en: A Brief Commentary on the Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Original Life and Mind-Contemplation, Volume One, Part One.
Written by the Śramaṇa Lai-zhou of Candana Monastery in the Capital of Qing.
△ Nine: General Explanation of the Title.
The title serves as the general table of contents for this scripture; therefore, it is explained first so that future generations may understand its great significance.

"Great" (Mahā) has the sense of distinguishing itself from the "small. This is because the Śrāvakas do not realize that all is but mind, but instead rely solely upon the six consciousnesses and the three poisons.
It establishes the root of both defilement and purity; even if one were to realize the ultimate fruit, it would be nothing other than that of a single arhat.

Because such a person lacks the great mind, has not yet made the great vow, has not yet practiced the great conduct, and has not yet realized the great fruit, but merely relies on and abides in the small, this is called the Hīnayāna.
At the very beginning of this sutra, a single large character "Great" (大) is placed to make it known that this is not the Dharma of the Small Vehicle, but rather...
This is a Mahāyāna dharma-gate. "Vehicle" (yāna) is so named because it conveys and carries; it is like the boats and carriages of the world.
If people mount them, they can travel from near to far, reaching that destination from here. The gate of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground is likewise thus.
If a person awakens to this, practices it, and realizes it through direct experience, they may immediately proceed from the state of an ordinary being to the rank of a sage;

they may immediately pass from birth and death to nirvana. This is because it is that upon which all Buddhas have fundamentally ridden, and because all Bodhisattvas ride upon this Dharma to reach the stage of a Tathāgata.
One should know that the two characters "Mahāyāna" (Great Vehicle) encompass the entirety of the Mahāyāna.
"Fa" (Dharma) is a general designation, as seen in titles such as the *Mahāyāna-saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Mahāyāna-śata-dharma-viśada-mukha-śāstra*.
Only the five characters "Ben-sheng-deng-wu" (Original Birth and Others) constitute the specific title of this particular scripture. Now, "Ben" (Original/Root) refers to the source of all phenomena;
"Sheng" (Birth) refers to the manifestation and development of all things. As the saying goes: "The gentleman applies himself to the root. The root...

Standing thus, the Way gives rise to faith—how truly so! We know that when the Sages bestowed their instructions, they did not fail to cause people to awaken to their fundamental nature and give birth to the Way.
This accords with the Will of Heaven and reaches the ultimate principle; beneath a single word, the ordinary is transformed into the sagely.
May we not, then, fail the Sages' intention. For this reason, this sutra begins by placing the two characters "birth-of-the-fundamental" (ben-sheng) at its head, desiring to...
To the reader: Investigate your own fundamental source; this is the Buddha-nature inherent in your very person.
Once the Buddha-nature is awakened, wisdom arises spontaneously, for through the manifestation of principle, wisdom is activated, such that essence and function are both fully revealed.
Therefore, it is called "Original Birth" (*pūrvajanman*). As for "Contemplating the Ground of the Mind," this expresses the correct meaning of "Original Birth.

Fearing that people might not understand the purport of "Original Birth," it further states that the "Original" is precisely the "Ground of the Mind," and that "Contemplation" is able to give rise to the Path. The primary purport of this entire sutra lies entirely herein.
Furthermore, there are two explanations: the general and the specific. The general explanation is as the sutra says: "The minds of sentient beings are like..."

Just as the five grains and five fruits grow from the great earth, so too do the worldly and transcendental dharmas of the mind give rise to the good and evil of the five destinies, as well as the distinction between the noble and the ordinary. For these reasons, the three realms are mind-only;
the mind is called "the earth. Those who can contemplate the mind attain ultimate liberation; those who cannot contemplate it sink into perpetual delusion.
Thus we know that the Tathāgata himself explained the contemplative method of the mind-ground.

This is because the sutra states that whether one is born in the mundane or supramundane realms, among the five destinies of good or evil, or as a sage or an ordinary person—the intent is that when one is deluded, these are precisely the deluded mind.
It can produce the fruits of karma; to awaken to it is itself the true mind, which can produce the fruits of sainthood.

That which is most important is that the contemplation of the character is the essential point. Now, "contemplation" refers to the luminous awareness reflecting back upon itself. When a single thought accords with this, all delusions are suddenly emptied. Nirvana is inherently possessed;
only then does one know that sentient beings have been Buddhas from the very beginning. Therefore it is said: "One who can contemplate the mind..."

This is ultimate liberation. Those who are unable to contemplate in this way will, in response to objects, grasp at conditions—like a dog chasing a clod of earth—and will naturally and ultimately sink into the depths, forever falling into the cycle of birth and death.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states, "All things are created solely by the mind," which carries the same meaning.
This is why the Buddha preached this sūtra and established this title; he intended that by seeing the title one would know the sūtra, and by reading [the title...]

The interpretation of the sutra’s meaning involves giving rise to wisdom and contemplative insight, culminating in the attainment of Buddhahood; from the outset, this does not fail to accord with its original intent.
Regarding the separate explanation: there are two kinds of mind. First is the true mind, which is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings and the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Second is the deluded mind, which is the root of the karma of sentient beings and the cognitive consciousness that conditions objects. However, the true...
Although delusions are distinct, they do not depart from a single essence. "Earth" (*bhūmi*) is a metaphor that possesses two meanings: first, the sense of "carrying.
This refers to the great earth being vast, firm, thick, and powerful; because all mountains, rivers, grasses, trees, and sentient beings are carried by the earth.
Second, the sense of "growing. This means that both sentient and insentient things all depend upon the earth.
It exists. Furthermore, because it can increase [the seeds], the mind is also like this. That is to say, the true mind follows conditions to form the myriad dharmas;

this is the meaning of "arising. The mutual perfuming and activation of seeds and manifestations is the meaning of "increasing. Since they manifest in dependence upon the mind, they do not depart from the mind.
This refers to the meaning of "carrying" (vāha). It is because seeds and manifestations mutually perfume and stimulate one another, thereby giving rise to the deluded mind.

Due to not knowing that the myriad dharmas are mind-only, one clings to the existence of phenomena external to the mind and further grasps at them; thus, the two attachments to self and phenomena suddenly arise and continue.
Furthermore, when one conditions them, the myriad dharmas fully manifest; when one does not condition them, all dharmas are fundamentally quiescent. Since—

When conditions are met, there is existence; this carries the meaning of "carrying" (like having a film on the eye, one falsely sees flowers in the sky; the flowers appear in dependence on the film, yet if the disease of the film is removed, the flowers in the sky vanish of their own accord).
Thus, the two characters "mind" (*xin*) and "ground" (*di*) constitute the object of contemplation, while "contemplation" (*guan*) constitutes the wisdom that contemplates.

This means relying on the mind to perform contemplation, thereby contemplating the mind itself. Furthermore, there are three types of contemplation: namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the middle (*madhyama*). Emptiness is not...
Cessation is the sublime function of the true essence of the mind. However, the true nature is like space, and the contemplation of emptiness is like sunlight;

when light and space merge, there is no differentiation between them. Therefore, at the time of correct contemplation, one does not perceive the myriad dharmas, as they are in profound union with the true nature, pervasive and pure, such that not a single dharma is seen to confront the mind—this is what constitutes emptiness.
Furthermore, a sutra states: "The Buddha expounded the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground for Maitreya.
If a person hears this but once with their faculty of hearing, they will gather their thoughts to contemplate the mind, thereby perfuming the seeds of Bodhi; before long, they shall attain Bodhi.

Thus we know that once one gathers the thoughts to contemplate the mind, the wisdom of emptiness naturally illuminates itself. Departing from delusion and severing all marks, its very substance is the Truth. This is called the Contemplation of Emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā).

This is the contemplation of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Second, as for the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*), it consists of generating the resolve [for enlightenment] by repaying the four debts of gratitude, and practicing cultivation while dwelling in an *araṇya* (hermitage).
This observation of phenomenal characteristics is the contemplation of the provisional; it serves to subdue deluded thoughts and give rise to profound shame and remorse.

(The four debts of gratitude are: the debt to one's parents, the debt to sentient beings, the debt to the king, and the debt to the Triple Gem. As for the practitioner, they abide in the four stainless natures according to the Buddha’s teaching, single-mindedly practice the twelve dhūtas, and employ the three gates of contemplation.)

To cultivate the practice of patience is called true renunciation. This consists of three contemplations: first, to contemplate all sentient beings as emanations of the Buddha, and to contemplate oneself as a truly ignorant person; second, to contemplate all sentient beings with the thought of them being honorable masters, and to contemplate oneself with the thought of being their servant;

third, to contemplate sentient beings as one’s parents, and to contemplate oneself as their son or daughter. Constantly performing these contemplations, even when struck or reviled, one never retaliates, but skillfully employs expedient means to subdue the mind.

Regarding the four types of stainless nature: these refer to clothing, bedding, food and drink, and medicinal requisites. Whichever of these four things one obtains—whether coarse or fine—if they satisfy one’s needs, one remains free from greedy seeking; this is [the fourth].

The nature of defilements is entirely a provisional observation. Third is the contemplation of the Middle Way: observing that all afflictions and the myriad phenomena are unified within one’s own mind, and thoroughly comprehending these dharmas so as to be capable of realizing bodhi.
This is what is meant by engaging with existence without being obstructed by the contemplation of emptiness;

it is to realize the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) through the very phenomena themselves, remaining unattached to either emptiness or existence. This constitutes the contemplation of the Middle Way, as described in the "Chapter on the Adornment of Merits" and elsewhere.

The *Guanxin pin* (Chapter on Contemplating the Mind) and other texts state that one should know that the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) is the contemplation of the mind’s ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);

the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) is the contemplation of the mind’s conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); and the contemplation of the middle (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*) is the contemplation of the mind’s truth of the primary meaning (*paramārtha-satya*).
This constitutes the mutual fusion of principle and phenomena, the ultimate pinnacle of liberation. All of the above are what is elucidated by this single scripture. The scripture is...
It is that which can express [the meaning]. Furthermore, the Sanskrit term *sūtra* is translated here as "holy teaching" (*āgama*), or alternatively as "seated discourse" (*śikṣā-sūtra*).

Regarding the fact that "seated discourse" (*śikṣā*) and "agreement" (*kīrti*) have been omitted and only "discourse" (*sūtra*) remains: this is because the holy teachings of this land are called "discourses" (*jing*).

It is named "discourse" because its meaning accords with that of this land. Moreover, it possesses four meanings: penetration, inclusion, constancy, and dharma. That is to say, it penetrates the meanings expressed [by the words].
The capacities of those to be gathered and transformed remain constant, unchanged across past and present; the Dharma is equally observed by both ordinary beings and sages.

Furthermore, the earth serves as the analogy, the Jātaka tales and other such works serve as the teaching, the Mahāyāna is that which designates, and the Jātaka tales and others are that which is designated.

The mind constitutes the essence (*tattva*) of this single scripture, while the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*) serves as its function for cultivation and realization (*bhāvanā-sākṣātkriyā*).
Taken together, these—the essence, the function, the method, and the analogy—form the title; by combining the subject and the object, a single heading is established.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the text’s meaning has two parts. First, the explanation of the preface has three sections. First, the title of the preface based on the sutra:

The Preface to the Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground in Past Lives describes and clarifies the beginning and end, briefly outlining the general framework so that future generations may understand its origins and development. Furthermore, as for the preface:
The walls of the east and west. By observing the walls, one knows the depth of the entire residence; by seeing the preface (*xu*), one knows the great significance of the beginning and the end.
△ Second, identifying the dynasty of the author of the preface.
Emperor Xianzong of the Tang composed this preface.

"Tang" was the national designation of the dynasty. This serves as a preface to the era of translating the scriptures. The Li clan succeeded the Sui in possessing the empire; the national designation was the Great Tang.
Emperor Xianzong was the tenth sovereign. His personal name was Chun. He was the crown prince of Emperor Shunzong. The Emperor was upright, intelligent, and resolute.

He severed the rebellion of Zhiping. Capable of employing loyal counsel, he was not swayed by popular opinion and ultimately achieved success. The prestige and authority of the Tang dynasty were nearly restored; he was truly worthy of being a sovereign of the Restoration. Emperor Xianzong conferred upon him a posthumous title. One who is extensively learned and possesses many abilities is called a *xiàn* (exemplar). *Zōng* (founder) means "venerable," "law," or "lord.

One who transforms the world through the Correct Law (*zhèngfǎ*) is honored as the lord of men and is revered by the world; hence, he is called a *xiànzōng* (Exemplary Founder). A *huáng* (August One) is a sovereign.

Among the ancient emperors, only Fuxi, Shennong, and Huangdi were designated as the Three August Ones (*sānhuáng*). According to the *Shìfǎ* (Canon of Posthumous Titles): "To bring peace to the people through the law is called *huáng*."
The term "Di" (Emperor) is also a designation for a sovereign. The *Lüshi Chunqiu* states: "The Di is one to whom the world conforms;
the Wang (King) is one to whom the world proceeds. The *Shangshu* lists the Five Emperors as Shaohao, Zhuanxu, Gaosin, and Tang Yao.

Yu Shun was known as one of the Five Emperors (Wudi). The Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties were known as the Three Kings (Sanwang). Only the Qin of the Ying lineage obtained the empire and first assumed the title of Emperor (Huangdi).
He declared that his Way surpassed that of the Three Sovereigns (Sanhuang) and his merit exceeded that of the Five Emperors;

thus he styled himself the First Emperor (Shihuangdi). Thereafter, all sovereigns were titled Emperor. The preface to this present scripture was composed by the Imperial Hand of Emperor Xianzong of the Tang Dynasty.
"Preparation" (*zhi*) means to measure, fashion, and construct. △ Third, the actual explanation of the preface has three parts.
First, the opening remarks praising the world, which is divided into two. First, the actual praise of emotional desires.

Alas! Since self and objects are distinct, and cravings are in full blaze, the six sense-faculties fall into the realm of causes and conditions, while the seven emotions rush toward the field of profit and loss.
Thus, the True is entangled and bound by the delusive; love and hatred assault from within, while a profusion of splendors overwhelms what lies before.
The mind is like a leaping monkey; the body is like a mad elephant.

"Fu" (夫) is a particle used to introduce a statement; "yi" (噫) is a sound of resentment. This refers to one's own regret for failing to recognize the original truth and thus vainly giving rise to passions and desires;
it is also an expression of lamentation. The two lines concerning "things" and "self" specifically describe the delusion regarding reality. This is because the mind pervades all things.
The Dharma-realm: the myriad phenomena share the same reality. Heaven and earth share the same root as I; the myriad things share the same substance as I.

It is only because of ignorance and lack of awakening that True Suchness follows conditions, transforming into the consciousness of karma, and further giving rise to the two divisions of subjectivity and objectivity.
Because the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) resembles an external object, the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) grasps and clings to it;

failing to realize that all is but mind, the *darśana-bhāga* transforms into self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*), and the *nimitta-bhāga* transforms into external objects. As it is said: "One's own mind grasps its own mind; what is not illusory becomes illusory phenomena.
Thus it is said, "Objects and self are already distinct" (*ji* meaning "already"). "Desires" refers to the five desires, namely: wealth, form, fame, food, and sleep. Or...
Forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles are all objects desired by sentient beings. "To relish" means to like, to desire, or to take pleasure in doing.
This refers to the grasping mind itself. "Just blazing" refers to the intensity of craving and desire. This merely indicates the general state.
The six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are explained below: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. All are capable of giving rise to consciousness and serve as the foundation for the six consciousnesses;

therefore, they are called the "six faculties. As for "sinking," it means falling into [samsara] such that one cannot extricate oneself. Now, since the faculties give rise to consciousness, grasping and attachment act as the cause.

The objects are the six sense-fields (*ṣad-viṣaya*); they act as the conditions by way of enticement. Through the mutual drawing and grasping of faculty and object (*indriya-viṣaya*), [the cycle] unfolds.

It grows ever more intense. Sentient beings are submerged within it; thus, it is said they "fall into the realm of causes and conditions. (The six dusts refer to form, sound, fragrance, flavor, touch, and phenomena;

as each possesses the quality of defilement, they are called the six dusts. The seven emotions refer to joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hatred, and desire. To "rush" means to pursue and chase after them.
Taking favorable circumstances that bring satisfaction as "benefit," and unfavorable circumstances that snatch away such benefit as "harm. A "field" refers to a place.

It is said that humans possess seven emotions, all of which are pulled along by external objects; thus, one may say that every place within the three realms serves as a field for the creation of karma. "Gai" (葢) means to envelop or to obstruct; there are five kinds: first, desire; second, anger; third, sleep... [and so forth]. This clarifies that when the mind is bound by these, it is deluded by external objects, and sentient beings have no portion of freedom whatsoever. "Gai" refers to covering and hindering. There are five types: 1. Greed and desire; 2. Hatred and resentment; 3. Sleep... [and so forth]. This explains that when the mind is entangled beneath these, it is bewildered by its environment, and sentient beings lack any share of autonomy. "Gai" signifies concealment and obstruction. There are five varieties: 1. Craving; 2. Malice; 3. Torpor... [and so forth]. Essentially, this demonstrates that the mind is obscured by its surroundings, leaving sentient beings entirely without any capacity for self-mastery. "Gai" means to cover and to hinder. There are five: 1. Lust; 2. Wrath; 3. Drowsiness... [and so forth]. Thus, below the section on "entanglement," it is shown that the mind is deluded by objects, and sentient beings possess no part of independence at all. "Gai" is to cover and to block. There are five kinds: the first is greed; the second is hatred; the third is sleep... [and so forth]. There are five types: first, sensual desire; second, anger; third, drowsiness... [and so forth]. This clarifies that when the mind is entangled beneath these, it is led astray by external objects, and sentient beings have absolutely no share of autonomy. "Gai" means to cover and to hinder. Sleep; fourth, restlessness and regret; fifth, doubt. All sentient beings possess these five delusions, which shroud their true nature and obscure their wondrous luminosity, such that they cannot clearly perceive the various right paths. Because they function as coverings, they are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*).

"Envelopments" (*paryavasthāna*) means the sense of being bound. There are ten kinds: namely, anger, concealment, drowsiness, sleep, frivolity, restlessness, lack of shame, lack of remorse, stinginess, and envy.
Possessing these ten delusions, one becomes sticky and attached to all things, like a silkworm making a cocoon to bind itself;
they are also named according to their function, and are thus called "envelopments. "Reality" (*tattva*) refers to the Buddha-nature within each person. By means of these five...
Covered by the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and bound by the ten fetters (*paryavasthāna*), the true nature cannot attain liberation; hence it is said that "the hindrances and fetters shroud its truth.

As for "clinging," this refers to the sentient beings' mind of attachment to objects, which does not transcend the two categories of self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*). Because of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), they fail to realize the two kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*):

to claim that the body has a governing master is the clinging to a self (*ātma-grāha*); to claim that there are phenomena existing outside the mind is the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). This arises from...
These various forms of grasping and attachment prevent one from attaining liberation; therefore, it is said that one is bound by delusion. Regarding "love and hatred":
since one does not realize that all phenomena are but mind, one falsely gives rise to grasping and attachment—producing love for favorable conditions and hatred for adverse conditions.

The mind arises in pursuit of objects; hence it is said that one "assails the internal. To speak in terms of delusions: the "frivolous and ornate" refers to universally objectifying various realms and creating all manner of karma;
the "dissolute" refers to acting with spontaneous disregard for restraint. The former applies to everything encountered by the eyes;
thus, objective concerns are unstable, like the leaping of a monkey, and the body is dragged along by objects, like the charging of a mad elephant.

They gallop [away]. Therefore it is said that the categories of the mind are equal. △ Second, the conclusion regarding delusion and the failure to return, in two parts. First, lamenting one's own inability to attain clarity:
"How could one further awaken to the nature of Bodhi? One must settle the dust to clarify oneself, realize the principle of True Suchness, and find joy in its fundamental emptiness and quiescence."
"How could they possibly do so? means they are unable to reflect back upon themselves; this applies to the following two phrases as well.

*Bodhi* is here translated as "the path of awakening" (*jue-dao*), which is a specific name for true nature (*zhen-xing*). "Awakening" (*wu*) refers to being alert and conscious; it is the functional wisdom that realizes one's fundamental source.

This means that while *bodhi* is inherently present, because of delusion one fails to realize it, and thus cannot reflect back upon oneself. "Dust and grime" (*chen-ai*) refers to circumstantial phenomena (*shi-yuan*). This means...

Dusty affairs swirl and stir without ceasing; the deluded mind flickers from moment to moment without rest. How could one, amidst such a turbulent current, quiet the mind to awaken to the source and thereby realize its own original nature?
True Suchness (*tathatā*) is neither delusive nor subject to change; it is another name for Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). "Principle" (*li*) refers to the essence (*tattva*);
because it is vast and free from even the slightest speck of dust, it is called empty and quiescent (*śūnyatā-praśānta*). To penetrate this is to become a Buddha.

Therefore, it is called "joy" (*rati*). Furthermore, being quiescent and non-active is *original enlightenment* (*mūla-awakening*); "realization" (*prativedha*) means clear illumination, which is *initial enlightenment* (*ādi-awakening*).
"Joy" refers to the enjoyment of one's inherent nature. Taken collectively, this describes the nature of *bodhi*, which is primordially present yet not realized.
The affairs of dust and defilement are fundamentally non-existent yet not clearly understood; the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) is inherently possessed yet not realized.
How, then, could the bliss of the dharma-nature (dharmatā) be attained? Thus, the author of the preface concludes his lamentation in this manner. Question:
Are the nature of bodhi and the principle of True Suchness identical or distinct? Answer: They are the distinction within identity. Generally speaking, when one speaks of bodhi...

This is explained in terms of wisdom (*jñāna*). Generally speaking, "true thusness" (*tathatā*) is explained in terms of principle (*li*). That is to say, wisdom that is identical with principle is called *bodhi*;
principle that is identical with wisdom is called true thusness. Therefore, *bodhi* is called "nature," which is the nature of wisdom; true thusness is called "principle."
This is the very essence of principle; let the student know this. △ Second, concluding that one cannot save oneself:
Were it not for the Wondrous Enlightenment, who could rescue those drowning in this [suffering]?

"Wondrous awakening" (miao-jue) is precisely "wondrous enlightenment" (miao-wu). This concludes the preceding section: since one cannot awaken to bodhi or fully comprehend true suchness (tathatā), it means that within oneself there is no wondrous awakening.
The phrase "who then" (qi shu xia) concludes the point that one cannot save oneself; "to rescue" (zheng) refers to lifting up and extricating.
"Drowned" (*nì*) means to sink and submerge. "This" (*sī*) refers to the aforementioned craving, hindrances, and entanglements.

It means that when people are deluded by craving and the like, they are like a person fallen into the midst of mud, unable to extricate themselves by their own strength. "Not having" (*bù yǒu*) means non-existence.
"Who" (*shú*) is a term used for general reference. This states that sentient beings pursue sensory objects and drown themselves, becoming so deluded that they cannot awaken on their own.
If there were no wondrous awakening to deliver oneself, who could save one? This concludes the preceding section on exclaiming at the state of the world.
II. Fortunately Encountering the True Exposition (in four parts). 1. The Wise Transmit the Dharma and the Flowing Multitude of Deluded Beings Attain Deliverance.

"From this, the Perfect Ones opened the Dharma; the Great Beings transmitted the teachings. They rescued the deluded masses to the other shore and extinguished all delusions at this gate. Regarding the phrase "from this":
it is a term used to connect what precedes with what follows. It connects to the preceding point that sentient beings are unable to save themselves, and it introduces the following...

The Buddha is able to uplift [beings]. The "Ultimate Person" (zhiren) is none other than the Buddha; this means that the Buddha is the most ultimate among humans. (Above the heavens and below the heavens, only the Buddha is uniquely honored;

therefore, he is called the Ultimate Person. "Opening" (kai) means to reveal and instruct; its meaning is to open what is closed. "Dharma" (fa) refers to the mind-dharma; its meaning is to serve as a guide and to maintain.
This means that it guides sentient beings to produce understanding and sustains their own nature. This is truly because it is that which all Buddhas...
This is what Bodhisattvas cultivate and what sentient beings inherently possess; it does not transcend spiritual, luminous awareness and cognition.

Therefore, it is called "mind" (*citta*). Because its cultivation and practice lead to the realization of the Way, it is called "Dharma. Since the Buddha has realized this, he takes pity on those who do not know it.
Therefore, he opened the way for transformation and gave instruction, desiring that others might also know this, so as to manifest the Great Sage’s impartial mind toward all things.

"Dashi" (Great Being) is a title for a Bodhisattva; throughout India and China, all the successive patriarchs who have expounded the Buddha-dharma and transmitted it from one to another are called Dashis.
"Jiao" (Teaching) refers to words of instruction and guidance; "Chuan" (Transmission) refers to proclaiming [the truth].
It is spread throughout the world. "The multitude of deluded ones" refers to sentient beings who do not awaken to their Buddha-nature. "The other shore" is a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*.

Using "this shore" as a metaphor for birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), it signifies that there is suffering here; using "the other shore" as a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*, it signifies that there is bliss there. Delusions and karma are like the water in the river.
The teaching is a metaphor for a ship or boat. Bodhisattvas are like those who pilot the vessel. If the sentient beings of the world rely upon...
Instruct them to practice accordingly. It is like boarding a boat to reach dry land; one can thereby depart from birth and death, transcend delusion and karma, and realize nirvana.
Thus it is said that "the multitudes of the deluded are ferried to the other shore. *Si* means "exhaustion" or "end. All delusions refer to the eighteen realms (*dhātus*).
This "gate" (men) refers to this very sutra. That is to say, by relying on the sutra to practice contemplation, all delusions are suddenly eliminated;

hence it is said, "to dissolve all [delusions]" (the term "gate" takes its meaning from "penetration," as this sutra is the thorough path to Buddhahood, and is therefore "penetrating"). II. Sublime Contemplation: The Arising and Ceasing of the Mind-Ground Returning to Suchness.
Neither extinguished nor born: one perceives that form and emptiness both vanish. Neither coming nor going: one contemplates that nature and characteristics are both thus.
The former phrase eliminates delusion; the latter phrase accords with truth. Both attribute their efficacy to this Dharma-gate.
Birth and extinction are the deluded mind; form and emptiness are both deluded objects. The two instances of "not" constitute the practice of contemplation for dissolving delusion. It is said:
If a person relies on this Dharma and skillfully contemplates the mind-ground, they will suddenly turn back from delusion to return to the truth;

thus, both form and emptiness are extinguished (*ming*, meaning "exhausted"). Coming and going are merely shifting fluxes that do not abide. These two characters "wu" (no) are the true mind of immovability.
Just as a person skillfully contemplates the mind-ground, they harmonize and integrate all phenomena so that they all return to the original nature; this single nature is eternally abiding.
Therefore it is said: "All are thus. △ Third, the True Principle is difficult to comprehend and must rely on the expressive means (*nirukti*).

Thus, for one who seeks to dissolve form and emptiness, there is no way to reach their ultimate limit without words. For one who seeks to understand nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there is no way to realize their final destination without texts.
These traps and snares are established to lead all beings onto the broad highway.
Thus, the two characters [“然則”] are words that承接 (receive/lead over) from what precedes. “致” means to arrive at; it carries the sense of reaching the ultimate limit.

“歸” means to return; it carries the sense of tending toward. “文” refers to literary composition; “言” refers to speech; both belong to the category of *nirukti* (explicative expression), meaning that the Way is manifested through speech and principle is made manifest by means of literature.
The phrase “泯色空者” (those who dissolve form and emptiness) restates the preceding text to serve as a counter-illumination (*pratisedha*). If it were not so...

Language serves as a manifestation; it cannot by itself extinguish delusive objects. To penetrate to the ultimate limit is like the case of "nature" (svabhāva) and "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa), which also refer back to the preceding text:
conversely, it is made clear that if there were no expressive words, how could one realize the principles expressed?
Since one does not awaken to this by oneself, one cannot integrate the delusive with the return to the True. A *quān* (筌) is a bamboo trap for catching fish;
a *tí* (蹄) is a rabbit's footprint, though it is also written as *dì* (罤), referring to a device for catching rabbits. These two both serve as metaphors for the expressive words and texts.

The intended meaning is that the fish and the rabbit represent the principle (*li*) being expressed. Thus, when the Sages established their teachings, they employed written characters and spoken language.
By explaining the mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*), people of the world are finally able to see their nature and clarify their minds. *Quai* (逵) also means "path.
*Na* (納) means "to receive" or "to attain. This refers to the practitioner who, having attained the words and phrases, awakens to the ultimate truth—just as a traveler attains the path.
If one wishes to reach the place of ultimate refuge, there shall never be any obstruction. △ Fourth, the conclusion which reveals the sacred teaching and attributes its grace to the Buddha:
This is indeed the great teaching of the divine beings of the Western Land.
"This" refers to the aforementioned subject and object of expression. "Gai" (葢) is used here as a particle. "Western" refers to the land of India.

"Divine Person" (shénrén) refers to the Buddha. "Great Teaching" (dàjiào) conveys the sense of veneration; it means that the Divine Person established the teaching, which is discourse in accordance with the nature of reality—how great it is!
The character "ye" (也) is a concluding particle. (The reason for referring to him as a "Divine Person" rather than by the name "Buddha" is to praise his spiritual subtlety and unfathomable nature.)
It is not comparable to the spirits of ghosts and deities). △ Third, the account of its provenance, in two parts. First, the source from the Western Regions, in two parts.
First, the formal citation of the scripture’s title.
Regarding the *Mahāyāna-mūla-jātaka-citta-bhūmi-parīkṣā-sūtra*:
Second, it was personally taught by Śākyamuni.
At Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, together with Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and other great bodhisattvas...
This is what the Bodhisattva has taught.
The first phrase identifies the Teacher of the sutra; the second phrase identifies the location where the sutra was taught.

The subsequent text, beginning with the mention of the Head (Śākyamuni) together with the assembly, refers to those who are the recipients of the teaching—the sentient beings to be converted. "Śākya" is the clan name of the Buddha; here it is translated as "Able Benevolent One" (Nengren).
This means he possesses the skill to respond appropriately to sentient beings and the benevolence to bestow grace upon them. "Tathāgata" (如來) is a title modeled after the virtues of former sages;

it is the foremost of the ten epithets. It signifies that both his physical marks and his wisdom are identical to those of the Buddhas of antiquity, as if he were the re-manifestation of a previous Buddha.
Furthermore, it is said that he "came riding the path of suchness" to achieve perfect enlightenment, meaning that he manifested his traces from his original essence.
This sutra was spoken by the Buddha; therefore, the Buddha is the Teacher. Mañjuśrī is translated here as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode).

This Bodhisattva attained perfect enlightenment long ago; yet, after the realization of the fruit, he practices the causes, assisting the Buddha to propagate the transformation [of sentient beings] and manifesting himself as a Bodhisattva.
Thus, he is titled "Wondrous Virtue. Maitreya is translated here as "The Kindly One" (Cishi), meaning that his kindness flourishes in this world and his compassion reaches its fulfillment.

In a future kalpa, these two will raise their heads; the term "and others" includes the assembly at large. Because they requested the Dharma and questioned the Buddha, they initiated this Great Teaching;

they are precisely the assembly of those who are ready to receive it. II. The Source of the Text in the Eastern Land (China), in three parts: 1. The era of its first arrival from the Sanskrit original.
As for these Buddhist scriptures (Sanskrit: *brahmapustaka*), they were presented by the Kingdom of Siṃhala during the reign of my illustrious ancestor, Emperor Gaozong.
Having been treasured for many years, they were kept secret within the inner palace.
“Fan” (梵) is a designation used in the Western Regions; it refers to the fact that all those to the west of the Pamir Mountains are of Fan stock.
“Fan-jia” (梵夾) refers to Sanskrit manuscripts. “I” (我) is the self-designation of Emperor Xianzong. “Liezu Gaozong” (烈祖高宗) is his posthumous title.

According to the *Shifa* (諡法), one who upholds virtue and honors great achievements is called “Lie” (烈). He was the third sovereign of the Tang dynasty. “Dai” (代) refers to a dynasty. This is a Sanskrit manuscript.
Regarding its initial arrival: Siṃhala Island was a subordinate kingdom of India. It was said that because the sovereign possessed the Way, guests from all quarters came to visit;
thus, they brought this Treasure of the Dharma as an offering. "Secret" (mi) means to store away; "inner palace" (zhōngjìn) refers to the imperial court;
"throughout the years" (lìnián) refers to the great length of time elapsed. △ Second, the Sage Sovereign examined the text and found it accorded with his own spiritual capacity.

I, the Emperor, have succeeded to and guarded the great enterprise, reverently upholding the illustrious design. In the intervals between attending to the affairs of government, I have bathed my mind herein.
I believe that the principle of concentrating the thoughts provides assistance to the present age, and the merit of its subtle guidance may supplement the administration of justice.

Furthermore, while the Great Hero brought about transformation through compassion, I have been born without having suffered harm; and while the Dharma King takes purity as his primary tenet, I abide in peace.

Without causing disturbance, one spreads the teachings to those below, thereby conforming to the gateway of skillful means. Diligently applying oneself with focused thought, one accords with the ground of spiritual practice.
Is the benefit of non-action not ultimate?
"Zheng" (朕) is the self-designation of the Son of Heaven. "Sì" (嗣) means succession. "Shǒu" (守) means to uphold and maintain.
This refers to that which was established by our ancestors; I merely uphold, maintain, and protect it. "Pīyè" (丕業) refers to the great enterprise.
The Son of Heaven regards the entire realm and the altars of soil and grain as one grand foundation. "Tú" (圖) means to draw or depict; this is because divine beings bore the diagrams.
And so it emerged. The Sage drew the hexagrams, and thereafter all mountains, rivers, and lands were collectively treated as one great map of the imperial house;
thus they are called the "Imperial Chart" (huangtu). "Prosperous" (chang) means flourishing; it is also an auspicious omen. "Devoutly" (qian) means sincerity.
This refers to the great enterprise of one's ancestors; I merely maintain it with constant vigilance and care. Hence it is called "reverently serving" (*qiánfèng*).

"Serving" (*fèng*) is synonymous with "honoring" (*zūn*); it signifies that one does not dare to treat it with negligence or contempt. "Administration" (*zhèng*) refers to state affairs; "listening" (*tīng*) means managing them.
"Leisure" (*xiá*) refers to moments of free time; "washing" (*zǎo*) means cleansing. This meaning constitutes the fundamental principles of this scripture. In sum, this refers to the Son of Heaven.

Every day he attends to ten thousand matters of state. Once all affairs of governance have been concluded, whenever there is even a moment of leisure, he must cleanse his heart and purify his thoughts to investigate this scripture.
This serves to gather and restrain discursive thoughts and to contemplate the ultimate truth in stillness, thereby providing benefit in supporting the administration of current affairs.

(The term "bu" means to assist; it refers to the fact that the affairs of the time are not limited to ten thousand matters. If one were to critique these with a distracted mind, errors might occur. Therefore, through investigation and quiet contemplation, one proceeds from stillness...)

Examine this in detail; it will surely accord with correct principle. Therefore, it is said that there is assistance for the times. "Latent" (*qian*) means secret. "Guiding" (*dao*) refers to inciting or leading forth.

"Aiding" (*bi*) means assisting. "Principle" (*li*) is the essence (*ti*). This concerns the great substance of the fundamental human relations (*gangchang*) between ruler and subject in the administration of the court.

By perusing this scripture, there may be those who turn their hearts toward the Way, transforming customs and changing social mores, thereby perhaps providing assistance to the national constitution (*guoti*).
This is the merit of his assistance. His name, "Huó" (活), signifies decisiveness.

As for "guiding from within," it means that through morning study and evening contemplation, accumulating [virtue] day by day and month by month, one becomes unaware and unperceiving, yet profoundly accords with the intent of the Buddha. By harmonizing Buddhist principles with statecraft, one may say:
"The August Heaven has no dual paths; the Sage has no two minds. Since ancient times, Buddhists and Confucians have shared a common way; therefore, regarding the state—

There is indeed a supporting benefit to be derived from this principle. Furthermore, "da" (大) and below serve to further explain the merit of assistance and support. "Qie" (且) is a particle used as an introductory phrase, or it may be borrowed for the sake of rhetorical expression.
"Daxiong" (大雄) refers to the Buddha; as the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The Great Hero, the Fierce World-Honored One.

This means that the Buddha possesses great kindness (*maitrī*), being able to bestow upon sentient beings the joy of the Dharma, and great compassion (*karuṇā*), uprooting the suffering and affliction of sentient beings. "Hua" (化) refers to the teaching.
"Transformation and deliverance" refers to *hua* (transformation). As for "while I am below," it means that my six sense organs are complete and function with clarity;
this is all due to the power of the Buddha’s compassion being bestowed upon me. The Dharma King is called "Buddha," which carries the meaning of "sovereign mastery.

As for "with purity below," it means that the Buddha’s correct principle dwells amidst the dust of the world without being stained, and remains unsullied by the turbid age, serving as the source of the Pure Teaching. As for "with me presiding over... [the text continues].
Since ascending the Great Throne, Your Majesty’s person has been in harmony and peace; the palace retinue remains free from ailment;
the four seas enjoy tranquility, and there is an air of great peace. Thus it is said: "Peaceful and undisturbed. This, too, is the result of the Buddha’s power of purity being bestowed upon us.
Is this not a great assistance to the empire, the state, and the people? To "spread the teaching" below means that one desires to establish and propagate the Buddhist Dharma.

The intention is to bestow instruction and grace upon those below; "below" refers to the myriad officials and the common people. A *fu* (seal-token) means "to assist. It is that by which trust is assisted.
Furthermore, according to Han regulations, bamboo six inches long was divided and joined together;

thus it is said that *fu* signifies "to support" (*fu*), meaning that the two parts support and join one another without discrepancy. The current preface employs this meaning, drawing from Buddhist teachings.
This harmonizes with Confucianism. As for the "gate of expedient means" (*upāya-mukha*), it refers to the method by which the Son of Heaven instructs the people.

It means that the sovereign uses benevolence, righteousness, and morality to instruct the people as his "method" (*fang*); when the myriad subjects rely upon this instruction and carry it out, they obtain its benefit.

"Gate" (*men*) refers to the thorough path for coming and going; thus, the gate is itself the expedient means. Taken collectively, it signifies that the Son of Heaven desires to establish and propagate the Buddha-dharma.
The teachings are used to assist the royal law; thus, the two perfectly support and harmonize one another without discrepancy.

"Exerting diligence" (*li-jing*) below means that the Son of Heaven desires to practice cultivation so as to attain his proper place. "Exerting" (*li*) means to apply effort; it carries the sense of refining and uplifting oneself.
"Harmonizing" (*xie*) is the same character as "cooperating" (*he*), meaning to act in concord. The Son of Heaven, in governing the state through the cultivation of the self, must...

However, following the legacy of Yao and Shun and establishing the statutes of Wen and Wu constitutes the practice of cultivation. Now, in contemplating the principles of the Buddha with refined thought, there is ground for harmony.

For instance, the "Chapter on Repaying Kindness" shares a great congruence with the national essence. As for the "Dharma Gate of Contemplating the Mind-Ground," its thorough investigation of principle and exhaustion of nature mutually support and coincide with our own teachings.
That which is called "non-action" (wuwei) refers to the unchanging nature of True Suchness (tathatā), which is, in its very substance, non-existent.

It acts in accordance with conditions without changing; it employs the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) while in motion, yet remains eternally still. Its tranquil illumination and its essence are identical—this is true unconditionedness.

"Beneficial" (*yi*) means increasing excellence; it is auspiciousness (*kalyāṇa*). Since there is already assistance for the state, there will be the merit of increased excellence and the beauty of auspiciousness for the nation.
Is this not a term that reveals through negation (*paryudāsa*) in order to positively manifest the Buddha?

The benefit of this sutra is ultimate and exhaustive. △ Third, the transmission of the imperial decree, the translation, and the circulation, in three parts. First, stating and determining the intent of the translation:
"In this way, it is possible to expound the True Doctrine and elucidate the profound meaning."

The word "fu" (夫) is a particle used to introduce a statement. "Rúshì" (如是) is a term that points to the Dharma; it specifically refers back to the aforementioned benefits of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
"Débù" (得不) is also a term used for contrastive emphasis. "Yǎnchàng" (演暢) and "chǎnhóng" (闡弘) both carry the meaning of circulation and propagation.

The profound mysteries of the True Doctrine are collectively termed the essence of Buddhist principle. The intent is that since the sutra possesses such benefits as these, how could it be kept secret?
"Stored within the inner palace and not circulated in the world"—this is a concluding phrase. △ Second, regarding the scholars of meaning who translated the scriptures:
he brought out the Sanskrit original at Liquan Temple and issued an imperial decree to the great virtuous masters of the capital’s school of meaning, including the Tripiṭaka Master from Kaśmīra.
The eight persons, including Prajñā, translated its essential meaning; the four persons, including Meng Jian, Grand Master for Palace Memorials, refined its prose.
It was arranged into eight fascicles and compiled as a single work. The secret treasury of the Tathāgata has been opened for the first time after passing through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust;

the true principle of the Mahāyāna is now realized after transcending worlds as vast as grains of sand. To illuminate the darkness and provide a bridge across the ford, it is hereby established that...
For those who peruse it, ambrosia is sprinkled upon the field of the mind; for those who awaken to its meaning, the finest essence flows within the realm of their nature.
These words of succession now emerge from within and proceed outward, as the Sanskrit manuscript is transmitted from within the palace to the outside world.
He was at Liquan Monastery, which was the place for translating the scriptures. "Shao" (詔) means to proclaim. "Jingshi" (京師) is the name of the capital;
"jing" (京) means great, and "shi" (師) means multitude. This refers to the residence of the Son of Heaven, which must be designated by terms signifying its vastness and grandeur.
Below the section on "Yixue" (義學), all are persons who translated the scriptures. "Yi" (義) means appropriateness; it refers to one who has extensively studied the Buddha’s...

The *sūtras* [he studied] were those whose realization penetrated the principles of nature and whose literary intent was appropriate; furthermore, he was well-versed in the Confucian classics and the various works of the "Hundred Schools.
This is what is called "learning in meaning" (*yixue*). The title "Mahādeśa" (Great Virtue) is a term of address for those who possess moral integrity, learning, and renown;
thus, he was addressed by this title. "Kaśmīra" is the name of a kingdom in the Western Regions, which was the birthplace of the translator. Three.

"Zang" (藏) refers to the threefold Dharma of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma; it is an honorary title for the Master of Translation, signifying that his learning was thorough across the Tripiṭaka, and thus he was designated as "Tripiṭaka.
"Bānrě" (般若) means "wisdom" (prajñā); this is the Master's personal name. The term "etc. (等) includes others.
The names of the eight individuals are not detailed, but all were translators. "Fanyì" (翻譯) means "to transform and translate."

That is to say: furthermore, regarding the intention of substitution—since these sections of the Sanskrit original are all written in the Indic script of the Western Regions, the meaning of the characters is unknown to people here in this land.

One must employ someone who is proficient in the languages of both countries to first substitute the characters of this land for those of the Western Regions, and then further replace the phrases of this land with Indic script.
Regarding such phrases, one may substitute "namo" for "taking refuge," or "buddha" for "the Awakened One," and so forth;

this is how one comes to recognize the characters of the spoken sounds, which is called "translating the phonemes. Alternatively, there may be *saṃyukta* (conjunct) syllables, *trisaṃyukta* (triply conjunct), retroflex sounds (*mūrdhanya*), protracted vowels (*pluta*), and so on in the Sanskrit text.

When one encounters characters in this [Chinese] language for which there is no equivalent, one must inquire in detail regarding both the Chinese and the Indic (Sanskrit) versions, striving to ensure they correspond appropriately; this is what is meant by "translating the words" (*fan yu*).

As for the "meaning" (*zhi*), it refers to the doctrinal principles (*artha*) of the sutra. The "words" (*yu*) serve as the means of expression (*vācaka*), while the "meaning" (*yi*) is that which is expressed (*vācya*).

Since understanding the means of expression leads to an understanding of that which is expressed, one should know that translating the text is itself the translation of the meaning. [The section] following "Commanding and Admonishing" is the "Preface and Polishing."

"Person of letters" (*wenzhi ren*) refers to one who possesses literary talent. "Decree" (*ming*) refers to an imperial edict; it carries the sense of an official command or order. "Censor" (*jianyi*) refers to an officer of speech.
"Grand Master" (*dafu*) is a high-ranking office for promoting talent through the recommendation of those with eloquence; it is a prestigious position for nurturing and supporting human resources.

Meng Jian was the personal name of such a Grand Master. As for the other three individuals, their names have not yet appeared; they are merely designated by the collective term "equals" (*deng*). All [are officials].

Those who received the mandate and refined the text did so because the translators’ words and phrases were occasionally crude or vulgar, and their literary style was overly prolix or inconsistent with the conventions of this region.
Thus, four individuals revised, polished, and finalized the wording, embellishing it with elegance; this process is termed "refinement" (*rùn-sè*).
"Arranging" (*liè*) means to divide, and "binding" (*lè*) means to collect and organize; that is to say, they divided [the work] into eight sections.
[The text] was compiled into a single volume. "The secret treasury" refers to the mind-dharma of the Tathāgata, which is not bestowed upon those who are not yet ready vessels.
"Dust-aeons" (kalpas) refers to the long duration of time; it means that the period during which [the teaching] was hidden and obstructed has already been long.

"Initially opened" refers to the commencement of its translation and dissemination. Regarding "dust-aeons": one takes all the atoms of dust existing throughout the great earth and uses them to calculate the number of obstructed kalpas, with one atom corresponding to one kalpa. Since the atoms are infinite, the kalpas are likewise [infinite].

It is immeasurable. This merely indicates its long duration; furthermore, "immeasurable" does not mean it is beyond measure. Indeed, for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one may not encounter the appearance of a Buddha;

yet even when a Buddha appears in the world, he does not preach at an improper time. When the time for preaching arrives, [the teachings] exist only in the Western Regions; and even upon reaching this land, they are preserved in the innermost palace.
It was only until the reign of Emperor Xuanzong that they were translated—this constitutes their initial revelation. Tracing back to the very source, it is truly because [the Dharma] is subtle.

Dust motes compared to kalpas are still insufficient as a metaphor. Nevertheless, Emperor Xianzong initiated the translation and circulation [of this scripture], which has brought great benefit to the world.
How can those who have fortunately obtained the Dharma ever repay it? Regarding the phrase "the Lesser Vehicle" (*xià dàshèng*):

it refers to the principle of the *tathatā*-nature, which cannot be fully attained by those of meager merit; therefore, it uses dust motes to compare with world-systems, and world-systems to compare with persons, thereby making it manifest.
To encounter this sutra is no easy matter. "Sand" refers to all the sand within a river; "worlds" refers to the lands within the world-system.
"Transcending" carries the meaning of surpassing or exceeding. To speak of "sands and worlds" means to take each grain of sand from a river and compare it to one world-system.
Since the sands are immeasurable, the worlds are likewise immeasurable. This, too, is not... [text truncated]

"An analogy is for the purpose of analogy; 'then one realizes' refers to being in accord with the Way. However, this phrase, when contrasted with what precedes it, is somewhat difficult to comprehend.

It may be explained through two meanings. First, the Tathāgata preached the sutras in the Western Regions (India), and they fortunately flowed into our country, where they were translated and circulated, enabling people to see, hear, contemplate, and realize them; only then can one enter into realization. This is because from the Western Regions to this land...

The multitude of lands is like the sands of the Ganges; yet the people of this region, without straying even a single step from their place, realize the true principle of the Buddha—this may truly be called surpassing the realms of sand.

(The intent is that although one has traversed worlds, they have never been translated [into words]; though there are people within those sandy realms, they do not grasp the essential meaning and cannot personally realize it.)

That this has now been translated and verified is a source of the greatest joy. Second, this refers to the Dharma-treasure of the Mahāyāna; it cannot be cultivated or realized by those of meager merit.

It must be in our Great Tang Dynasty that sentient beings possess both merit and wisdom, and are thus able to realize it through direct experience. Though the sands of the world are numerous, [only here can this be attained].
Without encountering this profound teaching, one cannot cultivate and realize [the truth]. That people of this land have realized it may be called "transcending sands of worlds.
The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "In immeasurable lands, even the name [of this teaching] cannot be heard, let alone being received, upheld, read, or recited.
This is also like that; both meanings apply. As for "being obscured and ignorant," it refers to sentient beings whose ignorance obstructs their wisdom.
The ignorant do not realize this for themselves. This sutra’s wondrous contemplation is like a candle; it can illuminate the celestial realm of one's nature and can shatter delusion and confusion.
Therefore, it is said that it "illuminates their darkness. "Ferry" (*jin*) refers to a landing place for crossing; "bridge" (*liang*) refers to a bridge. "To show" (*shi*) means to point out.
The meaning is that birth and death are like a great river, and afflictions are like the water within that river; without a ferry-boat or a bridge, one cannot cross.
"Is able to cross over. This indicates that this sutra serves as a bridge within the cycle of birth and death, by which sentient beings are enabled to cross over.
"Enabling them to open" (*pi*) correctly clarifies the benefits obtained by sentient beings; "enabling" (*bi*) means to cause or command. "Opening" (*pi*) refers to unrolling the scroll.

"Reading" (yue) means to look over and examine. The character "one who" (zhe) refers to the person who opens and reads the text to understand its meaning. "Ambrosia" (ganlu) refers to the medicine of immortality;

a single drop that moistens the lips is well able to bring life forth from within death. This serves as a metaphor for the wondrous contemplation of the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*) found in this sutra.
If a person follows this practice, they can escape birth and death and realize Nirvana at a high level.
How is this any different from sprinkling nectar upon the mind? Now, as for calling the mind a "field," it is because it possesses the capacity for growth:

a deluded mind can give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*), while an awakened mind can give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*). The intent is to eliminate delusion and generate wisdom. Those who have attained clear awakening also understand this.

Regarding the meaning of this statement: *tīrtha* (clarified butter) is a superior flavor in the Western Regions (*Sī-yù*). *Xìng-jìng* (nature-object) is also an alternative designation for the "mind-ground" (*xīn-dì*).
*Liú* (flowing) means to pour in. The ancients spoke of "pouring *tīrtha* upon the crown of the head" to express attaining the true essence of the flavor of the Dharma.
As for calling "nature" an "object," it is that which is illuminated by wisdom; because one thus treads upon it, it is termed an "object. This concludes the first two lines.
All say that one who can awaken to this principle is like nectar sprinkled upon the mind; one who can give rise to true wisdom is like clarified butter (ghṛta) moistening one's nature.
△ Third, the conclusion returning to the era.
My admiration is inexhaustible; how could I ever forget to open and study this work? Having transcribed it, I have composed this brief preface.

Although it is free from all words and letters, how could it not require elucidation? Thus, I shall reveal its fundamental source and preserve its chronological record. At this time, our Great Tang dynasty governed all under heaven.
It has been one hundred and ninety-four years.
"Alas! is an expression of lamentation. "Insufficient" means incomplete. The intended meaning is: not seeing the Buddha-nature is like losing a supreme treasure;
though one’s rank may reach the pinnacle of human honor, one has not yet escaped birth and death, nor has one heard the True Dharma.
I have still not yet escaped being driven by karma and lack any share of autonomy. Now, fortunately, I have obtained the True Dharma and realized my original nature;
it is as if I have acquired a supreme treasure. My joy is so extreme that it turns into sorrow, lamenting that I attained it so late.

Thus, my sighs of admiration are inexhaustible. How could I ever forget to open and contemplate this? I wish to keep it close day and night, never parting from it. Furthermore, since I have already transcribed it...

"Translation" means transcribing. "Merely providing a preface" means describing and clarifying the great meaning. Although [the text] is separated from the following, it employs both affirmation and negation as a concluding summary;
though these are words that do not exhaust the full sense, the characters themselves constitute the preface. All such particles are merely syntactic markers.
"Jù" (詎) means "how could it be? "Jiǎ" (假) means "to employ. "Fāhuī" (發揮) means to manifest and reveal; this refers to the fact that the True Dharma is fundamentally free from words and letters.
How could this be introduced merely by the preface? Nevertheless, as I now seek to reveal its fundamental source and calculate its chronological era, I cannot help but provide this introduction.
"Yu" (御) means to govern and to administer; it is the title by which I, Emperor Xianzong, refer to myself.
This was at the time when the Great Tang unified and governed all under heaven, and the translation was completed.
From the time of the High Ancestor (Emperor Gaozu) until now, one hundred and ninety-four years have passed.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Prajñā and others of the Kapiśī Kingdom of the Tang Dynasty, by imperial decree.
△ Second, the commentary on the scripture, in two parts: first, the translators.
*Kaśmīra* is here translated as "low-born. It is within the territory of North India.

Once Madhyāntika had reached that region, he established five hundred monasteries (*vihāras*). He purchased low-born people from various foreign lands to serve as laborers for the service of the Saṃgha.
After Madhyāntika entered parinirvāṇa, those low-born people established their own rulers, and consequently...

Regarding the country: the present translator is a native of that land; since a person is manifested by way of their country, [this is noted]. The "Three Piṭakas" and so forth are explained as in the preface.
△ Second, the Sūtra Text has three parts, namely the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Dissemination. As for these "parts," each of the three sections possesses—
This refers to the "divisions" (*vibhāga*). It means that all sutras possess a *nidāna* (introduction) section, a *saddharma* (main body) section, and a *pariṇāmana* (circulation) section.
Beginning from the Jin dynasty, the Dharma Master Dao’an of Xiangyang categorized and demarcated the various sutras, asserting that they all consist of these three divisions.

He held that when the Sages establish their teachings, they must rely on conditions for their arising; in order to transmit their subtle words, they first manifest the causal origins. Therefore, there is the *nidāna* section. As for the causal origins...

Once this has been clarified, one should present the correct exposition (*bhāṣya*). By discussing the profound subtleties of the fundamental meaning and opening the path of awakening for sentient beings, there is the "Correct Teaching" (*saddharma*).
When the correct exposition is complete, it is transmitted from one to another so that the assembly may practice it and ensure its reach to distant lands for ten thousand ages;
thus, there is the "Circulation" (*saṃprakāśana*). Although the teaching is divided into these three parts, those who propagated the Dharma at that time feared that...

This accords with the Buddha’s intention, yet for the most part it was not followed in practice. Later, when the Bodhisattva Bandhuprabha’s *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* arrived, it also consisted of three parts:

first, the section on the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; second, the section on what is expounded in the holy teachings; and third, the section on practicing in accordance with the teachings.

This corresponds in meaning to the [threefold division of] introduction, main body, and dissemination. Only at that time were those who propagated the Dharma finally able to follow it in practice. What was...
This refers to the fact that Master Fenzhou’s commentary accords perfectly with Bandhuprabha; this is what is meant.

Thus, it is known that Master Daoshi was the progenitor of the *pin-pian* (chapter/section) classification system for all time under the Great Song dynasty in China. The first part, the Introduction, is divided into two sections. First, the title of the chapter.
Chapter One: The Introduction.
There are three meanings to "introduction" (*nidāna*): first, sequential order; second, causal origin; and third, narrative account.

This refers to the sixfold perfection [of the sūtra] listed at the beginning of the scripture, serving as the introductory lead for the opening chapter; thus, it constitutes sequential order. The Tathāgata enters meditative absorption and emits light.
The manifestation of auspicious omens serves as the opening for the commencement; this constitutes the *nidāna* (preface).

The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda, beholding the signs of light, alerted the assembly and declared that the Tathāgata had emerged from meditative absorption out of compassion and would surely preach the sublime Dharma; he thus briefly recounted the Buddha’s intention. This constitutes the *anukrama-nidāna* (sequential preface).
In the Sanskrit language, this is called *varga*; here it is translated as "chapter" (*pin*). Those [sections] whose meanings and categories are similar are gathered together into one.

A section (*varga*). Therefore, it constitutes a chapter (*parivarta*). As it is the beginning of all chapters, it is called the "First. Now, there is a general introduction (*sāmānyanidāna*) and a specific introduction (*viśeṣanidāna*).
From "Thus have I heard" up to "each bowed at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side" constitutes the general introduction, because it is common to all sūtras.
From "At that time, the World-Honored One" up to the end of the chapter constitutes the specific introduction, because it is particular [to this sūtra].
Because it initiates the subject matter. △ Second, the Sūtra Text has two parts. First, the General Introduction has four parts. First, the indication of faith and hearing: "Thus have I heard.
This is also called the Sixfold Preface of Certification of Faith, meaning that all sūtras universally contain the phrase "Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha...
In a certain place, there are several lines of text that serve as evidence that this was spoken by the Buddha; one should therefore give rise to reverent faith.
If such [evidence] is absent, then it was not spoken by the Buddha and is not worthy of belief. Hence, it is called "evidence for faith. Such is the meaning.
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: Among the six types of accomplishment, for the sake of accomplishing faith, the two characters "thus" (*evam*) are used as words of faithful compliance.
This means that regarding the great ocean of the Buddha’s Dharma, faith is that which enables entry; if one has faith, one says "it is thus," and if one lacks faith, one says "it is not thus.
Therefore, among the five stages, the stage of faith comes first. Furthermore, among the eleven wholesome dharmas, faith is...

It is also the foremost. Prior to the mind of faith, there is no dharma more excellent. It is by relying on this foundation of faith that understanding, practice, and realization first establish themselves.
Liu Qiu said: "When the Sages preach the Dharma, they do so only to manifest *tathatā* (suchness). Only suchness is the truth; therefore, it is called 'Thus' (*evam*).
As for 'I heard' (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*), 'heard' signifies accomplishment. This 'I' refers to the conventional self of the five aggregates, namely Ānanda; 'heard' refers to the ear."

The sense organs give rise to consciousness; thus, setting aside the particulars for the sake of the general, it is said, "I heard. Combining this with the preceding "Thus" (*evam*), it serves as a term to indicate the Dharma:
"This Dharma, I heard from the Buddha. There are four kinds of "I": first, the *parikalpita* (imagined) self of ordinary worldlings; second, the *ātman* (self) of non-Buddhists;
third, the provisional self of those in the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna; and fourth, the true self of the *dharmakāya*.

Now, in order to distinguish this from others, it is called the "provisional self" (*prajñapti-ātman*). Since the sages have already severed the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*), they employ the term "self" in accordance with worldly convention to distinguish between subject and object, referring to it provisionally as "I.

As for the previous statement regarding "discarding the particular to follow the general," it means that since it is said that consciousness is produced by the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*), one would properly say "heard by the ear"; yet it says "heard by me" because the ear is a specific instance among the six faculties.

I am the totality of the single body, for I have set aside the particulars; it is because [the self] follows this totality that it is called "self. △ Second, the time, the principal figure, and the location.
First, as for the time: The Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
"At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) refers to the perfection of the time; that is, an auspicious occasion. Even in worldly affairs, when matters converge, one still awaits a propitious period.

How much more so for the grand proclamation of the Great Dharma—how could it fail to coincide with a sublime era? Furthermore, because the Way of teacher and disciple was in perfect accord and the discourse reached its ultimate conclusion, it is said to have occurred "at one time.
This does not refer to specific seasons such as spring, summer, autumn, or winter, nor to specific hours such as midnight, noon, dawn, or dusk. For the Buddha’s teaching lasted forty [years].
The nine years [of teaching] constitute, in total, one great period of temporal teaching. "Buddha" is the full term; here it is translated as "the Awakened One.

This means awakening oneself and awakening others, such that the perfection of awakening and practice is achieved. Regarding "awakening oneself": it is to realize that the nature is truly eternal and to understand that delusions are empty and false, thereby distinguishing this from the lack of awakening in ordinary beings.

Regarding "awakening others": it is to employ unconditioned compassion to deliver the multitude of sentient beings, thereby distinguishing [this from the awakening of those who do not benefit others].
The self-enlightenment of the two vehicles is fulfilled at the fifth stage (*pañcama-vihāra*), where causes are exhausted and fruits are perfected;

this refers to the Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) which distinguishes it from the partial enlightenment of Bodhisattvas. He who is the master of the Dharma for preaching this sutra is the "Principal Accomplishment" among the six accomplishments, namely Śākyamuni Buddha.
"Abiding" (*vihāra*) means dwelling or residing; it encompasses both the subject and the object. The "subject that abides" is...
The Buddha’s place of residence refers to locations such as Rājagṛha. Regarding "Rājagṛha" and so forth, this signifies the perfection of the location.
In the past, King Vṛṣabha (or Vṛṣagaṇa) established a palace-city together with a thousand kings; thus it was named Rājagṛha (King’s Abode). It is the capital city of the kingdom of Magadha.

(In the commentaries on various sūtras, all cite King Vṛṣagaṇa; the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, however, calls him King Śuddhodana or Śūdrasoma. This may be due to differences in the Sanskrit terminology, or...)

"Bōzú" (駁足) is a term used for the sake of phonetic inversion. Regarding the differences in Sanskrit terminology: there are five regions of India, each with its own distinct language. For instance, what is called "qián" (錢) by the people of our own land [China] is called "zhěhā" (者哈) in Manchuria and "chāosù" (嘲素) in Mongolian;
the same applies to their respective languages. "Gṛdhrakūṭa" is translated as "Spiritual Vulture Peak" (Língjiù) and also as "Vulture Head Peak" (Jiùtóu fēng).

This refers to the mountain's shape resembling the head of a vulture, a name derived from its physical form. Furthermore, because the Buddha—a spiritually enlightened Great Sage—resided here to preach the Dharma, it is so named.
Therefore it is named Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak). That the Sanskrit term remains here is out of respect, and thus not translated.

Furthermore, these few phrases were spoken when Ānanda inquired of the Buddha as he was about to enter *parinirvāṇa*: "What words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras? The Buddha commanded that they be placed thus: "Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was dwelling in a certain place, together with such-and-such persons. This was done so that future generations throughout the world might [know the source].
One should know that the Buddha-dharma has its source and origin; it is not something that can be fabricated at will by worldly people.

Furthermore, there are three purposes: first, to sever doubt; second, to quell contention; and third, to distinguish the heterodox. Because these three purposes exist, the Buddha commanded that they be placed at the beginning of the sutras. Regarding the severing of doubt:

when Ānanda ascended the seat, his physical marks and signs were perceived as being identical to those of the Buddha, and the assembly gave rise to three doubts. The first was the doubt that the Buddha had arisen once more.
Second, there was doubt that a Buddha from another direction had arrived; third, there was doubt that Ānanda had attained Buddhahood.

By uttering such words as these, the three doubts were immediately extinguished. Regarding the "extinguishing of disputes": if one did not say, "I heard this from the Buddha," it would be considered one's own fabrication, and thus contentious debate would arise.

Regarding the "discrimination against the heterodox": it means that at the beginning of the sūtras of the heterodox non-Buddhist teachings, the two syllables "A-u" (Āyuṣmat) are always placed [as a title].

Regarding the characters: "A" means non-existence; "you" means existence. The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) claim that although the myriad dharmas are numerous, they do not transcend the auspiciousness of existence and non-existence.
The Buddha-dharma differs from theirs; therefore, it is said to "distinguish from the heterodox. △ Third, the extensive listing of the audience has eight parts.
The first two concern the assembly of Śrāvakas of the Two Vehicles. Part five: first, citing their category.
"Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.

From this point downward, the "perfection of the assembly" is established; that is to say, if there were no one beneath the seat [of the Buddha], for whom would he preach? "Together with" (sārdham) means "in company with.
Ānanda said: "It was not heard by me alone from the Buddha; because it was shared with the assembly, it serves all the more as a basis for testimony and faith."
"Great" (*mahā*) means that his capacity and measure are venerable, and he is honored by great beings such as celestial kings.
He is called "great" because he possesses the Great Path, because he possesses great function, and because he possesses great knowledge. Regarding "bhikṣu," the *Jingming shu* states:

some say there is a translation, while others say there is none. As for those who say there is a translation, it is rendered here as "one who removes hunger" (*divasa-kṣapa*). Sentient beings have meager merit; regarding their causes...
Being unable to sustain oneself, one receives retribution characterized by great scarcity and deprivation. The monastic precepts and conduct constitute a fertile field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*);

they can produce wholesome qualities in sentient beings and eliminate the deprivation caused by cause and effect. Therefore, they are called "removers of deprivation" (*poṣadha*). Regarding the statement that there is no corresponding term [in other languages], the name contains three meanings:
