first, destroying evil; second, terrifying Māra; and third, the mendicant (*bhikṣu*). The precepts prevent misconduct of the body, while meditative concentration removes the confusion of the mind.
Wisdom awakens one to the emptiness of perceptions; it can destroy the evils of view and affliction, and is therefore called "Destroying Evil.

Once evil has been destroyed, Māra thinks to himself: "Since he has left the household life, he will further convert others to leave the triple world together with him; this runs contrary to my intentions."
Māra was filled with sorrow and fear; thus he is named "Terrifier of Māra" (Bhikṣu). As for householders, there are three types of lawful means of livelihood to sustain their bodies and lives:
first, agriculture; second, commerce; and third, service as a craftsman. For those who have left the home life, the Buddha did not permit these; they may only sustain themselves by begging for alms.

When the body is at peace, the Path endures, and they bring benefit and merit to their donors; thus they are called "Alms-seekers" (Bhikṣu). Regarding the term "Assembly" (Zhòng): in the Sanskrit language it is *saṃgha*.
This translates as "the harmonious assembly. "Harmony of affairs" means there is no separate group; "harmony of Dharma" means there is no separate principle. △ Second, indicating the number:
thirty-two thousand people.
The number of sūtras in various collections differs; however, the fundamental canon consists of thirty-two thousand [verses].
△ Third, the praise of their virtues:
All are arhats whose minds are well-liberated and whose wisdom is well-liberated; they have accomplished what was to be done and are free from all heavy burdens.
He has taken up the burden and attained his own benefit; he has exhausted all fetters of existence, attained great mastery, and dwells in pure precepts.
Adorned with skillful means and wisdom, he has realized the eight liberations and reached the further shore.

Arhat. Formerly translated as "The Unattached" (wu zhu), "The Non-arising" (busheng), or "The Worthy of Offerings" (yinggong); alternatively, it is said that there is no direct equivalent, as the name contains three meanings.
Because the husks of ignorance have been shed, one will not receive the retribution of birth and death within the fields of future lives; hence, it is called "Non-arising.

Because the ninety-eight latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) have been severed and exhausted, one is called a "Slayer of Thieves. Possessing the merits of wisdom and abandonment, one is fit to be a teacher for others.
Because they are a field of merit for the heavens, they are called "Worthy of Offerings" (*arhat*). Regarding liberation in contrast to bondage:

sentient beings have their wisdom covered by ignorance and are bound by the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), thus failing to attain liberation. This Arhat, however, has exhausted both views and afflictions and is already free from birth and death;
therefore, his mind is liberated. Having shed the husk of ignorance, the nature of his wisdom is unobstructed; therefore, his wisdom is liberated. Mind...
This is the very essence of nature; wisdom is the function of insight. "Skillful" is a term of praise, which by contrast reveals the unskillfulness of ordinary beings.

"Having completed what was to be done" means that delusions are exhausted and reality is fully realized, such that there is nothing further to be done; the fruit of the Path has been attained, such that there is nothing further to be accomplished.
"The heavy burden" refers to birth and death (*saṃsāra*); it means that as long as one does not leave birth and death behind, one is like a person weighed down by a heavy load.

Regarding the term "all" (*sarva*) in "having abandoned all heavy burdens": there are two interpretations. First, it is an auxiliary particle. Second, although it metaphorically refers to birth and death, it also encompasses afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma;
because these are manifold, they are called "all. Since one has now departed from them, it is said that one has "abandoned all heavy burdens.

"Attaining" (*prāpta*) means "reaching. "One's own benefit" (*svārtha*) refers to self-benefit. This is the self-benefit of the *śrāvaka*, which differs from the bodhisattva’s self-benefit, which is the benefit of others.

People merely plan for their own selves. By extinguishing the fetters of affliction arising from views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* and *kleśa-saṃyojana*) within the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*), they cause the causes and effects of the triple world to perish.
Therefore, it is said: "exhausting all fetters of existence. "Existence" (*bhava*) here carries the sense that the causes and effects within the three realms have not yet perished.

"Fetters" (*saṃyojana*) means bondage; it refers specifically to the causes and effects of views and thoughts. From "attaining the great... downwards: having already departed from the bonds and fetters of the three realms, then...
Possessing the three vidyās and six abhijñās, they act according to their will; seeking only benefit and never causing harm, they are simply autonomous.

"Great" means that merely being free from the fetters of bondage constitutes autonomy, yet they further possess supernatural powers that follow their mind; thus, it is called "Great Autonomy. Regarding the phrase "abiding in purity":
since they are devoid of both *darśana-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya* afflictions, their intrinsic nature is unturbid, which is termed "purity"; in its very essence, it is unstained.

It is called "pure. Being pure and free from transgression is called "precept" (*śīla*). Being the basis for the noble ones (*ārya*) is called "abiding" (*vihāra*). Therefore, it is said: "abiding in pure precepts.
The latter two lines [of the verse] briefly indicate the virtue of benefiting others. Wisdom is of two kinds.

The wisdom of the emptiness of birth is for one’s own benefit; the wisdom of skillful means is for the benefit of others. Because the merit of benefiting both self and others adorns the essential nature, [it is called "adornment"].
Question: Above, it was stated that this is for one's own benefit; yet in the commentary, it is explained differently, as the Bodhisattva’s twofold benefit. How are these two accounts reconciled?
Furthermore, does it not contradict [the previous statement] to say that there is the virtue of benefiting others? Answer:

It is simply not the same as a Bodhisattva manifesting in various forms according to the type of being and preaching the Dharma according to their capacities—such as the thirty-two manifestations of Avalokiteśvara.

While this [present case] also benefits others, it is merely skillful means according to conditions; yet it is certainly not without [the quality of wisdom], such as the wisdom of Śāriputra or Kātyāyana.
If the debates of Pūrṇa and the like were entirely incapable of benefiting others, would it not be the case that all such efforts are useless?
Moreover, this Venerable One possessed the traces of "inner secrecy and outer manifestation"; how can one speak of him in such general terms?

As for the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), these are what are attained by Arhats through the cultivation of the eight stages of liberation (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*). There are eight kinds of liberation; they are not...
Bound by the eight internal and external matters, one is therefore said to be "liberated. (For those who have read widely and seek clarity, please consult the *Daming Sanzang Fashu*).

Regarding "reaching the other shore" (*pāra*): this is a metaphor used to manifest the Dharma. A "shore" refers to the edge of water; it is the dry land on either side of a great river. There is "this" and there is "that":
this shore is a metaphor for birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and the other shore is a metaphor for nirvāṇa. Within the river...

The water is a metaphor for the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃyojana-kleśa*). This means that by practicing the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*), one attains liberation.
Taking meditative concentration as a boat or raft, one who can board this vessel leaves behind birth and death, crosses over the afflictions, and reaches nirvāṇa to enjoy the bliss of the Dharma.
The above concludes the praise of his virtues. △ Fourth, the listing of names.
Their names were: the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Mahānāmapratyayika, Mahākāśyapa, Gavāmpati, Revata, and Uruvilvākāśyapa.
Nadī-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākātyāyana,
Mahākapphiṇa, Cunda, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and Aniruddha.
Subhūti of the Subtle Arms, Bakula, Sundarananda, Rāhula— these venerable Arhats,
as well as the learners such as Ānanda and others, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of followers.
From Kāśyapa to Ānanda, these twenty-two individuals were all the foremost leaders among the assembly; "raising their heads" implies they represent the entire multitude.

Furthermore, they are divided into those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and those still in training (*śaikṣa*). Those who have reached the ultimate truth and exhausted all delusions, having nothing further to learn, are called "beyond training.
Those who investigate the truth and sever delusions while still in the stage of learning are called "in training. From Kāśyapa to Rā... [text fragment]
Uruvilvākāśyapa and the others were all Arhats beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Ānanda and the rest were all still in training (*śaikṣa*), namely those who have attained the first three fruits.
As for why the foremost among the assembly beyond training is addressed as "Venerable" (*āyuṣmat*), the Sanskrit etymology may not be fully detailed;
however, according to its meaning, it is a title for an elder. Because they are advanced in years and senior in ordination age, they are called "Venerable. *Ājñātakauṇḍinya*.

He was one of two individuals from his maternal clan and belonged to the family of the Buddha’s maternal uncle. The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) states: "Ajñāta" is his name; this translates as "Already Known" (*jīzhī*).
Alternatively, it is said to mean "Without Knowledge," yet this does not mean he lacked knowledge; rather, it means he knew "non-existence" (*wu*). It is also translated as "Understanding.
The *Lengyan jing* says: "I was first called 'Understanding'"; the full title is "Understanding the Ultimate Limit" (*jie benji*), making him the foremost in understanding.
"Dharma" is his name; "Kauṇḍinya" is his clan name, which translates here as "Fire-vessel. He is of the Brahmin caste.
His ancestors served the fire, and from this they derived their lineage; he is also called Kauṇḍina, differing only in the Sanskrit pronunciation. ○ Aśvajit:
since the meaning of this Venerable One’s name has not been translated [into Chinese], both the Chinese and Sanskrit versions remain undetermined. ○ Mā... [text ends]
*Hānamapātirikka*. *Mahā* means "great," signifying that his path and practice are great;
it is a term of praise. The specific name is also not clearly known. *Mahākāśyapa*. This is translated as "Great Kūrma" (Turtle Clan).

His ancestors studied the Way, and a numinous tortoise appeared bearing a divine chart in response. Because of this virtue, the clan was named after it; people of the time commonly addressed him by his surname. His...
He truly had a name; his name was Pippala, which is the name of a tree. He was born through the prayers of his parents to a tree deity, and thus he received his name from that tree.
"Great" (*mahā*) is a term of praise or a term of distinction. This is because among the disciples of the Buddha, many were named Kāśyapa.

Just as with the Ten Powers (Daśabala), so it is with the three Kāśyapas. This Venerable One is not one of them; therefore, he is renowned by his great title. Alternatively, it is translated as "Drinking Light" (Kāśyapa).
Because the radiance of his body shines so brightly that it can swallow up and drink in the light of the sun and moon, this became his name.
Due to causes in past lives, having used gold to gild the forms of Buddha images, he was moved to experience a body of golden light in every lifetime and birth.
Gavāmpati is translated here as "ox-chewer. In five hundred past lives, he had once been a bull king;

because after eating, he would chew his cud long afterward, he is called a "chewer. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that in past lives he had mocked śramaṇas, which resulted in him having the affliction of chewing the cud in every successive birth.
The Buddha ordered him to dwell in retreat in the heavens, yet [the Buddha] remained apprehensive.
The retribution for the slander of worldly people. ○ Līlāvatī (Lípōduō). This means "constellation. He was born through the prayers of his parents to the constellations;
he was named after the place of his request. ○ Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa (Yōulópíluójiāshè). This means "Papaya Grove."
Because he lived near this forest, Guishan says: "Pāṭaliputra" (木瓜) refers to a "tumor" (*gaṇḍa*); because there was a tumor on his chest like a *pāṭala* fruit, he was so named.
○ Nadi-Kāśyapa: *Nadī* is the name of a river; he lived near this river, and was named after his place of residence. ○ Gayā-Kāśyapa:
Guishan says that *Gayā* is the name of a mountain, namely Elephant Head Mountain (*Gajapadaka-parvata*). He lived near this mountain.
They were named after the mountain upon which they resided. These three venerable ones were originally three brothers living as laymen;
when the eldest brother returned to the Buddha, his younger brothers followed him. Śāriputra is translated here as "Son of Śārī. He was named after his mother.
Śārī is the name of a bird in the Western Regions, translated here as "crane" (shùlù). Its eyes are bright and beautiful, and the eyes of the Venerable One’s mother resembled them.
Thus she was called Śāriputrī. "Fu" (弗) is a transliteration of the Western term for "son. It means the son of Śāriputrī;
this "son" refers to the Venerable One, who was foremost in wisdom. ○ Mahāmaudgalyāyana is his clan name. Kauṣṭhila is also the name of a tree.
He prayed to the tree deity and obtained a son, and thus he was named after it. However, since he already had a [given] name, and...

As for those addressed by their clan names, this is because people of that time frequently called them by their surnames. Alternatively, he is translated as Caishu Shi (氏). "Shu" (菽) is the name for beans;
because his ancestors were fond of eating beans, they named their clan accordingly. This Venerable One was the foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
Mahākātyāyana is translated here as Wenshi (文飾), meaning "Ornamentation. He was the foremost in formal debate and exposition.
○ Mahākāpyana. ○ Sandhāna. These two venerable ones are also not included in the *Yìjí* (Collection of Meanings).
Their Chinese and Sanskrit names are not detailed. ○ Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. This venerable one’s name is given in full, including his parents.
"Pūrṇa" means "Fulfiller of Vows," which is the father's name. "Maitrāyaṇī" means "Compassionate Woman."
This is the name of his mother. "Only the son" refers to the Venerable One, meaning the son of the daughter of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇī, who was foremost in preaching the Dharma.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Apart from the Tathāgata, there is none who can exhaust the eloquence of his discourse.
○ Aniruddha: sometimes called Aniruddha, or Anuruddha; these are all variations due to differences in the Sanskrit pronunciation.
"Ear. This is translated as "As One Wishes" (*yathā-īpsita*) or "Without Poverty. In a past age of famine, he once offered millet rice to a *pratyekabuddha*.
As a result, for ninety-one *kalpas*, he experienced wondrous happiness among gods and humans, never suffering from any lack.
He was free from poverty; hence he was called "The Poorless. He was the Buddha’s younger cousin and was foremost among those with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

○ *Miaomiao bi* (Subāhu): This does not correspond to the Sanskrit term, nor is its meaning clear. Perhaps it means his arms were more exquisite than those of others, and he was named after his arms. ○ *Subhūti*:
This is translated as "Born of Emptiness" (*Kongsheng*), also as "Good Auspiciousness" (*Shanji*), also as "Well-Manifested" (*Shanxian*), and also as "Good Deeds" (*Shanye*). His...
On the day he was born, his household became entirely empty; thus he was called "Empty-born" (Śūnyatā-jāta).

His parents were struck with wonder and consulted a diviner, who declared it auspicious and named him "Good Fortune" (Kalyāṇa-bhadra). Later, when a treasure trove reappeared, he was named "Good Manifestation" (Kalyāṇabhadrika).

By nature he was kind and charitable, never contending with others. Upon leaving the household life, he perceived emptiness and attained the Way, while simultaneously cultivating a mind of loving-kindness.
He attained the *araṇā-samādhi*. For this reason, he was always able to guard sentient beings with his mind;

thus it is called "wholesome karma. This Venerable One was the foremost person in understanding emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Bakkula means "Good Appearance" (*Sukhavarṇa*) because his physical features were upright and handsome;
he is also called "Venerable of Weighty Lineage. In the *Madhyama Āgama*, in the "Questions by the Heretics," [it is said]: "For eighty years, you have given rise to thoughts of desire."
"No. He replied, "One should not ask such a question. For eighty years, I have never once given rise to a thought of desire, nor have I ever entertained a single thought of arrogance.

I have never accepted a robe from a householder, nor have I ever worn a robe made of cut patches, nor have I ever borrowed a robe from another, nor have I ever sewn a robe with a needle. I have never accepted invitations, nor have I ever begged for alms from great households."
He never leaned against a wall; he never looked at the face of a woman; he never entered a bhikṣuṇī’s quarters; he never exchanged greetings with them;
even on the road, he did not speak with them. For eighty years, he sat constantly and did not lie down. Jingxi said:
"Those who propagate the Dharma should take this as a mirror for observation. Regarding Sundarananda: *Sundara* means...
"Sujāta" (Good Love) is the name of his wife; "Nanda" means "Joy," which is his own title.

To distinguish him from Nanda the cowherd—who loved his wife while living as a householder—the name is given in conjunction with his wife. This Venerable One was the Buddha’s own younger brother and the second son of King Śuddhodana.
○ "Rāhula" means "Obstruction"; he was so called because he remained covered within his mother's womb for six years.
Because of this obstruction, he is a son of the Buddha. He is also called Rāhula; there is a translation meaning "Born in the Palace.
When the Prince renounced the world, the Crown Princess remained in the palace; how could she have become pregnant?

The Buddha and King Śuddhodana later provided testimony that he was the biological son of the Prince and born within the palace, and for this reason he was named "Palace-Born" (Kūṭadanta). Some say that six years after the Prince renounced the world...
In the year [of his birth], when Yaśodharā gave birth to a son, all the Śākya clan were filled with doubt. Consequently, the Great Consort Yaśodharā prepared a fire pit beneath a high tower;
she carried her son up to the tower, burned incense, and prayed to Heaven: "If this child is indeed the physical heir of the Crown Prince..."
"May my mother and I remain unharmed; if there is any misfortune, may both my mother and I be consumed by fire. Having finished this prayer, she leaped into the flames.
At that moment, the fire pit was transformed into a cool, refreshing pool, and mother and son remained unhurt.
Through this divine testimony, all doubts were extinguished. Thus, the Venerable One who is an Arhat has attained the supreme state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
This is one category. ○ Regarding the *śaikṣa* Ānanda: this further cites another instance of the *śaikṣa* category. "Ānanda" is translated here as "Joy.
On the day the Buddha attained enlightenment, King Droṇodana gave birth to a son. A household messenger came to inform King Śuddhodana, saying, "Your noble younger brother has fathered a son.
The king’s heart was filled with joy, and thus he named him accordingly. Furthermore, the entire kingdom celebrated with great delight. It is also...

He is named Ānanda (Joyful), which is also translated as "Untainted. Although his residual latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) were not yet exhausted, he followed the Buddha into the palaces of devas, humans, and nāgas;
because his mind was free from defiled attachment upon seeing women, he is so called. The term "etc. (*ādi*) collectively encompasses the general assembly of those in training (*śaikṣa*).

Regarding the phrase "each with [the others]": "each" (*pratyeka*) means individually, and "with" (*saha*) means together. This refers to the group of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) being together with those beyond training.

It is the same for those in training (*śaikṣa*). Regarding "several" (*aneka*): there is a number contained therein; because they are numerous and cannot be fully enumerated, it is stated generally as "several hundreds or thousands.
Regarding "retinue" (*parivāra*): a teacher refers to his disciples as his retinue, meaning they are his dharma-retinue, his disciples, and those under his authority.
Regarding "all" (*saha*): this means "everyone," referring to all who are present here.
...Thus. △ Fifth, the assembly concludes:
each bows at the Buddha’s feet and withdraws to sit on one side.
As for bowing at the feet, this is the standard protocol for a disciple serving a teacher; however, such reverent devotion must be sincere and may never be perfunctory.
Furthermore, regarding those who withdraw to sit: this is the established ritual for determining the seating order according to rank.
Nevertheless, as there are regulations governing the details of ceremony, the positions must not be disordered. The temporary gathering of teacher and disciple is a model for a thousand generations;
will those in the present and future who observe the rites of a disciple not likewise take this as a standard to emulate? △ Second, the Mahāyāna.
The fifth section concerns the assembly of Bodhisattvas. First, the category is introduced:
"Furthermore, there are Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
*Bodhisattva* (菩提薩埵) is the correct transliteration; *bodhi* is the name for the Buddha-way, and *sattva* here means "great mind" (*mahācitta*).

Sentient beings possess a great mind because they enter the Buddha-way; thus they are also called *bodhisattva*. They are called "opening beings" (*kaishi*) because their minds have first opened, and they are called "beginning beings" (*shishi*) because they have first resolved to attain enlightenment.
An ancient manuscript also calls them "exalted beings" (*gaoshi*). Since the translations were not fixed, the original Sanskrit term has been retained.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains that *bodhi* means the Buddha-way, and *sattva* means a sentient being who is bringing [the path] to completion; this refers to all...
"Buddha-way" means the fulfillment of sentient beings. It is also called "Awakening Sentient Beings," which refers to the supreme awakening of the Buddha-way while transforming sentient beings below;
it is the honorific title for one who benefits both self and others. As for "Mahāsattva," *mahā* means "great," and *sattva* refers to a being;

thus, it denotes the greatest among Bodhisattvas, namely those on the stages (bhūmi) at the level of Equal Awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), who differ from those of the Three Degrees of Worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*).
Therefore, he is called "Great. △ Second, the indication of the number:
"accompanied by eighty-four thousand people.
△ Third, the praise of his virtues, in three parts. First, a general praise of his rank as being adjacent to the Sublime Enlightenment (Samyak-saṃbodhi).
All are those in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), great sons of the Dharma-king, possessing great majestic power like great dragon kings;
this is a general reference to them all. "One birth" does not refer to the birth within the cycle of birth and death, but rather to the transition from cause to fruit.

One currently abides in Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). Myriad practices are already fulfilled; myriad virtues are already complete; the ultimate truth is already reached. Only one portion remains:

the ignorance of the mark of birth (*utpatti-nimitta-avidyā*), which has not yet been exhausted. If one employs the ten kinds of diamond-like samādhis (*vajropama-samādhi*), in a single kṣaṇa that ignorance will be severed and exhausted, and one immediately enters Sublime Enlightenment (*pratyaksa-buddhatva*).
This transformation of Equal Enlightenment into Sublime Enlightenment is called "one life."

"Supplementer" (bǔ) means to fill. "Position" (chù) refers to the rank of a Buddha. Just as when the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma of a preceding Buddha have already ended, a subsequent Buddha fills that position;
hence, he is called a "Successor" (bǔchù). Regarding the "Great Dharma Prince": the Buddha is the Dharma King and the Bodhisattva is his son.
Since both are able to shoulder the affairs of the Buddha, they possess the significance of being a "son. All Bodhisattvas are...
O Son of the Buddha! Because the stage of Solitary Equal Enlightenment is immediately adjacent to Great Awakening, it is called the "Prince of the Great Dharma.
Regarding those of "Great Majestic Virtue," they possess both the two gates of subduing and gathering; they have majesty that is awe-inspiring and virtue that is venerable.

The phrase "like a great dragon king" employs a metaphor to manifest their supremacy: a king governs and commands all dragons, and the "great" one is the most honored, serving as a metaphor for Equal Enlightenment.

Bodhisattvas—since all those of the three stages of worthiness and the ten bhūmis are governed by the state of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) and are thus ranked as supreme, this serves as a metaphor.
Furthermore, there are many other intentions: the dragon is considered a spirit among yang-natured beings and the sovereign of scaly creatures;

its ability to raise clouds and bring rain is used to metaphorize the compassion of the Bodhisattva, while its power to overturn seas and move mountains is compared to the Bodhisattva’s [great spiritual power].
His wrath transcends its kind, likening him to the Most Honored among Bodhisattvas. He is hidden within the abyss, likening him to the profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of a Bodhisattva.
His great virtue is nameless; these metaphors merely provide a brief illustration of one or two aspects.
△ Second, the specific praise of the adornment of the ten thousand virtues, in two parts. First, the general heading.
"Perfected by a hundred blessings.
"Blessing" (*puṇya*) refers to virtue, goodness, and auspiciousness; it is a general term for all that is favorable. "A hundred" is a designation for the completion of a number.
As with "a hundred things" or "a hundred kinds," so too, "ten thousand virtues" refers not merely to ten thousand, but is a general designation for the Buddha’s virtues.
The same applies to the virtues of a Bodhisattva; they do not stop at one hundred, but encompass all virtues, all goodness, and every auspicious quality.
Therefore, it is called "perfectly complete. Part Two: Specific Praise, in Six Sections. First, praising the circular halo that dispels darkness.
Virtue.
The radiance of his body shines forth like a thousand suns, destroying all darkness.
This refers to the Bodhisattva emitting light from his entire body, which is capable of dispelling all obscurity; the excellence of its illumination is likened to a thousand [suns].
The suns arise together. For instance, while a single sun can illuminate one set of four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*), the illumination of a thousand suns is of infinite extent.
Although the darkness of the world is great, it does not equal that of the hells. When sentient beings fall there, they are moved by the power of their karma;
there is no light from the sun, moon, or lamps. They dwell perpetually in darkness, where a collection of sufferings more intense than this cannot be found.
If one is graced by the illuminating light of a Bodhisattva’s body, suffering ceases and bitterness halts; this is called the light of great compassion that uproots suffering.
For example, sentient beings among humans and devas who follow the path of goodness, though not in physical darkness, possess minds that lack clarity.
Chasing after sensory objects, they create karma and do not know the essential way out; they, too, are in darkness. If they are touched by the holy light, they then give rise to [awakening].

With thirsty longing, one transforms ignorance into wisdom; thus, one can turn the mind toward the Path and seek deliverance from birth and death—this is the light of Great Compassion that bestows bliss.
Therefore, it is said: "It shatters all darkness and obscurity. △ Second, praising the merit of the two types of wisdom that benefit both self and others, in two parts:
first, praising the merit of Real Wisdom (bhūta-jñāna) for self-benefit.
Wisdom is clear and transparent, surpassing the great ocean; it thoroughly penetrates the secret realm of all Buddhas.

Wisdom is the awakening illumination of the essence of reality (*dharmatā*). Nevertheless, there is a distinction between self-illumination and awakening others. These four lines are explained here primarily in terms of self-illumination.

"Clear and transparent" refers to the wisdom of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which, although still accompanied by the ignorance of the phase of arising (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*), [remains luminous].

It appears as if it exists, yet is as if non-existent. Therefore, that which cannot be turbidified by delusion is called "clarity" (*ting*); that which cannot be obstructed by dust is called "penetration" (*che*).

This is the "arising enlightenment" (*shiqiao*) initiated based upon "original enlightenment" (*benjue*). By using this arising enlightenment to reflect back upon original enlightenment, one becomes free from turbidity and obstruction;
this is true wisdom (*zhishi*). Regarding the phrase "even more like the great ocean": the seawater is a metaphor for true wisdom. The crystal-clear limpidity of the water is like [true wisdom].
The clarity of wisdom is like the vastness of the ocean. "As penetrating as wisdom" means that while the capacity of the ocean is great, it ultimately has limits;
wisdom, however, has no limits, for it exhausts the vertical and pervades the horizontal. Although the seawater is clear, [it is not so with wisdom].

When wind encounters water, waves arise; wisdom is not like this, and therefore it is called "transcending" (*yu*). That which is mentioned above is the wisdom that acts as the means of realization (*pramāṇa*);
that which is understood below is the principle realized (*prameya*), the secret realm, which is the very mind-ground of all Buddhas.

Regarding the statement that "it is not transmitted to those who lack the capacity" and "it is not taught when the time is not right," the two characters "understanding" (*liao*) and "penetrating" (*da*) apply to both the subject and the object. "Understanding" (*liao*) refers to illuminative comprehension, while "penetrating" (*da*) refers to...
Realization. That which is thoroughly understood is the wisdom of ultimate reality; that which is thoroughly understood is the secret realm.
This is originally the mind-ground of all Buddhas, yet it is called a "realm" because it is that which is illumined by wisdom. Thus one treads upon the realm. II.
Praising the virtue of expedient wisdom in benefiting others.
He kindles the great torch of the Dharma to guide sentient beings across the ocean of birth and death, acting as a great captain.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, as if for his own infant children, he constantly bestows peace and happiness at all times; his fame is heard throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Since it is called the "Great Dharma," it must be for those of great capacity. "Dharma" refers to the rules for cultivating causes and realizing fruits.
"Torch" (*jù*) means a firebrand; "to kindle" (*rán*) means to burn. To "kindle a great torch" is a metaphor for preaching the Great Dharma.

Because sentient beings have heavy obstructions from the two attachments (*dvaya-grāha*), their Buddha-nature is obscured and they cannot awaken on their own; therefore, the Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma to guide them.
This mind causes the two attachments to be eliminated and the two emptinesses to be attained, like holding up a torch to dispel darkness.
These two lines illustrate, for the time being, the grace of destroying delusion and achieving awakening. The following two lines are a metaphor for leaving suffering behind to attain the fruit.

"Fully responding to capacities" means teaching others without weariness. "Mastery" refers to the fulfillment of one's wishes.

Since the preceding passage describes how the three wheels respond to sentient beings such that nothing fails to accord with their minds, they fulfill their original intent; thus, there is a spontaneous and effortless mastery. "Exquisite goodness," etc. [follows].

"Uninvited" explicitly reveals unconditional compassion (*nirālambana-maitrī*); if one were to appear only after being invited, that would merely be a manifestation of emotional attachment.
Compassion. It is not so with the Bodhisattva. Rather, they act in accordance with conditions and according to capacities, responding to whatever is felt by others.

"Throughout immeasurable kalpas" below refers to the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of causes, which does not occur in a single lifetime. "Diligent cultivation" means that one keeps [the teachings] in mind at every thought-moment and practices them without slackening.

Transgressions are overcome as follows: patience overcomes anger; vigor overcomes laziness; meditative concentration overcomes distraction; and wisdom overcomes ignorance.

(Generosity must necessarily include the three types of giving: material gifts, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of Dharma. Patience must necessarily encompass both the phenomenal and the principled. Phenomenal patience refers to the two kinds—patience toward living beings and patience toward dharmas. Regarding living beings: when mosquitoes, gadflies, birds, beasts, and various wicked people cause all manner of disturbances and harm, the Bodhisattva’s mind remains firm and unmoving; this is called patience toward living beings. Patience toward dharmas refers to remaining unmoved by cold winds, heat, or cold.)

Regarding the mind: these two are both patience regarding phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti*). Diligence also has two types: first, not being weary in one's own cultivation; second, not being weary in benefiting others.

If there is even a moment of weariness or indolence, one will fall back and decline. Therefore, seeing ever-newness in every thought-moment is the practice of a Bodhisattva. Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) must be like a *nāga*: amidst the four postures, one is never outside of samādhi. Wisdom also has two aspects, namely the two functions of skillful means (*upāya*) and reality (*tattva*). By means of the wisdom of reality, one illuminates and shatters ignorance, thereby being able to realize the ultimate truth; this is self-benefit. They do not serve, attend upon, or make offerings [to them], nor do they study and practice the Dharma. The second refers to traversing all places;

Regarding "all afflictions": the character "not" (不) extends down to the following phrase. They neither abide in nirvana nor do they sever the afflictions.

"Nirvana" (涅槃) is here translated as "perfect quiescence" (圓寂). This means that true nature is fundamentally perfect and delusive confusion is fundamentally quiescent; the Bodhisattva skillfully realizes this.
Since the true nature is fundamentally perfect, Nirvana is my own self-nature; why then should I dwell in it? Therefore, I do not dwell in it.
Since delusive confusion is fundamentally quiescent and afflictions are inherently empty from the beginning, they are my very Bodhi; why then trouble myself to sever them?
Therefore, I do not sever them. If Nirvana were fixedly dwelt in and afflictions necessarily severed, one would be no different from those of the Two Vehicles.

If one were to rely solely on provisional language for exposition and expression, sentient beings would have no gateway through which to enter the Path.

To speak of "forgetting words" is itself not to lose their wondrous essence; thus it is said that one expounds the wondrous Dharma.

Since they are called "transformation bodies," they are not of a single type; this may be described as being like the motes of dust [in the universe].
"Manifesting bodies throughout the lands" means appearing according to the various types [of beings].

As for "various," it means there are many kinds of non-Buddhists, such as those who worship fire or revere water, those who speculate on eternalism or nihilism, and those who observe the precepts of cattle or dogs.

As for "restraining," it refers to using the correct to refute the erroneous. Regarding "erroneous mind," it means that while the mind is fundamentally not erroneous, it becomes so due to associating with false teachings.
A false teacher perfumes [the mind] so as to form seeds; through such defiled habituation, one becomes perverse. "To crush and subdue" means to break, defeat, and bring under control.

One sees a deep pit, yet there is no descent below. This precisely explains the meaning mentioned above: it is the wondrous function of serving the Buddha, preaching the Dharma, benefiting sentient beings, and subduing the heterodox.
It means that while the true body of the Bodhisattva remains unmoving, its manifestations pervade the ten directions.
This is the inconceivable intersection of resonance and response, like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers: the water does not rise upward, nor does the moon descend.
At one time, for one month, his reflection appeared in all the waters; thus it is said that he possesses no marks of coming or going.

Bodhisattvas teach and transform others so that all may abandon evil for good and turn from the heterodox toward the orthodox, taking goodness as their adornment.
Second, regarding the environment of retribution (*niśraya-vipāka-loka*):

It is merely called "abiding" in a figurative sense because it accords with this reality and constitutes the meaning of ultimate perfection. Although it abides, it does not abide; therefore, it is said to "abide in non-abiding."

"numerous" here means many. The two lines beginning with "There is nothing... appear inverted in the text;
if one reads the preceding line as the subsequent one, the sequence becomes smooth. "Dharma-joy" refers to the joy of the dharma-nature (dharmatā); that is to say, the dharma-nature.

Within the essence, there is bliss because it is free from all karmic suffering. "Vast" means that it is coextensive with the nature (*dharmatā*). Furthermore, it is said to "accept nothing that is not [already contained]";
this refers to the fact that within the essence of the *dharmatā*, the ocean-like sands of inherent virtues are fully possessed; once attained, they are all attained.
Therefore it is said that there is nothing not received; this is precisely the public mind of the Bodhisattva. Having realized what he himself has attained, he leads others to realize it as well.
△ Fifth, praising the destruction of Māra and the accomplishment of the Way and its Virtue.
Donning the armor of diligence and grasping the sword of wisdom, one shatters the hosts of Māra and beats the Dharma drum.

With the body constantly seated throughout all sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the Bodhisattva practices and severs delusions; this is to wage war against the multitudes of Māras. To succumb even momentarily to indolence is to be defeated by Māra.
Because one is bound, one must apply diligence as if donning armor so as not to be wounded by Māra. In the Sanskrit language, *māra* means "the slayer.
This refers to that which wounds and kills the life-force of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*) and damages the wealth of the Dharma; it is a metaphor for the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
For example: the Māra of greed harms liberation; the Māra of hatred harms right nature; the Māra of delusion harms natural wisdom; and the Māra of pride harms humility.
Doubt harms right faith; malevolent demons harm right view, and so forth.
When a Bodhisattva once applies the illumination of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), all delusions are extinguished, like wielding a sharp sword to slay bandits.
This diligence and wisdom are both powerful weapons for subduing Māra. The two lines following "subduing Māra" specifically illustrate their application at the moment of need. As for the drum...

The merit of advancing [the troops] is like the time of clashing in battle: when the drums are beaten at the camp gates to augment the spirit and urge on the fight, the army and officers exert their valor and break through the multitudes of rebels.
As for the so-called *dharmadundubhi* (Dharma-drum), it means that the wondrous Dharma is like a drum;

it is the concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) of the moment. Contemplative observation is like the striking [of the drum]; by applying diligent effort without interruption, all demons are thereby destroyed.

Only then does one achieve perfect enlightenment; hence it is said that the body constantly sits pervasively in all places of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*). This is the manifestation of the image of Great Peace.
Now, regarding the term "all" in "all places of practice," it is as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:

when Vairocana Buddha attains enlightenment in a single location—the place of enlightenment according to the *āraṇyaka* dharma—then simultaneously throughout the worlds of the ten directions, even down to the most minute...
Within every pore of the dust, there is the attainment of the Way by a Tathāgata; this is identical to what is meant by "the body is eternally omnipresent in all places.

The site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) has two meanings: the phenomenal and the noumenal. The phenomenal site of enlightenment refers to a secluded and tranquil place, which is the ground for cultivating and realizing *bodhi*.
The noumenal site of enlightenment is the perfect concentration (*samādhi*) inherently possessed by one's own nature. It can be...
This refers to the true *araṇya*, the place of authentic practice. △ Sixth, the praise for the virtue of awakening all classes of beings:
He blows the great Dharma conch to awaken all classes of beings; all sentient beings receive its benefit, whether they hear his name or behold his person.
There is no passing away in vain. Possessing the three types of penetrating knowledge (*trividyā*), he awakens to the phenomena of the three periods of time.

He skillfully knows the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings, administering medicine according to their ailments without further doubt. He spreads the great cloud of Dharma and pours down the rain of ambrosia.

He turns the wheel of the Dharma of the non-retrogressive wisdom-seal, closing the prison of birth and death and opening the gate of *nirvāṇa*. He makes vast vows to endure until the end of the future.
To deliver all sentient beings.
The blowing of the conch is a metaphor for the Dharma; thus it is called the "Dharma-conch. The conch carries the meaning of awakening;
that is to say, these bodhisattvas, having themselves attained the Way, are further able to awaken all sentient beings, preaching the Dharma to alert the multitude, just like blowing [the conch].
The conch shell is used to alert people; it is like our Great Qing, which during the two seasons of spring and autumn, blows the conch at its nine gates as a signal.

This causes the soldiers and generals of the Eight Banners to hear the call and be alerted, repairing their armor and practicing martial arts with their halberds to prepare for the occasional needs of the state.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: he speaks of how the matter of birth and death is great and how impermanence is swift.
It causes the beings who are alerted by this to generate the bodhicitta for the sake of escaping the suffering of birth and death;

therefore, it is said that "all sentient beings receive benefit. Regarding the phrase "upon hearing the name": they deeply understand its supreme virtues, and those who undergo transformation are vast in number—some hear the name and look up to its virtue, while others see the physical marks and take refuge.
Thus, those who have not yet generated the mind do so, and those who have already generated it engage in practice.
Those who have already practiced advance further; those who have already advanced realize the fruit. Thus it is said that none pass by in vain.

"Possessing the three," and so forth, clarifies that the Bodhisattva observes the capacities of beings and teaches the Dharma accordingly, such that the capacity and the teaching meet, like a skilled physician administering medicine.

The "three types of penetrating knowledge" (*trividyā*) are not excluded from the categories of phenomena; this is another designation for the three types of clear knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*), namely, the clear knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-vidyā*). It is able to...
Knowing that which has already passed—the causes and effects of all defilement and purity for oneself and others—is the clarity of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

Being able to know all causes and effects of defilement and purity in the present is the clarity of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Being able to know all causes and effects of defilement and purity for oneself and others in the future is the clarity of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Because one can penetrate the three periods of time, it is said that one awakens to the dharmas of the three periods. Through this awakening, one clarifies the three periods.

Dharma. This is why one skillfully knows the sharpness or dullness of the faculties (*indriya*) of sentient beings. There are two interpretations of these faculties. First, the faculty is the cause itself;
it refers to knowing their past—whether they cultivated causes or created karma—which thus brings about the inequality of sharpness or dullness in this present life.
Second, it refers to the six faculties of the present life. Those with sharp faculties have thin afflictions and deep wisdom; upon hearing once, they awaken to a thousand things. They attain...
For those of great *dhāraṇī*-capacity, he teaches the Dharma of the Great Vehicle’s perfect and sudden ultimate reality.

For those whose delusions are heavy and faculties dull, he employs skillful means to teach the Four Noble Truths or Dependent Origination, or he teaches the dharmas of human and celestial precepts and virtues, causing them to practice and realize them.
Thus, there is no superfluous word in the Dharma, and no faculty left unaddressed in the person; it is like a skilled physician who prescribes medicine according to the illness.
Regarding the administration of medicine: the aforementioned medicines for the illnesses of sentient beings all consist of two types.

First, concerning the illnesses of ordinary beings within the six realms of existence—namely, the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*), and birth-and-death through segmented transformation (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*)—the medicine consists of the methods of practice for investigating reality and severing delusions.
If the six realms are further divided, there are distinctions between the wholesome and the unwholesome, according to the capacities of those encountered.
The teachings are likewise not the same. Second, there are two types of supramundane sages:

first, those who have the affliction of a class of *śrāvakas*, namely, the *dharmadhātu*-external dust-like afflictions (*rajas*), the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*), and the non-extinction of attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
Therefore, observing that the three realms are truly existent, they fear them as a burning house and loathe them as shackles.

To such practitioners, the Bodhisattva accordingly administers the medicine of the Dharma, teaching that the environment and its inhabitants are non-dual, and that defilement and purity share a single source.

He shows that nirvana and birth-and-death are equal to flowers in the sky, and that their very substance is the true mark (*dharmatā*). Thus, he causes them to turn away from the Small Vehicle and toward the Great, to resolve upon bodhicitta, and to practice universal [compassion].
The "Virtuous Practice" (Śubhakārin) refers to one who becomes a bodhisattva by means of being a śrāvaka. Second is the bodhisattva of the Initial Teaching (Ādikarmika-yāna).

Although for them there are no phenomena external to the mind, they must still transform defilement into purity and undergo cultivation over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; furthermore, they do not yet realize that both defilement and purity are empty.

Even "the single true suchness" is still a sickness. For such a capacity, the Bodhisattva provides the medicinal medicine of the sudden and perfect teaching, causing their single thought-moment to become empty of mind;
this is immediately named Buddhahood. It does not rely on stages or gradual realization, but leads them to the one true dharma-realm.
When their ten levels of faith reach fullness, they immediately encompass the five positions and achieve equal and right enlightenment.
Awakening. Such is the thorough penetration of seeing the opportune moment; the teaching is thus appropriate for them. Therefore, both the teacher and the taught are entirely free from doubt.
"Spreading widely" (布大) means that the Great Dharma possesses the grace of providing shelter, like clouds;
it possesses the virtue of moistening and nourishing, like rain; and it possesses the power to restore life, like nectar (*amṛta*). This is because it is the treasure of the Dharma King.
It is like a seal; because it possesses the power to crush and overturn [samsara], it is like a wheel. Because it can block and sever birth and death, it is like closing a prison.
Because it can lead one into entry upon nirvana, it is like opening a gate. Why is this so?

It is truly because sentient beings have their minds scorched by afflictions and are oppressed by birth and death, much like the intense heat of summer. If they obtain the protection of the Great Dharma, it will not allow them to be distressed.
Scorched by afflictions, they are likewise not oppressed by birth and death, just as clouds can dispel the heat.
When sentient beings do not encounter a sage and have not heard the Great Dharma, their minds lack the water of wisdom to nourish them; they are utterly parched and withered.

Upon hearing the Great Dharma for the first time, it can nourish the ground of the mind, causing the seeds of wisdom to sprout, just as rain nourishes the fields. Sentient beings, while [still] un-...
If one hears the True Dharma, one may act according to one's own whims and thereby injure the Dharma-body and shorten the life of wisdom.
Conversely, if one hears the True Dharma, it causes the Dharma-body to abide eternally and prevents the life of wisdom from being cut short; it is like the sprinkling of nectar upon the mind.

From the eighth stage onward, Bodhisattvas follow the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*), flowing spontaneously into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience); therefore, it is said that they do not...

[The practitioner] may regress. Yet, taking this Dharma once more, they transmit it to others. If people obtain it, they can crush and grind away afflictions and karma, transporting themselves into Bodhi like the operation of a chariot wheel.
Sentient beings who have not heard the True Dharma do not know that their own minds are the Buddha, nor do they know that all phenomena are suchness (tathatā).
Upon hearing the True Dharma for the first time, they are then able to establish a definitive seal [of realization].
All sentient beings shall all become Buddhas. All phenomena (dharmas) should be understood as their true reality, just as one gains confidence from the impression of a seal.
Sentient beings are entangled by birth and death, like those within a prison.

If they hear the True Dharma and practice in accordance with it, they will block off the causes of birth and never create them again, just as one who has closed a prison cannot re-enter. This is the nature...
Pure nirvana is inherently possessed within one's own mind; because of delusion, it is not realized—how could it otherwise be entered?

Upon hearing the True Dharma but once, one immediately turns from the false back to the true, entering directly and transcending all at once, like opening a door and stepping into a room. The above are various metaphors.
Although a bodhisattva possesses supreme virtues, if they are not sustained by great vows, even if they are able to deliver sentient beings, they cannot do so for long.
Because he has made great aspirational vows, he shall deliver all living beings until the end of the future.
The above concludes the separate praise of the adornment of his myriad virtues. △ Third, the concluding praise that he will soon attain Buddhahood.
These bodhisattvas shall, before long, attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Anuttara" and so forth means "Unsurpassed Perfectly Equal and Right Enlightenment," which is the complete virtue of the fruit of Buddhahood.
Since they have already been praised as having no merit incomplete and no virtue unprepared, they are those whose rank is adjacent to Great Enlightenment.
The conclusion states: "Before long, they shall attain [enlightenment]," and so forth. △ Fourth, the enumeration of names:

Their names are Bodhisattva Vimala, Bodhisattva Maitreya, Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda, Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti, Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and King Vajragarbha.
Bodhisattvas: Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha-rāja, Bodhisattva Gaganagañja-rāja, Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīśvararāja, Bodhisattva Samādhiśvararāja, Bodhisattva Sumeru-rāja, and Bodhisattva Mahāsāgaragambhīra-rāja.
The Bodhisattva King of Sublime Eloquence, the Bodhisattva King of Exalted Joy, the Bodhisattva King of Great Supernatural Transformations, the Bodhisattva King of Sovereignty over Dharma,
the Bodhisattva King of Pure Rain, the Bodhisattva Medicine King, the Bodhisattva Superior Medicine, the Bodhisattva Healer of the Disease of Afflictions,
the Bodhisattva Jewel Mountain, the Bodhisattva Jewel Wealth, the Bodhisattva Superior Jewel, and the Bodhisattva Jewel Virtue.
Bodhisattva Ratnagarbha, Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa, Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta,
Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha, Bodhisattva Ratnadatta, Bodhisattva Ratnadhvaja, Bodhisattva Mahāratnadhvaja,
Bodhisattva Ratnavarṣa, Bodhisattva Ratnagati, Bodhisattva Ratnadaṇḍa, Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin, Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī, and Bodhisattva Ratneśvara.
Candana-gandha Bodhisattva, Mahā-ratna-ulkā Bodhisattva, Mahā-ratna-vyūha Bodhisattva, Sūryaprabha Bodhisattva, Candraprabha Bodhisattva,
Jyotiṣprabha Bodhisattva, Tejaprabha Bodhisattva, Vidyutprabha Bodhisattva, and Smṛtimatī-prajñā Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Destroyer of Māra, the Bodhisattva Conqueror of Māra, the Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent, the Bodhisattva Unceasing, the Bodhisattva of Uninterrupted Great Vows,
the Bodhisattva of Great Renown, the Bodhisattva of Unimpeded Eloquence, and the Bodhisattva of Unimpeded Turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
Regarding the sacred names of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, there is a debate among the ancient masters as to whether they should be explained or not.

Some maintain that because a Buddha possesses ten thousand virtues, they cannot be fully exhausted by a single word; fearing that one might fail to encompass the totality of these virtues, they do not provide an explanation.

Others say that although he possesses ten thousand virtues, one may still explain the meaning based on the name, for citing a single instance can encompass the rest—just as with the benevolence of Yao, the virtue of Shun, and the [wisdom of] Yu.
Jian was frugal while Tang was magnanimous. How could it be that Yao alone was benevolent but lacked virtue, or that Shun alone possessed virtue but lacked benevolence?
The virtue of the sages is such that by citing one particular strength, all virtues are understood to be fully present; this is how the matter is resolved. Now, I follow the latter interpretation.
Nevertheless, I do not dare to provide an extensive explanation, fearing that later worthies might grow weary of prolixity; therefore, I have explained it briefly. As for "Vimalakīrti" (Wugou):

he takes afflictions (*kleśa*) as his defilement. While they pollute the Buddha-nature, now that his rank is adjacent to Great Enlightenment and the five stages of dwelling are nearly exhausted, he is thus named "Stainless.
As for "Maitreya": this is translated as "The Kindly One" (*Maitrī*). His kindness flourishes in the present world, and his compassion reaches its fulfillment.
Because it refers to a future kalpa. ○ As for "Lion’s Roar" (Siṃhanāda), it is so called because his preaching of the Dharma is fearless, like the roar of a lion.
○ As for "Mañjuśrī," this is a transliteration of the name of Mañjuśrī; it refers to the time when the Bodhisattva manifested his birth.
There were ten kinds of auspicious omens: first, light filled the chamber; second, sweet nectar overflowed the courtyard; third, the earth gushed forth the seven treasures;
fourth, spirits opened the precious treasuries; fifth, roosters gave birth to phoenix chicks; sixth, sows brought forth dragon piglets;
seventh, mares produced qilin; eighth, oxen gave birth to white-zhai; ninth, granaries transformed into golden millet; tenth, elephants possessed six tusks. These were the ten kinds.
His auspicious signs are all unfathomable; therefore, he is called the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. ○ Vimalakīrti was a transformation of the Tathāgata Suvarṇapuṣpa into the body of a layman.
This is translated as "Pure Name" (Vimala-kīrti), meaning that while dwelling amidst the dust [of the world], he remains unstained, taking "purity" as his name.
His supernormal powers and eloquence are both unfathomable. During the assembly of the Vaipulya sūtras, he once rebuked the provisional teachings.
Because they are minor. ○ Regarding Avalokiteśvara: this means observing the sounds and voices of the world;

seeking out cries to save beings from suffering, manifesting bodies to preach the Dharma, acting without partiality and universally pervading all—therefore, he is called "Sovereign" (Īśvara). ○ Mahāsthāmaprāpta refers to Mahāsthāmaprāpta (Great Power Attained).
This means that when the Bodhisattva moves or acts, the great earth trembles and shakes, awakening the minds of the multitudes and causing the Māra King to feel dread.
Regarding "Vajragarbha-rāja" (King Vajragarbha): it refers to the accumulated store of the realized qualities of nature, which is like a treasury; the nature itself is firm and sharp.
He is like a vajra. The essence and function of a vajra are such that it is both firm and sharp.
Being firm, no object can destroy it; this is like the essence of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*). Being sharp, it can destroy all things; this is like the function of inherent virtue.

Generally speaking, its essence is eternally abiding, while its function is able to subdue demons. Because its essence and function are sovereign, he is honored as a King. As for the King Kṣitigarbha:
All phenomena in the world arise from the earth; the earth is a treasury of jewels. This serves as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva’s vows, which are vast and profound;

all merits arise from these vows, and the vow itself is like a treasury. Because this is the name derived from the analogy between the phenomenon and its metaphor, he is called Kṣitigarbha (Earth Treasury).
He presides over the dark realms of the netherworld and acts with sovereign mastery according to his vows; therefore, he is honored as a King. ○ As for the King of Ākāśagarbha (Space Treasury):
This also employs a metaphor to clarify the name. All the myriad phenomena (*dharma*) of the world are encompassed by empty space;

empty space is the treasury. Empty space is a metaphor for the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena). This means that the *dharmatā* is all-pervasive, vast, profound, and inclusive; thus, the *dharmatā* itself is the treasury.
Because one is free to take or reject [phenomena] within it, it is honored as the King. Regarding the "King of Sovereignty over *Dhāraṇī*": *Dhāraṇī* is a Sanskrit term. [...]
*Ni* (尼): This is translated as "Total Retention" (*dhāraṇī*). Because the mind encompasses all phenomena and is able to sustain all phenomena, it is sovereign as a king.
*Samādhi-vaśavartirāja* (三昧自在王): *Samādhi* in Sanskrit is translated here as "Right Concentration.
It means that without departing from right concentration, one manifests all dignified postures; therefore, it is sovereign as a king. *Merurāja* (妙高山王): This is also borrowed [from the Sanskrit].
This is an illustration by way of metaphor. In the Sanskrit language it is called *Sumeru*; here it is translated as "Sublime High Peak. A peak is a mountain.
It is composed of the four precious substances and sits firmly within the great ocean, rising higher than all other mountains to serve as the king among them.
The path realized by the Bodhisattva is likewise: wondrously luminous, supreme, and unsurpassed by any of the multitude of sages; he reigns as a sovereign with mastery. ○ The Great Ocean.
Regarding the "Profound King" (Shenwang): the former stage has a Way as lofty as a mountain; this stage has a Way as deep as the ocean.

Furthermore, the metaphor of the mountain specifically clarifies the aspect of Principle (li), while this metaphor of the ocean specifically reveals the aspect of Wisdom (zhi)—namely, the two wisdoms of Expedient Means (quan) and Reality (shi).

He is honored as King because he brings about the freedom and benefit of both [self and others]. ○ Regarding "King Adorned with Sublime Eloquence" (*Suvicitravāgīśvara*): "Eloquence" refers to verbal skill; "sublime" refers to the profound and mysterious.
By employing brilliant eloquence, he manifests provisional teachings that accord with reality. Through the merit of preaching the Dharma, he adorns his own nature (*svabhāva*).
Because he possesses mastery over the provisional and the real, he is honored as King. ○ Regarding "King of Exalted Joy": this refers to the path realized within oneself.

Gao (High). He delighted in preaching for others, benefiting both himself and others. Because he was most honored and supreme, he was made King. ○ Da Shenbian Wang (King of Great Supernatural Transformations).
He skillfully employed supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), his transformations were unfathomable, and he subdued demons and heretics with effortless ease;
therefore, he was honored as King. ○ Fazizai Wang (King of Dharma-Sovereignty). Regarding the Dharma he had realized himself, he explained it to others; the provisional and the real were non-dual.

The principle and phenomena are interfused; sovereign and autonomous, he acts as the King. ○ Regarding the "Pure Rain King": the path of self-realization is vast and free from even the slightest speck of dust, hence it is called "pure.
In delivering sentient beings and preaching the Dharma, he moistens and nourishes all living things, and is thus metaphorically likened to rain.

The virtue of benefiting sentient beings is honored as kingship. ○ As for the Medicine King (Bhaiṣajyarāja): in his causal stage, he was a skilled physician who treated the physical illnesses of people;
in his resultant stage, he is the Dharma that responds to capacities to treat the mental illnesses of people. Because the entire world rejoices, he is honored as the Medicine King.

○ As for the Superior Medicine (Bhaiṣajyasamudgata): he and the former position were brothers during their causal stage; [the one] practiced the medicine of phenomena (dharma-bhaiṣajya), while [the other] practiced the medicine of principle (li-bhaiṣajya).
The Venerable Elder has ascended the Path; therefore, he is called Bhaiṣajyarāja (Medicine King). ○ Regarding "healing the disease of afflictions":

the afflictions of sentient beings are like a disease, and the Dharma-medicine of the Bodhisattva can heal it. Because it can cure the disease of the mind, this name was given. ○ As for "the Jewel Mountain":

Jewels emerge from within the mountain; thus it is called a "Jewel Mountain. The mountain is a metaphor for the *dharmakāya*, and the jewels are a metaphor for the qualities of intrinsic nature (*prakṛtiguṇa*).

Since the *dharmakāya* contains these qualities, just as a mountain produces jewels, it is given this name. "Jewel Wealth" (*Ratnadhana*) refers to the true treasure of the wealth of the Dharma; "Direct Realization" (*Sākṣātkriyā*) is its designation.
"Jewel Supreme" (*Ratnottama*) means that among all treasures, the Jewel of the Dharma is supreme. Since the Bodhisattva has realized this, [it is so named].
These are taken as names. ○ *Ratnaguṇa* (Jewel Virtue) refers to the multitude of virtues realized; they are honored as jewels.

○ *Ratnagarbha* (Jewel Treasury) refers to the great treasure of the Dharma King, accumulated like a storehouse. ○ *Ratnakūṭa* (Jewel Accumulation) refers to the accumulation of all Dharma-jewels, applied without fail.
○ *Ratnapāṇi* (Jewel Hand) refers to one whose hands produce precious jewels to relieve the poor. ○ *Ratnamudrāpāṇi* (Jewel-Seal Hand) refers to the hand... [text continues]
Holding the jewel-seal, he wields the authority of the world; holding the Dharma-seal in his mind, he wields the authority of the Dharma-King.

The "Jewel Light" refers to the Bodhisattva emitting light to gather and sustain sentient beings; the entire world receives his grace, and because they hold him in high esteem, he is regarded as a treasure.

The "Jewel Giving" refers to bestowing the Dharma-treasure upon others with a public-spirited heart, without stinginess. The "Jewel Banner" refers to erecting the Dharma like a banner, held in supreme honor.

It is a treasure. Because it subdues the heterodox and manifests the orthodox, it is given this name. ○ As for the "Great Treasure Banner," it subdues the heterodox and manifests the orthodox throughout all places.
○ As for the "Treasure Rain," the Dharma that is taught moistens the minds of sentient beings, causing the seeds of wisdom and the sprouts of insight to emerge from this point onward;
therefore, it is named the "Treasure Rain. ○ As for "Treasure-Penetration," it is the true wisdom that illuminates itself, penetrating one's own nature.
It is a treasure. Expedient wisdom illuminates others; penetrating their capacities is a treasure. ○ As for the "precious staff," it supports the Dharma-gate just as a staff props up an object.
It strikes and rouses sentient beings, bringing life forth from death. Wisdom and spiritual powers are likened to this precious staff.

Regarding "Jewel-Crest" (Ratnaśikhin): The uṣṇīṣa on the Tathāgata’s crown is the "jewel" due to its supreme secrecy; the marks and signs of a Bodhisattva are similar to those of a Buddha. Regarding "Jewel-Auspiciousness" (Ratnaśrī): Among all auspicious things, peace and happiness are supreme. Through the Bodhisattva’s wisdom and supernormal powers, the Dharma-realm is protected and sustained; thus, there are no three calamities in the land and no eight difficulties for the people, taking peace and happiness as the jewel. As for "That which exists": one attains the Great Dharma Jewel; whatever one directs toward is as one wishes, taking sovereignty as the treasure.
○ As for "Sandalwood Incense": when this incense is applied to the body, neither water nor fire can harm it. When a Bodhisattva exercises their spiritual power, they protect sentient beings;
thus, the afflictions of birth and death cannot cause them any harm. ○ As for "The Great Jewel Torch": using wisdom to shatter delusion is like holding up a torch to dispel darkness.
Darkness. ○ "Great Jewel Adornment" refers to the Dharma-jewel of the Mahāyāna, which adorns the Dharmakāya.

○ "Sunlight and Moonlight" means that as the sun and moon spread their radiance, heaven and earth shine brightly; so too does the true light of Prajñā illuminate both the ultimate and conventional truths simultaneously.
○ "Starlight" means that the constellations are arrayed across the void and silver light dots the emerald green; when myriad virtues gather within the mind, Prajñā increases its brilliance. ○
Regarding the light of fire: fire is able to emit radiance, transforming darkness into clarity; the mind is able to emit radiance, transforming consciousness into wisdom.

Regarding the light of lightning: lightning is the swiftest, followed immediately by the crash of thunder; the light of wisdom illuminates the capacities [of beings], and spiritual powers manifest accordingly.
Regarding the wisdom of mindfulness: the karmic suffering of sentient beings is what the Bodhisattva is mindful of; the Bodhisattva’s wisdom illuminates it.
Benefiting sentient beings. ○ Regarding "destroying Māra": concentration and wisdom support one another, and the five māras are severed together. ○ Regarding "conquering Māra":

while Māra may prevail over sentient beings, causing deluded followers to fall into the pit, wisdom prevails over all māras, as one ascends high upon the shore of awakening. ○ Regarding "constant diligence":
with a focused mind free from distraction and a forward-striving mind free from weariness, one dwells perpetually in the world, transforming and benefiting humans and devas. ○
"Unceasing" means that the dual benefit of self and others never ceases. "Undying Great Vows" means that the Four Great Vows are engraved upon the heart.
"Great Renown" means that myriad virtues converge in the mind and an excellent reputation is universally acclaimed.
"Unimpeded Eloquence" means that brilliant eloquence and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge are in full bloom. "Unimpeded Turning" [of the Wheel of Dharma].

Regarding the "Dharma Wheel": it is the Bodhisattva who turns the Dharma, moving freely and without obstruction in all directions. Sentient beings obtain the Dharma, which is then transmitted and circulated from one to another.
The enumeration of names above is now complete. △ Fifth, the conclusion of the assembly.
Thus, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas such as Vimala each came accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of attendants.
This is a term used to indicate the aforementioned names; "Vimala" is the foremost among those of a similar class.
"Attendants" refers to the disciples under their guidance, the number of whom varies for each individual; hence it is said:

"Several," whether hundreds or thousands, are all indefinite in number. Because both the teacher and the disciples are present, it is called "together. This concludes the section on the assembly of Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas.

△ The third part, the division of the assemblies of the Devas, Nāgas, and the Eight Divisions, has eight sections. First, the assembly of the Devas; second, [the assembly of the Nāgas]; first, the assembly of the various Devas of the Desire Realm;
fourth, [the assembly of the Form Realm Devas]. First, indicating the number and citing the types.
Furthermore, there were hundreds of millions of devas from the six heavens of the desire realm.
"Furthermore" (fu you) means "in addition. The assembly at this Dharma gathering consisted not only of those of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas, but also included various devas and others;

their number is indicated as "hundreds of millions" (yi wan) to express their great multitude. As for the "six desires" (liu yu), it refers to the fact that there are six [heavens] situated above and below.
They are heavy with the same [defilements]: food and drink, sleep, and sexual desire; therefore, they are all called "desire" (*kāma*). As for the heavens, their nature is spontaneous intentionality:

towers, palaces, jeweled trees, and flower ponds appear according to the mind's inclinations; exquisite scenes, rare treasures, delicious foods, and celestial garments likewise manifest spontaneously following one’s will.
There are also subjects, ministers, men, and women; thus, they have not yet escaped the realm of form and desire (*rūpa-kāma*). Nevertheless, although...
They possess desire, yet it differs from that of humans. All the devas are born by transformation;

they do not enter a womb, their bodies contain no semen or blood, and they unite through spirit alone rather than through physical coupling. There are six tiers, ascending and descending, each higher level being increasingly subtle.

The Son of Heaven (the ruler) is the king. As for the six layers: first is the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*), situated halfway up Mount Sumeru, to the east, west, south, and north.
In the north, each resides on one terrace (*pada*), each presiding over two divisions of spirits and deities, and each protecting one continent.
They are situated forty-two thousand *yojanas* above the earth. ○ Second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is located at the summit of Mount Sumeru; Śakra, the Lord of Devas, dwells in its center.
The four directions—east, west, south, and north—each govern eight heavens, totaling thirty-three heavens. These are situated eighty-four thousand *yojanas* above the human realm.
Both the Four Heavenly Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*) and the Trāyastriṃśa heavens are terrestrial deities (*bhūmi-cara*).

Although they dwell upon mountain peaks or at their waists, because there is still slight obstruction below them, they are classified as terrestrial. When the desire-thoughts of these two classes of gods are stirred, men and women embrace one another. Their...
The mind then ceases; before the two organs have moved, they take mutual embracing as their desire. ○ Third is Yāma Heaven. In Sanskrit it is called Yāma;
in Chinese it means "time-period" (shífēn), also known as "Good Time" (Shànshí). This is because one experiences constant exhilaration at every moment, and it is named for its delight in goodness.
Therefore, it is called "Good Time" (*Sukhāvatī*). Because day and night are distinguished by the opening and closing of lotus flowers, it is called "Time-Portion" (*Kāmadhātu*).
The gods of this heaven dwell supported by the void; when a desire arises, they merely hold hands as man and woman and their passion subsides. ○ Fourth is the Tuṣita Heaven.

This is also a Sanskrit term; in the language of China, it means "Contentment. Because they know how to find satisfaction regarding the objects of the five desires—namely, form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch—they are called so.
These devas also dwell supported by space. If a desire arises, their laughter as man and woman ceases immediately.
○ Fifth is the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*). This is because they take pleasure by themselves emanating the five sensory objects of desire. They also dwell supported by space.

Dwelling. ○ Sixth, the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*). This refers to those who accomplish their own pleasure by means of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) emanated by others.

They also dwell supported by space. Some say this is the Heaven of the Māra King. Regarding these two heavens above, if a desire-thought moves, it is merely stilled by the mutual gazing of men and women.
As the verse says: "In the Four Kings and Trāyastriṃśa heavens, they embrace; in Yāma, they hold hands; in Tuṣita, they smile; in Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin, they gaze at one another."
Behold! These are the six divine pleasures of desire). △ Second, the names are listed in order. Their names are:

the Son of Heaven Virtuously Abiding (Śubhavyūha), the Son of Heaven Majestic Virtue (Tejodhipati), the Son of Heaven Universal Radiance (Samantaprabha), and the Son of Heaven Pure Wisdom (Vimalamati).
The auspicious devaputra, the Great Auspicious devaputra, the Sovereign devaputra, the Great Sovereign devaputra,
the Sunlight devaputra, the Moonlight devaputra— such devaputras as these, with Śakra Devānām Indra as their leader.

"Skilfully Abiding" (Susthitamati) means abiding in and upholding the wholesome path; he is fit to be a son of heaven. "Majestic Virtue" (Vīryadeva) refers to a majestic and dignified appearance, with a transformative virtue that excels all others.
"Universal Radiance" (Samantaprabha) refers to the light of his body shining everywhere. "Pure Wisdom" (Viśuddhamati): because the faculty of wisdom is unstained, it is called "pure.
"Auspiciousness" (Śrī) and "Great Auspiciousness" (Mahāśrī) refer to the manifestations of the Bodhisattvas. "Wholesome" (Kuśala).
Teaching the Dharma to others is the most auspicious of all things. Regarding "Sovereign" and "Mahāśvara":

Sovereign refers to the King of the Heaven of Delight in Transformations (*Nirmāṇarati-deva-rāja*); Mahāśvara refers to the King of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin-deva-rāja*).

As kings of these heavens, they possess sovereignty over everything according to their every wish. Regarding "Sunlight" and "Moonlight": the sun and moon adorn the heavens, causing heaven and earth to shine with brilliance.
They are able to dispel darkness and bestow grace upon the world. Such devaputras as these refer collectively to those mentioned above.
Śakra-devānām-indra (meaning "the Able One," because he is able to act as the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven) is none other than Śakra. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"In the past, there was a Brahmin of the Kauśika clan who, together with thirty-two close friends, jointly cultivated merit and virtue. When his life came to an end..."
They all dwell upon the summit of Mount Sumeru. Kauśika serves as the Lord of Devas, named Śakra Devendra.
Thirty-two beings serve as his ministers, residing in a surrounding array, while Śakra alone occupies the center. Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states:
"In the past, after the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a woman who resolved to build a stūpa; as a result of this merit, she was reborn as the Lord of Devas."
There are thirty-two beings who assist in his cultivation; as a reward, they become his ministers. When the sovereign and his ministers are combined, there are thirty-three.
The one who serves as the leader is the one who governs and oversees all the devas. If one were to discuss those situated above him, there are further celestial kings dwelling in the void;
