yet Śakra is necessarily made the foremost because, whenever the Buddhas appear in the world, it is only the Brahma Kings and Śakra [who receive their teachings].

Explanation: Because Śakra made offerings of incense and flowers and requested the Buddha to preach the Dharma, whenever the Buddha preaches the Dharma, Brahmā King is on the left and Śakra is on the right.
Having merit in requesting the Dharma, he is thus the foremost. △ Third, manifesting his origin and extolling his virtues.
May they all take joy in the wondrous Dharma of the Mahāyāna, vow to serve and attend upon the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, enter the inconceivable secret realm,
and adorn the assemblies and sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas.

"Manifesting in all forms below" refers to manifesting in the body of a celestial king (*devendra*) while practicing the Bodhisattva path. The "wondrous Dharma of the Mahāyāna" is the heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of all Buddhas.
Since it is said that one "loves and delights" in it, this is the *bodhicitta*. Regarding the two characters "follow" (*sui*) and "accord" (*zhan*), they signify mastery;

they refer to assisting the Buddha in propagating his transformation [of beings]. As for "following the affairs of the Tathāgatas of the three periods," this necessarily involves traversing through past and present, and further includes the future.
"Come. This clarifies the inconceivability of external protection. "Entering" refers to the inconceivability of the internal resonance (*samaya*).
As for "secret," it is not spoken at the wrong time and is not transmitted to those who lack the capacity. As for "realm" (*viṣaya*), it is another name for *tathatā* (suchness).
One must have the wisdom and principle merged in profound harmony before one can be said to "enter"; this is the merit of realizing what the Buddha has realized. It adorns the Path.
The "site" (the place) serves to further manifest the great protection.

Just as in the present-day Dharma assemblies, a monastic who has seen the Way constitutes the adornment of the Dharma community, so too within the assemblies of the Buddhas, the presence of the holy multitudes as assistants constitutes the adornment of the Buddha’s assembly.
This interpretation is entirely based on those who manifest through great skillful means (*mahopāya*). Furthermore, there is another interpretation: [it refers to] those who delight in the Great...
The "Dharma" refers to the initial arousal of the bodhicitta. "Wishing to follow and serve the Buddha" means studying the Buddha’s path and teachings.

"Necessarily passing through the three periods of existence" means that one's great vows are inexhaustible. "Entering the realm of the Buddha" means attaining the fruit through the fulfillment of causes.

"Adorning the site of enlightenment" means expressing gratitude and assisting in the transformation of beings. This explanation is spoken for those of sharp faculties who practice according to the reality [of the teaching]. Indeed...
These two interpretations each have their own basis. Considering the two characters "three" (tri) and "time" (kāla), the former interpretation is highly comprehensive;
considering the two characters "craving" (tṛṣṇā) and "delight" (rati), the latter interpretation is also consistent. △ Fourth, the conclusion that clarifies the celestial hosts.
Each was accompanied by several hundred thousand retinues.
△ Second, the assembly of devas from the form realm (rūpadhātu), in four parts. First, indicating the number and citing the types:
Furthermore, there were color-realm (*rūpadhātu*) sons of gods as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.

Regarding the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*): "form" refers to material substance, because it possesses physical bodies. This means that although one is free from the foul and corrupt forms of the desire realm, there still exist pure forms.
Beginning with the Brahmā heavens of the first *dhyāna* and ending with the Akaniṣṭha heaven, there are altogether eighteen heavens.
In all of them, there are no women and no defilement of desire; therefore, they are called "Brahmā heavens."
"Brahma" (brahman) means purity. It refers to being without food or drink, without sleep, and without sexual desire;

all are born by transformation (*upapāduka*). Because they still possess material form (*rūpa*), it is called "Form" (*rūpa*). "Realm" (*dhātu*) means limitation and distinction; it refers to the boundaries of the three realms, as each is distinct and different from the others.

(The eighteen heavens are: the Heaven of the Brahma Assembly, the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā, the Heaven of Great Brahmā, the Heaven of Limited Light, the Heaven of Immeasurable Light, the Heaven of Radiant Sound, the Heaven of Limited Purity, the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity, and the Heaven of Pervasive...)

The Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) Heavens, the Puṇyaprasava (Merit-Born) Heavens, the Puṇyaprasādaka (Merit-Loved) Heavens, the Bṛhatphala (Vast Fruit) Heavens, and the Asaṃjñisattva (Non-Perceiving) Heavens—these thirteen heavens belong to the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

From the Abṛha (No Affliction) Heavens, the Atapa (No Heat) Heavens, the Sudarśana (Good Vision) Heavens, the Sudṛśa (Good Appearance) Heavens, and the Akaniṣṭha (Ultimate Form) Heavens—these five are where the noble stream-enterers (*ārya-srotāpanna*) who are *anāgāmins* (non-returners) reside. Together there are eighteen, which are also called the Dhyāna Heavens, because they cultivate contaminated meditative concentration (*sāsrava-dhyāna*).

Regarding "Ganges sands": this river is forty li in width, and its sand is as fine as flour. To calculate vast quantities, one uses sand as a standard; one grain of sand corresponds to one heaven. In total...
This means they were as numerous as the sands [of the Ganges]. The explanation of the *devaputra*s is the same as before. △ Second, the names are listed in order.

Their names are: the *devaputra* Universal Radiance, the *devaputra* Stainless Adornment, the *devaputra* Sporting in Supernormal Powers, the *devaputra* Sovereign in Samādhi, the *devaputra* Sovereign in Dhāraṇī, and the *devaputra* Mahānārāyaṇa.
The celestial son Pūrṇapraṇidhāna, the celestial son Apratihatapratibhāna, the celestial son Śrīpuṇyajñāna,
the celestial son Nityamahāpraṇidhānapravartaka, and other such celestial sons, with the Great Brahmā King Mahābrahmā as their leader.

Regarding the phrase "The Great Light Shining Universally": based on the section praising his virtues, since it states that he has realized the Buddha’s secrets and has attained non-retrogression toward Bodhi, he is a Bodhisattva of great expedient means (*mahopāya*) who manifests in the body of a celestial king to gather and transform those of a similar kind.
Being a Bodhisattva, his bodily light shines universally, causing all who touch it to attain supreme benefit. ○ *Vimala* (Stainless).
Regarding "adornment": from the perspective of its manifestation, because one has already departed from the defilement of desire, it is called "stainless"; thus, purity serves as the adornment.

From the perspective of its fundamental nature, departing from tainted afflictions (*āsrava*) constitutes being "stainless," while attaining untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) constitutes the adornment.
Regarding "sporting with supernormal powers" (*abhijñā-vikrīḍita*): manifesting the body of a celestial king is likewise the sporting of samādhi. 3. [End of section]
Mastery over Samādhi: *Samādhi* means "right concentration. In terms of its outward manifestation, it refers to contaminated (*sāsrava*) meditative absorption;
in terms of its fundamental nature, it refers to uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) meditative absorption.

Because one possesses mastery over this concentration, it is so named. Mastery over Dhāraṇī: Having attained total retention (*dhāraṇī*), one thereby possesses mastery. Great Nārāyaṇa: *Nā...* [text fragment]

Rāyaṇa, the celestial Malla, is said to possess the greatest divine power among the devas; endowed with great supernormal powers (*mahā-ṛddhibala*), he subdues all māras and gathers in all classes of beings.
Regarding the "fulfillment of supreme vows": the supreme vow consists solely in attaining Buddhahood and delivering sentient beings.

Because the practice and the vow must mutually support one another, they attain fulfillment. Regarding "unimpeded eloquence" (*anāvaraṇa-pratibhāna*): it clarifies that eloquence is brilliant and flowery, and [it] explains...

Unimpeded in the Dharma. ○ Regarding "Auspicious Virtue and Wisdom": it refers to the merit of both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) realms, as well as the wisdom that benefits both oneself and others;
because these are the most auspicious. ○ Regarding "Constantly Making Great Vows": it means desiring to realize Bodhi, with vows that never cease.
○ From "In this way" onwards, the ten names mentioned above are summarized; "etc. indicates their innumerability. [This is] the Great Brahmā King of Radiance.

Regarding those who are designated as "foremost," there are ten names; it cannot be definitively determined which heaven they belong to, as there are no explicit textual passages in the sutras to clarify this.
However, as for this Great Brahmā King (*Mahābrahman*), although there is likewise no explicit textual passage, he is certainly of the First Dhyāna.

This is because he possesses *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) internally, and speech externally, thereby enabling him to preside over and govern all the devas; thus, he serves as the foremost. △ Three.

Manifesting his original vows and extolling his virtues, he was fully endowed with samādhi, supernormal powers, and the eloquence of joyful exposition; he had served all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
When he sat upon the Vajrāsana beneath the Bodhi tree, defeated the hosts of Māra, and realized awakening, [the Bodhisattvas] went everywhere to the assemblies and, at the very outset,
exhorted the Tathāgata to turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma, to open the gate of the ambrosia, and to deliver the multitudes of devas and humans.
He has thoroughly realized the secret intentions of all Buddhas and shall no longer regress from great bodhi.
"Spirit" (shen) refers to the celestial mind; "penetration" (tong) constitutes the life of wisdom. Emerging from samādhi, he is sovereign and unimpeded.

By means of his skillful eloquence in discourse, it is evident that he never tires of instructing others. Thus, throughout his service to various Buddhas, he possesses the capacity to assist in their transformative teachings.
This is virtue. Regarding "throughout the three periods" and below: this means that one has experienced more than a single lifetime and served more than a single Buddha.

Since it speaks of passing through the three periods, it necessarily implies a horizontal pervasiveness throughout the ten directions. Whenever a Buddha attains enlightenment, he invariably desires to request the Dharma. *Bodhi* in Sanskrit is translated here as "the Way of Awakening";
this is the title for the fruit of Buddhahood. It is not the tree itself that is *bodhi*; rather, it is because the Buddha attained enlightenment beneath the tree [that it is so named].
The Bodhi-path is named after that which is realized; thus it is called the Bodhi-tree. "Vajra" refers to the hardness of the five metals; it is a name for a jewel.
Its shape is like that of buckwheat, its color is like purple-gold, and it is most firm and sharp.
Regarding "sitting upon the Vajra-seat": the Vajra is not the seat itself, but rather the seat upon which the Buddha sits is metaphorically likened to a Vajra, such that Māras cannot delude him.
As firm as a vajra, it can shatter the armies of Māra; as sharp as a vajra, it is an inevitable principle that one must destroy Māra before attaining the Way.
There are many kinds of Māras, all of whom can harm the Way and cause the mind to be unsettled;
these are all the works of Māra, such as the afflictions of the five abodes, the two types of birth-and-death, and the various māras of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*).
The Bodhisattva shatters them; ignorance is about to be exhausted, and the state of conditioned transformation is about to be left behind.

At this, the celestial Māra becomes terrified and, leading his hosts of demons, comes specifically to cause disturbance and harm. He may manifest the body of a beautiful woman or employ awesome supernatural powers, employing hundreds of schemes and thousands of methods in an attempt to destroy the Bodhisattva’s meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
However, by means of the power of the diamond-like concentration (*vajrasamādhi*), the Māra cannot cause any harm; he flees in retreat.

"Depart! This is called the destruction of Māra. Once the hosts of Māra have been destroyed, one attains correspondence with the One Thought (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta*) and immediately enters wondrous enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) to become a Buddha.

Therefore, it is said: "Having already destroyed the army of Māra, at the time of realizing Bodhi... The passage from "pervadingly reaching down to" below is a formal eulogy of the virtue of requesting the Dharma.
"Assembly" (*sabhā*) refers to the gathering of host and guest. "Great assembly" (*mahāsabhā*) does not refer merely to a single time or place;
it refers to assemblies throughout the three periods of time and assemblies throughout the ten directions. Whenever all Buddhas attain enlightenment, these various devas [are present].

Relying on samādhi and employing supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), they arrive everywhere at once; that is to say, by dividing their forms and dispersing their shadows, they are present in all places and manifest at all times.
Therefore, it is said that they "arrive everywhere at the assemblies. Regarding the phrase "all [the Buddhas] below":

when the various Buddhas attain enlightenment, if they were only able to benefit themselves and did not rely upon preaching the Dharma, how could they benefit others? Thus, as soon as they have attained perfect awakening, they must be exhorted and requested [to teach].
This refers to the preaching of the Dharma. However, the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is like the turning of a wheel, which has two meanings: first, the sense of crushing and grinding;
second, the sense of transporting and carrying. Wherever a wheel turns, all shards and debris are shattered, and it is also able to transport various objects from here to there.
This serves as a metaphor for the Buddhas’ preaching of the Dharma, which enters into the minds of sentient beings and crushes [their afflictions].

It grinds away afflictions and karma, transporting one to Bodhi; therefore, it is called "turning the wondrous Wheel of Dharma. "Opening the gate to the sweet and descending" means that the Tathāgata’s wondrous Dharma is like nectar (*amṛta*).
The term "gate" has the sense of a passage, serving as a metaphor for the Buddha’s teachings. The Buddha preaches the Dharma for the sake of humanity.
It is like opening a door. If a person enters according to the teaching, they will receive the sprinkling of ambrosia upon their mind;

thus, delusions can be shattered, obstacles removed, and one may transcend birth and death. Therefore, it is said that "he delivers the multitudes of humans and devas. Regarding the phrase "skillfully awakening," etc., this praises the attainment of the Buddha-mind-dharma.
There are three kinds of secrecy: namely, body, speech, and mind. As for the secrecy of the body: the Tathāgata’s single... [text fragment ends]

The body does not change; it appears differently according to the perceptions of sentient beings—sometimes large, sometimes small; sometimes good, sometimes evil; sometimes compassionate, sometimes majestic;
sometimes superior, sometimes inferior—all of which are inconceivable. Therefore, it is called the "secret of the body. As for the "secret of speech":
A single sound is uttered, yet it differs according to the capacities of beings: some hear the precepts and virtues, some hear the Truths and conditions, and some hear the Six Perfections;
all are inconceivable. Therefore, it is called the "Secret of Speech. As for the "Secret of Mind," it refers to the observation of capacities and the thorough examination of all modes of guidance;

these are known only by the Buddha himself, while others cannot fathom them. Therefore, it is called the "Secret of Mind. Furthermore, as for the "Intent": (Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "意趣者。復", which translates to "As for the Intent: Furthermore...")
This reveals the subtle and profound essence of the secret teachings. Since he is thus able to awaken skillfully, he has attained the heart-dharma of all Buddhas;
for this reason, he shall never again regress from Great Bodhi. Judging by these praises of his virtue, he is indeed a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body.

Manifesting in the body of a celestial king, he practices the bodhisattva path to assist the Buddha and propagate his transformation. (There are three kinds of non-retrogression: first, non-retrogression of stage; second, non-retrogression of practice.)

Third is the non-retrogression of mindfulness (*smṛti*). The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra clarifies that at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), one attains the Tathāgata’s single body and infinite bodies, possessing the three types of non-retrogression. If these are explained by mapping them onto the sequential stages, then the seventh level of faith is called the non-retrogression of position; from the eighth level of faith onward is called the non-retrogression of practice;

and from the first stage onward is called the non-retrogression of mindfulness. Furthermore, entering emptiness is called the non-retrogression of position; entering the provisional is called the non-retrogression of practice; and entering the Middle Way is called the non-retrogression of mindfulness. In the first stage of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), one partially possesses the three virtues (*tridharma*).

These are called the three non-regressions: Prajñā is the non-regression of stage, because it is free from the two types of death; Liberation is the non-regression of practice, because all practices are complete; and the Dharma-body is the non-regression of mindfulness, because it realizes the true mark.
(These descriptions are all praises of the virtues of the Bodhisattvas. △ Fourth, the conclusion that reveals the assembly of those with form.
Each was accompanied by several hundred thousand retinues.
△ Second, the assembly of nāgas, in three parts. First, indicating the number and citing the class:
Furthermore, there were forty-eight thousand great nāga kings.

In the Sanskrit language, this is *nāga*; here it is translated as "dragon. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The dragon is the sovereign among scaly creatures. It can become hidden or manifest; it can become large or small.
At the spring equinox it ascends to heaven; at the autumn equinox it enters the earth. That which has scales is called a *jiaolong*;
that which has wings is called an *yinglong*; that which has horns is called a *qiulong*; that which lacks horns is called a *chilong*. Before ascending to heaven..."

It is said: "The Coiled Dragon. Generally speaking, these are all entities of divine spirit. As for the term "Dragon King" used here, it refers to the king among dragons, who governs and oversees the multitude of dragons.
All sutras state that they are able to protect the Buddha-dharma and serve as benevolent deities;
therefore, whenever the Buddha preaches the Dharma, there are always assemblies of dragon beings. △ Second, the sequential listing of names.
The Nāga King Mānasa; the Nāga King Takṣaka; the Nāga King Nanda; the Nāga King Upananda; the Nāga King of Lake Anavatapta;
the Nāga King Mahāsuvarṇamukha; the Nāga King Maṇiratna; the Nāga King Varṣa-sudhana-ratna;
the Nāga King Nitya-madhusrava; the Nāga King Mahātejas; and the Nāga King Balavaśitva.

Such nāga kings as these, with Sāgara Nāgarāja as their leader—Mānasī (translated here as "Great Body" or "Great Power")—when the asuras pushed back the ocean waters to submerge the city of Sudarśana, this dragon coiled its body to stem the tide;
therefore, it is called "Great Body. ○ Takṣaka (translated here as) ...
Manifesting poison; also called "Many-Tongued. ○ Nanda and Upananda were two brothers who were nāgas.

Nanda means "Joy" in this language, and Upananda means "Good. They constantly protected the country of Magadha; the wind did not rustle the branches, the rain did not break the clods of earth, and the rains fell in due season.
Thus, there were no years of famine in the kingdom. Therefore, King Bimbisāra held an assembly once every year.
In response, the common people heard this and were all filled with joy; from this point on, he received his name. This refers to the one subdued by Maudgalyāyana.
○ Anavatapta Lake: this is translated as "Without Affliction. The Āgama Sūtras state: "On the Snow Mountains there is a lake named Anavatapta.
Within the lake is a hall supported by five pillars where the dragon deity constantly resides. It is named after the lake upon which it relies. ○ Great...
"Golden-faced" means that his facial features are golden in color; he is named from this. "Wish-fulfilling jewel" refers to the jewel beneath his neck, which is called the *cintāmaṇi*.

"Raining down exquisite treasures" means that because the dragon possesses divine power and also a compassionate heart, out of pity for the poor and destitute, it rains down precious treasures. "Constantly pouring down sweet rain" refers to sweet rain.

Immediately, a fine rain fell in accordance with the season, so that the grain crops could reach maturity. ○ Those of great majesty and virtue possess a majesty that inspires awe and a virtue that commands respect;
their majesty subdues demons and enemies, while their virtue transforms the good and virtuous. ○ Those of powerful strength and sovereignty.

"Powerful" (*balavān*) means robust and flourishing. It is named according to its mastery resulting from the abundance of strength. The phrase "and so forth" below concludes [the list] as the leaders.
*Sāgara* is translated here as "Salt Ocean. Because the waters of this region are salty, it is named after the sea.
The leader immediately took charge of the assembly. △ Third, the praise of their virtues and the conclusion regarding the assembly:
They all cherished and delighted in the sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna; they gave rise to great vows and reverently upheld it, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of followers.
Delighting in the Great Dharma is itself the bodhicitta; furthermore, upholding it through vast vows is the practice of a bodhisattva, which is likewise inconceivable.
△ Third: The Assembly of Yakṣas. Part One: Indicating the Number and Enumerating the Types.
Furthermore, there were fifty-eight thousand yakṣas (yakṣa is erroneously called *yecha*;
this means "valiant and strong," also "violent and evil," and also "light and agile").
There are three types: first, those on the earth; second, those in the void; and third, celestial yakṣas. Earth-dwelling yakṣas possess only wealth.
Because they did not practice giving, they were unable to fly. Because the two yakṣas of the empty sky and the heavens practiced giving by offering chariots and horses, they were able to fly.
These spirits are those who practiced while harboring a murderous intent; they are like the Five Peaks and Four Rivers today who claim the title of Emperor or King.

In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there are three grades: the superior grade consists of powerful ghosts (*mahābala-piśāca*); the middle grade consists of flying yakṣas (*khecaratva-yakṣa*); and the inferior...
The *Rākṣasa* who practices the stages and levels. △ Second, the sequential listing of names:

the Yakṣa King Mahāsiṃha (Great Lion), the Yakṣa King Cakravartiprabhāsa (Light of the Turning Wheel), the Yakṣa King Sunārāyaṇa (Exquisite Nārāyaṇa), the Yakṣa King Atibhīṣaṇa (Extremely Terrifying), the Yakṣa King Padmaprabhavarṇa (Lotus Light Color), and the Yakṣa King Surucira-indriya (Exquisite Faculties).
The *kṣa* yakṣas; the yakṣas who externally protect the True Dharma; the yakṣas who make offerings to the Triple Gem;
the yakṣas who rain down various precious jewels; the Maṇibhadra yakṣas—such yakṣas as these, with the Saṃjñeya yakṣa as their leader.
The "Great Lion King": the lion symbolizes fearlessness; by his majesty he subdues all species and rules as a sovereign king.

Regarding the "Light of the Turning Wheel," there are two interpretations: either the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma, and the light arrives as it shines forth; or [the wheel-turning king's light arrives].
Alternatively, he may personally turn the Dharma and illuminate sentient beings. The former interpretation identifies him as a *yakṣa* of actual practice;
the latter identifies him as a Bodhisattva manifesting in this form. Regarding "Mānārāyaṇa": *Nārāyaṇa* refers to the celestial "Powerful One.
When this deity is further qualified as "Sublime" (*māna*), his power becomes inconceivably great. Regarding "Extremely Terrifying": this is because his physical form is manifest as fierce.
As for the name: since he is present in the Buddha’s assembly, he must be outwardly stern yet inwardly compassionate. Regarding the "Lotus Light and Color": this is a metaphorical designation.
A lotus dwells in the mud yet remains unstained; when it emerges from the water, it is fragrant and pure, thus possessing both light and color.
Although this deity is among the yakṣas, he is not affected by evil habits, just like a lotus emerging from the water whose light and color are radiant.
Loving-kindness. ○ Regarding "the exquisite faculties": this deity is called "exquisite" because the six sense-faculties are keen and sharp, and the physical form is upright and dignified.
○ Regarding "guardian of the True Dharma": one is so named for the purpose of protecting the Dharma. ○ Regarding "making offerings to the Triple Gem":
knowing the Triple Gem to be supreme, one makes offerings as an act of reverence. ○ Regarding "raining down various precious jewels": this is through the practice of compassion.
Manifesting the Name. ○ *Maṇi-prabha*: *Maṇi* means "as one wishes" (*yid-bzhin*), and *prabha* here means "extreme" (*mchog*). Thus, it means "the extreme of fulfilling wishes.

Alternatively, if one wears this jewel around the neck, whatever is sought is fulfilled as wished; or if the mind is like this jewel, that which is realized is fulfilled as wished, with no meaning left unexhausted.
Therefore, it is named after this. ○ *Saṃśīrṣa*: This is a term for which the Chinese and Sanskrit [phonetic transcriptions] have not yet been established.
Detailed [explanation] will be provided for reference later. △ Third, praising their virtues and concluding the assembly:
All were fully endowed with inconceivable light of wisdom, inconceivable torch of wisdom, inconceivable conduct of wisdom, and inconceivable accumulation of wisdom.
For the sake of sentient beings, they subdue malevolent spirits to bring them peace and happiness; they are able to extend merit and wisdom, and protect the Mahāyāna so that it shall not be severed.
Each is accompanied by several hundred thousand retinues.
Since it is said that this is inconceivable and utterly unfathomable, we know for certain that this deity has manifested in the body of a yakṣa while practicing the bodhisattva path.
His light of wisdom can illuminate the capacities of sentient beings; his torch of wisdom can shatter the darkness; his conduct of wisdom can traverse the Buddha-way;

and his accumulation of wisdom stores up both skillful means and ultimate reality. For the sake of living beings, he restrains demons and spirits, manifesting the majestic power of subjugation to bring them under control.
May peace and prosperity prevail. May the compassion of guidance and instruction be fully manifested; may the banner of the Dharma of desire be eternally established and protected;
and may the constant radiance of the Buddha-sun never cease to be seen. △ Fourth, the Gandharva assembly, in three parts: first, indicating the number and citing the class.

Furthermore, there were eighty-nine thousand gandharva kings—here called *xiāngyīn* (Fragrance-Body), also known as the spirits who soar through the air—who do not consume alcohol or meat, but sustain their bodies (*yīn*, meaning "body") solely on fragrance.
They are the deities of music who serve Śakra, tossing up the *yaṣṭi* banners; they reside in the Vajra Cave to the south of Mount Sumeru.
Abiding. O Lord of Devas, when music is performed, this deity manifests a distinct transformation upon his body and subsequently ascends to heaven.
He is also called "Fragrance-Seeker" (*Gandharva*), for when Śakra desires to perform music, he burns incense and this deity arrives seeking its fragrance.
△ Second, the names are listed in order.
The Gandharva King Jewel-Crown on the Summit; the Gandharva King Universally Radiating Light; the Gandharva King Vajra-Jewel Banner;
the Gandharva King Pure Exquisite Sound; and the Gandharva King Pervading All Assemblies.
The Gandharva King Universal Manifestation in All Directions, the Gandharva King Delighting in the Mahāyāna,
the Gandharva King Turning the Non-retrogressive Wheel, and such Gandharva Kings as these, with the Gandharva King Pure Faculties as their leader.
The jeweled crown reveals the dignity of the Honored One who adorns the head; the emission of light allows one to know the virtue of his physical marks;

the diamond-jeweled banner possesses the function of subduing demons; the pure and wondrous voice is endowed with the merit of assisting in transformation; reaching everywhere and manifesting universally.
All possess the spiritual power of resonance; they delight in the turning of the wheel [of Dharma] and are not without the excellence of benefiting others.
Their faculties are pure, like flawless fine jade; therefore, they preside over their respective divisions as supreme leaders.
△ Third, the praise of virtues and the assembly:
They all conceived deep love and reverence for the Mahāyāna; they constantly benefited and brought joy to sentient beings without ever succumbing to weariness or indolence;
each was accompanied by several hundred thousand retinues.

The first two lines reveal the profundity of his protection of the Dharma; the next two lines reveal the urgency of his protection of living beings (these spirits all possess the virtues of Bodhisattvas;
do not interpret them as being of the common run). △ Five: The Assembly of Asuras, in three parts. First, stating the number and citing the types.
Furthermore, there are ten billion asura kings;
this term is translated as "the Ugly," because while the males are hideous, the females are beautiful.

It is also translated as "Non-Gods" (asura), for although their divine retribution is most excellent, they are not gods, being ranked immediately below them. During the causal stage, they harbored a mind of suspicion and jealousy; though they practiced...

Regarding the Five Constant Virtues: because one desires to prevail over others, yet performs meritorious deeds while harboring anger, this constitutes a lower grade of goodness that brings about this retribution body.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "There are four kinds of asuras. If, within the realm of ghosts, by the power of protecting the Dharma, they ride upon supernatural powers to enter the void—these asuras are born from eggs and are categorized within the destiny of ghosts. If, within the realm of devas..."
Their virtue has declined and they have fallen. The dwelling place they have chosen is adjacent to the sun and moon.
These asuras are born from a womb and are categorized within the human realm (*manuṣya-gati*). There are asuras who uphold the world;

their power penetrates all things and they are fearless, able to contend for authority with Brahmā, Śakra Devendra, and the Four Heavenly Kings. These asuras exist through transformation and belong to the celestial realm (*deva-gati*).
They are included therein. There is another class of inferior asuras who are born in the heart of the great ocean and dwell at the mouths of underwater caverns;
they roam through the void by day and return to their watery abodes by night. These asuras exist due to moisture and are categorized within the realm of animals (tiryagyoni).
△ Second, the listing of names by order:
Rāhula, King of Asuras; Vemacitra, King of Asuras; Prabhāsa-tejas, King of Asuras;
Mahāsthāma-dṛḍha, King of Asuras; and Manojña-svara, King of Asuras.
The Asura King Universal Radiance, the Asura King Ever-Victorious in Battle, the Asura King Skillful in Illusion,
and other such Asura Kings, with the Asura King Vast and Sublime Eloquence as their leader.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The body of Rāhu, King of the Asuras, is seven hundred yojanas long;
his manifested form is sixteen thousand eight hundred yojanas long. Emerging from the great ocean with half his body, it is level with Mount Sumeru.
The commentary on the text says: "This translates as 'Obstructing-Holder' (*rāhu*). His manifested body is eighty-four thousand yojanas long. This is cited.
The palms of his hands can obstruct the light of the sun and moon.

Vemacitra—here translated as "Pure Mind," also named "Various Doubts"—manifests majestic and steadfast power, thereby subduing Māra and protecting the Way, never retreating when encountering adversaries.

With the radiance of his wondrous voice, he discerns the capacities of beings to preach the Dharma, ensuring that none who are ready for transformation are overlooked. In battle, he crushes the heterodox and upholds the orthodox.

Skillful in illusion, he benefits the multitude according to their needs. As for one of vast and wondrous eloquence, he must possess a torrential flow of speech and the meaning of brocade-like patterns;
thus, he is more than capable of serving as a leader. △ Third, praising his virtues to conclude the assembly.
They were well-versed in cultivation, free from all conceit, upholders of the Mahāyāna, and respectful toward the Triple Gem;
each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of followers.

"Cultivation" refers to upholding the Buddha-way. To be skillfully able to praise [the Dharma] is called "attaining its essential meaning. To rely on oneself and look down upon others is "self-conceit" (*māna*).
When both the seeds and the manifestations are extinguished, it is called "being free from all. However, self-conceit is not of a single kind; therefore, the term "all" is used.

For example, there are those who, relying on their own noble lineage or official family, look down on others and treat things with arrogance; or those who, by means of extensive learning and broad knowledge, look down on others.
Those who are arrogant toward others may do so by means of eloquent speech and sharp rhetoric;

those who are arrogant toward others simply because they possess some excellence and look down upon the shortcomings of others—all such instances constitute *māna* (self-conceit). Since this deity has cultivated the Buddha-way, he must certainly sever all of these;
therefore, it is said that he is "detached. The Mahāyāna is precisely the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground. One who upholds it will necessarily transcend words and see the Way. Three.
The "Treasures" (ratna) are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. They are collectively termed "treasures" because they are revered. The Buddha is the Honored One among those with two feet;

the Dharma is the Honored One that transcends desire; and the Sangha is the Honored One within the assembly. As long as the Three Jewels abide in the world, they are like a compassionate vessel upon the ocean of suffering.
A bright torch in the long night; a rain of moisture upon the burning house. For those who take refuge, merit increases immeasurably;

for those who pay homage and recite [his name], sins are extinguished as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Because there are such supreme benefits, he is held in high esteem. There are three types of Triple Gems; fearing prolixity, they are not detailed here.
(This Asura likewise possesses the virtues of a Bodhisattva; do not regard him as an ordinary being. △ Sixth, the Kāla-garuḍa King, in three parts: first, the heading.
To cite further examples by number:
there are also five hundred million *garuḍa* kings—
here translated as "Golden-Winged"— whose wings and pinions are golden in color, and the distance between their two wings is three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li*.
They have wish-fulfilling jewels upon their necks and take dragons as their food; these are the Garuḍa deities. △ Second, the names are listed in order:
the Garuḍa King Ratnaśikhin, the Garuḍa King Vajraviśuddhaprabha, and the Garuḍa [King] Swift as the Wind.
Rāja-garuḍa; Śuddhaprajñā-garuḍa-rāja; Vistīrṇakāya-garuḍa-rāja; Avivartyacitta-garuḍa-rāja;
Viśālākṣaviśuddha-garuḍa-rāja; Pūrṇodara-garuḍa-rāja; Mahātejas-garuḍa-rāja; Jñānaprabhāsa-garuḍa-rāja. Thus [they were].
The Garuḍa Kings, with the Garuḍa King Jewel-Light as their leader. As for "Jewel-Crest" (Ratna-śikhin):
on his crown there is a fleshy protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) that is as venerable and sublime as a jewel; hence he is so named. The diamond (vajra) is a metaphor as explained previously.
That its essence is unstained is called "pure" (viśuddha); that its function has illumination is called "light" (prabhā). This is what this deity has realized.
Its essence and function are like a diamond (*vajra*). Its flight is beneficial, and thus it is as swift as the wind;
its pure wisdom is vast and penetrating, and thus its measure is like space. Its wondrous body is expansive, so it is named according to its physical form;
its mind does not regress, so it is designated by its aspiration. Its sublime vision is pure, remaining unobstructed by any sensory dusts.
His great belly is full, yet he is constantly nourished by the milk of the Dharma, which fills his heart; do not consider yourself satiated merely by being a dragon who eats.
To praise his virtue is to have the benefit of sentient beings; it is through this benefit that one attains true satiety. His majestic power and virtue are both great.
One sees the dual practice of *saṃgraha* (gathering) and *vinaya* (subduing). The radiance of wisdom possesses the complete virtue of the two benefits.
As for "Jewel Light" (*Ratnaprabha*), in terms of the essence realized, it is as solid and real as a jewel; as for the function of that essence, it illuminates objects like light.
Since both essence and function are fully manifested, he is the leader among the assembly. △ Third, praising his virtues to conclude the description of the assembly.
They all fully accomplish the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and skillfully bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
Each is accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
"Non-arising" is precisely "non-birth. If one accomplishes this dharma, one does not perceive even the slightest [existence] within or without the three realms.
When dharmas arise, there is not even a slight dharma that ceases.

Thus, having realized within oneself this dharma of neither arising nor ceasing and having brought it to patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) in the mind—just as when a person drinks water, they know its coldness or warmth by themselves—it is called "dharma-patience" (*dharmakṣānti*).
This phrase praises the virtue of self-benefit; "well-attained benefit" praises the virtue of benefiting others. "Benefit" (*yōeki*) refers to abundant profit.
Benefit. This deity, through the application of his power of vows, may increase merit or prolong life;

as when seeking an official position one obtains it, or seeking children one obtains them, as well as eliminating calamities, resolving misfortunes, and bestowing auspiciousness—all these are matters of benefit.
All such beings are objects for whom benefit is intended. △ Seven: The Assembly of Kinnaras, Part Three. First:
To indicate the number and cite the types:

furthermore, there are nine hundred million *kiṃnara* kings—this term translated as "doubtful deities"—who resemble humans and have a single horn upon their heads; thus they are called "those who are neither human nor non-human" (*amanuṣya*). They are [the retinue] of the Heavenly Emperor.
The deity of Dharma-pleasure (Dharmarati) dwells on the Ten Jewel Mountains. His body possesses extraordinary marks. Whenever Śakra ascends to heaven, this deity immediately plays music;
when the Buddha preaches the Dharma, this deity likewise sings with strings and chants verses on the gates of the Buddha-dharma. △ Second, the names are listed in order.
The Kinnara King Earth-Shaker; the Kinnara King Wondrous Jewel Flower Banner; the Kinnara King Radiance of Jewel Trees;
the Kinnara King Radiance of the Good Dharma; the Kinnara King Supreme Adornment; the Kinnara King Radiance of the Great Dharma;
the Kinnara King Upholding the Sublime Dharma; and the Kinnara King Adorned with Wondrous Jewels.
King Rāja, King Kṣemadṛśya, King Kinnara, and so forth— these and other Kinnara kings,
with King Manojñaghoṣa as their leader.

"Shaking the earth" means that either a deity possessing supernatural power shakes the earth with every step to admonish and stir the human mind, or the exquisite strains of stringed music move the depths of the human heart;
for this reason, it is so named. "Exquisite Jewel Flower Banner" means that the banner symbolizes the crushing of heterodoxy.

It is the actual practice for protecting the Way; it is the manifest expression of causal conduct. It serves as the true provision for entering the Way, and is therefore designated by the term "wondrous jewel" (*ratna*).
A tree can provide shade and possesses the virtue of coolness; light can dispel darkness and possesses the virtue of illumination.
The deity is endowed with these virtues and is thus worthy of honor and esteem, which is why he is called a "jewel. As for the "light of the sublime Dharma":

This means that when one attains realization of the wholesome dharmas, the light of the mind becomes naturally luminous. Regarding "the most supreme adornment": among all adornments, the sublime Dharma is foremost;
because one realizes this sublime Dharma, it is taken as the name. Regarding "the great light of the Dharma":
the entire body arises as function, with wisdom and principle serving as its name. The sublime Dharma is the mind alone; by upholding it, one awakens. Sublime wisdom is the treasure. Thus...

Adorned with exceptional dignity and having perfected wondrous contemplation, his wisdom and principle were in profound accord. With a voice of pleasing melody, he surely attained the Way through the lute and pipes;
his spiritual faculties were preeminent, and thus he was the foremost leader. △ Third, praising his virtues to conclude the assembly.
They all possess pure and wondrous wisdom; their bodies and minds are joyful, and they sport with sovereign ease.
Each is accompanied by several hundred thousand retinues.
"Pure" (清淨) means that the light of the mind is bright and clear, illuminating objects as wisdom (*prajñā*); being unstained while amidst turbidity is called "pure. It dwells...
To be unstained by dust is called "purity. To be neither stained nor defiled is "wondrous. To attain the mind and respond to the body is "joy.
Because it arises from the essence to manifest function, it is called "sovereignty. Because its wondrous response is without fixed direction, it is like "play.
△ Eight: The Assembly of Mahoragas (3). First: Indicating the number and citing the class.
Furthermore, there were ninety-eight thousand mahoraga kings—here translated as "Great-Bellied Crawlers.
These are earth-dwelling dragons, specifically great serpent deities that move by crawling on their bellies. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states:
These are the temple deities of the world who receive people's offerings of wine and meat; they all enter the belly of a python.

Alternatively, those who violate the precepts, are perverse and sycophantic, full of anger and stingy with almsgiving, and greedily crave wine and meat—falling into the realm of ghosts and spirits due to their laxity regarding the precepts—will have worms enter their bodies to devour them.
They are also called *mahoragas*. This explanation refers to the body received as a result of karmic retribution. This scripture...
Regarding those referred to as "Kings" within the text: this means they preside over their respective classes; they are also manifestations of Bodhisattvas. △ Second, the names are listed in order:
King of the Mahoraga with the Wondrous Topknot, King of the Mahoraga Possessing Great Majestic Virtue, and King of the Adorned Jewel Topknot.
The Mahoraga King; the Mahoraga King Subtle Pure Eye; the Mahoraga King Jewel Banner of Radiance;
the Mahoraga King Lion’s Chest; the Mahoraga King Immovable as a Mountain;
the Mahoraga King Lovely Radiance—and these and other such Mahoraga Kings sported there.
The King of the Mahoragas with Supernatural Powers was the leader.

As for "Wondrous Topknot" (Miaojì): he has a fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) upon his crown; he is so named because of his exquisite beauty. He possesses great majesty and virtue, by which he subdues the multitude;

he wears a solemn topknot, thereby distinguishing himself from the mundane. His pure eyes allow him to perceive the wondrous Path, and his light-bannered standard manifests the crushing of heterodoxy.
"Siṃha" (Lion) symbolizes fearlessness; "Acala" (Immovable) symbolizes supreme dignity; "Vairocana-prabha" (Light of Loving Radiance) symbolizes the brilliance of wisdom.
Because he dwells at ease beyond all phenomena, he is called "Wandering in Play" (*vihāra*). Because his wondrous functions are unfathomable, he is called "Supernatural Power" (*abhijñā*).
As he is the leader among the assembly, [the section] concludes by praising his virtues and summarizing the multitude.
Having already been able to cultivate skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they cause all sentient beings to forever leave behind the entanglements of craving.
Each is accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues;

"having already been able to descend" refers to being endowed with various provisional wisdoms (*prajñā*). Skillfulness (*kauśalya*) does not manifest outward traces, whereas skillful means (*upāya*)...
Without regard for scale, [the teaching] addresses all those below. "Craving" refers to sensual craving; that is, although objects of craving are many, desire for form is the most significant.
Craving and desiring form serve as the cause of birth and death. When the multitude is bound by these fetters, it constitutes the fruit of birth and death.
Whether bound by the entanglements of affection or driven by the continuity of karmic results, sentient beings are deluded and ignorant, failing to awaken to their own nature.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva manifests in their form and engages with them through common activities and shared endeavors, employing skillful means to guide and transform them, striving to cause them to turn their minds away from desire.
When both the seeds and their manifestations have perished, one is said to be "permanently detached. Having ceased to create causes, one will ultimately not undergo the results.

This may be called great skillful means; it is merely a sublime practice for gathering and transforming beings according to their respective types. Each [category] is concluded below with a summary of the assembly. The common tradition says:

if one is strict regarding the precepts but lax regarding the vehicle, one will be reborn in the heavens. Being captured by the realms of pleasure, one lacks the leisure to see the Buddha or hear the Dharma.

When the retribution is exhausted, one falls back again; there is falling but no ascending. If one’s vehicle is urgent but one’s precepts are lax, one falls among the seven classes of ghosts and spirits.
One falls because the precepts are lax; yet because the vehicle is urgent, one does not forget the original vow and does not abandon the Buddha-dharma.
Thus, one constantly stays near the Buddha to hear the Dharma and cultivates through the Dharma; there is ascending but no falling. If both the vehicle and the precepts are urgent, then...
If one transcends the world to become a sage, yet both vehicle and precepts are lax, one will fall directly into the three miserable realms; this is the general rule for ordinary cases.

However, this present sutra is not so. The eight classes of devas and nāgas are all great manifestations of expedient power, intended to govern and gather all categories of beings, causing them to see the Buddha and hear the Dharma as causes for transcendence. If it were not for the Bodhisattvas manifesting in the bodies of kings...
The transformation through guidance: the eight classes of devas and nāgas are all forever deluded. How true is the grace of the Bodhisattva! What can be done to repay it?
This concludes the section on the eight classes of devas and nāgas. IV. The Assembly of Universal Monarchs, Nobles, and Commoners.
1. The Gathering of the Universal Monarchs. a. The Universal Monarchs Assemble.
Furthermore, there were wheel-turning sage-kings from ten thousand billion lands in other directions:
wheel-turning sage-kings of the golden wheel, wheel-turning sage-kings of the silver wheel, wheel-turning sage-kings of the copper wheel, and wheel-turning sage-kings of the iron wheel.

A Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) appears during the aeon of increase (*utkarsa-kalpa*), whereas Śākyamuni appeared in the world precisely during the aeon of decrease (*apakarṣa-kalpa*). How, then, could there be a Wheel-Turning King [at that time]?
For this reason, the text first specifies "other lands," and the phrase "ten billion" indicates a great number rather than a fixed count.

According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it is stated only that for a Golden Wheel-Turning King, the precious golden wheel appears; however, according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, there are four [types of wheels].

Each of these kings has wheels that appear. Now, this sutra also mentions the seven treasures, the thousand sons, and so forth; from this, it is clear that each of the Four Kings possesses the seven treasures.
In this sutra, the names are listed with the Golden Wheel at the head because of the principle of honoring the superior before the inferior.
However, if one discusses the sequence of the *kalpa* of increase (*vivartakalpa*), then the Iron Wheel would come first. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* [states] that when human life spans...
One increase and one decrease constitute a small kalpa (*antarakalpa*).

This means that when the human lifespan is eighty-four thousand years, as each hundred years pass, the lifespan decreases by one year until it reaches ten years; then, after another hundred years have passed, it increases by one year.
When the lifespan increases in this manner until it reaches twenty thousand years, an Iron Wheel-Turning King appears, ruling alone over the single continent of Jambudvīpa.
Should there be any kingdoms that do not submit to his transformation, the king manifests his majesty and arrays his troops, causing them to return to submission.
Thereafter, he exhorts and transforms the people there, leading them to cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action; this is called an Iron-Wheel-Turning King.

Second, the Copper-Wheel-Turning King: This refers to when the human lifespan has increased to forty thousand years, a Copper-Wheel-Turning King appears and governs two continents—the Southeastern ones.
Should there be kingdoms that do not submit to his transformation, the King travels to those lands, proclaiming his majesty and spreading his virtue, causing them to...
They submit to him. Thereupon, he exhorts and transforms the people to cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action. ○ Third, the Silver Wheel-Turning King:
this refers to when the human lifespan increases to sixty thousand years, a silver wheel-turning king appears and governs the three continents of the east, south, and west.
In various kingdoms where there were those who did not submit to his transformation, when the King arrived in those lands, they immediately became his subjects through the majesty he displayed.
Thereupon, he exhorted and transformed the people, leading them to cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action. ○ Regarding the four types of Golden-Wheel Kings:
it is said that when the human lifespan increases to eighty-four thousand years, a Golden-Wheel King appears, ruling over the four continents. By means of the [fifteen... [text fragment ends].
On that day, having bathed, he ascended the throne hall. Suddenly, the precious golden wheel appeared before him; it had a thousand spokes and was perfect in its radiant color.
If the king wished to go toward the east, the wheel would turn eastward. He would then lead his armies and follow behind it.
Before the golden wheel, four divine beings would also guide the way. Wherever the wheel halted, the king would immediately bring his carriage to a stop.
In the south, west, and north, wherever the wheel arrives, it is likewise so. Throughout the four continents, he universally exhorts the people to cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action.
II. The Seven Treasures Follow in Succession.
Along with the seven treasures, a retinue of a thousand sons, and immeasurable adornments; elephants, horses, and chariots;

countless jeweled banners with great precious streamers suspended from them; flower garlands and jeweled canopies; silken fabrics and white fly-whisks; various rare and wondrous things, and exquisite jewel necklaces.
There were ointment incenses and powdered incenses, blended from ten thousand varieties, of subtle and exquisite fragrance.
As for the seven treasures: first is the golden wheel treasure (*cakraratna*). Its wheel has a thousand spokes, its diameter is one zhang and four chi, and it is complete with hub and rim.
It is carved and engraved, interspersed with various jewels; its radiance penetrates clearly, being fashioned by celestial artisans and not of this world.
He possesses them all. That is to say, once the Wheel-Turning Sage King has obtained this treasure, the wheel turns according to his mental intention.
As he travels across the world, he completes the circuit in an instant. This is the Golden Wheel Treasure. ○ Second is the White Elephant Treasure.
It is said that when the noble king ascends the throne at dawn, the white elephant treasure suddenly appears.
Its body is pure white, its head is variegated in color, and it has six tusks in its mouth; the tusks have the colors of the seven precious gems.

It possesses the power to fly, such that when the king mounts it, he can travel throughout the entire world in a single day—departing in the morning and returning in the evening—without fatigue or exhaustion. If he travels...
If it stands, its head and tail remain motionless; its eyes do not look askance; it is composed, gentle, and virtuous.
If it walks across water, the water does not ripple, nor does it even wet its feet. This is called the Elephant Treasure. ○ Third is the Dark Blue Horse Treasure.
There was a horse of blue-red color. When the king ascended the hall at dawn, a precious horse of deep-blue hue suddenly appeared.
Its mane and tail were threaded with pearls; when it was washed and groomed, the pearls would fall off, yet in a mere moment they would grow back as before.
The jewel is fresh and pure; its color is superior to the former. Its sound is heard from within a distance of one yojana. It possesses the power of flight;
if the king mounts it to tour the world, he departs in the morning and returns by evening, yet his strength never grows weary.

Wherever the horse’s hooves touch the dust, it all turns into golden sand. This is called the Horse Treasure (Aśvaratna). Fourth is the Jewel of the Divine Wheel (Cakraratna). When the king ascends the throne hall, [the wheel appears].
There is a divine jewel-treasure that suddenly appears; its color is brilliant and pure, free from any flaw or blemish.
When suspended in the air at night, it illuminates the interior and exterior of the kingdom according to its size, no different from daylight.
This is called the Jewel-treasure (which is the wish-fulfilling gem). Fifth is the Woman-Jewel: she is of upright countenance, endowed with perfect physical features, and her body is warm in winter.
She is cool in summer. From all her pores, sandalwood fragrance emanates; from her mouth, the fragrance of blue lotuses issues forth.
Her speech is soft and gentle, and her movements are composed and serene. Food is digested of its own accord, unlike worldly women who possess various impurities.
This is called the Woman-Jewel. (6) The Treasurer of Wealth, also known as the Minister of the Treasury:

whenever the king desires wealth or the seven precious jewels, the Minister of the Treasury bows his entire body toward the earth, and the earth produces the seven jewels; he turns toward water and the water produces jewels;
he turns toward mountains and the mountains produce jewels; he turns toward rocks and the rocks produce jewels. This is the Treasurer of Wealth. His...
Because this person’s past merit is profound and vast, his eyes can see through to hidden treasures buried in the earth. Whether they have an owner or not, he perceives and knows them all.
Those that have an owner, he protects and guards for them; those that have no owner, he takes to provide for the King’s use (also known as the *Gañjapati-ratna*).
7. The Treasure of the Military Commander (*Senāpati-ratna*): Also called the Minister of the Army or the General-Treasure. This king...

Suppose he intends to obtain fourfold armies—whether numbering in the thousands, tens of thousands, or even infinitely many—and in the mere blink of an eye, the troops are already assembled, their ranks and formations strictly orderly;
this is called "mastering the army. That man’s wisdom and strategy are heroic and fierce, and his military arts are uniquely outstanding.
He then goes to the king’s presence and says, "Great King, regarding any campaign of conquest you may have, there is no need for concern. If...
As for the fourfold army of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, the ministers are able to provide them immediately. Regarding the "thousand sons" (the numerical categories are not listed here;

please examine this further with care), the retinue consists of the thousand sons and the assembly of ministers. When the King travels, those who guard him from front and rear constitute his adornment.

From the phrase "immeasurable" below, the various adornments are extensively enumerated. "Elephants and horses" refers to the cavalry and so forth; "banners and pennants" refers to the imperial carriage ornaments.
As for the *dhvaja* (banner): it is made of various silks and brocades, fashioned into a cylindrical tube and colored in five hues with tiered layers hanging down.
Atop it is a six-cornered precious canopy (*ratnacchattra*), each corner of which has tassels (*dāma*) or small flags (*patākā*) hanging down;
alternatively, it may be adorned with jewels or embroidered with thread. It is mounted on a long pole, upon which a golden hook is fixed, and half of the banner is attached to this hook.
Above, it is held by a *bala* (powerful man) who leads the way, serving as a symbol for the crushing of heterodoxy. The banner (*dhvaja*) is likewise;

however, that which is circular is a *dhvaja*, while that which is flat is a *patākā*. Regarding the flower garland (*mālā*): [examine the meaning of the character]. A *mālā* refers to beautiful hair. It is used frequently throughout the sūtras, though its specific intent here remains unclear.

This was likely not an oversight by the translator, but rather an error regarding the term *mālya*. Now, explaining *mālya*: it refers to a curtain or drape. Because it is strung with flowers, it is called a "flower garland" (*huaman*).

A *chattra* is a parasol; it is suspended above the king. Regarding *vilepana* (unguents): they are used for bathing with water, and because their fragrance is subtle and profound, they are called "unguents.

*Cūrṇa* (powdered incense) refers to scented flour. As for "blended incense," it is that which is composed of various fragrances; while there are said to be ten thousand varieties, the marvelous ones are the most extraordinary.

"Extraordinary" (*shu*) means "superior. △ When a Prince of a Golden Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) succeeds to the throne, he takes the waters of the four great oceans and pours them over his crown;
only then does he succeed to his father’s position. △ He makes three offerings and praises the Buddha.
Each holding a priceless incense burner made of various jewels, they burned great precious incense as an offering to the World-Honored One,
praising the Tathāgata’s profoundly deep ocean of wisdom with exquisite words.

On the other hand, when a wheel-turning monarch comes to see the Buddha, he does not dare to act with disrespect; thus, he holds an incense burner and burns incense to manifest his sincerity in drawing near.
With "With wondrous [words]" and so forth, he may praise the Buddha’s physical marks and signs, or praise his supernormal powers, or praise his meditative concentration.
All [these verses] employ exquisite sounds and elegant phrasing to commemorate the Buddha’s virtues. Regarding "the ocean of profound wisdom":
the Tathāgata’s two wisdoms—expedient and ultimate—are likened to a great ocean; they are so deep as to be unfathomable and so vast as to be immeasurable.
Only a Buddha and a Buddha can truly know them. △ Fourth, the narration of his own aspiration to the Buddha.

He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I now do not seek the tainted fruits of existence within the three realms—whether as humans or devas—but seek only the supramundane *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?

Within the three realms, although one may occupy a position of honor through the blessings and joys of humans and devas, once the merit of previous lives is exhausted, one returns to birth in the evil destinies and undergoes immeasurable suffering. Who [could find peace therein]?"

Those who possess wisdom and delight in worldly happiness call the Buddha the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*), because among both the mundane and supramundane realms, the Buddha alone is uniquely honored. I now describe my resolve below:
the three realms—namely, the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm—are all abodes where sentient beings of ordinary nature receive their retributions.
This is the place [of such]. "With outflows" (sāsrava) means falling away; it refers to the nature of leaking away from the wealth of the Dharma of inherent virtue.

This is precisely the cause and effect of birth and death for ordinary beings. Because the grasping at a self has not been extinguished, both cause and effect are characterized by outflows, like a broken vessel that cannot hold anything.
These three—namely, the delusions of views and thoughts, the karma of body and speech, and the fruit of saṃsāra—are all [outflows].
If one remains [in this state], one cannot transcend the world and will thus be left behind in the three realms, perpetually undergoing birth and death.

Although the retributions of humans and devas constitute the wholesome paths, they all belong to the cycle of tainted birth and death; therefore, these are not sought after. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"Whether born in the heavens or among humans, there is the suffering of poverty and hardship, the suffering of separation from loved ones, and the suffering of enmity with those one hates."
It is suffering. Sentient beings are submerged within these various kinds of suffering such as these.
Furthermore, it is said that there is no peace in the three realms; they are like a burning house. Since it says "does not seek," this implies a weariness with the suffering of birth and death.
"Only seeks" below refers to the arousal of the bodhicitta. "Anuttara... below means "Unsurpassed, Perfectly Equal, and Perfect Enlightenment. This is the Buddha.
The ultimate fruit realized is precisely the path yearned for by the Wheel-Turning Kings (cakravartin). Below, the text interrogates and explains the preceding meaning:
namely, why it is that humans and devas regard goodness as a favorable fruit yet do not seek it.

This is because, although the status of fortune among humans and devas within the three realms is honorable and their dwelling therein is pleasant, it cannot endure for long. This is truly due to [the nature of] the past...
This is brought about by the meritorious karma of previous lives; thus, one experiences its karmic rewards in the present life. However, that actual pleasure is not permanent;

after a long time, it must inevitably decay and give rise to suffering, ending in a fall. Therefore, it is said that when the merit of previous lives is exhausted, one returns to the evil realms and undergoes immeasurable suffering.
Alas! The various distinctions between good and evil karma performed by human beings in this world all leave their impressions and form [karmic seeds].
Seeds are contained within the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). If the virtuous seeds are superior and ripen, one first experiences the retribution of virtue.

If one further cultivates virtuous deeds, they progress to ever higher levels. However, if one does not cease their craving for pleasure and fails to perform virtuous actions, then the unwholesome seeds contained within the eight consciousnesses will ripen;
one will inevitably fall away from the fruits of virtue and enter the evil realms to undergo [suffering].
To measure suffering is a logical necessity; how could it be avoided? As for why one speaks of "evil paths" (*durgati*) rather than simply "evil," *gati* means "direction" or "tendency";
it refers to the three miserable realms as the destinations toward which one is headed.

In the hells, there is the suffering of mountain-blades, sword-trees, copper snakes, and iron dogs; among the hungry ghosts, there is the burden of carrying sand and stones, filling rivers and blocking seas.
The sufferings of animals include such things as carrying heavy loads over long distances and having whips and sticks fall upon their bodies;
because these types of suffering are truly numerous, they are said to be "immeasurable. The phrase "Who would... serves as a counter-illustration to show that the wise do not seek [such states].

The first instance of the character *lè* (樂) is pronounced *yào*, meaning "desire"; the second instance of *lè* is pronounced *luò*, meaning "happiness. "Who would" is used here as a general reference.
This statement means: "How could there be such a thing? That is to say, how could there be a wise person who, desiring the pleasures of the five worldly desires, would instead fail to seek Bodhi?
(This clearly demonstrates that the Wheel-Turning King is indeed a wise person. △ Fifth, the prostration to conclude the assembly.
Having spoken these words, they each, together with several hundreds of thousands of retinues, joined their palms with single-minded devotion.
Their single-mindedness signifies the purity of their resolve; their joining of palms signifies their reverent submission. △ Second, the assembly of various kings, in five parts.
First, to cite the category:
furthermore, there were sixteen great kings whose territories were called "kingdoms" and who ruled with sovereign power.
As the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted all matters concerning the future to these ten [kings].
The kings of the Six States were none other than this very king. Now, a true king must establish virtue and achieve merit so that his legacy may be great and enduring.
He weaves the warp of benevolence and righteousness and the woof of martial and civil virtue. Deepening his roots and strengthening his foundation, he bequeaths his legacy to his descendants.
Every word and every deed serves as a model to be transmitted through ten thousand generations, remaining unalterable; such is the power of an Emperor.
It can stabilize the myriad states; the King’s majesty can subdue the millions of subjects.

Therefore, regarding the final testament from the Tathāgata’s golden mouth and the dying charge at the Crane Grove (Heli), [the Buddha] was concerned that the fourfold assembly might become weak and fragile, and feared that the Triple Gem might decline and fall.
Thus, he entrusted [the Dharma] to the sovereign’s majestic influence and borrowed the King’s power, entrusting it to the Emperor and relying upon the imperial edict to circulate it.
This is the general introduction. Now, as the Buddha intends to expound the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, these various kings have gathered like clouds. II. Listing their names:
King Śuddhodana of the kingdom of Kapilavastu; King Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Magadha; [King Mahāpraṇāda] of Vārāṇasī...
There was the Great King Kosiya; the Great King Yuntuo of the country of Yutuo; the King of Śrāvastī;
King Kapina; and these sixteen great kings, along with various minor kings, including King Prasenajit, the sovereign of Śrāvastī.
He was named Candraprabha and served as their leader.
"Kapila" is a partial transcription of a Sanskrit term; its full form is *Kapilavastu*.
*Kapila* means "yellow," and *vastu* means "place of residence. In ancient times, there was a rishi named Yellow-Head (*Kapila*) who resided there.

Because this is the place where the Path is cultivated, it is given this name. Alternatively, translated according to its meaning, it is called "The Abode of the Capable Sage" (Śākyamuni), which is the site where the Buddha descended.
It is located within the Great Trichiliocosm. As for "Śuddhodana," in the Sanskrit language it is *Ratnada* (or *Suddhoda*), which is translated here as "Pure Rice" or "True Purity.
This means that the King transformed and governed the world through the purity of his true path and virtue.
He is none other than the Buddha’s father. That the King, his father, has now arrived at the Tathāgata’s place of enlightenment does not mean he views his son merely as a son;
rather, he regards his son as a Great Sage. Thus, he honors the Way and admires the Virtue—a meeting unparalleled in a thousand ages.
How could he possibly be arrogant and self-important, looking down upon the Sage? It is as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, concerning the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
He attained enlightenment. His father, the Wheel-Turning Sage King, along with the royal grandson, the consort, and the queen, all arrived at the site of enlightenment;

this too was a rare occurrence. Magadha is translated here as "Excellent Victory" (Śubhavijaya) or "Non-Harming" (Ahiṃsā), because since the beginning of the eon, there has been no infliction of punishment or harm there.
Alternatively, it is called Magadhī, which is merely a difference in the Sanskrit pronunciation. Bimbisāra is translated here as...
"Of upright countenance" means that his physical features were exceptionally sublime; this refers to him by way of his physical appearance.
"Vārāṇasī" is translated here as "City Encircled by Rivers," or alternatively as "Deer Park. This is the name of the capital of the kingdom. As for King Kāśyapa:
He was the ruler of the country; his name, translated into Chinese, is not yet known. There is the country of Yudhā with its Great King Yu-ch'an;

these are all without historical verification, as they do not appear in the *Fanyi mingyi ji* (Collection of Translated Names and Meanings). Sāla means "firm" or "solid" in Chinese; it is the name of a tree.
The country is now named after this tree, either because the country is named for the tree itself or because such trees abound there. Kapiṇa is also not yet known.
"Lesser kings" refers to all the *kṣatriya* rulers, such as the feudal lords (*zhuhou*).
"Śrāvastī" is translated here as "Hearing Things," because precious objects abound in this city; it is also rendered as "Abundant Virtue," meaning that the kingdom abounds in four virtues:
wealth and treasures, the five desires, extensive learning, and liberation. This is the name of the country. The king's name is Prasenajit, which means "Victorious."

Regarding the army: The *Ratnaraśmi-rāja-sūtra* states that this king was already a fourth-stage Bodhisattva named Candraprabha during the Dharma of King Nāgaprabha ten thousand kalpas ago. This specific name is not seen in other sutras;
alternatively, "Prasenajit" may be his royal title while "Candraprabha" is his original name. He is called the "foremost" because he governs and oversees all the kings.
△ Third, the praise of their virtues:

They are all fully endowed with merit, wisdom, and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Possessing great majestic power (*mahā-tejas*), they naturally subdue all enemies, just like a wheel-turning king (*cakravartin*).
The populace is flourishing and the land is abundant and joyful. Having planted various roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) at the abodes of immeasurable Buddhas.
They were constantly protected and remembered by all the Buddhas. During the Kalpa of Adornment, when a thousand Buddhas appeared, these kings constantly served as their patrons.
During the Bhadrakalpa, when a thousand Buddhas appear, these kings likewise serve as their patrons.
In a future age, during the Constellation Kalpa (*Nakṣatra-kalpa*), when one thousand Buddhas appear, they shall serve as patrons;
indeed, until all the Buddhas of the future appear in the world, these kings, by the power of their original vows, will constantly practice the giving of alms.
He benefits sentient beings and skillfully enters various gates of expedient means as appropriate. Although he acts as a king, he does not crave worldly pleasures;

he feels weary of and seeks detachment from birth and death, cultivates the causes of liberation, diligently pursues the Buddha-way, delights in the Mahāyāna, and transforms and benefits all living beings.
They do not cling to any signs. They perpetuate the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it shall never be severed.
Regarding "merit and wisdom": merit is a general term for a hundred auspicious blessings. Because one possesses merit, the borderlands are peaceful and one enjoys great tranquility.
Because one possesses wisdom, the True Dharma is used to instruct people, and the myriad subjects delight in their vocations. As for "supernatural powers" (*abhijñā*): "spiritual" (*shen*)...
This refers to the Heavenly Mind. It universally constitutes the life of wisdom. When the Heavenly Mind gives rise to its penetration, its wondrous function is inconceivable.
An ancient worthy said: "A ruler (*jun*) is one who leads (*qun*). One who can lead the myriad things of the world and eliminate their harms is called a ruler.
Ban Gu said: "In his ruling of the world, he enflames it like the sun; he awes it like a deity. He encompasses...
He nurtures them like the ocean and sustains them like spring; he is like plants and trees growing in mountain forests, or birds and fish thriving in rivers and marshes.
He participates in the transformation of heaven and earth—how could this be said to depend on the thickness or thinness of human affairs?
Is this not the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the King? One who possesses great majesty and virtue has a dignified and solemn countenance, majestic without even appearing angry.
This is *wei* (majesty). To abide in the correct Way for oneself is *ren* (benevolence); to bestow kindness and righteousness upon all things is *de* (virtue).

The *Hongfan* says: "Without partiality and without factionalism, the King’s Way is vast; without factionalism and without partiality, the King’s Way is level. This is like the three lines following the "turning wheel" [in the hexagram].
This reveals the majesty that subdues the king. The two lines beginning with "The people" manifest the inspiration brought about by the king’s virtue.
All that precedes constitutes the fruits of virtue in the present life; the section beginning with "Immeasurable" refers to the causes of merit from the past.

Now, the reason for planting wholesome seeds specifically in the presence of a Buddha is that the Buddha serves as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*); it is like sowing seeds in a fertile field to reap a harvest.

It must be weighty. As for those who speak well of it, their praises are not of a single kind; it must involve the simultaneous cultivation of the myriad practices, benefiting both oneself and others—this is the profundity of the cause.
The latter two lines [of the verse] refer to the excellence of the conditions. "To protect" means to guard and preserve.
"Mindfulness" means cherishing and caring for others; that is to say, by providing protection, one can subdue Māra and prevent the resolve from regressing.

By cherishing them, one preaches the Dharma to them, ensuring that their wisdom necessarily increases. This may be called a virtue in which the causes are profound and the conditions are superior, whereby merit and wisdom increase and expand.

Regarding "Adornment" below, this clarifies the virtue of practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) through the power of vows, which is deep and vast. [This concludes] the *Kṣemadharman* Kalpa.
"Below" refers to the thousand Buddhas of the past. "Below" [the section on] the Bhadrakalpa refers to the thousand Buddhas of the present.
"Below" [the section on] the Nakṣatraprabhāsa-kalpa refers to the thousand Buddhas of the future. The phrase "and so forth" (*naiti*) is a term used for abbreviation;
it implies that this does not stop here, but extends even to all the infinite Buddhas of the future who shall appear in the world. These kings and others, by virtue of their original vows...
[The Bodhisattva] exerts power and extensively practices giving to benefit sentient beings. The perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) must necessarily possess three aspects.

Regarding "benefiting sentient beings," this is explained here primarily in terms of those who are impoverished. Regarding "giving," this is explained here primarily in terms of material gifts. Furthermore, it is said that one should "skillfully enter various doors of expedient means as appropriate";
thus, it does not stop at the single type of material gift, but requires that one adaptively comply with the timing and circumstances.
Through the gift of Dharma and the gift of fearlessness, he causes them to be transformed by his teaching.

Although he has set forth the following resolve, generally speaking, for those who are kings—honored as the most noble among men, possessing the wealth of the four seas and the rare treasures of the entire realm—who among them would not have their minds stained by the pleasures of the five desires?
Yet, that these various kings do not covet such things and instead feel weary of them may be called "wealth and honor not [corrupting] the mind."
That one's mind can be led astray by lust, yet the five desires cannot seize one's resolve, is because the matter of birth and death is of great importance.
