That which cultivates the cause of liberation refers specifically to the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), while explained generally, it is the transcendence of sensory dust (*vītaraja*).

The two characters "Buddha-path" (*buddhamārga*) are a general designation for the causes and fruits of the Three Vehicles. The latter two phrases, "loving and delighting in," constitute the specific function of the Bodhisattva.
Regarding the Buddha-path, it is primarily concerned with self-benefit; yet, through the transformation of sentient beings, it is also capable of benefiting others.

"Transformation" refers to the Bodhisattva’s instruction, while "benefit" refers to the gains acquired by the multitude of living beings. Furthermore, there are two explanations regarding this "multitude of living beings. [The first is] the specific...
"Speaking" refers to the myriad people. Taken collectively, it encompasses the ten categories. "Not clinging to various marks" means that both mind and objects are empty.
This is because the two characters "marks" (xiàng) generally refer to all virtues: such as giving, which pervades the three periods of time;
or teaching and transforming, which employs skillful means according to what is appropriate, serving as the cause for liberation and the path of twofold benefit. These do not depend on...
The emptiness of both self and dharmas ultimately results in the fruits of the conditioned; therefore, it is appropriate that one should practice emptiness.

Furthermore, "generosity according to circumstances" and so forth refer to the provisional contemplation (*parikalpita*). "Not craving worldly pleasures" refers to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

"Not clinging to various marks" refers to the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way, which simultaneously dispels both emptiness and existence. The section beginning with "continuing the Three Jewels" serves as a summary. Thus, the three contemplations are perfected.

As for "cultivation," it generally serves to perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas and ensure that the life of wisdom remains eternally present. (Regarding the three kinds of giving: they are the gift of material wealth, the gift of Dharma, and the gift of fearlessness.

Furthermore, giving can encompass the six perfections: rejoicing in bestowing upon others is the perfection of generosity (*dāna*); being unstained by attachment to material wealth and desires is the perfection of morality (*śīla*); diligence in practicing giving is the perfection of effort (*vīrya*);

not clinging to the marks of giving is the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna*); desiring to seek awakening is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā*); and remaining free from anger while giving is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti*). △ Fourth, the Manifestation of the Approach.
For the sake of hearing the Dharma, they made offerings to the Tathāgata, extensively preparing exquisite foods and solemnly presenting incense and flowers as they approached the Buddha’s presence.
That those who hear the Dharma do so with such urgency demonstrates their devotion to the Path; that those who make offerings do so with such sincerity and reverence demonstrates their piety.
That the exquisite foods must be "extensively prepared" indicates their great variety; that the incense and flowers must be "solemnly presented" indicates their dignity and gravity. Thus it is said:
That this majestic arrival does not even take note of the dignity of the royal way is sufficient proof that the Buddha-way is more esteemed than the royal way.
△ Fifth, the assembly is concluded:
each [deity] was accompanied by one hundred thousand, two hundred thousand, and so on, up to ten million followers. All these retinues were present together.
"Retinue" refers to one's kin and all the ministers and subjects.
It can be seen that the King manifests his body to practice the bodhisattva path and leads his retinue to know the existence of the Triple Gem, causing them to extensively cultivate merit and wisdom;
this is the great grace of the sovereign. △ Third, the assembly of the King’s ladies-in-waiting, in five parts: first, citing the category.
Furthermore, there were the consorts of sixteen great kings who said:
"The wife of a lord of a state is called the 'Lady of the Lord' (jun-furen). Since these people belong to great kingdoms, they are equivalent to the queens (feihou) of this region.
The reason they are not called 'queens' but are called 'ladies' is to conform to the customs of their respective countries. This is because..."
As for the women of the household, they are separated by the barriers of the inner chambers.

Were it not for the Bodhisattva manifesting in the form of a queen and consort to lead the palace officials, nobles, and various court ladies to see the Buddha and hear the Dharma, they would remain ignorant of the existence of the Triple Gem;
how then could they advance upon the Path? Therefore, the Queen Mother went first, desiring that her superiors lead by example so that those below would follow.
It was thus. Thereafter, the multitudes of women among the myriad people were all able to follow this transformation.
II. Listing the Names: Lady Vaidehī; Lady Māyāśrīmālā; Lady Atiramaṇīya; Lady Anupamā Triloka;
Lady Puṇyavipākaprabhā; Lady Cintāmaṇiprabhā; Lady Mallikā; Lady Guṇavatī.
As for these ladies, Lady Viśeṣacāritrā was their leader.

Vaidehī—here translated as "Contemplation" (Sīwei)—is described in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* as saying: "I only pray that the World-Honored One will teach me contemplation and teach me right reception.
She was the queen of King Bimbisāra and the mother of King Ajātaśatru. She was exquisite.
Regarding Śrīmālā: "Śrī" is not a Sanskrit term; "mālā" means beautiful hair. This lady was named after her exquisite hair.
She was the daughter of King Prasenajit and the consort of King Udayana. As for her being "extremely lovely": she was originally a bodhisattva who manifested as a queen;
possessing such noble virtues, who would not love her? One should know that she is truly beloved.
These two characters express a sense of reverence and respect; they do not imply defiled emotion. Regarding "incomparable within the three realms":

while the Bodhisattva possesses stainless, supreme virtues, how could the conditioned marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) of the tainted realm possibly compare to them? Regarding "the radiance of karmic reward":
although he possesses the merit of a queen, he does not cling to the appearance of retribution; rather, his natural light of the Dharma shines with brilliant clarity. Therefore, it is said:
"Radiant Light. Furthermore, it refers to the light of wisdom. As for "Light of the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel," it means that the jewel of the mind emits brilliance;
thus, it is called "Jewel Light. "Mallikā" is a Sanskrit term translated here as "garland"; she was also named after her beautiful hair. She was the queen of King Prasenajit.
"Wondrous Virtue" means being fully endowed with merit and wisdom. "Excellently Sublime Countenance" refers to her sacred virtue.
Within her heart, a wondrous countenance is manifested externally; as she is fully endowed with virtuous marks, she serves as the foremost leader. △ Third, praising her virtues:
She has already been able to skillfully enter immeasurable right concentrations. For the sake of delivering sentient beings, she manifests in a female body, employing the three gates of liberation.

He cultivates his mind, possessing great wisdom and perfect merit. With unconditional great kindness and unimpeded great compassion, he cherishes all sentient beings as if they were his own infant children.
"Right Samādhi" refers to the samādhi of intrinsic nature. Its essence is non-dual; it is pure from the beginning and fundamentally such, perfectly interfused and all-pervasive.

That it is now called "immeasurable" has two meanings: first, it reveals that the essence of samādhi is without limit, which carries the sense of exhausting the vertical [depth] and pervading the horizontal [expanse].
Second, while its essence is fundamentally a single dharma, its functions are immeasurable; this specifically manifests its multiplicity based upon those functions.

Establishing the name: "Entering" (*praviṣṭa*) refers to the gathering of function back into the essence. "Good" (*kuśala*) is a term of praise. To enter that which is not entered is called "skillful entry.
"Already" (*dīrghakāla*) means for a long time; it signifies that one has skillfully entered right concentration for a long duration.
From "for the sake of saving those below" onward, the text extensively reveals the virtue of benefiting others. That is to say, those who are to be saved by means of a woman's body—namely...
Manifesting in the form of a woman, she preaches the Dharma for them. "The three lower [categories]" refer to the gateway of practice for one's own benefit.
"The great lower" refers to the root of benefiting both oneself and others. The "three liberations" are the gateway of practice for Mahayana Bodhisattvas.

This is not comparable to the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of the Two Vehicles. As for those of the Two Vehicles who attain liberation through emptiness: they employ the contemplation of self-emptiness (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) to contemplate all phenomena as being without self or what belongs to a self.

Regarding "signlessness": since they are empty and without self, there are no signs of distinction such as male or female, or unity or difference. Regarding "wishlessness": since they are empty and signless, they claim for themselves that what was to be done has been accomplished, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is established, and the grasping at a self is exhausted.

There is no further existence to be received; what more remains to be done? Nor is there any further aspiration. Now, the three liberations of the Bodhisattva are precisely these: natural purity and cultivated perfection.
The arising of function refers to the three gates of contemplation. Regarding "inherently pure": the Bodhisattva’s contemplative illumination perceives that the self-nature is fundamentally pure;

it is perfectly luminous and spontaneously perfected, receiving not even a speck of dust. This is itself liberation, and it is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Regarding "accomplished through cultivation":

the Bodhisattva further contemplates that if one relies solely on innate spontaneity, ultimate realization will never be attained. Therefore, one gives rise to true wisdom and proceeds from nature toward cultivation.

This is the contemplation of the provisional (*parikalpita*). By not abiding in the characteristics of cultivation, one realizes the true characteristic (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*); hence it is called "cultivation and fulfillment. This is the liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).

Third, the arising of function refers to the contemplation for the benefit of others (*parārtha*). Having realized the true characteristic and understood that all phenomena are mind-only (*cittamātra*), the mind penetrates and phenomena pervade;
thus, function arises from the essence. Through skillful means (*upāya*) following conditions, although the myriad functions are fully manifested, they do not... [disturb the essence].
To depart from the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is the skillful means for the purity of liberation; this is precisely the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*). Regarding the cultivation of the mind:
although one is a bodhisattva, throughout the causal stage, one has never failed to cultivate as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

As for the perfection of merit and wisdom: these are the foundation of the two benefits. Through the perfection of self-benefit, one achieves fulfillment; because the cause is perfected, one thereby benefits others.
Therefore, he relies upon the compassion that is objectless and unimpeded, cherishing sentient beings as if they were his own infants.
Since all sentient beings share the same essential nature as himself, yet these beings are deluded and lack self-awareness—just like ignorant infants—how could the Bodhisattva not feel profound pity?
Furthermore, since this is called "objectless compassion" (*nirālamba-maitrī*), its manifestation...

The physical body performs the work of transformation. Furthermore, it does not limit itself to the single category of the female form; rather, it necessarily manifests in accordance with the various classes of beings and preaches the Dharma according to their capacities.
Just as with Avalokiteśvara, there is no land among the ten directions where he does not manifest his body—this is precisely the unconditioned and unobstructed compassion of a Bodhisattva.
△ Fourth, the Manifestation of Form.

By the power of his original vows, he encountered the World-Honored One. Desiring to hear the Dharma, he came to the Buddha’s presence and gazed upon the Honored One’s countenance, never for a moment averting his eyes.
He presented the World-Honored One with immeasurable kinds of supreme human offerings, as well as countless exquisite jewel necklaces, making offerings to the Tathāgata.
The great significance is the same as previously explained; the arrival of the kings is largely identical [to what has been described], so it will not be recounted in detail. △ Fifth, the assembly:
each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
△ II. The Assembly of Monastics and Laypeople. First, the classification of types and the manifestation of sincerity:

Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of innumerable people—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, various brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, śūdras, as well as elders and householders from all the kingdoms.
All the people and this great assembly gave rise to pure faith and a heart of profound reverence. Having planted roots of goodness in the past, they were born at a time when the Buddha-dharma exists;

seeking transcendence from the world, they conceived the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find, and thus came to the place where the Buddha was, joining their palms with single-minded devotion.
The two assemblies of bhikṣus are explained as before. Upāsaka means "male lay follower" (upāsaka); upāsikā means "female lay follower" (upāsikā).
These refer to male and female householders who have taken refuge in the Buddha and received the precepts, because they should draw near to and serve the teachings of all Buddhas.
They are also called "pure-faith gentlemen" and "pure-faith ladies," meaning that their conduct is pure and they believe in the existence of the Buddha.

It is the *Dharma*. O Brahmin—here translated as "Pure Conduct"—this was the lineage at the beginning of the kalpa. Because they dwelt in seclusion among the mountains and wilds, people called them by the name "Pure Conduct.

(Master Zhao said: This is an external meaning in the Chinese language. Their distinct lineage possesses its own scriptures, which have been transmitted from generation to generation; they take the study of the Way as their vocation, whether remaining as householders or leaving the home-life.)

Those who rely excessively on their own arts and techniques are people of *māna* (conceit). Furthermore, according to another interpretation, those who inherit and practice the dharma of Brahmā belong to a lineage that claims to have been born from the mouth of Brahmā; they are superior among the four castes (*catur-varṇa*) and alone take the name "Brahman.

This exists only in the five regions of India and not in other countries. The term *brahmacārin* found in various sūtras refers to this same name; it translates literally as "pure lineage," signifying that one is a scion of Brahmā. *Kṣatriya*: Master Guṇabhadra says this means "royal lineage" (*rāja-kula*). Alternatively, it is translated as "lord of the fields.
At the beginning of the kalpa, humans consumed the "essence of the earth" (*pṛthivī-rasa*); subsequently, they ate naturally growing non-glutinous rice. Later...

Human sentiments gradually became deceitful, and each person sought to establish their own private holdings. Consequently, those of virtue were established as leaders, and the land was divided among them;
this was the beginning of kingship. Thus, by tradition, they were given the name [Kṣatriya]; being noble and autonomous, they constitute the royal lineage.
Vaiśya is the same as Viśya; this is translated as "merchant. Śūdra is also called Sthavara; this is translated as "farmer."

"Fields" (kṣetra). These four types are the four castes of the Western Regions. "Elders" (gṛhapati): those who are either advanced in age and of high moral standing, or widely learned and well-informed, possessing the virtue of leadership;
people revere them as elders. "Householders" (kulaputra): those who abide in the Way while remaining at home.
Because he maintained himself with such purity, people called him a *gṛhapati* (householder). The above examples serve as illustrations.
Regarding these various manifestations of sincerity, "faith" (*śraddhā*) refers to that which is deeply patient, desirous, and free from doubt.
Conversely, it is made clear that if even the slightest doubt remains in one’s thoughts, faith is impure. What is here termed "pure" refers precisely to right faith.
This is doubt. Furthermore, it says that believing in worldly dharmas is not pure, whereas believing in supramundane dharmas is purity.

"With earnestness" (*yīnzhòng*) clarifies sincerity. "Past seeds" and so forth describe the existence of causes from previous lives. "Birth and encounter" and so forth celebrate the present meeting with the Buddha.

"For the sake of seeking" and so forth clarifies the purpose of his coming; that is to say, having failed to encounter the Buddha-dharma for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he now fortunately encounters it.
An era of a Buddha is one such rarity. Having encountered an era of a Buddha, it is further rare to hear the Dharma.

And having heard the Buddha’s Dharma, it is even rarer to encounter the Mahāyāna. Yet now that you have already encountered a Buddha, please be certain to preach the Dharma; though it is rare, it is no longer difficult.
If one does not seek the Dharma for transcending the world, one merely encounters an era of a Buddha (where "encountering" [zāo] means meeting). For this reason...
Seeking transcendence of the world, they have come to the Buddha’s presence; they simply join their palms with single-minded devotion. (A portion of the text is missing here;
it should state that they prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, which must have been omitted by the translator. △ Second, concluding by acknowledging his place among the assembly.
Each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of attendants.
△ Fifth, the assembly of non-Buddhist practitioners who have resolved their minds [on the path], in two parts: first, citing their types to demonstrate their sincerity.
Furthermore, there were countless assemblies of various non-Buddhists: non-Buddhists of ascetic practice, non-Buddhists of extensive learning, and non-Buddhists of worldly wisdom.
Delighting in seclusion from non-Buddhists— namely, the Lokāyata and Lokāyatika non-Buddhists who were their leaders—
he had attained the five supernormal powers and possessed mastery over flight. Struck with a sense of wonder, he came to the place where the Buddha was for the sake of hearing the Dharma.

Those who do not believe in the Three Jewels, who do not realize that all is mind-only, and who wander outside the Way with their minds—erroneously calculating and holding false attachments—are called non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

As for ascetics, they include those such as those who throw needles into themselves or lie upon thorns, those who pluck out their hair or smoke their noses, and those who observe the vows of cattle or dogs.

Thinking that the causes of suffering have already been exhausted and that the fruits of happiness will come of their own accord is a form of false seeking; therefore, such people are judged to be non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Their "great learning" is not the great learning of the True Teaching, but rather the study of non-Buddhist scriptures, such as the four Vedas and the treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), which they take as their fame.
These worldly wise ones are able to master worldly mathematics and arts, or the various *śāstra* traditions.
Those among the hundred schools who rely on petty cleverness yet fail to understand the True Dharma are all collectively categorized as non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Those who delight in seclusion are those who distance themselves from the mundane world and find joy dwelling in forest hermitages (*araṇya*).

As for those whose intent is to purify the mind and diminish desires, this has never not been the aspiration to seek the Way; yet they are nonetheless judged to be non-Buddhists because they have not encountered a Sage.
Master: "If one has not heard the True Dharma and practices blindly, though they may dwell in an araṇya (hermitage), they will ultimately achieve no authentic realization.
How can this be anything other than a non-Buddhist path? Lokāyata is here translated as 'Excellence in Debate,' also called 'The Teacher Refuting the Disciple,' or rendered as 'Evil Counter-argument.
Because their questions and answers do not accord with correct principle, they are considered non-Buddhists. *Lokāyata* (路伽耶): [As noted above].
"Trigati" cannot be translated. It is suspected to be *vilokāyata*, which is here rendered as "Left-handed Worldling" (*zuo-shi*).
It is also called "Evil Treatise" (*e-lun*) and "The Disciple Who Refutes the Teacher. This refers to those of the left path who delude the world;

because their calculations do not accord with the ways of the world, they are termed "Non-Buddhists" (*waidao*). Relying on the forceful sophistry of their evil treatises, they act as leaders. They have accomplished five—*//* (text fragmentary).
The "supernormal powers" (abhijñā) refer to the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of past lives, knowledge of others' minds, and the power of spiritual transformations;

because one can penetrate all things through these, they are called the five supernormal powers. Although one may possess these powers, when compared to those of the sages, they are not merely like heaven and earth apart—they are nothing more than faint approximations.
As for "sovereign flight," this refers to the power of spiritual transformations, meaning to travel by means of the void, with a momentum such that—

"Flight": because there is no obstruction for things, it is called "mastery" (*vaśitā*). (In the non-Buddhist practitioners of the Western Regions, five supernormal powers [pañcābhijñā] are possessed; as for the non-Buddhists of this land, it is further unknown how many such powers they possess.

If they do not possess them, they are merely called "heretics. One seeks after these non-Buddhists but does not find them. "To give rise to a mind of rarity," etc., is the intended meaning of the passage. That which is rarely encountered in the world is called "rare" (*āścarya*);
for example, before the Buddha appeared in the world, the six heretical teachers deluded the masses with arrogance and falsehood, and kings... [long]... [text continues].
He who revered me as his teacher suddenly heard that there was a Buddha whose wisdom, eloquence, and the wondrous application of his supernormal powers all surpassed his own.

Consequently, he looked up to him with thirsty longing and paid him homage, coming to listen to the Dharma. His intention was surely to turn away from the heterodox and return to the orthodox, abandoning himself to follow another.
This too was a great expedient means; by means of this matter, he gathered and transformed [beings], using the provisional to lead toward the ultimate reality. Therefore, he led...
The multitude approaches the Buddha. △ Second, the summary of their arrival together with the assembly:
each is accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
△ Sixth, the assembly of non-humans, ghosts, and spirits, in two parts. First, identifying the classes and stating their sincerity.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable and innumerable non-human beings and hungry ghosts, namely: the *akiṃcana* (destitute) ghosts; those who eat what people have vomited;
those who afflict sentient beings; those who eat mucus and saliva; those who are never satiated; the *piśāca* ghosts; the extremely foul-smelling ghosts;
those who eat excrement and filth; those who eat human fetuses; those who eat newborn children; those who eat impurities; and the *maṅgalaja* (auspicious-born) ghosts. Such was the case.
The various spirits, with the great ghost-king Vīrūḍhaka as their leader, abandoned their poisonous minds and took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
They all vowed to protect the True Dharma of the Tathāgata and came to where the Buddha was for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
Prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, they gazed up at the World-Honored One with yearning devotion.

The secular classics state: "Ghost" (*gui*) means "to return. This refers to when a person dies, their flesh and bones return to the earth, their blood returns to the water, and their *hun* and *qi* spirits return to heaven.
Only their subtle, yin energy remains alone, having no place to rely upon; thus they become ghosts. This explanation differs from that of the Buddhist scriptures.

According to the Buddhist scriptures, there are ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), namely the four noble ones and the six classes of ordinary beings. Furthermore, regarding these six classes of ordinary beings...
They distinguish between good and evil, each having three paths. There are three evil paths, namely: hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Thus, spirits and deities each have their own kind; they also have parents, wives, children, and so forth, but they belong solely to the realm of the Yin.

Human beings belong to the realm of Yang (the male principle). Humans cannot see them. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Ghosts (*preta*) mean 'those who fear. This refers to those who are empty, cowardly, and full of dread.

Furthermore, they mean 'majestic,' for they can cause others to stand in awe of their majesty. There are many categories of ghosts, as described in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*; fearing prolixity, I shall not enumerate them here.
As for the hungry ghosts (*preta*), they are specifically the "needle-necked" ghosts; their bellies are as vast as mountains, yet their throats are as thin as [a needle].
The Needle: Because they are unable to eat or drink and constantly suffer from hunger and emptiness, they are called *preta* (hungry ghosts).

As for those who are "ghosts without wealth," it means that because they lack merit and virtue, they cannot obtain food or drink; their throats are like needles and their mouths are like flaming torches. These are also specific names for hungry ghosts.
Those who eat what people have vomited or consume human nasal mucus and saliva—their hunger is evident. Those who "torment others" are those who harm people in the darkness. Not...
The "satiated" (*tṛpta*) are also *preta*s. The *piśāca*s are powerful spirits whose wealth and pleasures resemble those of humans and devas.

The "foul-smelling" (*pūtika*) and "extremely foul-smelling" (*atipūtika*) are the "hairy-foul" (*keśapūtika*) spirits; this means their body hair is coarse and foul-smelling, and they consume excrement, filth, and the like—these four types are thus to be known.
The "Born-Auspicious" (*jātamaṅgala*) are the virtuous among the powerful spirits (*mahābala*), such as those found in the world.
Those who seek fortune and long life shall be granted blessings; he provides protection and can bring forth auspiciousness.
As for *Vilūṭaka*, neither its Indic nor Chinese equivalent is clearly established; he is the sovereign king and thus serves as the leader.
"Abandoning the mind of toxic harm" refers to turning away from evil and returning to goodness. For when one has not yet taken refuge in the Buddha, all harbor a toxic mind in secret.

Those who harm others, having taken refuge in the Triple Gem, all become benevolent deities; hence it is said they "abandon" [harm]. As for those who "guard and protect," this is by virtue of their power of vows.

(Question: The Tathāgata’s supernormal powers are immeasurable; why is there a need for spirits and deities to guard him? Answer: The Buddha’s majesty is vast and great, so he certainly does not require them. However, to honor the Buddha and manifest respect, they attend upon and protect him. Regarding "prostrating with the five limbs":
this refers to both hands, both knees, and the head, all of which reach the ground, like the collapse of Mount Tai.
This is to manifest one's utmost sincerity. As for "those who thirst and yearn," because they have not yet heard the True Dharma, their minds lack the nourishment of wisdom;
they look up toward the True Dharma as one who is thirsty longs for a drink. △ Second, the conclusion and acknowledgment of being with the assembly.
Each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
△ Seven: The Assembly of Bird and Beast Kings. Part One: Identifying the Categories and Stating the Reality.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable and innumerable kings of birds and beasts, such as the king of the *jīvajīvaka* birds, the king of the parrots, and the [king of the] peacocks... [and so forth].
The king of sons, the king of elephants, the king of deer, and all such kings of birds and beasts— with the golden lion king as their leader— all took refuge in the Tathāgata,
the Great Teacher. Desiring to hear the Dharma, they came to the Buddha’s presence and, each according to the power of their vows,
made offerings to the World-Honored One.

Those with two feet and feathers are called birds; those with four feet and fur are called beasts (*śvāpada*). "Beast" (*śvāpada*) means "to guard," signifying that because their strength is great, they are not easily captured;
one must first surround and guard them before they can be caught. Furthermore, those in the wild are called beasts, while those in domesticity are called livestock.
Now, even these birds and beasts listen to the Dharma and are included among the assembly; this means that although their karmic retributions differ, their Buddha-nature is the same.
Because they are identical. The subsequent passage, which records his request for the Dharma, makes it clear that he was also a great master of expedient means (*mahopāya*) who led others by example.
Regarding the *jīvajīvaka* (life-and-life bird): the *Saṃyukta-ratnapiṭaka-sūtra* states, "On the Snow Mountains there is a bird called the 'Shared Life' (*sahajīva*).

It has one body and two heads; while their consciousnesses are distinct, they share a single karmic life-force. Therefore, it is called 'Life-and-Life. Regarding the *śuka* (parrot): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states, "A bird capable of speech."
The *Shanhai jing* states: "They have green feathers and red beaks; they possess human tongues and can speak. The term "Lion King" (*siṃharāja*) refers to various types of beasts.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Lion King is born of a pure lineage and dwells in deep mountains and vast valleys.
He has square jaws and large bones; his body is plump with flesh; his head is large and his eyes long; he is lustrous and clear; his eyebrows are high and broad."
His teeth are white and pure; his mouth and nose are square, large, thick, and full. His teeth are dense, even, and sharp. He extends his tongue, which is red and white.
His two ears are high-set. His hair is glossy and lustrous. His body is broad and expansive; his flesh is firm and well-adhered. His spine is long and his waist is slender.
Its belly is not protruding; it has a long tail and sharp claws. Its feet are firmly planted, and by the great strength of its body, it emerges from its dwelling place.

It stretches its back and yawns, striking the ground with its mouth to manifest great majesty. It does not eat past its time, displaying the signs of early morning to represent the power of the lion king.
Regarding the elephant, the *Yiwuzhi* (Record of Strange Things) states: "As for the elephant, this beast is unique in its physical form."
Magnificent! Its body is twice that of an ox, yet its eyes do not surpass those of a pig. Its nose serves as the servant of its mouth; when one looks at its head, it appears like a tail.

It is docile and obedient, kneeling upon hearing a command. Its tusks are naturally white and pure as jade—qualities praised in the ancient records. Capable of bearing heavy loads and traveling great distances, it is equal [to other noble steeds].
The deer is a wild beast of the mountains and forests; its longevity is like that of an immortal, and it is also called the "Immortal Beast. The male has antlers.
The Golden-Haired Lion King possesses a coat entirely golden in color, which is the manifestation of his virtue. As the sovereign leader of all birds and beasts, he is called the "Foremost.
That all [others] humbly express their sincerity and take refuge in him means that they, by means of their own...
They took refuge in the Buddha and made the Buddha their teacher; therefore, he is called the Great Teacher (*mahāśāstṛ*). (A "teacher" [śāstṛ] is the Dharma; it is the model for humanity.

It is a designation for one who instructs others in the Way; furthermore, it refers to the Lord. Regarding the phrase "desiring [to hear]," although even birds and beasts know to listen to the Dharma, they come to the Buddha's presence because they seek to transcend their kind.
Regarding the phrase "each according to [their capacity]," this means that they wish to create the causes for merit and thus offer worship. △ Second, presenting the cause and desiring the fruit.

They addressed the Buddha, saying: "We pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept our meager offerings, so that we may forever leave behind the seeds of evil karma that lead to the three miserable realms, obtain the retributive fruits of the blessings and joys of humans and devas, and have the Great Vehicle’s nectar-like Dharma-gate opened and proclaimed."
"Swiftly sever your ignorance; you shall attain liberation. Having spoken these words, the king of birds joined his palms with single-minded devotion and gazed up at the Tathāgata.
The final three phrases express a humble plea for acceptance. Regarding the offerings presented by birds and beasts:
they feel self-reproach for their own bodies, which are destined for retribution, and realize that the causes [of their current state] must have originated in previous lives.

Furthermore, they suppress themselves in the thought that if they do not cultivate meritorious causes again in this life, they will fare even worse in their future rebirth than they do in this one. For this reason, they look to the Buddha to accept their offerings.
Taking the Buddha as the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), if one receives [the teachings], it is like sowing seeds; thus one may look forward to the attainment of good fruits.

One shall certainly and forever leave behind the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*—namely hell, hungry ghosts, and animals), and the seeds of karma will naturally be extinguished. (The "three miserable realms" are the effects: namely hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

"Evil karma" refers to the direct causes that induce these three realms, namely the active seeds of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, greed, anger, and delusion. That which is perfumed by these active manifestations constitutes the seed; furthermore, it serves as the direct cause of karma. This is because when the seeds ripen...)

Thus, active manifestations arise; through these manifestations, one is able to attract karmic fruits. Riding upon these fruits, one must again perform karma, and by means of that karma, one further perfumes the seeds. For this reason, the three—afflictions, karma, and suffering—revolve without ceasing. This king of birds wishes to be eternally liberated from them. How marvelous! How marvelous!
"Obtaining and receiving" [the lower] refers to the formal seeking of wholesome fruits. "Expounding and clarifying" [the lower] refers to further seeking the supramundane Dharma.
Furthermore, it is called the Mahāyāna because its intent does not plot for minor fruits. The Mahāyāna is the Dharma; the ambrosia (amṛta) is...
This is an analogy. For a single drop of ambrosia can raise the dead and restore life; a single word of the Mahāyāna can transform an ordinary person into a sage.

As for the term "Dharma-gate" (*dharmamukha*): a "gate" has the sense of a passage, serving as the thorough path for transcending the world—that is, by means of the Buddhist gate, one exits the suffering of the triple realm.
The phrase "swiftly severing [delusions]" below indicates the intention to realize sudden enlightenment in a single lifetime, without passing through the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Ignorance is precisely delusion; liberation is precisely nirvāṇa. The subsequent description of the ritual at that time merely expresses the sincerity and reverence of the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind].

(Now, this king of birds and beasts did not merely see the Buddha and offer him tribute; he was further moved by emotion to seek the Dharma. He desired to sever ignorance as quickly as possible and vowed that he must certainly attain liberation.

How much more so for those who are the most spiritual among the Three Powers—none surpasses humans. If a human being does not act accordingly, I can do nothing for them. Question: The sutra says, "He addressed the Buddha, saying: 'I only pray... and so forth.
"Can birds and beasts speak human language? He replied, "There are three reasons. First, each species of bird and beast has its own language;
although humans do not understand it, the Buddha understands it. Second, because of the sincerity of their coming to pay homage, they are moved by the power of the Buddha's grace;
thus, even though they are birds and beasts, they are able to speak human language. Third, through the resonance of intent, although birds and beasts cannot [speak]..."

As for what people say and what they think, that which is silently recited within the mind, the Buddha knows it all himself. △ Third, the conclusion: acknowledging his participation with the assembly.
Each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of attendants.
△ Second, the assembly of Yama Rāja’s ministers. First, the categories are indicated and sincerity is invoked:
Furthermore, there are hundreds of thousands of Yamarāja kings, together with countless great rākṣasas of various forms and types.

As well as various wicked kings, the officials and subordinates of the netherworld, the jailers and judicial officers—all, by the Buddha’s majestic power, abandoned their malevolent intentions and came together with King Yama to listen to the Dharma. They addressed the Buddha, saying:
"All sentient beings, due to ignorance, crave the pleasures of the five desires and commit the five heinous crimes, thereby entering the various hells and revolving in saṃsāra without end."
Exhausted by the causes of their own karma, they undergo great suffering and affliction, like silkworms in cocoons entangling themselves with their own threads.

We only pray that the Tathāgata will rain down the great Dharma rain to extinguish the fires of hell, bestow the cool breeze, open the gate of liberation, and close the gates to the three evil realms.
When King Yama had spoken these words, he made offerings of various precious jewels to the Tathāgata with a single-minded heart.
He paid homage and circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times.
Some call him Yama; this is translated as "Quiescence" (Jìngxī), because he causes those who commit evil to rest from their unwholesome karma.

Alternatively, it is translated as "Obstruction" (Zhē), meaning he obstructs them so that they do not create evil. Or it is translated as "Twin Kings" (Shuāngwáng), for both the elder brother and the younger sister act as lords of the earth.

The Lord of Hell is the chief administrator among the officials of the netherworld. Because the elder brother governs the affairs of men and the younger sister governs the affairs of women, they are called the "Twin Kings.
They are also known as the "Dharma Kings" (*dharmarāja*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* asks: "Are they so called because they cause harm or because they bring benefit?
It answers: "Because they benefit sentient beings. When sentient beings arrive at the presence of the King, he causes them to remember [their past deeds]."
He then manifested a body resembling theirs and addressed them, saying: "You yourselves created these deeds; you shall now receive their fruit.

Because you have experienced the results of evil, do not accumulate new karma. Once the old karma is exhausted, there will be a time for liberation from suffering through the benefit of sentient beings."
Therefore, he is named the Dharma King. Five hundred *yojanas* beneath this Jambudvīpa lies the kingdom of King Yama;
its length and breadth are likewise the same. The *rākṣasas* are the wardens of hell, their forms being variously terrifying, hence they are called "of diverse kinds.
The various evil kings refer to those such as Qin Guang, Chu Jiang, and others, or those who preside over the eighteen hells, who are also so designated.
"King" refers to the Lord of the Netherworld. "Official" refers to the presiding officer. "Subordinates" refers to the retinue. "Jailers" refers to the adjudicators.
"Criminal officials" refers to those who administer the penal code. "Calculating merit and demerit" conveys the sense of weighing, evaluating, and investigating.

Whether through the examination of official records or the verification by the karma-mirror, evil karma is treated as transgression and met with painful punishments, while good karma is regarded as merit, leading one to rebirth among humans or devas.

Having received the Buddha’s descent [of power], they turn their gratitude toward the Buddha, saying that it is only by relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the application of his grace that they are able to abandon their evil minds; therefore, they come together with Yama to listen to the Dharma.
This serves as a counter-illustration: were it not for the power of the Buddha, there would be no leisure to hear the Dharma. Why is this?

As for these kings and others, if they are provisional manifestations, they are bodhisattvas and need not be discussed; however, if they are actual beings, they too have been moved by evil causes and must undergo suffering.

Furthermore, while attending to royal affairs, how could they find the leisure to practice? (Another sutra states: "In a single thought-moment of malice, King Yama takes charge of all matters in hell and undergoes suffering himself.")

This, too, cannot be discussed. In the past, King Yama was King Viśā; he fought against King Vaidarśi, but his military forces were no match for the enemy. Consequently, he made a vow: "In a future life, may I become the lord of hell to punish these offenders. His eighteen great ministers and a million followers all made the same vow.

King Viśā is the present King Yama; the eighteen great ministers are the present lords of the eighteen hells; and the million followers are the ox-headed *ābhas* (hell-wardens). The *Niraya Sūtra* states:

"Three times each day and night, a great copper cauldron filled with molten bronze appears spontaneously before him. A powerful ghost lays the king upon a bed of hot iron and, prying open his mouth with an iron hook, pours the molten bronze into it. From...

Passing down through the throat, there is nothing that is not scorched and consumed. It is the same for those great ministers; thus they undergo suffering. Just as when they did not receive [the teachings], each presided over their respective duties—how could they have had leisure for spiritual cultivation?

[The disciples] bowed to the Buddha and requested the Dharma. All [teachings] do not exceed ten categories. The five desires are: wealth, beauty, fame, food, and sleep; or alternatively, form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch—all things that can be craved.

These constitute the conditions of karma. The five heinous acts (*pañcānantarya*) refer to: killing one's father, killing one's mother, [killing an Arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and causing schism in the Sangha].

To murder an Arhat, to shed the blood of a Buddha, and to disrupt the harmonious Sangha that turns the Wheel of Dharma—according to worldly discourse, these constitute even greater acts of rebellion than regicide.
With ignorance as the cause, the five desires as the condition, the commission of evil deeds as the karma, and entry into the various hells as the fruit, one is like a silkworm in its cocoon:
entangled and unable to free itself. I only pray that you will descend and grant your request.

"Dharma. Fire is a metaphor for the suffering of hell; rain refers to water. Since water can extinguish fire and wind can dispel heat, these two both serve as metaphors for the power of the Dharma, which can rescue beings from all sufferings.
"Liberation" (vimokṣa) is *nirvāṇa*. "Opening the gate" is like preaching the Dharma.
"Gate" has the meaning of "passage," for by passing through it one exits the three realms (*tridhātu*). "Closing" has the meaning of "obstruction," so as not to allow [rebirth] again.
"Entering. The above—requesting the Dharma—is the cause for wisdom (*prajñā*); the below—making offerings—is the cause for merit (*puṇya*).
"Circumambulating" means to turn around; "completely" means all around. There are two reasons why one must circumambulate completely: first, it is the ritual standard of the Buddha.
Second, they serve as the outward manifestation of those who engage in the practice of the Way’s meaning. △ Second, the conclusion summarizing his inclusion with the assembly:
"Together with several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
△ Fourth, the general conclusion on the gathering of the assembly.
Each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit on one side.

Prostrating at the feet is the mark of reverence for seeing the Buddha; withdrawing to sit is the decorum for listening to the Dharma. When teacher and disciple assemble, there are fixed rules for such rites.
As for the phrase "each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet," it means that with their most honored heads, they paid homage to the Tathāgata.
To bow down with both feet is the ultimate expression of reverence and the sincerity of ritual propriety; it is also the established protocol for a disciple serving a teacher.
As for withdrawing to sit on one side: once the prostration at the feet has been performed, one sits with hands folded like wings;
this too is the fixed rule for maintaining order between the honorable and the humble. Thus concludes the general introduction.

△ Second, the Specific Preface (this serves as the formal cause for the occasion). 2. First, the assembly of the guest and host. 2. First, the sequence of the Buddha’s majesty.
[The Ritual Procedure].
At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon a lion throne of precious lotus flowers.
That lion throne was the color of deep blue lapis lazuli, adorned with various rare and wondrous jewels interspersed as ornamentation; its stem was made of crystal beads and refined purple-gold.

It was fashioned in the shape of lotus petals. Its lotus pedestal had filaments made of maṇi jewels, and it was accompanied by eighty-four thousand great precious lotuses of Jāmbūnada gold as its retinue.
"At that time" refers to the moment when the great assembly had gathered and the paths of teacher and disciple were in perfect harmony.

"World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*) is the title for the uniquely venerable Śākyamuni Buddha appearing in the world. "Seat" refers to the throne; its shape resembles a lotus flower, symbolizing fearlessness.
"Jewel" is a term of honor. Because the Buddha’s body sat upon it with both legs crossed in the *paryaṅka* posture, [it is called a "jeweled seat"].
"Seated, etc. and "The color is deep blue (*gāndārava*)," etc., clarify the essential characteristics of the precious throne.
"Deep blue" refers to a lustrous blue-red hue; "lapis lazuli" (*vaidūrya*) refers to a transparent precious substance. Thus, the throne is composed of *gāndārava* lapis lazuli.
"Of various kinds," etc., reveals the adornments of the throne. "Rare and wondrous" is a general term for all types of jewels; their intermingling manifests the splendor.
Their intermingled arrangement constitutes the general characteristics of the lotus pedestal (*padmāsana*). Below, *sphatika* (crystal) is specifically explained: the stalk is the body of the flower;
the leaves are the petals; the dais is the seed-vessel; and the filaments are the stamens. "Maṇi" means "wish-fulfilling.

Regarding the passage beginning with "eighty thousand," it demonstrates that virtues do not exist in isolation, as they possess their own retinue. "Jāmbūnada gold" refers to the finest among all golds.
This is like the finest gold. It is truly because the Sage’s use of ritual implements must embody symbolic teachings; it is not like worldly people who merely love ornate decorations.
The seat symbolizes the essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), and the Buddha symbolizes the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*).

The Buddha sitting upon that seat symbolizes the union of initial enlightenment with original enlightenment to achieve ultimate enlightenment (*nisthā-bodhi*). Now, these two—original and initial enlightenment—are present in every person.
It is inherently present; it also possesses its own causes for attaining Buddhahood as well as the fruits of adornment.
Furthermore, the lotus represents the cause and the Buddha represents the fruit; that the Buddha sits upon the lotus throne signifies that the fruit is accomplished in dependence upon the cause.
Moreover, the various [lotuses] represent the fact that the essence of nature is inherently endowed with myriad virtues. The "eighty thousand" below represents the eighty-four thousand dharmas.
The gates all exist in dependence upon nature; therefore, they constitute its retinue. The seats are shaped like lotuses to signify that while dwelling in the mud, they remain unstained;

emerging from the water, they are fragrant and pure, serving as a metaphor for the nature of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). Though existing within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), it remains unstained;
though in nirvāṇa, it is uniquely sovereign. The Tathāgata realized this, whereby causes were perfected and the fruit reached its ultimate limit, attaining bodhi in accordance with thought.
Indeed, it is because the Tathāgata has manifested this through the wordless Way to express and awaken the human mind (the Master is one who manifests fearlessness;

the lion is the king among beasts and has nothing to fear. This symbolizes that the Buddha is the "lion among men" and likewise has nothing to fear; therefore, it is called the Lion Throne). △ Second, the sequence on the assembly’s reverent sincerity.
Surrounded by the great assembly before and behind him, they made offerings, paid homage, revered, and praised him.
The Buddha sat in their midst while the multitude encircled him from without, like the myriad stars surrounding the North Star; his reverence was held deep within their hearts.

Regarding the offerings presented: when feudal lords have an audience with the Son of Heaven, as for their offerings, incense and flowers are arranged in rows and jade and silk are displayed in abundance;
as for their reverence, they are respectful and composed, their demeanor solemn and sincere;

as for their praise, they speak in eulogies, employing metaphors and analogies that are appropriate, such as the hymns of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, each according to its own particular theme. △ Second, the Invocation.
II. The Source and Lineage. Part One: The Tathāgata’s Formal Manifestation. Section One:
Demeanor Expressing Virtue. At that time, the Bhagavān sat cross-legged upon the lion throne;
his demeanor was exceptionally sublime, like Mount Sumeru composed of the four jewels, naturally towering high above the great ocean, or like hundreds of thousands of suns illuminating the void.
He emits immeasurable light that destroys all darkness, like a full moon disc among the myriad stars,
shining alone with cool radiance that illuminates the world with clarity.
"Bhagavān" is also called "Bhagavat. There are six meanings for this single name.

Among the "Five Non-Translations" elucidated by the Great Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty, this is categorized as "not translating because it contains multiple meanings. Regarding these six meanings, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Sovereignty, brilliance, and physical majesty; renown, auspiciousness, and nobility—since these six qualities are perfectly complete, [he is called Bhagavān]. Therefore...
The name *Bhagavat* is manifested as follows: "Sovereign" (*īśvara*) means that the Tathāgata is not bound by afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Blazing" (*tejasvin*) means that the Tathāgata’s fierce flame of the fire of wisdom penetrates to the infinite.
"Majestic" (*prabhāsvara*) means that the Tathāgata is adorned with the excellent beauty of the thirty-two marks. "Renowned" (*yaśasvin*) means that the Tathāgata is perfected...
"Because the Dharma-realm of Bodhi is universally heard. Regarding "Auspiciousness" (Śrī): it means that wherever the Tathāgata arrives, misfortune is extinguished and blessings arise.
Regarding "Noble and Honored" (Bhagavat): it means that the Tathāgata is surrounded by protection from both sages and ordinary beings, being uniquely honored throughout the ten realms.
Regarding "sitting in the full lotus posture" (*paryaṅka-bandha*) and so forth: it means to interlace the two feet with the soles facing upward, maintaining an upright and dignified body.
It is as follows: borrowing the mountain to manifest its virtue is a metaphor for the Buddha-body.

Sumeru is the same as Mount Sumeru; here it is called "Wondrous High Peak. It is composed of four treasures—gold, lapis lazuli, silver, and crystal. "Abiding" means dwelling; that is, it dwells within the great ocean.
Emerging from the water, it measures eighty-four thousand *yojanas*, towering above all other peaks; hence it is so called.

It stands far apart. (The metaphor of Mount Sumeru for the Buddha’s body has three meanings. First, its height and magnitude are immeasurable; it is the sovereign of the four continents and the support for the heavens of desire.

This metaphorically represents how the Buddha-way is great, serving as the support for the holy and the ordinary across the nine realms. Second, it is honored as the king of all mountains and remains unmoved by the eight winds. This metaphorically represents the Buddha’s majestic and dignified deportment; as the patriarch of a hundred spirits, he cannot be deluded by Māra.

Third, it is composed of various jewels, which metaphorically represents the Buddha’s possession of myriad virtues. Because there are these three meanings, it is compared to Sumeru. "Like hundreds of thousands" and so forth below metaphorically represent the Buddha’s light. It is like the sun traversing the sky.

Heaven and earth are universally illuminated; how much more so are hundreds of thousands? This is a metaphor for the light of the Buddha’s body, which is able to shatter the darkness of ignorance (the "darkness of ignorance" refers to *avidyā*) of sentient beings.
It is also as follows: it is a metaphor for the light of the Buddha’s wisdom. *Koṭi* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "jing" (a unit). One *jing* equals ten *zhao*; it is a vast number.
A *koṭi* full moon is a metaphor for the excellence of the Buddha’s wisdom. Furthermore, one— (Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at the end.)
The wheel is like the full moon; its pure radiance shines so brightly that it eclipses the brilliance of the host of stars, let alone those as numerous as *koṭis*.
As for the moon being called "cool," when the heat of a scorching summer is unbearable, the rising of the moon brings coolness, for it can dispel the affliction of heat.
Thus, the Buddha’s wisdom is complete and perfect like the full moon; it cannot be defiled by delusions, just as the moon [cannot be tainted].
Its purity can shatter afflictions like the coolness of the moon. The "multitude of stars" is a metaphor for the hundred spirits (*śatam ṛṣayaḥ*), manifesting the Buddha’s unique supremacy.
Furthermore, while the sun and moon illuminate only the four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*), the Buddha’s wisdom can illuminate the ten dharma-realms (*daśa-dharmadhātu*).
Even if one were to use hundreds of thousands of suns and *koṭi*s of moons as a metaphor, it would still fall short. Why? Because although there may be many suns and moons, in the end...
It is finite, for the Buddha’s wisdom is infinite. △ Second, the certain attainment of the various heavens has two parts. First, the ability to attain meditative absorption:
he enters the most excellent samādhi of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), called the "King Adorned with the Jewel Necklace of the Mind. Having dwelt in this absorption, ...
Body and mind are unmoving.
If one discusses the Buddha’s samādhi, fundamentally there is no entering or exiting; there is no time when he is not present, and no place where he is not in meditative concentration.
That he now demonstrates entering from a state of non-entry is because sentient beings cling to signs; it is also to manifest in accordance with their capacities. *Samādhi* is translated here as...

"Right reception" (*samyaksamādhi*) is explained as before. Regarding "the supreme goodness of the Peak of Existence" (*bhavāgra-parama-kuśala*): this also uses a metaphor to clarify meditative absorption.

The Peak of Existence is the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), which constitutes the ultimate summit of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*). "Supreme goodness" is a term of praise; it refers to having reached the highest level within the heavens.
This may be called the most supreme and most virtuous. It is likened to the Buddha’s meditative absorption (samādhi), which is as lofty and remote as that;
it is named "Lowering the Mind" (*hsin-hsia*), a designation for emerging from the Buddha’s meditative absorption. The worldly *kaṇṭhaka* necklace (*yǐngluò*) is composed of precious jewels;

this is likened to the Tathāgata’s mind in meditative absorption, wherein ten thousand virtues are gathered. This constitutes the adornment of the *dharmatā*. That body and mind do not move is the characteristic of meditative absorption.
It is like the bright moon over a cold pond, or a solitary peak against distant waters—majestic, vast, and inconceivable.
How could it fail to move and inspire the various devas? This is truly because the Tathāgata is the Great Sage of both the mundane and supramundane realms.

When spoken, it becomes a sutra; when applied, it becomes the Dharma. Now that he has entered meditative absorption, this is the place for directly pointing to the human mind to see one's nature and attain Buddhahood.
As a koan says: "When the World-Honored One ascended the seat, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said:"
Contemplate deeply the Dharma of the Dharma King; such is the nature of the Dharma King’s Dharma. It is likewise so now in this very certainty.

That which the Buddha realized and that which sentient beings inherently possess—the myriad virtues of the *dharmatā*—are revealed face-to-face right within the state where body and mind are unmoving.
This is called the teaching of wordlessness. If one wishes for people to realize it directly and immediately, this is precisely awakening to the Buddha’s vision and knowledge;

this is termed "sudden awakening. To manifest the Buddha entering meditative concentration is termed "sudden teaching. If one does not so realize, one must wait for the Tathāgata to emerge from concentration. Alas!
This may be called a song of the "Warm Spring" or "White Snow"—it is of no benefit to the mediocre or the ignorant. II. The Various Heavens.
The third section on making offerings: First, the offering of the gods of the formless realm.
At that time, all the sons of heaven in the formless realm rained down immeasurable varieties of subtle and wondrous flowers and incense, descending from the void like clouds.
Regarding the devas of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they possess consciousness but lack physical form. As for the statement that they now rain down flowers and incense:

since they lack physical form, their ability to cause such rain has two meanings. First, while they lack the physical matter resulting from karma (*karmaphala-rūpa*), they do possess the physical matter resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhiphala-rūpa*).

This refers to the manifestation of signs within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), such as seeing the Buddha and making offerings to Him. Second, although they lack physical bodies, they possess spiritual power;

thus, there is no reason why it would be impossible for them to manifest supernormal powers within concentration, see the Buddha, and present offerings. △ Second, the offerings of the various devas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The eighteen Brahmā kings of the various heavens in the realm of form rained down countless celestial flowers of manifold colors and hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of exquisite Brahmā-incense,
which filled the void and descended like clouds.
The meaning of the text is clear. Regarding the eighteen Brahmā heavens, they are as previously listed among the assemblies. △ Third, the offerings of the various devas of the desire realm:
the devas of the six heavens of the desire realm, together with the hosts of their sons, by the power of their celestial merit, rained down various flowers, such as *utpala* flowers.
The padma flower, the kuvalaya flower, the puṇḍarīka flower, the campaka flower,
the atimuktaka flower, the pārijātaka flower, the sumanā flower, the māndārava flower, and the mahāmāndārava flower.
Mañjūṣaka flowers and great mañjūṣaka flowers fell in profusion from the void, making offerings to the Buddha and the multitude of Dharma jewels.
Furthermore, there rained down priceless celestial incense;
its fragrance was like clouds of a hundred precious colors, and by the power of the devas, its scent filled all these worlds, making offerings to the great assembly.
The initial mention of "all devas" is a general term for ministers and subjects; it is only when they further include the Son of Heaven that they become "Heavenly Kings.

Regarding those who rain down flowers through the power of merit, this refers to receiving blessings as a result of having cultivated merit during the causal stage; it simply means making offerings to the Buddha with one's mind.
Flowers and incense arrive spontaneously; these manifest naturally through the power of merit.
As objects transform according to the mind, their varieties differ, hence they are called "diverse" (*nānāvidha*).

*Utpala*—here translated as "auspicious omen," or "blue lotus," or "spiritual omen"—is not a flower commonly found in the human world. It appears only when a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) is born. The wheel...
Before the King appeared in the world, these were utterly non-existent; however, because they existed in the heavens, it rained [flowers] as an offering to the Buddha.
The character for "rain" (雨) is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). That which falls from above is called "rain. *Pāṭhama* means "red lotus flower" (*raktapadma*).
*Kuvalaya* means "earth-delighting flower," or alternatively, "yellow lotus flower. *Puṇḍarīka* means "white lotus flower" (*śvetapadma*).
*Campaka*: translated here as "small yellow flower. *Atimuktā* (formerly called *shènsīyí*): alternatively translated as "dragon-licked flower.
This plant is shaped like hemp; it has red flowers and green leaves. Its seeds can be used for oil and are also suitable as incense. *Pāriśika*:
translated here as "summer-born flower," and also as "rain flower," because it grows only during the rainy season.
Sumanā; it is also called Sumana, which translates as "Well-Guiding the Mind" or "Flower that Satisfies the Mind.
It is yellowish-white in color and exceedingly fragrant. The tree does not grow very tall, reaching only three or four feet, with branches drooping downward like a canopy.
*Mañjuṣa* means "soft" or "gentle," and also refers to the "red flower. *Mahā* means "great. *Mandārava* means "pleasing to the mind" or the "white flower.

Regarding the phrase "falling in profuse, chaotic abundance": *pinfen* (profuse/chaotic) describes a state of intermingling or profusion. It signifies that flowers of various colors are intermingled as they fall from the sky;
viewed from afar, their variegated patterns appear like butterflies dancing across the vast expanse of space. Looking down upon them...
Fragrant, like brocade spread across the great earth—thus making offerings to the Buddha and the multitude of Dharma-jewels;

"the multitude" refers to the great assembly, meaning the universal offering to the Triple Gem. Furthermore, regarding the rain of priceless celestial incense: this refers to that which possesses color but lacks fragrance.
If one lacks the virtue of intelligence, how could they be considered a gentleman? This is why flowers rain down and incense rains down even more.
As for "the incense being like clouds," it refers to the smoke of the incense drifting and curling like auspicious clouds swirling through the great void.
Regarding the "hundred-jeweled colors," this refers to the intermingling radiance of fragrances and colors, like various precious gems clustered upon Mount Hua.
As for "the world," it refers to the inconceivable power of spiritual transformation; thus, clouds of fragrance pervade everywhere to make offerings to the great assembly.
The Great Assembly is precisely the Dharma-multitude of Vulture Peak; with masters and attendants intermingling, there is nothing that does not offer service.

The section on the fixed invocation of the devas is concluded. △ Third, the manifestation of auspicious omens by Bhagavat, in two parts. First, the transformation of the fixed state to bestow supernormal powers, in two parts. First, the transformation of the fixed state.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and, remaining on his original seat, again entered the Lion’s Rushing Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*).

As in the previous instance, he entered meditative absorption with body and mind unmoving, silently moving the various devas. The offering of flowers and incense by the devas also has its symbolic significance:
the samādhi represents movement within stillness, while the rain of flowers from the devas represents stillness within [movement].
Movement. Yet, as host and guest meet together, it signifies that movement and stillness do not depart from their proper place.

The rain of flowers and incense further signifies that cause and effect exist within a mere moment: the flowers represent the cause; the multiplicity of the flowers' colors represents that the cause is not of a single kind but must necessarily comprise the myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*).
The incense represents faith (*śraddhā*), meaning that without faith one cannot practice the cause, and without the cause one cannot achieve fruition.
Having first established faith, it further speaks of making offerings at a great assembly. This means that both the principal and the retinue are offered to.

The "principal" is the Buddha; the Buddha represents the fruition-Buddha of one's own mind. Offering flowers and incense to the Buddha collectively symbolizes that the causal capacity can achieve fruition.

Furthermore, offering to the assembly symbolizes that there is no category of being who does not possess this cause. Without leaving one's current location and without passing even a moment, [the offering is complete].
Thus, cause and effect are fully realized. Now, since this section states that he emerges from meditative absorption and enters it again, there is also a symbolic significance:
the former emergence symbolizes movement returning to stillness, thus entering; this present emergence symbolizes stillness giving rise to movement, thus arising.

Having arisen, he enters again, symbolizing being still while truly moving, and being moving while truly still. This may be called "movement and stillness sharing a single source. Indeed, this is the Buddha’s...
The meaning is profound; therefore, I have set it forth and explained it. I trust you will not weary of its detail.

As for why this samādhi is named "Lion’s Boundless Display" (*siṃhavijṛmbhita*), there is likewise a symbolic significance to the dharma it represents. Now, the lion is the king of beasts in the world, symbolizing fearlessness.
"Displaying" (*fèn*) means to spread wide or manifest; "speedy" (*xùn*) means rapid and swift. This is because the nature of the lion loves to roar.
*Qiú*. When the male and female dance and frolic most rapidly, one sees no lion, but only golden light; this expresses the height of joy.
To employ this as the name for a samādhi expresses the Buddha’s extreme joy, desiring to expound the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground to fulfill the Buddha’s heart-vow.

(The *Siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi* appears in the *Fajie Cidi*; there is such a name for this samādhi. It borrows a metaphor to manifest the Dharma, just as in the world a lion’s vigorous display is for two purposes. First, for...)

First, it vigorously shakes off dust and dirt; second, it is able to run forward and backward with such swiftness as to surpass all other beasts. This samādhi is also like this: first, it vigorously shakes off the delusions that obstruct meditative concentration; second, it is able to enter and emerge from various dhyānas with such swiftness and without interval.

This differs from the various *dhyānas* and *samādhis* in that it possesses both the meanings of "entering" (*praveśa*) and "emerging" (*vyutthāna*). First, regarding the "vigorous entry into *dhyāna*" (*dhyāna-vaśitā-praveśa*): this refers to departing from the unwholesome states of the desire realm and entering the first *dhyāna* with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).

Proceeding in this manner, one enters successively the second, third, and fourth *dhyānas*, as well as the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and finally the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*). This is called the vigorous entry. Regarding the "vigorous emergence from *dhyāna*" (*dhyāna-vaśitā-vyutthāna*): this refers to arising from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling and returning to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Arising from this concentration, one returns to the sphere of nothingness; likewise through the spheres of infinite consciousness and infinite space, down to the fourth *dhyāna* and the first *dhyāna*. Finally, emerging into the state of the distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), this is called the vigorous emergence. Nevertheless, although it leads [the practitioner]...

This is because their names are the same, yet their meanings are not entirely identical. Why? Because that [term] is a specific name for the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihāra*), and since it culminates in the cessation of feeling and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*), it is a concentration of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*). Since this present sutra belongs to the Mahāyāna, they are not entirely the same;
therefore, they are explained separately in the commentary (the wise should reflect upon this). △ Second, the application of the term to both [vehicles], in two parts: first, the general heading.
He manifests great supernatural powers, causing this trichiliocosm to quake in six ways.
With meditative concentration as the essence and supernatural power as the function, the function arises from the essence, whereby the wondrous meaning is fully revealed.
This is the Sahā world, the realm of the Buddha’s single transformation. As for "trichiliocosm," it refers to three times one thousand; taken together—
It is called a "great trichiliocosm" (mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu), not three thousand individual great trichiliocosms.
Just as one sun and moon and one Mount Sumeru constitute one set of four continents (cāturdvīpaka), one thousand sets of four continents constitute a small chiliocosm (sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu);
one thousand small chiliocosms constitute a medium chiliocosm (dvisāhasra-madhyama-lokadhātu); and one thousand medium chiliocosms constitute a great trichiliocosm.
The world is thus called "threefold," and when one speaks of "a thousand," it refers in total to a Great Trichiliocosm.

Within this, ten billion suns and moons, ten billion Mount Sumerus, and ten billion sets of four continents constitute a single Sahā world, which is precisely the realm governed by one transformation body of the Tathāgata.
For this reason, it shakes and trembles to awaken and stir the human mind. And therein...

This refers to obtaining benefit therein. As for the "six kinds," they are: shaking (*iṅgita*), surging (*utsarpaṇa*), trembling (*kampa*), striking (*nirghāta*), roaring (*nirghoṣa*), and bursting (*sphoṭana*).
These do not consist of both form and sound; rather, shaking, surging, and bursting constitute form, while trembling, striking, and roaring constitute sound (shaking is defined as tossing upward;

surging as rising up; trembling as having sound; striking as startling objects; roaring as a deep resonance; and bursting as splitting open. Generally, wherever an earthquake is severe, there must be a place where it splits open). △ Second, the detailed explanation has two parts. First, the transformation...

The marks were adorned and purified, meaning they shook, shook intensely, shook everywhere and intensely; surged, surged intensely, surged everywhere and intensely; trembled, trembled intensely, trembled everywhere and intensely; and quaked.
It shook violently; it shook everywhere and violently. It roared; it roared violently; it roared everywhere and violently. It crashed; it crashed violently; it crashed everywhere and violently.

Furthermore, this world surged in the east and subsided in the west; it surged in the west and subsided in the east; it surged in the south and subsided in the north; it surged in the north and subsided in the south; it surged in the center and subsided at the edges;
it surged at the edges and subsided in the center. Its ground was adorned and pure, and entirely soft and supple.
Moving directly is "movement. The movement of the four continents is "extreme movement. The universal movement of the great trichiliocosm is "pervasive extreme movement.
The same applies to the other five [types of trembling]. These correspond to the "movement," "pervasive movement," and so forth, as described in other sutras.
Each type has three aspects; together they form six sets of three, totaling eighteen aspects. These represent the purification of the eighteen realms (*dhātus*). Furthermore, below this...
It separately manifests the momentum of surging forth, meaning the east surges while the west sinks, and so on. "Surging" refers to rising upward; "sinking" refers to falling downward;
it does not mean being submerged and becoming invisible. The second line regarding the earth means that this Sahā world is originally a defiled land.
This is that which is produced by the defiled minds of sentient beings. That it is now purified through spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) also manifests both the phenomenal and the noumenal.
The phenomenal aspect refers to the exercise of spiritual power, whereby the defiled is transformed into the pure to awaken and stir the human mind.
The noumenal aspect refers to the analogy of the human mind-ground: it means that the human mind is originally pure, yet when defiled by delusions, it becomes impure; now, through this adornment...

This purifies the manifestation. It is intended to show that what is defiled can be turned into purity. Although the earth is fundamentally solid and firm, it now surges up in the east and sinks down in the west;
though firm, it is made supple by the Buddha’s supernatural power. Firmness represents the delusion of the human mind—being firm yet failing to awaken.
Now, the Buddha wishes to cause this delusion to be transformed into awakening; therefore, he uses the softening of the great earth as a symbolic representation.
...so it is. △ Second, the benefits obtained by all living beings:
It causes herbs and trees to flourish and brings benefit to all sentient beings, such that throughout the trichiliocosm there are no longer hells, hungry ghosts, or animals.

As well as other beings in the states of no-leisure and the evil destinies, all shall be freed from suffering. After casting off this body, they shall be reborn among human beings and the six heavens of the desire realm;
all shall remember their past lives and, with great joy and exultation, proceed together to the presence of the Buddha with a heart of profound reverence.

They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bringing various precious jewels and countless necklaces; having realized the emptiness of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala-śūnyatā*), they thereby repaid the Buddha’s kindness.

"Herbs" (*huì*) is a general term for grasses, further encompassing the sprouts and crops of the hundred grains; "wood" (*mù*) is a collective name for trees, likewise including flowers, fruits, gardens, and groves.
That "they flourish and grow" refers to the benefit obtained by insentient plants and trees. [The same applies to] all living beings.

This is for the benefit of all sentient beings. As for making the three thousandfold world-system free from hells and the like, this is brought about by the compassionate spiritual power of the Buddha, which transforms the three evil realms into the three good paths.

Regarding "hell" (*naraka*), the name is established according to its meaning: it is called a hell because it is a prison beneath the earth. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Jambudvīpa..."
Five hundred *yojana*s beneath the continent, there lies a hell. This hell consists of various large and small realms, namely the eight cold and eight hot hells and so forth.
Those who have committed extremely grave evil deeds in the world fall into these places;
yet, according to their respective causes, they experience different retributions. Collectively, these are known as the hells. There are also [realms for] hungry ghosts.
There are three types. The first refers to those whose karmic offenses are extremely heavy; for kalpas on end, they have not even heard the names of water or grain.
