The next type merely seeks out the human world to cleanse away pus, blood, excrement, and filth. The lowest type is satisfied at times with a single meal.
These sentient beings who commit evil deeds are born into this realm due to their stinginess and greed. As for the animals:
This refers to those with hair and horns, those with scales, shells, or feathers; those with four legs, many legs, or no legs;

and those that move through water, on land, or in the air—namely, sentient beings who have committed evil karma and, due to their ignorance, are born into these realms, as well as other beings in the unfavorable states (*akṣaṇa*) and miserable destinies (*durgati*).
Regarding this, there are two interpretations: first, those who commit evil karma while within the human realm.
These are the states of no leisure (*akṣaṇa*). These are those who do nothing but commit evil; they are like workers who have no leisure.

They are also the "evil destinies" (*durgati*) among humans. Second is the Avīci Hell (*Avīci-naraka*); the sentient beings suffering there endure immeasurable pain that constantly oppresses their bodies, and thus they have no leisure.
This is the true evil destiny. May all who attain liberation from suffering cause their evil karma to be suddenly [exhausted].
[The karmic] retribution is eliminated; thus it ceases. The above demonstrates the World-Honored One’s compassion (*karuṇā*) in uprooting suffering.

From "Having abandoned this body" onwards, it demonstrates his loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in bestowing happiness. As for "abandoning the body": the previous retribution is already exhausted. As for "being born among humans or devas": the subsequent fruit is immediately attained. Regarding "all [of them] know their past lives":
this is self-evident through the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) possessed by devas, whereas such is not the case for the human realm. This is because...
"Empowered by the Buddha’s power," they also recognized their past lives. "Rejoicing," and so forth, means they were moved by the Buddha’s profound kindness.
"Rejoicing" refers to the joy within the mind; "leaping for joy" refers to the outward manifestation of that state.

"Solemnly and respectfully" refers to the height of sincerity; "prostrating at the feet" refers to the ultimate expression of reverence. "Holding [the Buddha’s feet]," and so forth, represents the etiquette of showing respect upon meeting. "Awakening to the three," and so forth, refers to the vision.

This is the merit of repaying [the Buddha’s] kindness. Regarding the three wheels: first, one is free from attachment to a self; second, there is no perception of external phenomena; and third, one even discards the mind that realizes this.

Thus, both the self and phenomena are empty (*ātma-dharma-śūnyatā*), and even emptiness itself is discarded. To realize and witness in this manner is truly the profound repayment of the Buddha’s grace.

(Question: Realizing the emptiness of the three wheels is merely for one's own benefit. How can this be considered repaying his grace? Answer: Being able to achieve one's own benefit is precisely what constitutes repaying his grace. This is because [the realization] causes the sixfold earth tremors.)

Originally, this was intended to startle and awaken the human mind, causing it to turn its heart toward the Way. Now that you have realized the true principle and attained self-verification, which accords with the holy intent of the Buddha, this is precisely what constitutes repaying his kindness.

Thus far, we have moved from the evil realms to the human and celestial realms, and from the human and celestial realms to sudden awakening. Having awakened to the three voids, one will inevitably enter the ranks of the sages.

However, the interpretations provided above all rely on the literal text to explain the meaning, attributing the entirety of the merit to the Buddha. If one were to seek the meaning beyond the literal text, it would also...
All is but a manifestation of the mind; it merely borrows the power of the Buddha as a superior condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

This is because the Tathāgata’s shaking of the earth, his purifying of the world, and so forth, are truly external conditions that awaken [the mind]. When sentient beings of the three evil realms encounter such a superior condition, their minds become empty in a single thought-moment, and the three miserable paths are instantly stilled.
They are reborn among humans and devas, and by further awakening to the three emptinesses, they spontaneously realize Bodhi.

It is manifested. If judged according to the teachings: merely attributing gratitude solely to the Buddha constitutes the Initial Teaching (śāsanā). If the mind realizes emptiness through self-attestation, this is the Sudden Teaching (tongjiao).
If one is born from the evil realms into the human or celestial realms, and from the human or celestial realms cultivates the three kinds of emptiness—this is the Gradual Teaching.
A long time had passed, yet it was still not as long as the brief interval of the Tathāgata’s shaking of the earth; thus, there is no obstruction to either prolonging or abbreviating time.
Furthermore, this also contains the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). △ Second, the actual manifestation of auspicious omens, in three parts: First, the Tathāgata emits light.
At that time, the Tathāgata emitted a great radiance from the region of his chest and from all his pores,
named "The Playful Supernatural Powers of the Bodhisattvas," which causes those who have not yet regressed from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* to do so.
The color of this radiance was like Jāmbūnada gold.
Regarding the places where light is emitted from the chest and the pores: on the Tathāgata’s chest there is the *svastika* mark (*śrīvatsa*), which is the auspicious sign of ten thousand virtues.
From this, light is emitted, symbolizing that the light itself possesses ten thousand virtues.

Furthermore, each of the various characters represents the eighty-four thousand pores, all of which are capable of emitting light; the light from the chest is the primary one, while the lights from the various pores are secondary.
"Attendants. Furthermore, the light of a single hair serves as the principal, while the lights of all the other hairs serve as its attendants.

Because one observes that these principal and attendant lights mutually illuminate and mutually enter one another, with each light encompassing every other light in infinite layers, they constitute a single treasury of light, perfectly interfused and unimpeded;
this is what is meant by "all below. This name is established according to the meaning: because the principal and attendants intermingle their lights, it is like the wandering of a Bodhisattva.

The playful exercise of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) is of inconceivable and wondrous application. From the phrase "causing [them] not to regress" onwards, the chest represents the essence (*tattva*), while the various lights represent wisdom (*jñāna*).
Their essence is one, yet the functions of their wisdom are immeasurable. "Anuttara" and so forth refer to the ultimate fruit (*phala*).
Since it is said that one does not regress, we know that realization is certain. Yanfu says that "superior gold" refers to the color within the light;

because it flashes like gold, he uses refined gold as a metaphor for it. II. The Manifestation of Signs Within the Light. This has two parts. First, the manifestation of the signs of the six classes of ordinary beings.
This has two parts. First, the signs of the environment (the world of dependent retribution). This has two parts. First, the general characteristics.
This golden light universally illuminates the trichiliocosm as well as other worlds.
This trichiliocosm is this very realm; "other realms" refers to the worlds of the ten directions beyond this great trichiliocosm.
While this realm is the principal one and the other realms are its companions, once they have received the illumination, they too are able to radiate light and achieve fusion with it.
The realms are likewise identical to the light, layered upon one another without end; such is the general characteristic of all worlds. △ Second, the specific characteristics:
extending even to the ten billion Sumeru Kings of Mountains, including all the Snowy Mountains, Fragrant Mountains, Black Mountains, Golden Mountains, and Jewel Mountains.
As well as Mount Meru, Mahāmeru, Mucilinda, Mahāmucilinda, the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains, and the Great Iron Ring Mountains;

the rivers, great oceans, flowing springs, and bathing pools; and the ten billion sets of four great continents, the sun, moon, and stars, the palaces of the devas, the palaces of the nāgas, the palaces of all the honored spirits, and all the kingdoms and cities.

In royal palaces and villages, within the realm of Yama, and in all the eight cold and eight hot hells—even using the abbreviated expression "down to two syllables"—this refers to the ability to illuminate.
That is to say, this light does not merely illuminate general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), but illuminates even specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
"Miaogao" (Wondrous High) refers to Mount Sumeru; "one hundred billion" refers to [one hundred billion] Sumerus.
Regarding these numbers: "King" means that Mount Sumeru spans across the ocean; none of the other mountains can equal it, for it alone is honored as king.
"All" refers to the fact that within every world-system there are such mountains. The Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*) are the place where the Tathāgata practiced the path.
*Mīlū* (Mount Meru) is translated here as "Radiance"; this refers to the seven golden mountains, which, having gold as their substance, possess light.
*Vimala*. *Mucilinda* is translated here as "Stone Mountain. *Mahā* means "Great," thus it is the "Great Stone Mountain.
The Great and Small Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*) both surround Sumeru outside the Seven Golden Mountains, acting as its outer protection. The rivers and other features are easy to understand.
As for the Four Great Continents, they are on the four sides of Sumeru: Pūrvavideha in the east, Jambudvīpa in the south, Aparagodānīya in the west... [and so forth].
The continent of Videha, the continent of Uttarakuru, the sun and moon below—all these encompass the myriad phenomena as well as various palaces and celestial mansions.

"Celestial mansions" refers to the fact that each of the devas has their own palace. "Dragon palaces" refers to the fact that within rivers, streams, lakes, and seas, there are all residences where dragon kings dwell.
As for the "various spirits," this refers to those among the Five Peaks and Four Rivers who are honored by being titled Emperors or Kings.
As well as the various ghost generals and their like, each having their own palaces and dwellings, including all those below;
next, extending to the human realm, with its territories and kingdoms, administrative districts, villages, market towns, and settlements.

Within the realm of Yamarāja, that is, amidst the profound darkness, there are all those below who have emerged from the specific manifestations of the underworld: the eight cold and eight hot hells. All... [the rest of the passage].
This is the appearance of many hells. △ Second, the appearance of sentient beings as their primary retribution:
the appearance of sentient beings with sinful karma undergoing suffering, and even the appearance of animals and hungry ghosts throughout the ten directions undergoing suffering.
All the worlds and the various states of suffering and pleasure experienced by sentient beings within the five destinies are all manifested within this great golden light.
The first two phrases describe the manifestations of suffering within the hells, such as copper snakes, iron dogs, and mountains of blades.

The sword-trees and other such instruments oppress and harm people, causing them to suffer with cold, meanness, and terror, leaving them with no means of escape—such are the characteristics [described].
All of the above refers to the manifestations of suffering in the hells within this single realm of Sahā;

however, there are omissions in the text, as the meaning implicitly includes the realms of hungry ghosts, animals, and various other destinies. As for the phrase "even throughout the ten directions," this refers to Sahā.
Beyond this, it exhaustively encompasses the characteristics of all sentient beings subject to outflows (*sāsrava*). Regarding "beasts and below," ghosts and beasts are separately mentioned;
however, they alternate between being manifest or hidden relative to their primary realm. In the primary realm, the hells are manifest while ghosts and beasts are hidden;

here, ghosts and beasts are manifest while the hells are hidden. This is likely due to the ingenuity of the translator. Regarding "all [sentient beings] and below," this generally enumerates various classes of beings in the world.
"Interval" refers to the world of humans, the world of devas, and so forth; as these categories are extremely numerous, it is called "all.
The "five destinies" consist of the three evil paths, as well as the two paths of humans and devas. "Destiny" (gati) means to head toward or to fall into.
Thus, the retributive fruits of these five paths are the places where sentient beings head toward and fall into. Regarding the characteristics of suffering and pleasure, [it says] "three..."

The realms of the hells and so forth are the marks of suffering; the realms of humans and devas are the marks of pleasure. Because one receives the five desires with a satisfied mind and experiences them with joy, they are called the "marks of pleasure.
This is identical to what is said in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "The karmic conditions of good and evil deeds result in retributions that are beautiful or ugly;

all of these are seen here. Thus it says, "All such things appear," and so on. Having finished manifesting the marks of the six ordinary states of existence, [the text proceeds to] two: manifesting the various...
The second section concerns the sacred marks. First, the general heading:
furthermore, within this light, there appear the various manifestations of Bodhisattvas practicing the Buddha-way.
Although it says "Bodhisattvas," this also includes all Buddhas. △ Second, the detailed enumeration has two parts. First, the specific manifestation of Śākyamuni’s causal stage.
The characteristics of the fruit are twofold. First, a general explanation of cause and effect:
In the distant past, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was King Prabhāsa;
he first gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and eventually attained the Way of the Buddha beneath the Bodhi tree in the Śāla grove.
He entered into *nirvāṇa*.

Śākya is the clan name of the Buddha; here it is translated as "Capable Benevolence" (*Nengren*). "Capable" refers to his skillfulness in responding to sentient beings, and "Benevolence" refers to his compassion that benefits both self and others.
Thus, he takes compassion as his clan name. One who is called a Bodhisattva bears this title prior to the realization of the Way.
Furthermore, in the section below, it is clarified that in a previous life as a cause, he was a great king named *Prabhāsa*.
This king was the first to generate the bodhicitta, which constitutes the very root for attaining Buddhahood.
However, since one cannot attain Buddhahood without the bodhicitta, the tree named "Bodhi" refers to the Pippala tree; it is not the case that the tree itself is the bodhi.
Because he attained the path of Bodhi while sitting beneath this tree, the name of the tree is designated by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound based on the enlightenment he realized.

As for his attainment of the Buddha-way: having practiced in the Snowy Mountains, on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, upon seeing the morning star appear, he suddenly attained great awakening;
all delusions were completely emptied, and he realized that the nature [of reality] is inherently present. Therefore, it is said that he became a Buddha. This...
This marks the beginning of his attainment of the Way. The mention of the *śāla* trees below further clarifies the end of his life:

internally encompassing over three hundred assemblies of sutra discourses and preaching the Dharma for forty-nine years, he finally completed his work of transformation before passing away within the *śāla* grove.
He entered *nirvāṇa*. "Śāla" means "firm and solid" (*kaṭhina*) in this language. "Entering *nirvāṇa*" refers to withdrawing one's traces and returning to the True.

(Because it does not change with winter or summer, it is called "firm and solid. Its bark is greenish-white and its leaves are glossy. It is also translated as "High and Remote," meaning its stature is the highest, towering loftily above all other groves.

It is also called the "Crane Grove" (*haṃsa-vana*). It is also called the "Pair of Trees" (*yugma-vana*), because on all four sides there are pairs. The pair in the east symbolizes permanence and impermanence; the pair in the south symbolizes bliss and non-bliss; the pair in the west symbolizes self and non-self...)

The "pair" in the north represents the pure and the impure. On each side, one tree withers while the other flourishes. A pair is behind the Buddha, a pair is in front of the Buddha, a pair is at the Buddha’s feet, and a pair is at the Buddha’s head.

After he enters *nirvāṇa*, the two pairs in the east and west merge into a single tree, and the two pairs in the south and north likewise merge into a single tree; all hang down and cover the Tathāgata. Those trees appear dismal, turning entirely white.
II. Specifically explaining cause and effect. 1. First, explaining the duration of the process.
Within that interval, there are three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
A *kalpa* is also called an *asaṃkhyeya*; "asaṃkhyeya" means "innumerable. "Saṃkhya" means "to exhaust.
This refers to a number such that even those among humans and devas capable of calculating cannot know it through the utmost reckoning; this is called one *asaṃkhyeya*. As...
This process occurs three times; thus it is called the "three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. This refers to an exceedingly long duration, beyond the reach of thought.
Furthermore, the mention of "one million" is a general expression for the vastness of time.
This is the length of time Śākyamuni spent practicing the path from his initial generation of the bodhicitta until now, all occurring within the single period of the emission of light.
It can be manifested in a brief moment; thus it may be said that throughout the ten periods of past and present, the beginning and the end never depart from the present thought.
△ Second, clarifying the path practiced, in two parts: first, a general clarification of all practices.

All forms of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), as well as the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*, constitute the Buddha’s four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). First is immeasurable loving-kindness:

it consists of cherishing sentient beings and constantly seeking what brings them happiness, benefiting them according to their specific needs. Second is immeasurable compassion: this refers to feeling pity for [sentient beings].
All sentient beings undergo various kinds of suffering; constantly harboring a sense of sorrow for them, one immediately uproots their suffering and rescues them, causing them to attain liberation.
This is the immeasurable joy (*muditā*). Whenever one sees sentient beings free from suffering and obtain happiness, one’s heart is filled with delight and rejoices.
This is the immeasurable equanimity (*upekṣā*); that is, regarding the sentient beings who are the objects of focus, to be without feelings of either aversion or attachment is called equanimity.

Furthermore, one contemplates all sentient beings as equally attaining a state free from hatred, free from attachment, free from resentment, free from anger, free from enmity, and free from affliction;

therefore, it is called the immeasurable mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-apramāṇa-citta*). Regarding the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*: the Sanskrit term *pāramitā* is translated here as "reaching the other shore.
This means that birth and death (*saṃsāra*) are like this shore, while afflictions (*kleśa*) are like the middle of the stream, and *nirvāṇa*—[is the other shore].

It is "the other shore. Because Bodhisattvas, by means of the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates, benefit both themselves and others and thereby attain Nirvana, they are metaphorically described as having "reached the other shore.
(The *Bhadrapāla-kalpika-sūtra* states that the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Joyful King (*Nandirāja*) regarding the methods for cultivating practice:

from the first "Radiance" up to the "Distribution of Relics," there are three hundred and fifty *pāramitās*. Each of these dharma-gates possesses the six perfections of giving, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, totaling two thousand one hundred.)

The *pāramitās* (perfections). Regarding the four types of sentient beings—those characterized by greed, hatred, delusion, and equal proportions—he teaches and awakens each through these two thousand one hundred *pāramitās*.

Combined, they total eight thousand four hundred *pāramitās*. Each of these is further multiplied by ten, resulting in a total of eighty-four thousand *pāramitā-dharmaparyāyas*. These *dharmaparyāyas* serve as the unsurpassed medicine for the three realms; for hundreds of thousands of kinds of people, they eliminate the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśas*).
(As explained extensively according to the numerical categories of the Dharma). 2. Specifically manifesting cause and effect. Part three. First, the characteristics of past causal practices.
In the past, he was a Golden Wheel-Turning King who ruled over the four continents as far as the limits of the great oceans.

His subjects were numerous and flourishing, and his lands were prosperous and joyful. He governed the world through the True Dharma for immeasurable eons, and all manner of rare treasures filled his realm.

At that time, that wheel-turning monarch, observing that all worlds are entirely impermanent, grew weary of the pleasures of the five desires and renounced his position as a wheel-turning monarch to leave the household life and study the Way.
Or, as the beloved son of a king in a great kingdom, he abandoned his body and life to throw himself before a starving tigress.
At times he acted as King Śibi, cutting his own body to save a dove; at other times he saved a pregnant deer by sacrificing his life as a deer king;
and at other times, on the Snowy Mountains, he gave up his entire body to seek a half-verse of the Dharma.
"Past" refers to that which precedes the present; it is a general term for bygone times. As for the "Golden-Wheel King," he is explained as previously mentioned in the general introduction.
The word "king" (王) is pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*); it signifies arising and flourishing.
One who presides over the world with their person is called a king. The "four" refer to the four continents, as explained before, all of which are governed by the Golden Wheel.
Therefore it is said: "He rules over the four quarters of the world. This refers to the entirety of the great earth; taken collectively, it expresses the vastness of his sovereign governance.

"The people" below indicates the atmosphere of Great Peace (*taiping*). "True Dharma" (*saddharma*) refers to the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśala-karmapatha*) or the supramundane teachings.
"Transforming the world" means instructing and transforming worldly people toward goodness. "Throughout immeasurable *kalpas*" indicates the long duration of time. "All" below refers to the kingdom.
When the land was at its peak, it was during a time of abundance and peace; this refers to the conditions for generating the bodhicitta.

It is said that while the kingdom was in the midst of such prosperity, the king, amidst the turbulent current of worldly affairs, perceived that all phenomena in the world are impermanent—namely, that the world undergoes the cycles of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, and that sentient beings are subject to birth, aging, sickness, and death.
Regarding his "aversion to the pleasures of the five senses," it means that the king observed that although these pleasures were present before him, they were [ultimately unsatisfactory].
The arising of suffering from the destruction of pleasure is entirely impermanent. Furthermore, because one creates various karmas within the midst of craving for pleasure, one comes to loathe it;
thus, he relinquished his throne, left the household life, and studied the Way. The above describes the characteristics of the Wheel-Turning King’s study of the Way.

Alternatively, regarding the instance below where he gave up his body to feed a tiger, as described in the *Bao'en jing* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness): during the Buddha's causal stage, he was King Śatrujit.
The Prince went into the mountains for recreation and saw a starving tigress with seven cubs. The tigress was emaciated and weak, unable even to move;
the lives of both mother and cubs would soon come to an end. Prince Sattva then reflected:

"In this world, human life is spent in vain, a mere drifting through birth and death without any true benefit. It would be better to sacrifice my own body to save the lives of these tigers. He then gave himself to them.
A karmic connection was formed. [The Buddha] made a vow to seek the path to Bodhi by means of this [story]: that of King Śibi, who cut his own flesh to save a dove.
"Śibi" is translated here as "giver," which conveys the meaning of the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā).
When the Buddha was in the causal stage as King Śibi, a frightened dove flew to the king's presence, seeking his compassionate rescue. Subsequently, a hawk also flew before him, demanding the dove.
He wished to devour it, saying, "This is my food. If you rescue him, then my life shall end. Why does Your Majesty pity him and thus afflict me?
The King, mindful that the hawk was starving, then cut flesh from his own body to substitute for the pigeon.
Regarding the one who saved the pregnant doe and relinquished his body as a deer king: during his causal stage, the Buddha once acted as a deer king, presiding over a herd of deer. There was one...
There was a pregnant doe who, while carrying her young, was captured by a hunter intent on killing her. When the deer king saw this, he said to the hunter, "She is with child;
to kill her would mean the death of two. I am willing to take her place; do not kill her.
Upon seeing this, the hunter was moved by his benevolence and felt shame within his own heart, thinking, "If even a beast knows such kindness, why should I commit evil?"
He then purified his mind and repented his transgressions, vowing never again to take life. Regarding the one who sought the gāthā on Mount Himavat:

while the Buddha was in the causal stage, he was a *ṛṣi* practicing the Way on Mount Himavat. Having not yet attained the true transmission, he practiced asceticism in vain; realizing this was not the truth, he sought the Dharma everywhere.
At that time, a celestial being manifested in the form of a *rākṣasa* and, standing upon the mountain, recited the gāthā: "All conditioned phenomena..."

"Impermanence! This is a phenomenon of arising and ceasing. Upon hearing this, the seer gazed at him from afar, prostrated, and said to the rākṣasa, "This pure Dharma of the nectar of immortality—I have obtained but half of the jewel. I pray that you, O benevolent one, will explain it directly to me.
The rākṣasa replied, "My belly is famished; I have no strength, so how can I speak? If you wish to obtain it, provide me with offerings. [The seer] asked, "What do you desire, O benevolent one?"
[The Bodhisattva] offered [himself]. The rākṣasa said, "Only human flesh and warm blood can satisfy my hunger.

The seer said, "If you will tell me the way, I am willing to offer it; I am prepared to sacrifice my entire body to seek this half-verse. The rākṣasa said, "'When birth and death have ceased, extinction is bliss.
The seer rejoiced and immediately transcribed it upon wood, stone, and other surfaces. He then ascended swiftly.
The mountain-dweller cast himself as an offering. At that time, the rākṣasa was originally a manifestation of Śakra;

he immediately revealed his true form and prostrated with the utmost reverence, saying, "When you attain Buddhahood, you must deliver me first. This is the account of sacrificing one's entire body for half a verse, as recorded in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
If one were to discuss the immeasurable causal practices, they would be infinite; here, however, the broad is encompassed by the concise. All [is thus accounted for].
What among the myriad practices does he not manifest? △ Second, the manifestation of the signs of the beginning and end of his life in the world, in six parts. First, the sign of taking birth:
he may manifest taking birth in the household of King Śuddhodana.
Regarding his manifest birth: when the Buddha had completed his practice over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, he resided within the inner court of Tuṣita Heaven as the Bodhisattva Mahāprajñāpāla (Huming).

At that time, observing sentient beings and giving rise to compassion, he mounted the sun-disk scented elephant and entered the royal palace as a kinsman in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, with King Śuddhodana as his father and Queen Māyā as his mother.
For his mother, on the eighth day of the second month, she went to the Lumbinī Garden beneath an Ashoka tree;
raising her right hand to pluck a flower, he was born from her right side. At that time, nine dragons emitted water to bathe his golden body.
He then walked seven steps in every direction, looked around the four quarters, and said: "In the heavens above and on the earth below, I alone am honored.

This was his descent from the primordial source to manifest his traces in birth. The *Puyao jing* (Sutra of Universal Radiance) states: "He emitted a great light everywhere, illuminating the three thousandfold world-system.
The *Zhou shu yiji* (Record of Anomalies in the Book of Zhou) states: In the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao, the year of Jiayin, on the eighth day of the fourth month...
One day, the rivers, streams, springs, and ponds suddenly overflowed; the wells all spilled over; and the palaces, dwellings, mountains, rivers, and the great earth all shook violently.
That night, an aura of five colors entered and pierced the Taiwei constellation, pervading the western quarter and appearing entirely in shades of blue and red.
King Zhao immediately questioned the Grand Astrologer Suyou: "What omen is this? Suyou—
Suyou said, "There shall be a Great Sage born in the West; therefore, this auspicious omen has appeared. King Zhao asked, "What will become of it in the world?
Suyou replied, "For the time being there will be no other change, but after a thousand years, his fame and teachings will reach here.
King Zhao immediately dispatched someone to engrave this upon stone and bury it before the Tianci Temple in the southern suburb. 2. The Signs of Leaving Home.
He renounced sixty thousand palace ladies and abandoned all manner of exquisite music and entertainment. He left the city walls to enter the homeless life;
having traveled through the four gates, he resolved to renounce the world.

Abandoning his noble golden wheel-turning sovereignty, the wealth of the world, the abundance of the five desires, and the pleasures of the palace ladies, he mounted a white horse and followed Chandaka, while a celestial deity supported the horse’s hooves as he departed.
He traveled through emptiness; hence it is said he "surpassed the city walls and left the home. "Surpassing" (*yú*) means to transcend. This signifies that the city walls could not obstruct him.
There are two kinds of "leaving the home": first, leaving the secular household; second, leaving the household of the triple world (*tridhātu*).

Since he was manifesting transformative teachings after having already attained the fruit [of enlightenment], he served as a model for worldly people. As for leaving the household of the triple world, he had done so long ago. For now, we shall speak of leaving the secular home.
Regarding the worldly household: it is said that wealth and honor cannot corrupt him. △ Third, the aspect of ascetic practice:
for six years he practiced austerities, consuming only hemp and wheat daily.
As for "ascetic practitioner," this means that having already renounced the position of the precious wheel-turning monarch, he went to the Snowy Mountains because there was a Way to be sought.

Aware that he possessed a body, cold winds assailed his frame and scorching heat invaded his person. It reached the point where sparrows nested upon his head and spiders wove webs between his eyebrows;
reed shoots pierced his knees, and hemp and wheat served as sustenance for his hunger. No predatory beast or venomous insect failed to assail him.
Six years had already passed, which may be called the height of solitude and destitution. Yet he never wavered in his resolve—this is what is meant by being "poor and lowly."
He could not be moved. △ Fourth, the aspect of destroying Māra:
subduing all non-Buddhists. Having destroyed the armies of Māra beneath the Bodhi tree, [it is said that] "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika) are those whose minds wander outside the Way;
they do not know the Great Way of their own mind, but instead rush outward in pursuit. Therefore, they are so named.

"Non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). "To subdue" means to bring under control. At that time, the Tathāgata would either subdue them through supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) or refute them through the power of wisdom and debate, causing them to admit defeat and return home;
this is called "subduing all non-Buddhists. (This phrase is more appropriate if placed after the account of defeating Māra and attaining enlightenment.
Regarding "defeating the army of Māra": in Sanskrit, *māra* means "one who can snatch away life. This refers to when a Bodhisattva...
Beneath the Bodhi tree, as he was about to attain enlightenment, the great earth shook and he emitted a vast radiance that eclipsed the palaces of Māra.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān dispatched his three daughters to disturb the Bodhisattva’s pure conduct; however, by means of his supernatural power, the Bodhisattva [repelled them].
The demonesses were transformed; they all became old women. The Demon King was greatly incensed and issued commands throughout his retinue.

Above, thunder shook the heavens and hot iron balls rained down; blades, wheels, and weapons crisscrossed through the air. He drew his bow and loosed arrows, but the arrows suspended in mid-air turned into lotus flowers.
Unable to inflict harm, the host of demons fell into sorrow and dispersed in all directions. This is...
This is the mark of destroying Māra: namely, that his majestic power cannot be humbled. △ Fifth, the mark of attaining Buddhahood:
he realizes *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Attainment" means realization. *A* is a Sanskrit word; here it is translated as "non-. *Anuttara* is translated as "unsurpassed.
*Samyak* is translated as "right and equal. *Saṃbodhi* is translated as "perfect enlightenment. Combined, they are called "Unsurpassed Right and Equal Perfect Enlightenment."
This means that above the fruit of Buddhahood, there is no further dharma; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). Because it is the Middle Way, it is called "right" (*samyak*).

Because it is identical to the Buddha-nature of sentient beings, it is called "equal" (*sama*). Because it distinguishes itself from the lack of awakening of ordinary beings, it is called "awakening" (*bodhi*).

Because it distinguishes itself from the partial awakening of the two vehicles and the incomplete awakening of bodhisattvas, it is called "perfect awakening" (*samyaksambodhi*). This is what the Buddha has realized.
This is the ultimate fruit. Following his previous defeat of the demonic armies, he emitted a great radiance and immediately entered meditative absorption.

On the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, beholding the morning star, he attained great enlightenment and reached the final realization of Buddhahood; this constitutes the sign of attaining Buddhahood.
△ Sixth, the summary of the manifestation of light:
Such hundreds of thousands of Ganges-sands of inconceivable practices and vows, along with all their various manifestations,
were all suddenly revealed within this great golden light.
These are the vows the Tathāgata made during his causal stage and the deeds he performed; indeed, they are as manifold as the sands of the Ganges.
Since the compiler of the sutra could not describe them all in detail, it says "all such" and so forth. This concludes the section on the characteristics of the beginning and end of the present life.
△38. The Characteristics of the Eight Sites of the Spiritually Efficacious Stūpas. Part One: General Introduction.
Furthermore, within this light, there appear the inconceivable eight great precious stupas of the Tathāgata.
There are two meanings to the term "inconceivable": first, the inconceivability of the spiritual efficacy of the precious stupas.

This means that although the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, these precious stupas remain in the world; thus, while all sentient beings are engaged in making offerings and prostrations, by virtue of their spiritual power—
It should be augmented so that those sentient beings may obtain merit and longevity; or, for those of sharp faculties, they may clarify their minds and awaken to the Way.
Are such benefits conceivable? Second, the number of stupas is inconceivable.
This is because the Tathāgata’s water-moon transformation bodies number in the hundreds of thousands of billions, and worlds are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River. Within a single world...

These eight stupas exist in every world-system; they are numerous, immeasurable, and beyond all conception. In the Sanskrit language, *stūpa* means "sacred shrine" (*ling-miao*) or "lofty and manifest.
Because the world constructs these to enshrine the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) and honors them with great respect, they are called "Jeweled Stupas.
II. A detailed enumeration of the eight: First, the Jeweled Stupa at the place of birth.
The Kingdom of Kośala; the palace of King Śuddhodana; the birthplace stūpa.
Kośala is merely a different Sanskrit term for Kapilavastu. Although it is called a royal palace, it was actually beneath the Aśoka tree in the Vairañjā Garden.
This is the place where the Buddha descended into birth; thus, a jeweled stūpa was constructed to commemorate it.
Miraculous traces. △ Second, the Jewel Stūpa at the Place of Attaining Buddhahood.
In the kingdom of Magadha, by the side of the city of Gayā, beneath the Bodhi tree, is the Jewel Stūpa where [the Buddha] attained enlightenment.
The *Sūtra of the Eight Great Sacred Stūpas* states that he attained perfect enlightenment on the banks of the Nairañjanā River, and thus a stūpa was erected there for veneration.
This present sūtra, however, says it was on the outskirts of the city of Gayā. These two accounts are not contradictory;
for the Nairañjanā River is within the jurisdiction of Gayā, and being near this river is equivalent to being on its outskirts. His attainment of Buddhahood is as previously described.
Explanation: A stūpa was erected at this site so that future generations, upon seeing the stūpa, would look up to his virtue, resolve to cultivate the Way, and practice the path.
△ Third, the precious stūpa at the place where the Dharma was first turned.
In the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, the first turning of the Wheel of Dharma took place; this is the Jewel Stūpa for Delivering Beings.
In Sanskrit, it is called Vārāṇasī, which here [in Chinese] is translated as "Deer Park" (Luyuan). This scripture provides both the Chinese and Sanskrit names together;
because the park is located in this country, "Vārā" refers to the country, and "ṇasī" refers to the park. In ancient times, kings raised deer there, hence the name.

It is named Mṛgadāva (Deer Park). Regarding the "first turning of the Wheel of Dharma": when the Buddha first attained perfect enlightenment, he preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths here to deliver the five bhikṣus and others.
These people consist of five individuals: namely, three from his paternal clan and two from his maternal clan.
Therefore, a stūpa was erected there as an offering to mark the place where the True Dharma first arose. (Pārāyaṇa is translated as Jiang [River]).

It encircles the city; it is the capital. It lies within the borders of North India. This garden is a dependency of this kingdom (the name is derived from its connection to the capital). △ Fourth, the identification of the location of the non-Buddhist heretics' precious stupa.

In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, at the Jetavana Grove, he debated with various non-Buddhist teachers for six months; having attained omniscience, his fame was such that a precious stūpa was erected [in his honor].
Śrāvastī is here translated as "Abundant Virtue. The kingdom was abundant in the four virtues, as explained previously. "Giver of Orphans" (Anāthapiṇḍada) is the virtuous title of the elder Sudatta;
he was a high minister of King Prasenajit who was able to provide for all widowers, widows, orphans, and the solitary.
Because people praised his virtue, he was called "Giver of Orphans. This garden belongs to the elder Anāthapiṇḍada.
He purchased the site by scattering gold and established a vihāra and a Dharma hall. He invited the Buddha to dwell there during the rainy season retreat and preach the Dharma.
There were ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist practitioners who debated with the Buddha for six months; they were all defeated and fell into error.
Those non-Buddhists praised him with the utmost eloquence as the "All-Knowing One" (Sarvajña), and from this point on, the Tathāgata’s fame spread far and wide. Therefore...
The construction of this stūpa serves as a manifestation to regulate those outside [the Buddhist fold]. △ Fifth, the site of divine wonders:
the precious stūpa at the edge of Kanyākubja in the kingdom of Andhra ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, together with the Brahmā King.

Together with Śakra, Lord of Devas, and a multitude of one hundred and twenty thousand beings, they descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven via three jeweled stairways manifesting in mid-air to Jambudvīpa;
at that time, a miraculous jeweled stupa appeared.
Andhra has not yet been translated. Kanyākubja (Curunüchéng) is so named because of the "crooked girl. It is within the borders of Central India.
Formerly, there was a great tree-dwelling ṛṣi who settled his spirit in meditative absorption for tens of thousands of years; he then arose from his concentration.
He saw the king’s hundred daughters coming to the palace to request his presence; however, only the youngest daughter was permitted to serve as an attendant.
The rishi, harboring anger, uttered a malevolent curse: "May ninety-nine of the daughters have their waists bend all at once.

From that time on, it was named the City of the Bent Women (Kanyākubja). *Trāyastriṃśa* means "the Thirty-three"; there are eight heavens in each of the four directions, with Śakra residing in the center.
The Emperor [Śakra] and others are collectively named the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa). Regarding the mention of "the Mother" and so forth: the Mother is Lady Māyā;
after giving birth to the Buddha, she was reborn in this heaven. When the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, wishing to repay his mother’s kindness, he ascended to this heaven to preach the Dharma.
The Brahma King and Śakra, leading a retinue of one hundred and twenty thousand, escorted and protected him as he followed the Buddha. As for the manifestation of the three precious staircases:
Because the Buddha had been in the heavens for a long time, the people of the world did not see the Tathāgata; they stood gazing intently throughout the day.

Moved by their devotion, the Buddha employed his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) to manifest three jeweled staircases. "Staircase" (*krama*) refers to a flight of steps, specifically the successive tiers descending from above.
He caused them to be seen, a marvel so extraordinary as to startle the beholders, so that all were able to see the Buddha and give rise to great joy.
"Jambū" refers to Jambudvīpa in the south. Regarding those who build stupas and make offerings:
although the Buddha is a Great Sage, his not forgetting the kindness of his mother is a manifestation of supreme filial piety. △ Sixth, the place where the Mahāyāna was preached at the Jewel Stupa.
In the kingdom of Magadha, on Vulture Peak near the city of Rājagṛha, he preached the Great Prajñāpāramitā, the Lotus Sūtra of the One Vehicle, the *Cittabhūmi-sūtra*,
and other Mahāyāna texts such as the *Ratnakoṭi-sūtra*.

The name of the country is as explained previously. Regarding Rājagṛha (the City of the King’s Abode), it is the name of the capital city of the kingdom of Magadha, just as Beijing is the name of the capital city of Great Qing China.
Although the name "King’s Abode" was briefly mentioned before, its meaning has not yet been detailed;
I shall now set forth its original cause, so please do not weary of this prolixity. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: In the past, there was a Śūdraka...

O King, this king was diligent in observing the precepts and always relied upon truthful speech. One morning, he mounted his carriage and, accompanied by his court ladies, entered a garden for recreation.
As he was exiting through the city gate, a certain brahmin came to beg and addressed the king, saying:
"Your Majesty is a person of great merit, while my own body is destitute; please take pity on me and grant me whatever you can spare."
The king said, "I respectfully accept the Tathāgata’s instruction; I shall practice this giving as soon as I have returned from my excursion.

Having spoken these words, he entered the park to bathe and amuse himself. At that time, a king of birds named Mṛgapāda (Deer-foot) flew through the air and seized the king from among the court ladies, carrying him away.
The women wailed and wept, their cries shaking the entire kingdom and startling everyone within and without the city. They scratched [at the ground] in distress.
Agitated and terrified, Mṛgāra carried the king back to his original location. He placed the king among nine hundred and ninety-nine other kings.
King Śuddhodana said, "I do not fear death; I only regret that I have failed to keep my word.
Since my birth, I have never spoken a falsehood. This morning, as I was leaving the gate, a certain brāhmaṇa approached me."
"I begged for it, and at that time I promised him, saying, 'I shall give it back. Failing to consider impermanence, I betrayed his heart and have brought this sin upon myself;
that is why I weep. King Mṛgapada said, "If that is your intention, you fear this falsehood."
"I permit you to return. Once you have finished giving alms to the Brahmins for seven days, you must come back immediately.
If you exceed the seven days, I shall possess the power of wings and it will not be difficult for me to seize you. King Sutasoma returned to his own country and gave alms to his heart's content.
He installed the crown prince as king, assembled the people in a great gathering, and offered this apology: "My wisdom was..."
Zhou: At first, my governance was largely improper. You should regard me with loyalty and benevolence, as I do myself today.
This body is not my own; I am truly departing now. The people of the entire kingdom and all his kinsmen prostrated themselves to detain him, saying:
"We pray that Your Majesty will take heed and provide compassionate protection for this land. Do not worry about the ghost-king Lu-zu. We shall prepare iron houses and extraordinary troops."
"Though Mṛgāra is divine, he is not to be feared. The King said, "That cannot be," and spoke this verse: "Truthful speech is the foremost precept;
truthful speech is the ladder to heaven. Truthful speech makes one a great man; false speech leads to hell. I now uphold truthful speech;
even if I must abandon my body and life, my heart shall feel no regret. Having reflected thus, the King—
He set out immediately and arrived at the abode of Mṛgāra. Seeing him from afar, Mṛgāra spoke with joy:
"You are a man of truthful speech; you have not violated your pledge. All people cherish their own lives and bodies, yet you have escaped death and returned to fulfill your promise.
You are a great man. Mṛgāra further said, "It was well said by you. Now you shall be released."
Nine hundred and ninety-nine kings also bestowed [their kingdoms] upon you; as you pleased, each returned to his own country.
Because these thousand kings resided together here, it is named Rājagṛha (the City of the Kings). Gṛdhrakūṭa is explained as before. Regarding the phrase "preaching the Mahāyāna":
because the Buddha was on this mountain preaching various Mahāyāna teachings, those who erect jeweled stupas to make offerings thereby symbolize the Great Dharma of the One Vehicle.
It originates from this. △ Seven: The Appearance of the Illness at the Jewel Stūpa.
In the country of Vaiśālī, in the Āmrapālī Grove, the Elder Vimalakīrti, in an inconceivable manner, manifested an illness at the Jewel Stūpa.
Vaiśālī is here translated as "Extensive Splendor" (Guǎngyán) and also as "Extensive, Vast, and Pure" (Guǎngbó yánjìng). The kingdom is broad and level, hence it is called "Extensive" (Guǎngbó).
The cities and towns are magnificent and elegant, hence they are called "Pure" (Yánjìng). Āmrapālī, or sometimes Āmra, is here translated as "Peach" (Nài), which is the name for its fruit.
This fruit resembles a peach but is not a peach; it resembles a crab-apple (nài) but is not a crab-apple. It is also translated as "Difficult" (Nán).
Discrimination. Furthermore, it is said that the raw and the cooked are difficult to distinguish. "Forest" (*vana*) refers to a multitude of trees forming a grove;

this is the site where ancient Buddhas manifested their traces. *Vimalakīrti*—here translated as "Pure Name"—is the name assumed by the ancient Tathāgata Suvarṇapuṣpa when he manifested as a lay elder.
Regarding the "Inconceivable": formerly, during the assembly of the Vaipulya sutras, he manifested the appearance of illness, and the Buddha dispatched [monks]...

Mañjuśrī led a group of arhats and others to visit him to inquire about his illness. That elder invited them to dine at the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhakūṭa) Hall and borrowed seats from King Lamp (Dīparāja).
With a single hair he swallowed the vast ocean, and a mustard seed contained Mount Sumeru. He disparaged the partial and rejected the small, extolling the Great Vehicle and praising the Perfect.
Thirty-two bodhisattvas each discoursed upon a single gate of the non-dual Dharma; Vimalakīrti alone remained silent, a marvel that has stood peerless for a thousand ages.
Mañjuśrī praised him with the utmost eloquence, declaring this silence to be the true gate of the non-dual Dharma. Such was his supernormal power, wisdom, and eloquence.
It cannot be fathomed by the path of thought, nor can its reality be grasped through words; therefore, it is entirely inconceivable.
Consequently, a jeweled stupa was erected as an offering (to manifest his divine eloquence). △ Eighth: The Jeweled Stupa at the Site of Parinirvāṇa.
In the kingdom of Kuśinagara, by the side of the Bhāṭī River, within the Śāla grove, is the *parinirvāṇa* stūpa.
The name of the kingdom is explained as before. "Bhāṭī" is half of a Sanskrit term; in its entirety, it is called Āriravati.
This is a territory belonging to the kingdom of Kuśinagara. It is translated here as "The Golden River," because golden sand flows mixed with [the water]. By the side of this river, there is...
The Śāla Grove is explained as before. "Parinirvāṇa" (perfect quiescence) signifies that the essence of reality is perfect and the essence of delusion is quiescent;
it is a designation for the fruit of the path of true permanence. When the Tathāgata was seventy-nine years old, he came to this grove and preached the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.

Having finished preaching the sūtra, he immediately entered extinction. This is the place where the Buddha attained parinirvāṇa; therefore, those who erect jeweled stupas to make offerings thereby manifest the Buddha.
Even for the Great Sage, there is still a time of end; how could ordinary beings in the cycle of birth and death endure forever? (The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

On the fifteenth day of the second month, at the time of his approaching nirvana, he emitted various kinds of light. The earth shook violently, and the sound reached the Summit of Existence (*bhavāgra*). The light pervaded the three thousandfold world system. This corresponds to the *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Record of Anomalies in the Book of Zhou):

In the fifty-second year of King Mu’s reign, the year of Renshen, on the morning of the fifteenth day of the second month, a violent wind suddenly arose, destroying people's houses and breaking trees. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth all shook. After midday, the sky became overcast and dark; from the west came twelve white rainbows that stretched vertically through the south and north.)

It burned without ceasing throughout the night. King Mu questioned the Grand Historian Hu Du, saying, "What omen is this? He replied, "A Great Sage of the West has entered parinirvāṇa; therefore, these signs have appeared. △ Third, the conclusion.

These eight stupas represent the transformative manifestations of the Great Sage; they are the places of refuge for sentient beings among humans and devas. To offer worship and reverent homage to them constitutes the cause for attaining Buddhahood.

The first phrase specifies the eight stupas; the following expresses the Buddha’s intention. "Great Sage" refers to the Buddha himself. "Means of transformation" (*huayi*) refers to the ritual methods for delivering beings.
This means that when the Buddha was in the world, he could preach the Dharma so that those who heard it would awaken to the Way.

When the Buddha was no longer in the world, he left behind these precious stupas so that by seeing their forms, one might clarify the mind. To see the stupa is equivalent to seeing [the Buddha] himself.
The Buddha is the place of refuge for all beings among humans and devas. By making offerings, one can obtain merit;

by showing reverence, one can increase wisdom. To speak generally, whether it be a single color, a single fragrance, a single glance, a single prostration, a single praise, or a single exaltation—if the mind can revere the Buddha, then that very mind is the Buddha.
Is this not indeed the cause for attaining Buddhahood? II. Specific Explanation.
This concludes the explanation of the causal and resultant characteristics of Śākyamuni.
Such sounds and all manner of reflected images— all inconceivable matters throughout the three periods of time— completely manifest and enter into this great radiance.
These two matters—the formation of the mudrā and the sound—do not emerge from anything other than a single light.

Such "sounds" collectively refer to the sounds of the Tathāgata’s speech and preaching during both his causal and resultant stages, as well as the sounds used for subduing Māra and overcoming externalists.

Furthermore, the voices of all sentient beings—whether those of devas or humans, down to the cries of monkeys, the roars of tigers, the songs of orioles, and the chatter of swallows—as well as the sounds of all insentient things such as wind and rain, and all reflected images, are the differentiation of the *dharmadhātu*.
These various forms and shadows are explained in terms of horizontal [spatial] manifestation. As for "the three periods of time and so forth," this refers to...
The youth said: "This is the matter of causes and practices from immeasurable kalpas past; the matters of all causes and effects in the present world;
and after my extinction in the future, the legacy of stupas and the circulation of the teachings, which every person shall follow and practice until the very end of the future limit.
All the various forms and shadows, as well as all causes and effects of defilement and purity, do not, in total, exceed this single ray of light for a brief moment."
This is all there is to it. △ Third, a general explanation of the distinct characteristics of all the sages.

Furthermore, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the Buddhas of the three periods of time, as well as the great Bodhisattvas and their assemblies at the sites of enlightenment, manifest supernatural powers and transformations.

Rare and marvelous are these things, and all the sublime Dharma taught by the Tathāgatas; they all resound like echoes, such that within this great golden radiance, there is nothing that is not seen or heard.
"Throughout the ten directions" below indicates that [the Buddha] vertically exhausts the three periods of time and horizontally pervades all places.

Because he horizontally pervades the dharma-realm of the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions, there is nowhere he does not pervade; because he vertically penetrates the three periods of past, future, and present, there is no time he does not penetrate.
Furthermore, "and the great" below extensively reveals that throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, the various Buddhas are the primary subjects. It also...
The great bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time serve as their companions. "Dōjō" (the site of enlightenment) refers to the place where one attains the Way;
"jō" (site) means location. For example, the *āraṇya-dharma* refers to the Bodhimaṇḍa.

Alternatively, it may be called the "site of preaching the Way," such as the seven locations and nine assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, or even down to a single mote of dust or a pore of the skin—all of these are sites for preaching the Way. As for the "assembly" (*shūe*), it is...
“The great assembly” refers to the gathering of all beings—bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings, as well as the lords of all vessel-worlds.
Because ten thousand spirits have all assembled, it is called a “great assembly. Their supernormal powers are such that within a single pore they manifest jewel-king lands;

within a single mote of dust they turn the Great Dharma Wheel; and they can make one become infinite and the infinite become one, manifesting the large within the small and the small within the large.
Manifesting as small, or subduing various māras and restraining various non-Buddhists—all these are matters of supernatural transformations and rare occurrences.
The above are all the manifested phenomena and characteristics. Furthermore, below this, one not only sees these signs but also hears the preaching of the Dharma;
that is to say, throughout all places and at all times, whatever is spoken is entirely provisional.
The various teachings—whether sudden or gradual, small or great, partial or perfect—all respond like echoes. An "echo" refers to the sound reflected from an empty valley;
Śākyamuni’s emission of light is like the great sound, and the ten directions are like the empty valley. Their manifestation is like the response of an echo;
that is to say, they respond according to the voice, never missing their proper time. Therefore, it concludes by stating: "All are like [echoes]."
...and so forth. Now, the auspicious signs manifested as described above are all realms of great inconceivability;
how do they differ from the *Avataṃsaka*? They are manifestly the four dharma-realms and ten gates of mystery, all appearing through a single light.

Furthermore, the realm as it is perceived is the phenomenal dharma-realm (*ji-fajie*); that the light can pervade everywhere represents the principle dharma-realm (*li-fajie*), just like the objects within the light.

The realms are spontaneously unrestricted; this is the principle not obstructing phenomena. It is like ten thousand objects being in turmoil while a single light remains unmoving—this is phenomena not obstructing the principle.
This is precisely the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena.

Just as boundless objects do not depart from a single light, and that light does not depart from the single body of the Buddha—wherein "one body" refers specifically to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body)—it does not... [the text continues].
If it exceeds sixteen feet, it is small; if it encompasses the entire realm of the ten directions and three periods of time, it is large. Yet it does not go beyond the single body of the Buddha;

thus, the large is manifested within the small. This is the gate of unimpeded mastery over breadth and narrowness within the *dharmadhātu* where each phenomenon is mutually non-obstructive—what is called "the ocean of boundless lands, wherein self and other are not separated by even a hair's tip. Thus the Tathāgata emits light.
Yet, while remaining for only a brief moment, it perfectly manifests the events of the three periods of time;

furthermore, because length and brevity are unimpeded, this constitutes the "Gate of the Ten Periods Formed by the Separation of Dharmas. This means that each of the three periods is divided into three, with a single thought-moment serving as the totality;

thus they are called the "Ten Periods. Because the three periods are distinctly partitioned without mutual confusion, they are termed "separated dharmas. Nevertheless, the three periods exist within one another.

Establishing one another in succession constitutes "mutual accomplishment. This is what is meant by the statement that the ten periods of time—past, present, and future, beginning and end—are never separate from the present moment of thought (*cittakṣaṇa*).
To explain this further through analogy: here in this world, Śākyamuni emits light to encompass the ten directions, and the Buddhas of the ten directions each emit light to encompass one another.
As these lights reflect and interpenetrate one another, they form a reality of infinite, layered profundity. Furthermore, it is for...
This is the gateway to the realm of Indra’s net. Furthermore, while the Buddhas preach the Dharma as the principal figures, the Bodhisattvas also preach as their companions;

all are contained within the light. One Buddha acts as the principal figure while the other Buddhas act as companions; likewise, the Buddhas act as mutual principals and companions, and the Bodhisattvas do the same.
Principals and companions interpenetrate one another, proclaiming [the teaching] simultaneously and instantaneously, fully manifesting the perfection of the principal and the companion.
This is the Gate of Virtue. Fearing that an extensive treatment might weary people with its complexity, I have set forth only the broad outlines of the major meanings.

Were one to elucidate them in minute detail, all ten gates would be fully contained; students may grasp these through their own discernment. This is because the phrasing is manifest while the meaning is profound;
fearing that it might belittle the sacred scripture, I could not help but point out and explain it. Thus ends the first major section: "The Manifestation of Signs within the Tathāgata’s Radiance."
△ Section Three: The Joyful Entreaty for the Dharma by the Three Assemblies.
First, the Introduction on Arousing the Mind: All sentient beings who encountered this radiance and beheld those auspicious signs all aroused the peerless *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* mind.

This refers to the great assembly at the Dharma-gathering. As for those who resolve their minds upon seeing signs, because of the signs within the light—whether it be virtuous causes and virtuous fruits, or evil causes and evil fruits—who would not seek auspiciousness and avoid misfortune, reforming their evil and following what is good?

Furthermore, seeing the Bodhisattvas cultivating the causes and the Buddhas attaining the Way, and again hearing the Buddhas preach the Dharma, who would not look upon the worthy and desire to emulate them? Moreover...
Among the great and inconceivable matters, who does not possess them? It is only because the deluded mind closes itself off that they have substance but no function.
If one were to turn the mind for even a single thought-moment and reflect back upon one's original nature, all delusions would be fundamentally empty; would one not then suddenly become a Buddha?
This is why the great assembly has resolved their minds. As for the term "unequaled" (asama-sama): "equal" (sama) means level or uniform. It is the same as...
It is because they are equal. This refers to the supramundane Dharma; the bodhicitta alone is supreme, and there is no other dharma that can be said to be equal to this mind.
Among the hundred parables of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, none are equal to the bodhicitta.
Therefore, what was stated in the preceding text—that the transformative rituals of the Great Sage serve as the cause for attaining Buddhahood—is precisely what is being explained here. II.
Preface to the Contemplation.
At that time, the great assembly, beholding the Buddha’s inconceivable spiritual power, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and said to one another:
Today the Tathāgata has entered into samādhi and emitted a great radiance that illuminates the worlds of the ten directions.

By this light, one may behold all the inconceivable deeds performed by the Tathāgata in the past, which subdue sentient beings with wrong views in this degenerate age and cause them to give rise to faith and understanding.
We are advancing toward Bodhi. How rare is the Tathāgata, who is able to act as the father of all worlds!

He is difficult to encounter even in immeasurable kalpas. Through our cultivation of various practices and vows over successive kalpas, we have now met the Great Teacher of gods and humans within the triple world.
"Supernatural power" refers to such portents as the shaking of the earth, the emission of light, and the manifestation of auspicious signs—unprecedented events that had never been seen before.
"Each spoke to one another" indicates their mutual deliberation. "The Tathāgata has descended today" correctly describes the subject of their reflection.
"Inconceivable matters" refers to deeds such as sacrificing his own body to feed a tiger and cutting off his flesh to save a dove, through which he tamed [beings].
Below, the inconceivable deeds of the Tathāgata are described and elucidated. "Taming" (*damana*) refers to the compassion that guides and nurtures;

"subduing" (*vinaya*) refers to the majesty that restrains and overcomes. "The evil age" refers to the period when the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) arise together, clouding and obstructing one's own nature.

Because the ways of the world are not good, it is called an "evil age. Wrong views refer to the erroneous calculations of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), such as denying cause and effect, or clinging to nihilism and eternalism;

these are incorrect views. To cause others to give rise to faith and understanding means that the Buddha now manifests signs so that the distinction between good and evil, and the clarity of cause and effect, are evident, leading people to believe in causality and awaken to the fundamental truth.
This is the nature [of the Buddha]. "Turning toward" means turning the mind toward the Way. "Bodhi" refers to the fruit of the Way toward which one is directed.
"Able to act as a compassionate father" praises the Buddha’s profound and heavy compassion. "All worlds" indicates that they are not of a single kind;
it encompasses the world of sentient beings, the world of insentient things, and the world of the Perfectly Awakened One (the *jñāna-saṃbuddha-loka*). It includes them all.

Regarding the reliance on the Holy and the Ordinary, both the primary and secondary realms, this reveals that the Buddha is able to provide guidance, support, and protection, just as a compassionate father loves his children.
All of the above constitutes the verbal expressions for mental recitation. From "Immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) onwards, he describes his own practice over successive kalpas;

that he has now finally encountered [the Buddha] demonstrates the joy and rarity of such an occasion. Because the Honored Buddha can serve as a model for humans and devas, he is called the Great Teacher (*śāstṛ*).
△ Third, the formal request for the Dharma:
We pray that the Compassionate Honored One, out of pity for the world, will arise from meditative concentration and preach the profound Dharma, providing instruction, benefit, and joy.
After all sentient beings had spoken these words, they gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance and remained silent.
Anticipating that since the Buddha had manifested such extraordinary signs of light, there must surely be extraordinary teachings to follow, they entreated him with earnest supplication, saying:

"We pray that the Compassionate Honored Ones will arise from meditative concentration. This requests the Buddha to emerge from his samādhi; "to preach the profound Dharma," etc., refers to [the request for his teaching].

This is the phrasing used when requesting the Dharma. Because the meaning of the Dharma is profound and abstruse, it is called "deep" (*gambhīra*). Because no one can reach its limit, it is called "profoundly deep" (*atigambhīra*).
It is the path of the Buddha’s own realization. "To show" (*darśana*) means to reveal; "to teach" (*deśanā*) means to instruct.

These two characters refer to the teaching that acts as the agent (*prabhāvaka*), while the following two characters refer to the capacity of those who receive it (*prabhāvya*). Because they obtain benefit and rejoice, it is said to be "beneficial" (*hitāya*).
"Joy. All that follows below clarifies the upward-looking gaze. The section on the Tathāgata’s formal manifestation is hereby concluded.

△ Second, the Great Being’s lateral penetration has two parts. First, the prose exposition has two parts. First, the narrative by the Sūtra compiler describing his virtues has three parts. First, the designation of his name and conduct.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Siṃhanāda (Lion’s Roar). He had cultivated merit and wisdom for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
This bodhisattva was given his name by means of a metaphor: the lion is the king among beasts and has nothing to fear.
When he roars, the hundred beasts hide their tracks and the flying birds fall to the ground.

One who takes this as his name is a person whose various afflictions are about to be exhausted and whose two types of death are on the verge of perishing, one who is about to realize the wondrous fruit; what, then, has he to fear?
As it is said in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, there is nothing that does not accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); thus, the celestial Māras pay homage and the non-Buddhists take refuge.
For this reason, the roar of the lion is used as a metaphor. Regarding "three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*" below: this clarifies the length of time spent in the course of cultivation.
The Sanskrit term is *saṃkhyeya*, which here means "immeasurable number. During the causal stage, a Bodhisattva undergoes three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; within these three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*...
There is no time when one does not practice them. Generally speaking, the six perfections and the myriad practices are all causes for merit and wisdom.

Specifically, however, the perfection of giving (*dāna*) and diligence (*vīrya*) are the causes for merit; likewise, ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are all causes for wisdom.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of wisdom: first, the wisdom of self-benefit that consists of contemplative insight and the realization of the Path.
Second is the wisdom of discerning capacities and preaching the Dharma for the benefit of others. By practicing through the three stages, one attains the full perfection of merit and wisdom;
thus, one is able to roar the lion’s roar, subduing Māra and restraining outsiders. △ Second, the description of the stages of sainthood.
Within this Bhadrakalpa, he shall next succeed to the seat of Buddhahood, receive the position of consecration (abhiṣeka), and act as a Great Dharma King.
Having fulfilled the causal practices of merit and wisdom through his prior cultivation, his rank shall correspond to the "final mind" of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi).
This Bhadrakalpa is the present eon; it is the same eon as that of Śākyamuni Buddha. "Next" refers to succession. He inherits these causes...
Upon reaching the fruit, there is only one further transition, whereby one immediately enters the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and attains ultimate Buddhahood.

"To supplement" (*bǔ*) means to fill or to continue. "Position" (*chù*) refers to the rank or station. This means that when the kalpa of a preceding Buddha has ended, a subsequent Buddha continues that position; hence it is called "successively supplementing the Buddha's position.
Regarding the reception of the position of empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "It is like a great king of a nation who divides the affairs of state..."

He entrusted the affairs to the crown prince. When that Kṣatriya king’s eldest son had grown to maturity, he performed the ritual of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), which is called "abiding in consecration" (*abhiṣekasthita*);

this is a metaphorical designation for his station. It is like a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) who, using a golden vessel filled with the waters of the four oceans, takes hold of the golden vessel and pours it over the crown of the crown prince’s head;
thus, the prince succeeds to the royal throne. This is the Buddha’s vision of the Bodhisattva whose causes are perfected and whose practices are fulfilled.

When [the vessel] is full and irrigated with the water of Buddha-wisdom, one enters wondrous enlightenment; thus it is said that one becomes a Great Dharma King, or a consecrated Bodhisattva (*abhiṣikta-bodhisattva*).
Having received the empowerment of the water of Buddha-wisdom, one possesses unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna*);
although not yet having entered wondrous enlightenment, one has already become a Dharma King. △ Third, manifesting the holy virtue.
He looked in the four directions at the great assembly gathered like an ocean and raised his voice, saying these words.
Regarding the phrase "noble virtue" (shèngdé): having surveyed the great assembly, he desired to speak in order to provide an exhortation;
yet, seeing the Bodhisattva’s public-spirited mind, he could not bear to remain silent. This itself constitutes noble virtue. The narrator has thus completed the description of his virtues. △
Second, speaking words to admonish the assembly. First, the actual admonition of the assembly. First, personally recounting one's own faults to admonish the minds of the multitude.
First, recounting that the time since first generating the resolve was long.
In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have already resolved my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
There are three kinds of bodhicitta: first, because of correctly recollecting the dharma of *tathatā*; second, because of delighting in the accumulation of all wholesome dharmas;
and third, because of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings. These are the two aspects of self and others...
This is the public mind of benefiting others. △ Second, recounting the service of all Buddhas.
One serves all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

the Buddhas serve as the supreme conditions (*pratyaya*), while the act of serving serves as the supreme cause (*hetu*). "Serving" means there is nothing that is not performed. This is what is meant by "veneration."

He served without declining even the most humble and lowly labors; he practiced his conduct without sparing himself from the hardships of heat and cold. In seeking the Way, he was determined to reach unsurpassed Bodhi;

in studying the Dharma, how could he have grown weary through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*? Thus, it may be said that because the cause is profound and the conditions are superior, his merit and wisdom are deep and vast.
Therefore, it is said: "Experiencing affairs," and so forth. △ Third, describing the sublime assemblies he encountered.
There was once a primary assembly at a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), where inconceivable supernatural transformations were witnessed.

This describes the realm of the spiritual responses of all Buddhas; as for the "primary site of enlightenment," none surpasses the *Avataṃsaka*, and "inconceivable" and so forth refer to the ten mysterious and wondrous functions.
△ Fourth, the account of the present encounter with the light and its signs.
Never before had they beheld this golden radiance, which manifests all the practices and vows of bodhisattvas as well as the various physical forms of the Tathāgata,
enabling them to see the inconceivable events of the three periods of time.
That which was seen in the past was never not marvelous; yet it did not yet equal the marvels of today.
And the marvels of today are even more marvelous than the marvels of the past. Nevertheless, who among those within the light does not see these objective appearances?
The Bodhisattva, acting as a narrator, fears that people might treat this with negligence;

therefore, he uses words to praise its extraordinariness and exhort the great assembly not to let it pass in vain, but to apply their minds and await the Buddha. Thus, the following section exhorts them.

△ Second, exhorting the assembly to revere sincerity and swiftly seek the Great Dharma, in two parts. First, the actual exhortation to the assembly, in five sections. First, exhorting the assembly to be sincere.
Gazing up with the mind, I pray that you, O Benevolent One, will single-mindedly join your palms and gaze upon the venerable countenance.
"I pray that you" is a word of urgent exhortation; "Benevolent One" is a term used by the multitude, referring to the great assembly as "benevolent ones."
A person of virtue (where benevolence constitutes the complete virtue of a gentleman). With a single mind, all conditions are set aside. Joining the palms signifies reverence and sincere devotion.
The honored countenance is the very appearance of the Buddha. Gazing up with uplifted diligence, one prostrates the five limbs to await the Buddha’s compassionate grace.
△ Second, the Buddha emerges from meditative concentration to preach the Dharma.
Rising from samādhi, he bestows the medicine of ambrosia to eliminate the disease of feverish affliction, enabling sentient beings to realize the eternal, blissful, self, and pure Dharmakāya.
Amṛta is the medicine of immortality; it is a metaphor for the Dharma taught by the Buddha.
