The Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom are both perfected; the divine light he emits is likewise peerless. That light is brilliant and radiant like the color of gold, shining everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions.
Regarding the manifestation of the seven suns at the end of a kalpa: a kalpa refers to the beginning and end of heaven and earth.
When the kalpa reaches its end and is destroyed, the calamity of fire is about to arise. At that time, all people commit evil deeds, which causes the heavens to withhold rain for a long duration.
What is sown does not grow, and all springs and sources of water completely dry up. After a very long time, the wind enters...
From the ocean floor, he takes the sun palace and places it within the sun’s path at the edge of Mount Sumeru.
It shines everywhere upon the world until the grasses and trees wither and fall; thus it proceeds for one day, up to seven days, in succession.

It dries up the waters of the great ocean, smoke rises from the earth, and heaven and earth become completely incandescent, reaching all the way to the Brahma Heaven, where everything is utterly consumed and wiped away. (Cited from the *Dharmapada*).

In the *Yuan zhulin*, "kalpa" (劫波) is translated as "distinguishing periods of time. However, what is used here does not refer to the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvarta-kalpa*), but serves merely as a metaphor for the excellence of the Buddha’s light.
For instance, when the sun traverses the heavens in a single day, heaven and earth are brilliantly illuminated.

How much more so the light of the simultaneous illumination of the seven suns, which manifests its even greater excellence. Now, the superiority of the Buddha’s light is illustrated by taking this as a metaphor;
hence it is said: "Blazing and radiant, emitting a thousand rays. The final two lines of the verse provide a comparative evaluation.

Just as in the world there is no light superior to that of the sun and moon, even though the bodily radiance of those up to the Brahma Heaven is excellent, it still does not equal the light from a single pore of the Tathāgata.
Yet a single pore accords with the nature (*dharmatā*) and pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*; how much more so his entire body?
Regarding "immeasurable and unimpeded": it is like the sun and moon, which alone illuminate the four continents, whereas Mount Sumeru—
It cannot illuminate what is above it; how much less could it illuminate the ten directions? This reveals that it possesses limits.
When encountering mountains or facing objects, it cannot pass through them; this reveals that it possesses obstructions. Now, the Buddha-light is the opposite:

above it reaches the limit of the *bhavāgra* (the peak of existence), below it reaches the limit of the *Avīci* (the Unrelenting Hell), and horizontally it pervades the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions. Therefore, it is called immeasurable and boundless.
"Obstructed," etc. The Tathāgata concludes with the four lines below as a eulogy. "Resplendent" (*he-yi*) means that the light is supreme.
△ Second, the verses on the manifestation of signs within the light, in two parts: first, the verses on the appearance of the world of the environment (*niśraya-bhājana-loka*) illuminated.
Within the manifestation of the Great Sage’s golden light, all the various forms and appearances in the world are clearly seen:
all the kings of mountains within the trichiliocosm, including the wondrous Mount Sumeru composed of the four jewels,
the Snowy Mountains, the Fragrant Mountain, the seven Golden Mountains, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Meru, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, the minor mountains, and the great oceans and rivers.
As well as bathing pools; countless hundreds of billions of four-continent worlds; the sun, moon, and stars; the palaces of various jewels;
the palaces of devas, nagas, and all deities; kingdoms, cities, royal palaces, and all villages—all such things were clearly manifested within this light.
"Sage" (*sheng*) refers to one who has nothing they do not penetrate. Without relying on study or practice, they are born with this knowledge.
This means their hearing is without lack of acuity, their sight is without lack of clarity, their thought is without lack of thoroughness, and their application is without lack of centrality.

They贯通 (penetrate) the Three Powers (*sancái*), respond to the myriad things, and share the same efficacy as Heaven and Earth. How could such a person merely assume the title and occupy the position while acting in name only? They are like the Three August Ones (*sanhuang*).
The Five Emperors, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius—those whom the present hymn calls "Great Sages"—are surpassed by none other than our Buddha, the World-Honored One.

Vertically, he penetrates the ultimate limit of reality; horizontally, he exhausts the boundaries of the Dharma-realm. He realizes that all phenomena are his own self; he understands that birth and death are themselves nirvana.
He is the God among Gods, the Sage among Sages; therefore, he is called the Great Sage. The rest is to be understood according to the prose section.
Explanation. △ Second, the verse on the illumination of the characteristics of the holy and the ordinary regarding the primary retribution (the physical body), in three parts.

First, the verse on the characteristics of Śākyamuni’s causes and effects, in two parts. First, the verse on the characteristics of his ascetic practices during the causal stage, in thirteen parts. First, the verse on the characteristic of cutting flesh to save the dove.
Furthermore, he manifests the Tathāgata’s past causes: how he accumulated merit and virtue while seeking the Buddha-way.

In the past, when the Tathāgata was in the kingdom of Śibi, he once occupied a position of honor as a king of men. His realm was filled with every kind of treasure, and he constantly transformed the world through the True Dharma.

Compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity were ever-present without weariness; he was able to renounce what is difficult to renounce in order to advance toward Bodhi, even to the point of cutting his own flesh to save a dove.
He has never had cause for regret. With a profound mind of compassion, he rescues sentient beings.

The first two lines provide a general summary; from "The Tathāgata" onwards, they are specifically revealed. Regarding the story of Śibi saving the pigeon, while the prose version is brief, the verse expands upon it.
The third and fourth lines manifest that his status is supreme among men; the line concerning his kingdom manifests his wealth.

There are four seas [of teachings]. He constantly uses a single phrase to manifest the True Dharma (*saddharma*) and transform the world. As for the True Dharma: if it is a worldly dharma, it is the goodness of the precepts (*śīla*);

if it is a supramundane dharma, it is the Truths (*satya*), the Bases of Mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the Factors of Enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the Faculties (*indriya*), the Powers (*bala*), and the Perfections (*pāramitā*).

A single phrase of compassion is the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). A single phrase of "ability to relinquish" is the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). That which is difficult to relinquish refers to one's head, eyes, marrow, and brain.
Regarding kingdoms, cities, wives, and children, worldly people do not abandon their attachment to self; when these are mentioned, they immediately become angry, so who would dare to beg from them?
The Bodhisattva is not like this. Because there is the Buddha-way to be sought, he does not perceive that his own body or life can be preserved;
therefore, whenever there is a beggar, he is able to give everything away, unaware of the difficulty involved. The final two lines refer to [the act of] cutting flesh to save [others].

The pigeon. This demonstrates that although [the task] is difficult, it is not ultimately so. *Bodhi* refers to the fruit of Buddhahood; *yāyin* means "one who proceeds," signifying one who, by virtue of the cause, moves toward the fruit.
"Deep mind" refers to compassion; "right view" refers to the bodhicitta. △ Second, the verse on the manner of seeking the Way in the Snowy Mountains.
In the past, when the Buddha was still an ordinary being, he entered the Snowy Mountains to seek the path of Buddhahood. With a focused mind, he applied himself with courageous and diligent vigor;

for the sake of seeking even half a verse, he sacrificed his entire body. Because of these causes and conditions in seeking the True Dharma, he transcended the suffering of birth and death for twelve kalpas.
All sages and worthies were originally ordinary people with blood and bone. Thus it is said: "In the past, they were among the common folk.
Regarding the second line, "One who seeks the Way must surely enter the mountains," this is because by leaving behind worldly toil (*rajas*), it is easier to gather and control the mind.
The reason why people of the world are unwilling to seek the Way is that they regard worldly conditions as heavy and the side of birth and death as light.
Lightness. The Sage reverses this: the side of birth and death is heavy, while the side of worldly conditions is light. Therefore, one lets go of all conditions and withdraws the mind.
To be courageous means not to be intimidated by difficulties; to be diligent means to take the realization of the Way as one's goal.
That one was able to sacrifice his entire body for the sake of a half-verse precisely manifests the actual practice of courageous progress. Regarding the phrase "seeking [the Dharma] below":
This concludes the preceding meaning. Although this half-verse is slight, it is the true Dharma that transcends the world.

Because he exerted himself to such an extent as to sacrifice his body, he surpassed twelve *kalpas*. (The character "surpassed" [超] logically ought to stand above "twelve *kalpas*"). [Question]: That which people value most are their bodies and lives.

Even if one possesses a heart that yearns for the Way, how can one go so far as to completely sacrifice both body and life? Is this not overly circuitous? [Answer]: Body and life are burdens upon the Way. This half-verse contains words of ultimate truth. When a person attains the correct principle, they transcend the mundane and enter the supramundane.

"Sages! If one clings to the body and turns one's back on the Way, one will sink forever into the depths of saṃsāra. To hear half a verse is like obtaining a precious jewel; to sacrifice one’s entire body is like casting off worn-out sandals. Such joy and fortune are more than sufficient—what slowness or hesitation could there be? It is not only the Buddha Śākyamuni who was able to act thus.

Here in this land, Yangzi loathed the body as a hanging tumor, and the Sage Confucius said that he would die at evening if he heard the Way in the morning. These were all those who held the Way as paramount and did not begrudge their own lives. From this we know that it is not that the sages do not love their own bodies and lives;
rather, because the body and the Way cannot both be preserved, they have no choice but to renounce the former.

To take the Way while still possessing a body. Nevertheless, one who has not realized the emptiness of self cannot [do so]. (One should know that the teaching of sacrificing the body was for later generations to deliberate upon.

If one is truly like a Bodhisattva, with both person and phenomena empty, then it is permissible; if the two attachments are not yet empty, then it is not. For if the attachment to self is not extinguished and the eye of the Way has not yet dawned, it will only increase the suffering of karma—what benefit would this bring to the Way?
△ Third, the verse on increasing the offering of hair to the Buddha.
In the past, when he was the sage Māṇava, he offered his hair as an act of worship to Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
By virtue of these causes and conditions of diligent effort, he transcended the ocean of birth and death for eight kalpas.
During two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of his causal career, the Buddha once spread his hair over the mud to provide a path for the Buddha Dīpaṃkara;
through the conditions of such diligence, he further transcended eight *kalpas*. △ Fourth, the verse on sacrificing his body to save a tigress.
In the past, when he was Prince Sattva, he sacrificed his beloved body by casting himself before a starving tigress;
through this cause and condition of benefiting both self and others, he transcended the causes of birth and death for eleven kalpas.
As in the prose section. △ Fifth, the expanded verse on the appearance of the Elder Śrotodāra saving the fish:
The Elder Śrotodāra, a great king of physicians, impartially protected and rescued all sentient beings;
thus the fish were each delivered and reborn in the heavens, where they rained down necklaces as an offering of gratitude.
During his causal stage, the Buddha once was a skilled physician. He happened to see that the water in a fish pond had run dry and that the lives of the fish were soon to end.
He then borrowed the water from the king’s elephants and camels to fill the pond to the brim and further provided them with food, whereby the fish were able to survive.
The Flowing Water [Bodhisattva] then reflected: "Water and food merely save their lives; they cannot save them from death. However, I ought to..."
The Buddha-Dharma delivers them; as long as they possess the karmic affinity, they must not fail to be delivered.

He then circumambulated the pond while reciting the name of the Tathāgata Ratnākara and further chanted the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. The fish in that pond numbered ten thousand.
Because he had heard the Dharma, he cast off his fish body and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Using his divine eye, he observed the situation and understood the reason for this.
Then ten thousand devaputras, each holding a necklace and emitting light while reciting praises of virtue, came to repay the kindness of Jalavāhana.
Thus it is known that Jalavāhana was the former body of the Buddha, and now he also appears within the light. (6)
The *Udānavarga* praises his diligent devotion to the Buddha’s marks:
for seven days he stood on one leg praising the Tathāgata. Because of this diligence, he surpassed nine kalpas [of practice].
While the Tathāgata was still in the causal stage, seeing the marks, secondary characteristics, and radiance of an ancient Buddha, a longing arose in his heart; he then stood on one leg.
With one foot planted on the ground, he praised the Buddha’s marks and signs and his meritorious virtues. Sustained by diligent effort, he did not flag for seven days;
thus, he surpassed nine *kalpas*. △ Seventh: An added verse concerning the elephant king’s appearance at the hunt.

In the past, he was the king of six-tusked white elephants, whose tusks were so exquisite that none could compare to them. For the sake of relinquishing his body and life, he threw himself before a hunter, seeking the unsurpassed great bodhi of the Buddha.
In a previous life, he was the six-tusked king of elephants. There was a hunter who, seeing this white elephant, deeply coveted its tusks.
He thought to himself, "If I can obtain these tusks and present them to the king, and if the king rewards me, I shall be delivered from my poverty and suffering.
He intended to kill it, but fearing the elephant's great strength, he reflected repeatedly and could find no effective plan. He then returned to his wife and told her.
The wife said, "I have heard that a white elephant with six tusks must surely be no ordinary creature; it is likely an emanation of a Bodhisattva and cannot be harmed.
When her husband heard these words, he went back to the elephant's location the following day and said, "I have heard that a Bodhisattva can renounce what is most difficult to renounce.
I desire your tusks to relieve me of my poverty and suffering; I do not know if you will grant this. Moved by his distress, the elephant felt compassion for him.
He then threw himself down to the hunter and said, "I relinquish my body entirely; take it as you please. He then made this vow:
"By the merit of my self-sacrifice, may I never fall into the three miserable realms in any future birth.
May I not be born among humans or devas, nor seek the lesser fruits; rather, I pray to attain unsurpassed bodhi. 8. Verses on Increasing the Practice of Giving Eyes.
Alternatively, he becomes a King of Perfect Merit and Wisdom; giving his eyes, he diligently seeks the path of the Buddha.
Possessing merit, he acts as a king; possessing wisdom, he gives his eyes. Because he desires the perfection of both merit and wisdom, he is able to give his eyes.
If one does not give away one's eyes, then merit will not be perfected. If one does not give away one's eyes, then wisdom will not be fulfilled. Why is this?

If one cannot relinquish that which is difficult to relinquish, then the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) will remain incomplete; how then could merit be fully realized? The eye is the cause of wisdom;
it is by virtue of relinquishing the eye that wisdom becomes complete. Seeking Buddhahood through this means, one will certainly achieve success. 9. Verse on the Deer King Relinquishing [His Body]
Regarding his physical marks:
furthermore, he manifested as a great golden deer king, sacrificing his body and exerting himself with diligence to seek the path of the Buddha.
In the past, when the Bodhisattva was a deer king with a golden body, his strength and power surpassed all others, and his benevolence and love covered all universally.
A herd of deer followed him with reverence as they roamed the nearby park. When a herdsman reported this, the King led his troops to surround them from all sides.
The Deer King then realized their plight and said through tears, "That you have fallen into this calamity is due to my own fault.
I shall sacrifice my life to save you, my small followers. The Deer King went to the enclosure, lowered his two front legs, and said, "Step upon me and leap across!"
"Come forth! You shall all be safe. The herd of deer did as instructed and were all delivered from danger. Their bodies were torn and mangled; their blood flowed like a spring.
They collapsed to the ground and could only just breathe, their pain beyond words. The deer cried out and wailed, lingering about and refusing to leave.
The king of men beheld its mutilated body, with blood flowing so as to stain the ground crimson, yet he did not see the herd of deer.

He asked, "What is this? The deer king replied, "My conduct was not virtuous; by my destiny I was born as a beast. Seeking water and grass to preserve my meager life, I trespassed upon your majesty's borders.
My crime deserves a heavy penalty. Though my flesh is exhausted, my two thighs and five internal organs remain intact."
[The deer king] still remained alive. He said, "I only pray that Your Majesty will grant me a single meal for one day. The King asked, "For what reason are you in such a state?

The Deer King then related the full account of his origins and explained the circumstances. The Human King was moved with compassion and shed tears, saying, "You are a king among beasts, yet you possess the vast benevolence of heaven and earth;
you have sacrificed your own life to save the multitude. I am a ruler of men, yet I am merely greedy for my own desires."
He was killed. Born from one who had been cruelly slaughtered, he immediately issued a solemn decree to the people of the land: "From this day forth, hunting is forbidden. Do not covet venison.
They untied the ropes and lifted the deer, placing him safely upon level ground. When the herd of deer beheld their king, they looked up to heaven and wailed in grief.
Each person came forward to lick the wound. They distributed themselves to gather *caiza* (healing herbs). When the King of Men heard of this, he beheld the scene and wept bitterly once more, saying:
"The ruler nourishes his people with the love one has for a child; the people cherish their ruler with the affection due to a parent. How could the way of a ruler fail to be benevolent?
From now on, I shall cease all killing and honor benevolence and righteousness. Heaven will surely protect him; the state will be prosperous and the people abundant."

Xi. Renown for his benevolence spread far and wide; the people returned to him like a flowing stream. This was when the Buddha, while still in the causal stage, manifested in the body of a different species to practice the Bodhisattva path;
now he has again manifested his radiance. △ Ten: The Verse on Increasing the Gift of the Body to the Yakṣa.
He was King Maitrībala of the kingdom of Kāśī, who gave his entire body to five yakṣas;
the full details of this account have not yet been seen, so it is provisionally retained for further investigation. △ Eleven: An additional verse on the manner of giving one’s wife and children.
Furthermore, he became the King Adorned with Great Sovereignty (*Mahā-rājavyūha*). He gave away his wife and children without any stinginess.
Because he had acted as a king in his causal stage and adorned his virtue through unstinting generosity, he was given that name.
Whenever anyone came to seek something, he did not oppose their wishes, and his fame spread throughout the eight directions. At that time, Mañjuśrī wished to go and test him.
He transformed himself into a young Brahmin and came from a foreign land to the king’s presence, seeking to have the king as his master and the queen as his slave.
The king was greatly pleased and spoke to the queen: "I have now granted his request;
what do you think? The queen was also delighted. Then the king and the queen followed him wherever he went. The practitioner said: "Since..."

He became a slave. He walked with shuffling steps and bare feet—(the character for "shuffling" is pronounced *duò*; the character for "bare" is pronounced *xiǎn*, meaning to tread upon the ground with one's feet alone, implying that shoes were not permitted)—and he obeyed his master’s commands.
Even when it came to selling both the king and the queen in separate locations, preventing them from being reunited, he felt joy in his heart and showed no sign of regret at all.
Mañjuśrī praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent! By means of your supernatural power, you have..."
The king and his consort were as if awakened from a dream; they had not yet left their place. This was but one instance of giving away his wife.

He gave away his head as did King Mahāprabha. While the Buddha was practicing the path of a bodhisattva, he served as a king; wishing to practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), he was able to relinquish that which is difficult to give.

A Wheel-Turning King possesses a thousand heads; only then is he fully perfected in the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).

This [story] is but one instance of such head-giving. Regarding the sacrifice of eyes, marrow, and brain: during the Buddha’s causal stage as the Prince of Forbearance (*kṣānti-rāja-kumāra*), his father the King fell gravely ill.

Though they sought medicine, no effective remedy could be found. At that time, a rebellious minister intended to harm the Prince and falsely claimed: "He who has never harbored anger throughout his life..."
"His eyes and his marrow—use these to compound a medicine, and by taking it, the illness will be cured. Upon hearing this, the Prince spoke to the rebellious minister:
"Throughout my life, my mind has never been moved by anger; he must be such a person as that. If my father’s illness is truly cured, I shall not shrink from ten thousand deaths.

The final verse dedicates [the merit] toward the Buddha-way; now, all of these appear individually within this light. △ Thirteen verses on the signs of the Wheel-Turning King’s renunciation of the world.
In the past, the Buddha was once a Wheel-Turning King. The four continents were filled with precious treasures, and he possessed a thousand sons and a vast retinue.

For hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he transformed people through the ten wholesome paths of action. His realm was peaceful and secure, like a celestial palace, where he enjoyed the pleasures of the five senses without end.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King realized that both himself and the world were not solid or permanent—just as with the gods of the Realm of No-Thought.
For eighty thousand years they remain, until their merit is exhausted and they return once more to the various evil realms. These are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows;
they are like morning dew or flashes of lightning. One must realize that the three realms are like a house on fire, filled with the eight sufferings and difficult to escape.
Until one attains liberation and crosses to the other shore, what wise person would delight in saṃsāra? Only the supramundane body of the Tathāgata is [not subject to this].
"Born, one does not perish; there is constant peace and bliss.

These first six lines praise the king’s wealth and nobility, as well as his transformation of people through the ten virtuous deeds. "For hundreds of thousands of kalpas" indicates that this was not merely for a single lifetime;

the detailed explanation is found in the prose commentary. The ten lines beginning with "At that time... represent the realization of the impermanence of the world, serving as the basis for renunciation.
At that time, that single phrase can awaken one's own self; this awakening is the sudden wisdom within the mind.
Yet worldly people, being defiled by the five desires, lose consciousness of their original nature; though they rush about all day long, they do not consider it suffering.
Life and death do not allow for security even from morning to evening. Who is willing to reflect upon this? One is born according to karma and dies by the force of natural progression.
Through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, there is no end in sight. Only the wise awaken with urgency, realizing that the body is impermanent;

they further realize that the world’s environment and its supporting conditions are likewise shifting and unstable, certain to undergo destruction and extinction. Even the state of non-conception—[is not secure].

This passage means that not only do worldly people fall, but even the various devas, up to those in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), suppress the activity of floating thoughts through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) so they do not arise;
they inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness and mistake this for the ultimate Way.

After eighty thousand years, when the power of their concentration is exhausted, they still fall back to the human realm and subsequently fall into the evil destinies. Therefore, it says "when merit is exhausted," and so forth. The character for "years" (*suì*) is not [to be omitted].
"Stable. This is merely an error for the character "kalpa" (劫). It is like the following three lines, which employ metaphors for contemplation:

that the two types of retribution—the primary and secondary—in the human and celestial realms are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; they exist yet are non-existent. They are also like morning dew or flashes of lightning, unable to endure long.
Furthermore, it is metaphorized that the triple world is like a house, filled with the eight sufferings which are likened to fire. And the eight...
Suffering oppresses the body like fire burning a house. Not yet having attained the latter two lines [of the verse] expresses the intent of wearying of the world and seeking liberation.
However, the character "not yet" (wei) is most dynamic: if one delights in and clings to the five desires of the three realms, one cannot escape;

yet if one loathes suffering and seeks liberation, there is no case where one does not escape. The two characters "liberation" (jie tuo) refer precisely to being free from fetters (*visaṃyoga*). Correctly...

Regarding the fetters of sentient beings: it is because sentient beings are defiled by the five desires and bound by birth and death, like a silkworm making a cocoon to entangle and ensnare itself, that they have not yet attained liberation and find it difficult to transcend to the other shore.

"The other shore" refers to *nirvāṇa*. [The text asks: "Who is below? The word "who" (*ka*) is also used here in its active sense; it means that the fool, through his attachment and delight, enters into saṃsāra.
The wise, being unattached, are able to transcend and be liberated. Thus, who among those possessing wisdom would delight in saṃsāra?
There are only the latter two lines which express the intent of yearning for true bliss, namely: "In the heavens above and the earth below."
All are bound by the five desires and the cycle of birth and death, unable to attain liberation. Only the Tathāgata is able to transcend them;
he is able to emerge from the mundane world, able to depart from arising and ceasing, and able to attain true, eternal, peace, and blissful nirvāṇa.
"Eternal" means forever free from arising and ceasing; "peaceful" means not being dragged by karma; "blissful" means not undergoing any suffering. Therefore:
They shall forever transcend saṃsāra and ascend high to the shore of enlightenment.

Regarding the statement in the preceding prose that he renounced the position of a wheel-turning monarch to leave home and study the Way, yet its absence from the verse, it is intended for those who possess wisdom: "Who among the wise would delight in saṃsāra?
△ Second, the summary of the whole manifestation.

△ Second, the verse on the characteristics of the numinous stupas upon fruition, in three parts: first, the verse that provides a general heading for the eight stupas.
Furthermore, within this light appear eight stupas, all of which are excellent fields of merit for sentient beings.

Just as the lands of the world can produce the five grains to sustain physical life and are thus called "fields" (*kṣetra*), the eight stupas of the Tathāgata can produce a hundred blessings to sustain the life of wisdom;
therefore, they are called "fields of merit. 2. A specific verse on the eight stupas:

Thus, the World-Honored One’s stupa of the eight treasures is constantly offered to by devas, nāgas, and spirits;
Vajrapāṇi, Guhyapada, and the Four Heavenly Kings protect and uphold it day and night, never departing from it.
Regarding "the devas and nāgas making offerings": this means that seeing a stūpa is equivalent to seeing the Buddha. There are two meanings to this: first, the Buddha’s grace is vast and profound;
thus, one does not forget his benevolence and virtue. Second, as it is a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), it is like sowing seeds in a fertile field.
Regarding Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada: he was originally a bodhisattva who manifested as a protector of the Dharma deity. He holds a vajra-pestle, using the pestle to manifest [his power].
He is so named because he is "Vajra" (Adamantine). He manifests fierce appearances that cannot be fathomed by others; thus, he is called Guhyapada (Secret Trace).
As for the Four Heavenly Kings, they belong to the first heaven of the Desire Realm. Situated forty-two thousand *yojanas* above the earth, they reside on the mid-slope of Mount Sumeru.
On each of the four sides—east, west, south, and north—there is a terrace. The eastern one is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Holder of the Nation) and dwells upon a golden terrace.

He leads two classes of spirits and deities to protect the eastern continent. The one in the south is named Vṛddhi; he dwells on a terrace of lapis lazuli and likewise leads two classes of spirits and deities to protect the southern continent.
The one in the west is named Virūpākṣa; he dwells on a terrace of white silver and leads two classes of spirits and deities to protect the western continent.
The one in the north is named Vaiśravaṇa; he dwells on a terrace of crystal and leads... [two classes of spirits and deities].
A class of spirits who protect the northern continent and guard it day and night without departing do so by virtue of their vow-power.

(Question: Since the precious stupa is a field of merit and receives offerings from humans and devas, why is it necessary to have it guarded? (Answer: When the Buddha was in the world, the Māra King would constantly come [to disturb him]. After the Buddhas entered parinirvāṇa, because the Buddha was present in the world, he caused the palace of Māra to be ill at ease. Therefore, [the guardians] protect it.

Furthermore, it diminishes the retinue of Māra. Once the Buddha has entered *parinirvāṇa*, he leaves behind stūpas to remain in the world, which also signifies that the Buddha is present. Fearing that Māra might come to harm or destroy them, these [stūpas] are thus protected and maintained. Moreover, they come to guard them in accordance with their original vows. Again, it was asked:

"The Sūtra says they do not depart day or night, yet the commentary states that the Heavenly Kings each protect one continent (*dvīpa*). Now, since the eight stūpas are located in different directions, how can a single body protect them all? Answer: There are two meanings.

First, it is like a worldly governor who resides in one place but whose majesty and authority command the eight directions. Furthermore, there are subordinate officials who each guard a specific continent or district; this case is also like that. While residing in one place, his majesty commands all directions, and he has various spirits and deities under his jurisdiction, some of whom are dispatched to provide protection and maintenance. Return.

He rendered service to the King; that is, he was protected by the King and others. Second, he outwardly manifested the body of a deva, yet in reality he was a bodhisattva. His emanations and reflected forms—what is called "the single body remaining unmoving while pervading the ten directions"—how could there be any doubt?
The above concludes the verse explaining the characteristics of Śākyamuni’s causes and effects. △ Second, an additional verse on the characteristics of obtaining merit from constructing stūpas.
If one constructs eight stupas and makes offerings to them, the merit and lifespan of this present body will naturally be extended;
wisdom will increase, and one will be honored by all. All worldly and world-transcending aspirations will be fulfilled.

Whether a person prostrates before them or merely brings them to mind—these eight stupas are inconceivable—and both individuals shall obtain equal merit without distinction, swiftly realizing the path of unsurpassed Bodhi. Thus it is throughout the three periods of time.
Beneficial matters—all of these appear within this light.
This verse describes the merit of constructing a stūpa. The first line indicates the abiding [of the merit]; the second line clarifies the increase of worldly fortune and longevity;
the third line clarifies the increase of worldly wisdom; and the fourth line concludes by manifesting [the result]. This is because both merit and wisdom are fully perfected.
Furthermore, one's lifespan increases; whom in all the world would not then revere?
With the extension of merit and longevity, the worldly aspiration is fulfilled. Wisdom increases, and one is honored by the multitude; thus, the supramundane aspiration is perfected.
One should see that the merit of constructing a stūpa is inconceivable. Next, the text explains prostration.

The merit of mental recollection is unfathomable. If these two persons were to compare their respective blessings—namely, the person who performs prostrations and recitations and the person who previously constructed a stūpa—the two would obtain equal merit without any distinction.
This concludes the section on swift realization. Thus, these two persons not only attain worldly merit, but shall also swiftly realize unsurpassed *bodhi*. Thus it is said.
The following summarizes the three periods of time: namely, stupas such as those at birthplaces and sites where the Dharma was taught belong to the present;

ascetic practices performed during the causal stage belong to the past; and since the Buddha has not yet entered parinirvāṇa, stupas marking the places where he will manifest parinirvāṇa belong to the future.
Therefore, it is said: "Thus, the three periods of time are equal. As stated above regarding the merit of constructing stupas: it is like the drum of ambrosia.

The *Rājanirdeśa-sūtra* states: "If a person were to fashion a stūpa from a lump of clay as large as an āmalaka fruit, with a *cakra* (parasol) atop it like a needle, a pinnacle (*yaṣṭi*) like a jujube leaf, and a Buddha image within it the size of a grain of barley."
Enshrining even a single *śarīra* relic the size of a mustard seed yields merit superior to that of making offerings of gold and jewels filling the four continents to Arhats of the four directions.
From this, one should know that the merit of constructing a stūpa is particularly sublime. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"By gathering sand to build a stupa for a Buddha, one shall all attain the Way of Buddhahood. Furthermore, the "Chapter on Heavenly Bestowal" (Tianshuo pin) states:
"After the parinirvāṇa of Tathāgata Devendra, stupas made of the seven precious substances were erected over his entire-body relics (*śarīra*).
Devas and human beings paid homage and made offerings with incense, flowers, necklaces, banners, pennants, and jeweled canopies; immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of Arhatship."
Immeasurable sentient beings awakened to the state of a Pratyekabuddha; inconceivable numbers of sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and attained the stage of non-retrogression.
Based on this, it is clear that it is appropriate for those who swiftly realize Bodhi [to do so].

Thus we know that the faculties of those in the Mahāyāna are sharp; for those who attain sudden awakening through prostration and mindfulness do not diminish the merit of remaining in the world. Furthermore, as for the Tathāgata...
His great vows of compassion and his transformative virtue were so preeminent that their lingering influence spread through later generations, yielding benefits such as these.
△ Third, the increase of verses on the gathering of clouds to provide for the assembly, in three parts. First, verses on the gathering of sages and ordinary beings.
Bodhisattvas from the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, various rishis who sport with supernatural powers, and wheel-turning kings from billions of lands,
all gathered together like a vast cloud following this radiance.
The first phrase refers to the sages; the second phrase and below refer to ordinary beings. *Ling* (spirit) signifies pervasiveness, such as the myriad spirits or the hundred spirits.

*Xian* (immortal) signifies distinction; it is merely one category within the realm of the spiritual. *Shen* (divine) refers to wondrous functioning that is unfathomable; *tong* (pervasive) refers to sovereign mastery that accords with the mind.
"Playful activity" (*yōgi*) is the application of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Regarding the aforementioned "ten directions" as the places from which the Bodhisattvas and others come, and "ten billion" as the native land of the Wheel-Turning King—why is it that such ordinary beings and sages from diverse regions all gather like clouds upon seeking this light?
It is because a Buddha’s appearance in the world is difficult to encounter, and the Great Dharma is difficult to find.
Thus have I heard. △ Second, the verse on the manifestation of supernatural power and the offering of worship:
Each, by means of their own supernatural power, comes to make offerings, raining down wish-fulfilling jewels to honor the Compassionate Honored One.

Hundreds of thousands of kinds of celestial music, though not struck, spontaneously produce wondrous sounds. Heavenly flowers fall in profusion, filling the void; various fragrances universally permeate [the air].
The great assembly [offers] countless jewel banners and various necklaces, holding them to make offerings to the Honored One among Men.

The first phrase indicates the purpose of their arrival; the subsequent lines clarify the precious offerings. The term "raining down" (yù, pronounced yù) signifies descending from above, whether lingering in mid-air or accumulating before the Honored One;
each expresses the reverence of their intent to come in this manner. The six lines beginning with "All the devas" provide a general summary.
These celestial flowers, incense, and so forth—offerings of rare and precious value—also manifest the sincerity of the intention to come and the urgency regarding the Dharma.

(Question: Bodhisattvas and celestial immortals all possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*); thus, the objects offered would rain down from above on their own. It is not known how this is for a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*). Answer:

Although a Wheel-Turning King lacks supernatural powers, he possesses the power of sincere aspiration. Thus, the objects offered transform according to his vow and may likewise rain down from the sky. What cause for doubt is there? △ Third, the verses:
A verse in praise of the Buddha:
With subtle and wondrous verses, one praises the Tathāgata: "Excellent is your ability to enter samādhi;
you manifest inconceivable great supernormal powers to subdue all sentient beings who are difficult to transform."
"Gāthā" refers to independent verses (*udāna*). To describe excellent words and sublime virtues is called "praise" (*stuti*); terms such as "well done" (*sādhu*) are all words of praise.
"Possessing great supernormal power" refers to shaking the earth to admonish the minds of the multitude and emitting light to array cause and effect;
these are all manifestations within the Tathāgata’s samādhi-concentration, which neither humans nor devas can fathom.
This is therefore called "spiritual power" (*ṛddhi-bala*). The section beginning with "subduing those who are inferior" correctly clarifies the efficacy of this spiritual power.
It means that sentient beings who are stubborn and hold false views are truly difficult to transform.

Now, seeing within the light the reflected images of the causes and effects of good and evil, distinct and unmistakable, how could they not seek auspiciousness and avoid misfortune, and reform their evil ways to follow the good? How excellent, World-Honored One! You are truly able to...

This concludes the subduing [of the obstacles]. The first major section, "The Tathāgata Properly Initiates [the Teaching]," is hereby finished. △ Second, "The Great Being Requests the Dharma," in four parts.
First, the formal request for the turning of the Dharma.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will arise from samādhi and turn the wheel of Dharma for all sentient beings,
forever severing all afflictions and causing them to abide in the great nirvāṇa of non-abiding.

"May it be so wished for" (*vīṣaya*) is the earnest expression of this Great Being on behalf of the assembly. The three characters "arising from concentration" (*samādher vyutthāya*) are a request for the Buddha to emerge from his meditative absorption.
If one were to discuss the Tathāgata, he is always in a state of nāga-like concentration and there is no time when he is not concentrated.

That he now manifests the appearance of emerging from concentration within a state that is fundamentally non-emergent precisely reveals the Tathāgata’s single-minded compassion (*vatsalya*), his intimate concern for others.
In this state, by remaining motionless in a single sitting, the wondrous Dharma is fully manifested.

Yet, while the Great Beings (Bodhisattvas) have never failed to embody the Buddha’s intent, how is it that ordinary beings do not enter [this state]? For this reason, the Bodhisattva, fearing he might fail the Buddha’s intent, requested to emerge from samādhi once more for the sake of all those below.

To clarify the purpose of emerging from samādhi, [the text] refers to "all sentient beings. As for the term "all" (*zhū*), it does not— (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on a Buddhist sutra or treatise, likely concerning the *Samādhi of the Lion’s Roar* or similar Mahāyāna teachings. The translation reflects the philosophical and exegetical tone of the original.)

It refers exclusively to the six classes of ordinary beings, while also including the minor sages; all of these constitute the intended audience. Regarding the "Dharma Wheel," there are two explanations: the general and the specific.
The general sense is that all provisional and ultimate, sudden and gradual teachings are the Dharma Wheel. The specific sense refers to the present *Cittabhūmi-darśana-dharmaparyāya*.
Now, the Great Being (the Bodhisattva) has attained communion with the Buddha’s intent; as for his request to turn the wheel, it is the *Cittabhūmi* teaching that serves as the means.
To "turn" this teaching is to transmit it. The Dharma is the very mind of sentient beings as well as the wisdom that contemplates the mind.

A "wheel" possesses the characteristic of motion; it refers to [the Dharma] issuing from the Buddha’s own mouth and being circulated into the hearts of sentient beings, causing them to investigate and realize it through spiritual insight, until they reach a state of expansive, great awakening. Because it possesses such efficacy, one requests that the wheel be turned forever.
A single phrase cuts through it all: compassion is the intention to uproot suffering. Since it speaks of "all afflictions," this encompasses the entirety of the five stages of dwelling.
Ordinary beings are vexed by views and thoughts; their minds are disturbed, they create out-flowing karma, and they are entangled in the fragmented cycle of birth and death.
Those of the provisional and small vehicles are obstructed by ignorance; though they may attain the fruits of sainthood, they are still unable to realize the high [truth].
Bodhi remains constrained by the cycle of death and rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāmi-śīta-bhava*); this is entirely the realm of the Tathāgata’s compassion.

Therefore, one requests the Buddha to teach the Dharma in order to sever it. If one were to merely extinguish manifest delusions while leaving their seeds intact, then delusion would arise again when encountering objects.
When the seeds and manifestations of the mind have all ceased, this constitutes eternal severance. "Abiding in one phrase" refers to the intention of compassion, which is able to bestow bliss;
*nirvāṇa* is the fruit of the path—true, eternal, and without cessation or arising—as realized by the Buddha. By adding the character "Great" (*mahā*), it is distinguished from the lesser fruits.
"Abiding in two words" points to the wisdom that is capable of abiding; the two words "non-abiding" refer to that which is to be abided in.

This is the principle. The principle is itself *nirvāṇa*. Yet, since it is said to be "non-abiding," and furthermore said that there is "that which abides" and "the place where one abides," this is because fundamentally there is neither subject nor object.
Now, in order to provide an explanation and bring about understanding, one cannot help but distinguish between subject and object.

However, when wisdom and principle merge in profound stillness, such that there is nothing realized in realization and no place where one dwells in dwelling, then it is originally pure and naturally so; only then does one truly attain it.

It is "non-abiding. Furthermore, it is said that "non-abiding" distinguishes [the Bodhisattva path] from the "abiding" of the Two Vehicles, because they have not yet eliminated the subject-object duality.
Thus, one should know that the upper character "abide" (住) carries the sense of "entering into accord," while the lower character "abide" carries the sense of "clinging attachment.

Only when both cognition and principle are simultaneously extinguished is this called "non-abiding"; it is not like the "abiding" of the Two Vehicles. △ Second, the manifestation of sincerity through his coming.
"Those of us whose minds are pure have come from ten billion lands to hear the Dharma.

Here, "I" is the Bodhisattva’s self-designation; "like" (*ru*) is a term used for self-reference; "those of our class" (*děnglèi*) indicates that it is not merely himself alone, but includes those of a similar kind.
Regarding "minds are pure," there are two explanations: in the case of a Bodhisattva, it refers to the purity of one's own dharmas.

The simultaneous absence of both [defilements] is called "purity" (*śuddha*). In the realms of humans and devas, the mind being free from discursive thoughts is called "clarity" (*viśuddha*). The second phrase expresses sincerity.

As for the statement that they have come from afar, it is because they have come to hear the Dharma. Regarding the term "ten billion" (*koṭi*), just as in the Sahā world-system one speaks of a single land, here it is named "ten billion.
There are two intentions regarding those who come from there: first, the intention of distance, which refers to the sūtra...
The lands traversed by him number as many as ten trillion. These two points constitute the pervasive meaning: that while his single essence remains unmoving, his response pervades the ten directions;
thus, he is present in all ten trillion lands. What is now called "coming" is likewise coming without coming.
Not listening yet listening; thus it is with the Great Being, so how could it not be so for the Buddha? When the Buddha is in meditative absorption, he moves while remaining in absorption;
without speaking, he speaks. Even when emerging from absorption, he remains in absorption while moving; in speaking, there is no speaking.
The former interpretation accords with the literal text; the latter interpretation accords with the underlying principle. Both interpretations are acceptable.
△ Third, making offerings while in samādhi is not an impediment.
By the power of samādhi, one constantly observes with clarity: "Out of compassion, please accept this humble offering of mine. [One contemplates] the donor, the gift, and the act of giving...
Regarding "objects": among the three periods of time, nothing is to be apprehended.
The first two phrases seek for the Buddha to accept the offering; the latter two phrases indicate that the three spheres are essentially quiescent.

The first phrase refers to the Buddha observing within meditative concentration to bear witness to one's own mind. "A meager offering" (*mīwù*) refers to a slight or humble offering; it is a term of modesty. This refers to what precedes.
Each has come with their own supernatural power to make offerings, raining down wish-fulfilling jewels as an offering to the Compassionate Honored One and others.

If you would graciously accept them out of compassion, it would be to not fail the intent of their arrival. The phrase "able to bestow" below expresses that within the gateway of present phenomena, there is not even a single dharma lacking.

Therefore, I hope for your acceptance. The phrase "at the three [levels]" below is a negation, expressing that within the ultimate truth of reality (*tattvārtha*), not even a single dharma is established.

Therefore, it is said that there is "nothing to be obtained. The "one who can give" refers to oneself from the perspective of the person; the "object given" refers to the other from the perspective of the Buddha;
the "one who receives what I give" refers to the recipient; and the "gift object" refers to the offering, such as a precious jewel and so forth.

The character for "world" (*loka*) in the phrase "the worlds of the three periods" should be understood as the character for "matter" (*vastu*). That which is "without attainment" means that all three matters are unattainable;

namely, one does not perceive a self, one does not perceive a Buddha, and one does not perceive objects. This is the emptiness of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala-śūnyatā*), which is an offering made in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, regarding the "three periods," it is taught that a single moment of thought (*ekakṣaṇa*) is complete with the three periods, just as in a single moment...
That which has not yet arisen is the past; the single moment of its actual arising is the present; and once that moment has passed, it is the future.
This means that a single moment fully encompasses the offering to the Buddhas throughout the three periods of time.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "there is nothing to be attained," it refers to being precisely within a single moment of the three periods of time, such that the three periods do not obstruct the single moment, and even that single moment is ultimately non-existent. This may be called the emptiness of mind and objects.
Silence is an offering that accords with the true nature (*dharmatā*). Indeed, no sincerity in making offerings to the Buddhas surpasses this. △ Fourth, the summary of the offerings:
"We abide in the most supreme mind, making offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions."
The supreme mind is precisely the mind of non-apprehension. To abide [in it] is like sitting in meditative seclusion;
that is, to sit in seclusion within the ultimate truth (*bhūtakoṭi*). This is what we mean by making offerings to the Buddhas through "non-offering";

hence the expression "offering and so forth. Furthermore, the supreme mind is the principle (*li*), while offering is the subordinate matter, the function, or the practice; this may be called "single-mindedness."
It is immovable, yet its function pervades the ten directions. As Samantabhadra says: "A single body further manifests as bodies as numerous as the atoms of all lands;
each one universally pays homage to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of all lands. Within a single atom are Buddhas as numerous as atoms, each dwelling amidst the assemblies of Bodhisattvas.

This is the perfect interfusion and universal pervasiveness: horizontally penetrating the ten directions and vertically traversing the three periods of time, such that there is nowhere it does not reach.
He makes offerings. There is no time when he does not offer. How sublime is this Great Being; nothing can surpass him. Thus concludes the introductory section.
End of the first fascicle of the *Abridged Commentary on the Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Original Life and Mind-Ground Contemplation*.
A Brief Commentary on the Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Original Life and the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground, Scroll Two.
Written by the Śramaṇa Lai Zhou of Zhantan Monastery in the Pure Capital.
△ Second, the Main Body of the Teaching, from the section beginning with the Buddha’s emergence from meditative absorption and his expressions of praise, up to the Chapter on Entrustment.

The textual body of this scripture consists of eleven chapters in total. Some sections were delivered in response to requests for instruction; others were taught according to specific circumstances or to suit individual capacities.
Some were provided through causal analogies and parables, while others employed verse to further elucidate what was not fully expressed in prose.
Altogether, these serve to reveal the mind-ground and demonstrate various contemplative gateways; they constitute the authentic seal of the Dharma King and the core essence of the entire work.
This is the main thesis; hence it is called the "Correct Main Section. The major divisions are fourfold.

First, the Buddha discusses the cultivation of the mind-ground to elicit the four debts of gratitude that ought to be repaid (this comprises volumes two and three). This section is divided into two parts. First, the title of the chapter.

Chapter Two: Repaying Kindness (Part One) To dwell above and bestow bounty upon those below is called "kindness" (*en*). To be below and move the heart of those above, recompensing them with sincerity, is called "repayment" (*hō*).
Since parents, sentient beings, kings, and the Three Jewels—these four types—all possess great kindness, it is only right that one should repay them.

Because it is a response, the title of the chapter is established. △ Second, the main text has two parts. First, the section on the formal discourse on the cultivation of the mind-ground, which is divided into three.
First, the emergence from meditative absorption and the expression of praise. Second, the emergence from absorption. [End of subsection]
At that time, the World-Honored One arose serenely from samādhi.
To gather function back into essence is called "entering"; to manifest function from essence is called "arising. To be at ease and self-possessed is called "serene."
Samādhi is concentration (*samāpatti*). Since one necessarily discusses the mental factors (*cittadharma*) upon arising from concentration, it serves as the opening of the main body of the teaching.
△ Second, the praise, which has two parts. First, the designation and praise: "Excellent! (*sādhu*).
He addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
He spoke these words before the assembly, praising him with the utmost effusiveness, exclaiming "Excellent. Furthermore, "excellent" (shan-cai) signifies the ultimate degree of goodness;
its meaning lies in the following section. △ Second, explaining and establishing the good intention.
"You great beings, all you sons of noble family: do you wish to draw near to the Father of the World?
Do you wish to hear the supramundane Dharma? Do you wish to contemplate the principle of suchness? Do you wish to cultivate the wisdom of suchness?"
They came to where the Buddha was, making offerings and paying him respect.
Now, when the Buddha was in meditative concentration, the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda extolled the Buddha’s radiance to awaken the great assembly;

furthermore, there were verses requesting the Buddha to emerge from concentration and preach the Dharma. Now that he has emerged from concentration, he in turn addresses Maitreya with words of praise.
This clearly demonstrates that the Great Sage is devoid of the notion of self or personhood (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and free from the mind of emotional views.
It is not merely addressed to a single individual, but extends universally to the great assembly; therefore, he says, "You, O Great Beings (*mahāsattva*)," truly without any ulterior motive.
"Great Being" (*mahāsattva*) is also an alternative designation for a Bodhisattva. Regarding the address "good man," it refers to these Great Beings who, above, cultivate the Buddha-way and, below...
He transforms sentient beings and bears the weighty task; he is able both to preach and to practice. For this reason, he is praised with words of excellence.

The following clarifies the correct meaning. "For those who desire" describes his single-minded devotion. "Approaching [the Buddha]," etc., praises his sincerity. "The Father of the World" refers to the Tathāgata.
"Only our World-Honored One" governs and encompasses the great trichiliocosm, transforming and nurturing the multitude of sentient beings. First.
All holy ones and ordinary beings are equally children of the Buddha; therefore, those who call themselves "Fathers" do not commit the error of arrogance. (There are three worlds in the world:

first, the world of sentient beings, which refers to the ten classes of ordinary beings; second, the world of the vessel, which refers to the great trichiliocosm as the environment and its retributions; third, the world of wise and perfect enlightenment, which refers to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
The Dharma is able to regulate and sustain; briefly, there are two kinds. First is worldly dharma, which includes all social institutions, ethical principles, and scriptures.
It can guide beings to produce understanding and enable them to fulfill their aspirations and achieve renown. Second, regarding supramundane dharmas:

all truths, conditions, the six perfections, and the sutras and treatises can likewise guide beings to produce understanding and lead them to ultimately realize the fruit. Now, we are selecting those that are not mundane.

Therefore, it is called "transcending the world," which refers to the *Cittabhūmi-darśana* (The Contemplation of the Mind-Ground). As for the "Dharma that transcends the world": to practice according to what is taught, to be able to eliminate afflictions (*kleśa*), to be able to leave birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and to be able to realize *nirvāṇa*—it is not in vain.
As for "Suchness" (*tathatā*), it is the wondrous essence of true permanence. It is called "Such" (*tathā*) because it has existed inherently from the beginning;

it is called "Such-Such" (*tathātā*) because it is fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing; it is called "Principle" (*tattva*) because it is the essential nature for attaining Buddhahood. Suchness...

Wisdom (*jñāna*) is the function of the essence itself. Principle (*li*) is like a mirror; wisdom is like its light. This is the function of the true mind’s spiritual awakening and illumination in human beings.
However, regarding the word "Dharma" (*dharma*), it is said that one does not know what is inherently present unless one hears it.

Regarding the word "principle," it is said that one must have the method of contemplation (*shengfa*) through investigation and inquiry. Regarding the word "wisdom," it is said that one must practice it.

"Practicing [the precepts] will surely give rise to true wisdom. This is because the three types of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) are the ladder and the vessel for all Buddhas to attain the Way;
therefore, the Buddha recounted them. The final two phrases conclude by praising their sincerity. △ Second, the permission to preach the wondrous Dharma has five parts.
First, to manifest the Buddha’s true compassion, I shall now expound the wondrous Dharma of the Mind-ground to guide sentient beings and lead them into the Buddha-wisdom.

Although the meaning of "Mind" is vast, for the time being it shall be explained in terms of *tathatā-jñāna* (suchness-wisdom). As for "ground," because it can carry and support all living beings, it must necessarily be understood in terms of suchness.

It is spoken according to principle. Yet wisdom must rely upon principle, just as the earth serves as a vehicle for transport; wisdom exists in dependence upon principle, just as the earth is able to give birth [to all things].
"Sublime Dharma" (Miaofa) is an elegant appellation for the mind-ground.

The reason the mind is called "sublime" is that if one is deluded by it, one becomes an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), whereas if one awakens to it, one immediately becomes a sage (*ārya*). Truly, it is beyond the reach of thought or speculation.
That which is forcibly designated as "wondrous" is that which leads one to enter; this is the accomplishment of the Buddha. Buddha-wisdom is itself bodhi.
If one enters Buddha-wisdom, sentient beings are themselves Buddhas. Because the World-Honored One views people with such intimacy, he acts for them in this way.
△ Second, praising the difficulty of encountering the Dharma:
Such a sublime Dharma as this has been preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only after the passing of immeasurable kalpas. Thus it is with the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One.
To appear in the world is extremely difficult to encounter, like the udumbara flower;
even if a Tathāgata were to appear in the world and preach this sublime Dharma, that too would be difficult.

"Passing through immeasurable [eons]," and so forth, simply states that a Buddha is not easily encountered and the Dharma is not easily heard. From "The Tathāgata descends" onwards, it specifically clarifies the difficulty of such an encounter.

Regarding "having appeared": this means that although he attained Buddhahood long ago, he subsequently gave rise to compassion; returning once more to bestow his transformative influence, he does not appear at inappropriate times.

Therefore, he is compared to the udumbara (Sanskrit for *udumbara*; here translated as "spiritual omen," or "responsive omen"), which likewise does not manifest at inappropriate times, serving as an analogy for the Buddha.
"Difficult to encounter" (as stated below) further reveals that encountering the Dharma is likewise rare, just as this flower. Why is this?

It is because regarding the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground, when the wise hear it, they immediately attain perfect enlightenment; yet when fools hear it, they fail to realize it and instead slander it.
Because their minds fall into suffering due to such slander, the Buddha, in order to protect those of limited capacity, does not speak of it lightly. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "The Buddhas..."
He has appeared in the world; it is rare and distant to encounter him. Even though he has appeared in the world, to preach this Dharma is further still more difficult.
Those who are able to hear this Dharma—such people are likewise rare. It is like the *udumbara* flower, which appears only once in a long while.
This is what is meant by saying that "the 'bright spring' and 'white snow' do not benefit the mediocre or the ignorant. △ Third, the inquiry and explanation of the reason why.
Why is this? All sentient beings have distanced themselves from the Mahāyāna and the practices and vows of Bodhisattvas; they incline toward the paths of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
These Bodhisattvas weary of birth and death, enter permanently into nirvāṇa, take no pleasure in the Mahāyāna, and constantly delight in the sublime fruits [of their own attainment].
First the inquiry, then the explanation. Why is it that a Buddha is difficult to encounter and the Dharma is difficult to hear? It is because the resolve of sentient beings is not great enough.
They distance themselves from what they ought to seek—the vows and practices of a Bodhisattva—and instead incline toward what they ought not to pursue—the intellectual fruits of a Śrāvaka.
While birth and death are fundamentally empty, they falsely give rise to a sense of weary detachment; yet, toward the *nirvāṇa* of the "transformed city," they joyfully and forever enter.
True permanence and true bliss are originally the fruit of wondrous enlightenment. Yet, having abandoned the great for the small, they are said to be "not delighted.

Because their aspiration was not vast, the Tathāgata concealed them and did not speak of them. It is not that the Buddha would not speak of them; rather, it is that their spiritual capacity could not receive them.

(The "Nirvāṇa of the Phantom City" refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which uses the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles as a metaphor for a phantom city. This is the fruit of eternal bliss and wondrousness.
These are the four virtues of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa: "wondrous" refers to the virtue of purity; "fruit" refers to the virtue of selfhood. The explanation follows that of the first fascicle.
△ Fourth, the Buddha is free from the four faults.

However, when the Tathāgatas turn the wheel of Dharma, they remain far removed from four errors and teach the corresponding Dharma: first, there is no inappropriate place; second, there is no inappropriate time;
third, there is no inappropriate recipient; and fourth, there is no non-Dharma. They administer medicine according to the ailment, causing it to be cured and eliminated.
This refers to the unique virtues of the Tathāgata;
it precisely demonstrates that the Dharma accords with the capacities of sentient beings. However, these are merely introductory words.

As for the following sections, they clarify that the preaching of the Dharma is free from the four kinds of faults. Regarding "corresponding Dharma" (*saṃprayukta-dharma*): whatever is taught must be appropriate for the recipient, such that it does not fail its own purpose.
The text says: "Externally not neglecting the occasion—this is what constitutes 'correspondence' (*samyoga*). Otherwise, both are lost. This merely provides a general indication;
there is no further detailed explanation below. "Place" refers to the location where the Dharma is preached. However, when one should abide, one abides, and thus there is no fault.
"Soaring before settling" is precisely what this means. "There is nothing untimely" means that one speaks only when it is the proper time.
Thus, there is no fault. Were one to insist on preaching at an improper time, one could not avoid the error of speaking out of turn. The *Lotus Sūtra* states:

"After the World-Honored One’s Dharma has endured for a long time, he must surely speak the truth. This also indicates that he was waiting for the right moment. There is no one who is not a suitable vessel.
The vessel is the very basis for receiving the Way; one must speak only when it is certain that the person is such a vessel, so as to avoid error.

If one were to speak forcefully to someone who is not a vessel, causing them to give rise to slander, this would not only be a failure of speech, but would also harm others and cause them to fall into suffering—this is what constitutes a failure.

The Buddha-mind does not act; this is what is meant by being without error. "There is nothing that is not the Dharma" precisely reveals the teaching that adapts to the capacity [of beings], whereby both [the teacher and the taught] attain what is appropriate.

Regarding the section beginning with "responding to the illness," it is further clarified through a metaphor: the Buddha is likened to a skilled physician; all afflictions, delusions, and karmic actions are like diseases;
and sentient beings are like those afflicted by disease. From the perspective of the Buddha, there is observation of the place, observation of the time, and observation of the person.
Contemplating the dharmas, all are found to be mutually appropriate. This is like a skilled physician who knows both the disease and the medicine;

if the medicine and the disease meet, there is no ailment that cannot be cured. Because it is free from the four errors, it is called "correspondence" (xiāngyìng). Thus, it causes one to attain recovery and freedom from illness.

If we speak according to the analogy, the character "fu" (復) is erroneous; it should be the character "fu" (服). This means causing that person to take medicine so that their illness may be eliminated.
In accordance with the Dharma, this corresponds to the Tathāgata teaching the appropriate methods so that those who practice them can eliminate birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
If the character "fu" (復) were used, it would result in the fault of "encircling the tongue" (a phonetic defect); thus, "fu" (服) is more appropriate. That is to say:

The concluding section on "unshared virtues" (*asādhāraṇa-guṇa*): These are the virtues of the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, which are not shared with the followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

This section provides a general explanation for the preceding section. As for why the Dharma remains difficult to hear even after the Buddha has appeared in the world, it is simply because the capacities [of beings] are small while the Dharma is vast;
he therefore endures [the lack of response] without speaking, waiting until their capacities have matured before he teaches. This is why it is difficult to hear.

(The Buddha’s virtues are not shared with those of the Two Vehicles. For instance, even Śāriputra, who was foremost in wisdom, was like one who fails to refine the furnace and bellows; he practiced counting the breaths but was not proficient, like a tomb-digger. If even such a wise man was thus, how much more so for others?
△ Fifth, the conclusion revealing the difficulty of hearing [this teaching].
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have not yet attained mastery; it is the uncommon realm of the assembly of bodhisattvas.
For these reasons, it is difficult to see and difficult to hear.
This refers to the stage of the Śrāvaka reaching the "unshared realm" (*asādhāraṇa-viṣaya*). Read it in one breath:

this "unshared realm" is precisely the Bodhisattva’s playful exercise of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*), the purification of Buddha-lands, and the maturation of sentient beings—things that are beyond the reach of the two vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), and therefore not shared with them.

Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva is free from both the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) and the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), and is thus able to realize that all dharmas are but [mind-only].
Mind. Outside of mind there are no phenomena. Afflictions are themselves bodhi; birth and death are themselves nirvana. Therefore, one attains great mastery.
Yet the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas merely empty themselves of the grasping at a self, while their grasping at phenomena remains entirely intact.

Consequently, they view the three realms as a prison and loathe the four modes of birth as sores and ulcers. Although their minds may be free, they have not yet attained mastery over phenomena. Its...
Lacking the necessary endowment and being unable to withstand the Great Transformation, for these reasons it is difficult to see and difficult to hear.
△ Third, attaining the Way through the contemplation of the mind.
Regarding the path of Bodhi and the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground: if there are good men or good women who hear this wondrous Dharma...
Once these words have passed through the ear, within a mere moment, one should collect the mind and contemplate the heart, thereby perfuming the seeds of unsurpassed,
great Bodhi. Before long, one shall sit upon the Vajra-jewel throne beneath the King of Bodhi Trees and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Bodhi is the fruit of wisdom; the Right Path is the mental dharma (*cittadharma*). It is called the "Right Path" because it distinguishes itself from the heterodoxy of external paths and the partiality of the provisional vehicles of the Two Vehicles.
Taking the earth as a metaphor, just as the great earth can sustain all things, the mental dharma is exemplified as being able to sustain all virtues.

These collectively belong to the "dharma that is explained" (*vyākhyeya-dharma*); the "gate" (*mukha*) is a metaphor for the "teaching that explains" (*vyākhyāna-śāsana*), for a gate has the function of providing passage.
Meaning (*artha*). Being able to penetrate the innermost sanctum; the Dharma has a penetrating meaning, being able to awaken one to one’s own mind.

Since both the Dharma and its metaphor are presented together, it is called the "Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground. The above consists of the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*), which together constitute the Great Dharma.

As for the phrase "If there be... and so forth: men and women alike are all addressed as having great capacity (*mahā-yogin*); taking it to the ear constitutes hearing. The Right Path is itself the Dharma. This is what is called "profound and subtle."
"Exquisite. "A brief moment" (*kṣaṇamuhūrta*) refers to a short duration. Once [the teaching] has descended, it means that what is heard is not much and the time is moreover limited.

(The above constitutes *śrutamayī-prajñā* combined with *cintāmayī-prajñā*). Taking the gathering of mindfulness and so forth as *bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*: "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is deluded thought; "gathering" (*saṃgraha*) is the cessation of thought;

"contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) is the turning of light back upon itself; and "mind" (*citta*) is the original awakening of numinous awareness. If even a single thought does not arise, the dust and toil of affliction are suddenly stilled.
"One directly returns to the truth. Regarding "perfumed and formed": if one compares this to the ultimate *bodhi* of a Tathāgata, it is certainly not yet so;

however, it is precisely at this point that the seeds of *bodhi*-wisdom are perfumed and formed. Regarding "before long": although one has not yet realized it immediately before one's eyes, in reality it does not require much time;
hence the phrase "before long," etc. (As for the "Bodhi tree," it means that *bodhi* is not a tree; rather, because [the Buddha] sat beneath a tree and attained [enlightenment], it is called such).

The Bodhi Path: it is called by this name because the path is manifested through the tree. "King" (Rāja) is a term of honor. The Vajra is likewise not merely a seat; it is a metaphor for the essence and function of the wisdom realized within oneself, with the "seat" serving as the means to manifest that meaning. "Jewel" (Ratna) is also a term of honor.

Therefore, it is called the "Vajra Precious Seat. How magnificent is the Holy Teaching! It is the perfect and sudden true exposition. Since it says that one will attain Bodhi before long, it can be said that "resting is itself Bodhi" and that "the task of a lifetime is accomplished.

This is truly like a single grain of elixir that transforms iron into gold; a single word of the ultimate principle turns the ordinary into the holy. For those of us who are lowly beings of this degenerate age, if we but cast our eyes upon it once or hear of it for a brief moment, will it not perfume us into the seeds of perfection?

Will we not have our share among the thousand Buddhas? Part Two: Eliciting the Four Kinds of Gratitude and Their Corresponding Repayments. First: The Elder’s Abhorrence of the Great and Seeking of the Small, Taken as Knowing Gratitude and Repaying It.
Part Two: The Introduction. First, the narrator designates their names and extols their virtues.
At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, there were five hundred elders. Their names were:

the elder Sudhana (Wondrous Virtue), the elder Śūra (Valiant), the elder Dharmika (Good Dharma), the elder Buddhanusmṛti (Mindfulness of the Buddha), the elder Sumati (Wondrous Wisdom), the elder Bodhi (Awakening), and the elder Subhāṣita (Wondrous Eloquence).
The Elder, the Elder Dharmacakṣu, the Elder Prabhāsa, the Elder Pūrṇamanoratha—
such great and wealthy elders as these possessed right view and made offerings to the Tathāgata and the assembly of noble ones.
The name of the city is explained in the first fascicle. "Elder" (*śreṣṭhin*) is a respectful title for a layperson (*gṛhapati*).

One who dwells at home yet possesses the Way and is revered by the elderly is called an elder; it need not be restricted strictly to the ten virtues. (In Tiantai’s commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra*, it is stated that an elder possesses ten virtues.)

That [term] may be used as a metaphor for the Buddha alone; however, this is a general designation, and thus it cannot be so restricted. As for the "five hundred," these refer to actual numbers and do not necessarily symbolize the Dharma.
Among those listed by name, all names are established according to their virtues—whether named after wisdom, or named after principle, and so forth—and need not be explained individually.
However, regarding those who have accomplished right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) is the discrimination of the human mind; it is known that they possess the Three Jewels.

Principle is correct; to act contrary to this is erroneous. Nevertheless, since one possesses right view and knows that there are the Three Jewels, the purpose of making offerings to the Buddha is to seek the Dharma, while the purpose of making offerings to the various sages is to obtain merit—thereby sowing seeds in a fertile field.
