Because a golden age is difficult to encounter (the various assembly of sages are all the Jewel of the Sangha; for instance, Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others are all holy monks).

△ Second, the elder’s own declaration of his aspiration, in two parts: First, seeing the evil and hearing [the teaching] (seeing what appeared within the light—ascetic practices—and hearing the Tathāgata’s praise of the Mahāyāna), divided into two:
First, clarifying the Buddha’s praise of the Mahāyāna.
These elders heard the World-Honored One praising this Mahāyāna Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground;
this was recorded by the compiler of the sutra as the beginning of the great evil. △ Second, the description of what was seen within the light.
He then had this thought: "I see the Tathāgata emitting golden light that manifests the difficult and painful practices of a bodhisattva.
I have no desire for a mind that practices such austerities. Who could dwell in birth and death for eternal eons and undergo all manner of suffering and affliction for the sake of sentient beings?"
"Recollection" (*smṛti*) refers to the mental deliberation within the mind that has not yet been uttered by the mouth. "I see" (*paśyāmi*) below serves to clarify the object of this recollection.
"Not loving" (*anapekṣa*) means aversion; it is the mind capable of practicing asceticism (*duṣkaracaryā*), which is precisely the *bodhicitta*.
"Asceticism" refers to the deeds performed by Bodhisattvas, such as the sacrifice of body and life. "Who could... is a phrase expressing the inability to dare to accept or undertake [such a task].
This is precisely the fundamental mindset of those with limited aspirations who are intimidated by what is great. As it is said: "We deeply detest ascetic practices;
who is capable of performing them? This is truly because limited knowledge does not comprehend great knowledge, and a short lifespan does not comprehend a long lifespan.

The body and environment of the Bodhisattva are entirely empty; the three spheres are quiescent in essence. With no obstruction between the extended and the abbreviated, principle and phenomena are harmoniously integrated.

Thus, they can perceive ten thousand years within a single thought-moment, and a single thought-moment within ten thousand years. Even if their bones were hung upon mountains of blades or their bodies pierced by trees of swords, [they would remain unshaken].
For immeasurable kalpas, they have undergone immeasurable suffering and practiced immeasurable deeds, yet throughout it all, they never harbored a single thought of discrimination.
Wherein, then, is there any cause for fear? Now, these elders perceive me as being self-conceited; they do not dare to take up the burden and instead harbor feelings of resentment.
This is merely the common human sentiment. II. The Second Part: Properly Expounding One’s Own Resolve. A. First, Seeing the Buddha.
Having formed this thought, he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms in reverence;
this is the constant rule for seeing the Buddha. "Baring" means to expose; he placed his left shoulder under the *kāṣāya* robe, thereby exposing it.
The right arm is shown in the posture of performing labor; the right knee touches the ground, like a servant before his master. There is no sincerity in honoring the Buddha that surpasses this.
△ Second, the words of confession, in two parts. First, the confession of great evil.

With one voice and in unison, they addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we do not delight in the Mahāyāna practices of the bodhisattvas, nor do we take pleasure in hearing the sounds of their ascetic austerities. Why is this? Because of all the practices and vows cultivated by the bodhisattvas..."

None of these constitute knowing gratitude or repaying kindness. Why is this? Having departed from one's parents to enter the homeless life, one gives away one’s own wife and children according to their desires;
one bestows head, eyes, marrow, and brain, granting them all in accordance with whatever they seek.

Thus, undergoing all manner of afflictions throughout three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one fully cultivates the various perfections (*pāramitā*) and the eighty-four thousand practices of the *pāramitās*, transcending [all obstacles].
The stream of birth and death leads only to the state of great peace and bliss that is bodhi.

From "with different mouths" below, it is a general statement regarding the cause: they detest what they hear because of what they see. From "therefore" below, it is a phrase of inquiry and explanation:
that which the Bodhisattva practices is not for the sake of one who knows gratitude and repays it; this is indeed the view of the mundane world.
I have heard it said that those in the world who practice filial piety naturally provide for their parents with warmth, coolness, sweet food, and fine drink;

they maintain the sincerity of preserving their hair and skin; they establish themselves in court and bring glory to the world, neither impairing their physical form nor bringing disgrace upon themselves.
Even the vastness of one's household wealth and the excellence of one's descendants are merely the ultimate expression of knowing and repaying kindness.
Yet, such is generally the worldly view; they do not even know the practice of morning and evening inquiry or the offering of sweet delicacies.
They benefit them only in life and not in death; they provide for their present existence but cannot provide for their [future state].

This is the Way of the Spirits (Shendao). Thus Guifeng said: "Even if one were to maintain a grave for the rest of one's life and offer ancestral sacrifices forever, though this may express filial thought, it does not assist the Way of the Spirits;

how could it suffice as a repayment of gratitude? Indeed, that which best enables one to repay the kindness of their parents' toil is none other than to resolve upon Bodhicitta and practice the path of a Bodhisattva; this is what constitutes true wisdom and supreme compassion."

Ultimate filial piety is the highest form of repaying one's debt of gratitude. Furthermore, when it is said that one distances oneself from parents to pursue the life of renunciation and so forth, this is entirely unknown to those who have not yet transcended the mundane world.

Regarding the act of giving away one’s head, eyes, marrow, and brain to fulfill the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), the intent lies in relinquishing the tainted body (*sāsrava-kāya*) to seek the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). It is merely known that there is a path, but the [deeper] meaning is not understood.

There is indeed the body. As for those who must cultivate and realize [the Way] over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, it is like a great ocean a thousand fathoms deep—it cannot be exhausted by a single scoop;

or like a multi-storied tower nine *zhang* high—it cannot be completed in a single day. Yet the delusions and karma of sentient beings are deeper than a thousand fathoms, and the expanse of birth and death is more vast than that.
The unsurpassed, wondrous Path of the Buddhas possesses layer upon layer of merit; how could it possibly be limited [to three *kalpas*]?
To reach the height of nine fathoms, one must necessarily pass through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

By practicing according to reality, fulfilling the six *pāramitās* therein, and eliminating the obstacles of delusion, one may only then personally become the Compassionate Honored One endowed with myriad virtues. How could this be accomplished with ease?
The eighty-four thousand practices of the *pāramitās* are themselves the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates; thus they are explained.
See the first fascicle. The state of great peace and bliss is precisely the Buddha-fruition of *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
This above has been explained according to the gradual teaching for bodhisattvas; because they are truly able to act in this way, they give rise to such fear.

Suppose there were a bodhisattva of the sudden teaching, such as the dragon girl who, by offering a single precious pearl, instantly fulfilled all practices and transformed [into a Buddha] in a single kṣaṇa.
When a man attains equal and perfect enlightenment, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics,
and suddenly proceeds to the Immaculate World in the south to preach the Dharma universally for gods and humans—

wherein three *kalpas* of cultivation are not separated from a single thought-moment and ten thousand practices are perfected in a brief instant— how should we, the many elders, conduct ourselves here? Furthermore, observe these elders!
This name and title are also a manifestation of great expedient power (*mahopāya*), intended to reveal the fourfold debt of gratitude and serve as an introductory guide.
If one were to insist on viewing him solely through the lens of his actual status as a householder (*gṛhapati*), one would fail to perceive what truly makes him a "great man.

(The cultivation of the bodhisattva practice over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* refers to the stage prior to the first bhūmi: during the position of the three sages (*tri-śaikṣa*), one passes through the first *asaṃkhyeya*; from the first bhūmi to the seventh bhūmi, another *asaṃkhyeya*; and from the eighth bhūmi to the tenth bhūmi, yet another *asaṃkhyeya*. [Therein lie] the eighty-four thousand afflictions.)

"Defilement" (*rajas*) carries the meaning of "staining. This refers to various false views and afflictions that exhaust one without ceasing, causing one to revolve through birth and death with no end in sight. If one discusses the root of these defilements, they do not exceed the ten fetters (*daśa-ānuśaya*).

Within these ten fetters, if any single one is taken as the primary factor, the other nine act as its assistants, thereby forming one hundred. Calculated across the three periods of time, each period forms one hundred, totaling three hundred. However, since the duration of the present life is short, the assistance of the other factors in the present hundred is not considered.

Regarding the two periods of the past and future, each of those two hundred likewise takes one fetter as the primary factor and the other nine as assistants, totaling two thousand. Combined with the previous hundred of the present, this makes two thousand one hundred. Furthermore, this is calculated based on those who have excessive greed, excessive hatred, and excessive delusion.

The equal portions: there are four types of sentient beings, each numbering two thousand one hundred, totaling eight thousand four hundred. Furthermore, based on the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the six decays (*ṣaḍāyatana*), each has eight thousand four hundred, totaling eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*).

(The ten "messengers" (*dūta*) are greed, anger, ignorance, pride, doubt, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the grasping at precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). "Messenger" means that which impels; for example, when greed or anger is stirred, it causes people to create karma, and thus they are named by their function.

The four great elements are earth, water, fire, and wind. The six decays are the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), so called because they can cause the decay and loss of wholesome dharmas). △ Second, expressing the delight in the Lesser Vehicle.

It is better to advance toward the fruits of the paths of the two vehicles, accumulating the provisions for three lifetimes or a hundred eons, severing the causes of birth and death, and realizing the fruit of nirvana;
only by swiftly attaining peace and happiness can one be said to have repaid their debt of gratitude.

It is not like those below [the Bodhisattva path], whose aspirations are set upon minor fruits. Both Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are termed "those of the Two Vehicles. Regarding the "path and its fruit":
"path" refers to causal practice, namely the dharmas of cultivation such as morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

"Fruit" refers to *nirvāṇa*, which is the fruit of cessation realized when delusions are exhausted and reality is fully penetrated. The phrase "three lifetimes or a hundred kalpas" refers to the duration of practicing the path. Furthermore...
Regarding the phrase "swiftly reaching bliss": because there is no birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) within the state of fruition, that is itself bliss.

However, since it is said to be "swiftly reached," yet also stated to take "three births or a hundred kalpas," how can it be considered swift? There are now two interpretations. First, according to the literal sense:

based on seeing that Bodhisattvas traverse three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one considers this to be an extremely long duration; thus, by comparing the distant with the near, [the time is perceived as swift].
Even if one were to pass through three lifetimes or as long as a hundred kalpas, this would still be closer than the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of a Bodhisattva.

Second, while the words are the same, the meanings differ: taking the present body as one lifetime, exhausting the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) and realizing the fruit of *srotāpanna* constitutes the second lifetime;
thereafter, exhausting the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-āsrava*) and realizing the fruit of *arhat* constitutes the third lifetime.

A hundred kalpas are equivalent to a hundred years. Since "kalpa" is a designation for a division of time, even if one were to pass a hundred years, how could that compare to the bodhisattva’s practice of various ascetic austerities throughout immeasurable kalpas?
This refers to the one who cultivates and accumulates the provisions [for enlightenment].
The name is derived from a metaphor. As Zhuangzi said: "One who travels a thousand li gathers provisions for three months.

For those who advance upon the Path, precepts and meditative concentration serve as their provisions, because they sustain the life of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*). In the Mahāyāna, the three stages of the Ordinary Beings (*pṛthagjana*) constitute the stage of provisioning.

Those such as the Elder [Śāriputra] set their aspirations on the Hīnayāna; thus, it is like the Hīnayāna precepts, the concentration on the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-samādhi*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Wisdom is the provision for entering the Path and realizing the fruits. The causes of birth and death are the two delusions of views and mental afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
That which is realized when these views and afflictions are completely severed is the fruit of *nirvāṇa*. [The phrase] "swiftly reaching the lower" refers to the stage of the Arhat.
The cycle of分段生死 (segmented birth and death) has been exhausted; one no longer undergoes future existence. Being unattached to the oppression of all suffering, one dwells in peace and bliss.

This is what is meant by "repaying kindness. The intention is that by relying on the Buddha’s teachings and practicing according to them, one thoroughly understands the suffering of birth and death and realizes the bliss of nirvana.
Not to transgress the Buddha’s command is precisely to repay the Buddha’s kindness. Furthermore, regarding the practice of householders...
He departed, yet did not leave his parents; thus he repaid the kindness of his parents.
Because the elder’s transgression was great while his request was small, this is considered knowing and repaying kindness. This first major section is hereby concluded.
△ Second, the Tathāgata extensively praises the four debts of gratitude (*catvāra ṛṇāni*) to lead them to turn away from the Lesser Vehicle and toward the Great Vehicle.

○ This was because the elder and others had sought the Lesser Vehicle while disparaging the Great, making it their aspiration. To repay their debt of gratitude, the Tathāgata immediately taught that there are four kinds of debts of gratitude that ought to be repaid;
this may be called a potent medicine suited to the disease. After the Tathāgata had finished speaking, the elder asked:
The Buddha said: "Regarding these four debts of gratitude, how should one repay them? For this reason, the Buddha taught that nothing other than the bodhicitta can repay them.
Consequently, all five hundred elders gave rise to the bodhicitta; this was merely the Buddha’s great skillful means (upāya) in accordance with their capacities.
Thus it is said: "Leading the small toward the Great. This is divided into three parts. First, the general section for the five hundred [elders], part six.
First, the praise and permission to speak, and second, the place of grace. First, the eulogy:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the five hundred elders: "Excellent, excellent! You have heard this praise of the Mahāyāna."
The mind gives rise to regression, yet it initiates the sublime meaning for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings who are ignorant of its great kindness and virtue in future ages.

If one were to judge this solely by the regression toward the Great Vehicle and the adoption of the Lesser Vehicle, there would be nothing to praise; however, what is praised here is the initiation of the sublime meaning.
It is for the sake of those sentient beings who are ungrateful that he was able to move the Buddha’s heart, leading the Buddha to praise him with the utmost words:
"Excellent! Regarding the one who initiated this profound meaning, there are two explanations: the provisional and the ultimate.

According to the ultimate explanation, although these elders and others spoke of repaying kindness, their aspiration was directed toward minor fruits. What the Buddha now praises is that they truly did not know where the subtlety lay.

As for where [this teaching originated], only the Buddha knows it himself. It is precisely by relying on this single exposition that one may administer medicine according to the illness, giving rise to the teachings on the four debts of gratitude and leading others into the wondrous meaning of Bodhi; thus, at once, it shall circulate through future generations.
Is it not so that this is done for the sake of sentient beings in the future who are unaware of the debt of gratitude, so that they may come to know gratitude and repay it?

If one examines the names listed among the elders, each possesses the marks and characteristics of a Bodhisattva; yet now they manifest the power of skillful means by appearing to regress from the Great Vehicle toward the Small.

This serves as an introduction to the Buddha’s teaching on the four debts of gratitude that must be repaid. Therein lies the profound meaning of "inner secrecy and outer manifestation," as evidenced by what precedes and follows.

The scriptural text states: "The meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*) is primary; if one relies on that which contains reality within its name, the meaning of expedient means (*upāyārtha*) is primary. △ Second, the admonition and permission:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively! Reflect upon this well. I shall now analyze and expound for you the mundane and supramundane [teachings]."
"In places where there is kindness":
"Listen attentively" means to admonish one to listen with careful scrutiny and not to be careless; furthermore, "listen attentively" is a term used for emphasis.
"Reflect well" means to seek the essential meaning within what is said and not to cling to the characteristics of the words. "Keep it in mind" means to cause [the mind] to be correct.
Contemplate and observe the mind; do not engage in deluded thoughts. To "analyze and explain" means to clarify and elucidate the meaning of the word *en* (gratitude).
"Analyze" (*fen*) means to dissect; "distinguish" (*bie*) means to interpret. Within the single character *en*, one analyzes it into four parts, thereby interpreting and extracting multiple meanings.
It is proclaimed with all one's might; therefore, it is expounded. "Worldly" refers below to those who are generally acknowledged as sources of kindness:
kings, parents, and sentient beings are the sources of worldly kindness, while the Triple Gem is the source of supramundane kindness.
△ Second, the detailed exposition of the four debts of gratitude that ought to be repaid, in three parts. First, the general heading.
"Good sons, what you have said does not accord with correct principle. Why is this? There are four kinds of worldly debts of gratitude:
first, the debt of gratitude to one's parents; second, the debt of gratitude to sentient beings; third, the debt of gratitude to kings; and fourth, the debt of gratitude to the Triple Gem.
All sentient beings equally shoulder these four debts of gratitude."

Regarding those who do not accord with correct principle, one rebukes their vague discourse, as they still do not know the names and numbers [of the debts], nor the reasons for the existence of such kindness.
Why? Because below this, the meaning of what is "not yet permissible" is investigated. Below the phrase "In the world," the names and numbers are formally listed:
namely, parents have the kindness of nurturing; sentient beings have the kindness of mutual birth; and kings have the kindness of providing shelter and protection.
"En" (gratitude). The Three Jewels possess the grace of salvation and deliverance. "To bear upon one's back" means to carry on the head, or to receive with reverence;

it carries the sense of accepting and internalizing. This refers to the four kinds of profound grace that bestow benefits upon all beings; therefore, it is called "bearing the burden with equanimity. II. Specifically revealing the four [debts of gratitude].
First, the debt of gratitude to parents. Part One: A general presentation of the name and meaning.
Good son, regarding the kindness of parents: the father possesses the kindness of compassion, and the mother possesses the kindness of pity.
As for the mother’s kindness of pity, even if I were to remain in the world for an entire kalpa, I could not fully describe it.
Regarding "kindness" (*maitrī*): "kind" refers to loving-kindness. No one loves their child more than a father.

Just as when instructing in the courtyard or seeking a teacher to master poetry and practice ritual propriety, he provides all that is necessary without begrudging his family wealth; his affection is deep and his concern grave, never failing to keep it in mind.

Regarding "compassionate kindness" (*karuṇā*): "pitying" the child is what is meant by compassion. This refers to the child emerging from the mother; this partial love is what is meant by "pitying. For one *kalpa*...
"Unable to exhaust" means that words exceed their measure; it simply says that the mother's kindness is so profound and heavy that no words can fully express it.
△ Second, extensively revealing the profound kindness has three parts. First, a rough comparison.

I shall now proclaim to you a small portion of it. Suppose there were someone who, for the sake of merit, respectfully made offerings to one hundred pure-practicing great brahmins, one hundred great ṛṣis possessing the five supernormal powers, and one hundred virtuous friends.
They were placed within a most exquisite hall made of the seven precious gems. There, hundreds of thousands of kinds of superior and rare delicacies were provided;

various necklaces and robes of many jewels were hung; sandalwood and aloeswood were prepared; and dwellings were established, adorned with a hundred treasures, complete with beds, couches, and bedding.

To treat various illnesses with a hundred kinds of medicinal decoctions and to provide offerings with a single-minded devotion for a full hundred thousand kalpas is not equal to dwelling for a single thought-moment in a heart of filial piety, using even a small amount of material goods to provide physical care and compassionate nourishment for one’s mother, according to her every need. Compared to the former, this merit is far superior.
Even by a hundred thousand millionfold, it cannot be measured.
"A small portion" refers to a brief summary of the general outline. That is to say, the kindness of one's parents is difficult to express fully in words;
therefore, I shall borrow a metaphor for a rough comparison. "Suppose" is used in the sense of a hypothetical construction, meaning: suppose there were a person who, for the sake of seeking merit...
Extensively promoting offerings to those who possess the Way, I move them with sincerity, and they respond with virtue.
In this mutual interaction of resonance and response, they will surely bestow blessings upon me; hence it is said, "With reverence, etc.

*Brāhmaṇa* is here translated as "Pure Conduct," which combines both the Chinese and Sanskrit meanings. Alternatively, it is rendered as "Pure Lineage," signifying that they are descendants of Brahmā. Here, it is simply called "Pure."

Regarding the term "practitioner of brahminhood" (*brāhmaṇa*): it carries a sense of discrimination. That is to say, although one may share the same lineage as others, there are those who separately practice pure conduct (*brahmacarya*);
I shall provide offerings to them to seek merit. If there were no such intention of discrimination, the statement would be redundant.
Regarding "immortals" (*ṛṣi*): "immortal" (*xian*) means "to transcend. It refers to transforming the coarse body into a subtle substance and exchanging a short lifespan for a long one.

"Shen" (神) refers to supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Because there are immortals who possess these supernatural powers, they are called "divine immortals" (*shenxian*). As for the five supernormal powers: first, the feet do not touch the ground;
second, knowing the minds and lifespans of others; third, turning one's gaze to see a thousand *li* away, with no objects able to obstruct the vision.
Fourth, upon calling their names, they arrive immediately. Fifth, they encounter no obstruction from stone walls; thus they are called those with the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

(They are not the same as those who have attained the exhaustion of outflows. Regarding "good friends": those who share the same aspirations are friends, and those whose virtue and realization are superior to one's own are good friends.
These are all persons to whom offerings should be made. "One hundred" refers to the number of people in the assembly. "To settle" means to arrange a place for them, causing them to...
"He dwells therein" refers to the location of the hall. "Made of the seven treasures" below expresses the height of sincerity and reverence;

thus, the hall is called the "Hall of Wondrous Jewels," the food is called "precious delicacies," the varieties are said to be "hundreds of thousands," and the clothing is further described as being of "various jewels."
The dwellings were constructed with various fragrant woods; the furniture was said to be adorned with a hundred jewels.
To prevent illness, a hundred kinds of medicinal decoctions were prepared. Necklaces hung down from without, while sincere faith was maintained within.

Having endured such conditions for the vast duration of a thousand kalpas, the person who offered these provisions may be said to have reached the ultimate in devotion. By seeking blessings through this, the resulting merit will surely be supreme.

This serves as the standard for comparison, whereas the former does not; it is that which is being compared. If one makes offerings to one’s compassionate mother, the merit exceeds that [of the former].
As for the time, it need not be the thousand kalpas mentioned before, but may be but a single thought-moment.
As for the material substances, they need not be as abundant as those previously described, but may be even the most meager. As for the manner of service, it need not be as elaborate as the former.
The merit obtained from this Jewel Hall, compared to the blessings obtained by those who previously made offerings to the immortals and others, does not equal even one-thousandth part of it;
ten-thousandth part is likewise so. Therefore, it is said that it cannot be measured.

Although it is due to the power exerted by the compassionate mother’s kindness, it is also moved by the filial piety of the son. Now, as it is with the compassionate mother, so it is with the compassionate father.
However, it is not that one is unfilial toward the father because of being filial toward the mother; rather, it is because the mother has partial affection that this is explained separately.
△ Second, the ten detailed distinctions: first, the unmanifested debt of gratitude.
The compassionate mother of the world has incomparable love for her child; her kindness extends even to that which is not yet formed.

From the moment of conception, throughout the ten months, she undergoes all manner of suffering and affliction while walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—suffering that cannot be fully expressed by words. Though she may obtain sensual pleasures, food, drink, and clothing, [she endures these hardships for her child].

Yet she does not give rise to craving; rather, her mind of anxious concern never ceases. She reflects only upon how, as she is about to give birth, she will gradually undergo various sufferings, filled with grief and distress day and night.
"Unformed" means not yet having attained a physical form. For instance, after birth, one perceives the dimensions of the body and the distinctions of facial features;
prior to the fetal stage, it is therefore called "unformed. [The mother] desires a child moment by moment.
This is already an act of bestowing grace; as for the matter of conception, it goes without saying that it is even more so. [The fetus] resides below the stomach and above the large intestine.
As the subsequent text states: "Sucking at the root of the mother's milk and consuming the blood of the mother's body, for ten months it undergoes inexhaustible suffering.
Because one considers the child within the womb, even if there be sensual pleasures, exquisite food, or fine clothing, they are all [of no avail].
She does not give rise to affection; her mind of anxious concern never ceases. She thinks only that upon giving birth she will surely undergo various sufferings;
therefore, she makes no distinction between day and night. △ Second, the kindness of being about to give birth.
If there is difficulty in childbirth, it is as if hundreds of thousands of blades are vying with one another to butcher and cut [the mother], ultimately leading to her death.
At the time of delivery, it is a great ordeal for the mother; hence it is called "difficult childbirth. Since it is said to be like being butchered by a thousand knives:
The pain was unbearable; his life hung by a thread. Hence it is said: "He thus reached impermanence" (meaning that birth and death are not fixed).
△ Third, the kindness of nursing.
If there is no suffering or affliction, one's kinsmen and relatives will experience inexhaustible joy, like a poor woman who has obtained a wish-fulfilling jewel.
When her child utters a sound, it is as if hearing music; she uses her breast as a place for him to sleep and rest, and his left and right knees as his seat.
He constantly wanders about within the mother’s breast, from which a spring of nectar flows;
thus, he who is free from suffering is truly born without ailment. For the mother, obtaining her son is like a pauper finding treasure;
when the son utters his first cry, the mother hears it as the beauty of celestial music. Compared to this, even the sensual pleasures she experienced prior to his birth are insignificant.
Yet no love arises [for others]. How is this so? At that time it was suffering; at this time it is joy, because there is a child.
Because the mother is lowly, it is said that while in the swaddling clothes, the child does not leave the mother’s bosom; thus, her breast becomes the place for peaceful sleep.
Since the breast serves as the bed, the knees become the place for wandering and walking. From within the breast, milk flows forth.
This sustains their lives, comparable to nectar (*amṛta*). Day and night it constantly arises like an inexhaustible spring.
Because the mother’s kindness is so profound, one strives with all one's might to describe it in this way. △ Fourth, the kindness of compassionate love.
The grace of her nurturing extends throughout the heavens; the virtue of her compassion is vast beyond compare. Among all that is exalted in the world, nothing surpasses the mountain peaks;
yet the kindness of a grieving mother exceeds Mount Sumeru. Among all that is weighty in the world, the great earth is foremost.
The grace of a compassionate mother exceeds even that;
"nurturing" means raising and sustaining. That which "pervades all under heaven" refers to the greatness of her kindness, such that there is nothing she does not cover.
"Compassionately pitying" and below: both the text and the metaphors are clear; there is no need for further explanation. ○ Yangzi said: "Parents are to a child as Heaven and Earth are.
Without Heaven, how could one be born? Without Earth, how could one have form? Zhihua said: "Heaven hangs its images; Earth carries forms. The father receives the vital breath;
the mother brings about the transformation. As the *Shijing* says: "Alas, alas, my parents! Their toil in giving birth to me was great. Without [Heaven and Earth], [how could this be?]
What can a father rely upon? What can one depend on when there is no mother? When going out, one carries grief; when returning home, there is nothing to reach.

O Father, you gave me life; O Mother, you nurtured me. You caressed me and raised me; you grew me and sustained me. You looked after me and returned to me; whether going out or coming in, you were ever with me.

Desiring to repay this kindness, [I find] the Great Heaven is boundless. (Regarding "Great Heaven" (*hàotiān*): according to the *Erya*, spring is called the Azure Heaven (*cāngtiān*), summer is called the Great Heaven (*hàotiān*), autumn is called the Compassionate Heaven (*míntiān*), and winter is called the White Heaven (*báitiān*).)

"High Heaven": "Hao" means vast and great. In the high summer, the sunlight and the heat pervade the six directions without end. The sprouts of the hundred grains and the plants of the gardens and forests all reach maturity because of this. Heaven possesses this grace, yet it never has a mind that declines the toil and labor involved. Parents are likewise; they are even more generous toward me.

They turn to the dry places for themselves and move to the damp places for me; they suckle and nourish me with milk. They swallow what is bitter and spit out what is sweet, providing compassionate instruction until I am grown.

Their heart of pity and concern has never abandoned me for even a moment. Such is their grace and virtue—they have never declined the toil and labor. Therefore, the debt of gratitude owed to one's parents is comparable to that of High Heaven. △ Fifth, the grievance regarding the child’s fall.

If there are sons or daughters who turn their backs on kindness and act insubordinately, causing their parents to give rise to thoughts of resentment, and if the mother utters evil words, the child will immediately fall accordingly—either into hell, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm. Among the maladies of the world, none surpasses the fierce wind.
The subtlety of malice is even more rapid than that; neither all the Tathāgatas, the Vajradevas, nor the ṛṣis possessing the five supernatural powers can provide protection.
To be fully aware of one's debt of gratitude and yet disregard it is called ingratitude; ingratitude is unfiliality, and lack of compliance is defiance.
As for "resentful thoughts," hatred arises from the heart; as for "malicious words," they issue from the mouth. When parents are thus provoked to anger—
The son immediately followed suit and fell. In this present life, he was punished by Heaven and struck by lightning; after death, he would inevitably fall into the three miserable realms.
This is illustrated by worldly analogies: when the wind is fierce, it topples trees and breaks flowers; when one utters words of resentment, calamity approaches and disaster arrives.

His punishment by Heaven was like that of Ni Jiu, and his being struck by lightning was like that of the Xu family. As for those whom even the Buddhas and sages cannot save, it is because they have acted in rebellion against the Way.

This was a transgression. (At Mount Qingtianmuzu, there lived a resident named Ni Jiu. Deluded by his wife’s words, he was unfilial toward his mother. His mother lacked sufficient food and clothing, and whenever she encountered matters, he would not permit her to speak. It happened that the autumn grain had just ripened; he ordered his mother to husk the new rice, fowl to be cooked, and rice to be prepared.

After he and his wife had finished eating, he gave the leftovers to his mother. She spat it out, unable to swallow it, and wept as she cried out to Heaven. That night, a violent wind and torrential rain arose.

A massive boulder split from the mountain peak and fell directly upon Ni Jiu’s sleeping bed. It then shattered the left wall and emerged, coming to rest on the west side of the stream. His mother remained unhurt. By dawn, when the villagers gathered to look, the house was already empty. The mother wandered along the cliffs searching and weeping, finding only her young grandson with several bleeding fingers stuck to [the remnants of the meal].)

At Stone Peak, the son and daughter-in-law were unaware of their mother’s death. Chen Zhongzhou was moved by this event and thus composed the "Record of the Execution of the Traitor at the Cliff. (Xue Shi was a commoner from Longyou. She had two brothers living more than ten *li* apart who took turns caring for their mother every five days.

The elder brother was very poor while the younger brother was somewhat well-off. The elder brother could not provide enough gruel and rice for his mother, and when it was his turn to care for her, he was still two days short. He said to his mother, "Let us go to my younger brother's house for now; I shall make up for the deficiency later. When the mother arrived at her brother's gate, he would not let her in, saying, "The elder brother's contribution is not yet complete.

When the mother explained her brother's intention, he refused as firmly as before. Hearing the sound of cooked rice, the mother begged for a little to satisfy her hunger. Her brother secretly ordered his wife to take the rice steamer and place it on the bed, covering it with a quilt. The mother then returned weeping. When the mother heard the rice was ready, she asked for a small portion to stave off her hunger. Her brother secretly instructed his wife to take the rice steamer and place it upon the bed, covering it with a blanket. The mother then returned home, shedding tears.

Before he had gone even a mile, thunder and lightning broke forth. A deity entered from outside the fence, seized the rice steamer, and struck him with it; he then shook his wife at the gate, and the husband died in his room. The husband was silent as if by divine decree—how swift was the retribution!
△ The Six Children Obtain Fortune through Filial Piety.

If a son or daughter of good family, relying on the instructions of their compassionate mother, obeys and complies without opposition, they will be protected and remembered by the devas, and their fortune and happiness will be inexhaustible.
Such sons and daughters are called the noble lineage of devas and humans; they may even be bodhisattvas.

To deliver sentient beings, manifesting as sons or daughters to benefit their parents and serve them with obedience and non-opposition—this is precisely the practice of filial piety. Filial piety can reach up to Heaven; therefore, all the devas protect and mindfully observe such persons.

Blessings arise from filial piety, and joy is obtained through obedience. Becoming ever more excellent in subsequent lives, it is thus called "inexhaustible. Such individuals are honored and noble among gods and humans.

Regarding "lineage" (*jāti*): it refers to those who practice filial piety; they do not fall into the three miserable realms (*trāya*) but constantly abide among humans and devas, thereby forming a lineage.
Within the three realms, a human body is difficult to obtain and is thus precious; among the various heavens, the higher ones are more venerable.
The Buddha used these words to exhort and inspire sentient beings, saying that not only is one of the lineage of humans and devas, but one is also [of the lineage] of Bodhi.
The Buddha manifests his body. Indeed, the power of filial piety can move heaven and earth: thus Dong Yong was granted a wife, and Liu Yin obtained millet.
When the thoughts of filial piety move the spirits and deities, Cheng’s wife delivered her entire family from calamity, and Lady Zhang avoided the cause for punishment by thunder.

(Dong Yong was a man of the Western Han; his family was so poor that he had no means to bury his father. He sold himself as a laborer, and with the money earned, he provided for the burial. The Supreme Lord took pity on him and sent down the Weaver Girl to be his wife. She wove one roll of silk daily, thereby redeeming his freedom.)

He gave birth to one son. After the Weaver Girl ascended away, [Dongfang Shuo] served as Commandant during the reign of Emperor Jing. His son, Zhongshu, was ranked first among those who responded to the imperial edict on the "Worthy and Virtuous" (Xianliang) during the early years of Emperor Wu's reign; he served as Grand Tutor to the Prince of Jiangdu and became a great Confucian scholar of his generation.

(○ Liu Yin of the Jin dynasty. At the age of seven, he was able to practice filial piety and support his parents. His great-grandmother, Lady Wang, once craved *jǐn* greens during the height of winter; she had not eaten for one night. Yin then wailed and wept in a marsh, his cries never ceasing, as he offered prayers upward to the August Heaven.)

He universally bestowed his compassionate pity. Suddenly, as if someone were saying "Stop, stop," he checked his tears and looked at the ground; immediately, *jǐn* grass grew there. He took it back home to offer to his mother. Furthermore, one night he dreamed that a deity said to him, "There is millet beneath the western hedge. Upon waking, he dug it up.

In the end, fifteen *zhong* of grain were obtained. The inscription read: "Seven years' worth of millet, bestowed upon the filial son Liu Yin, so that he may provide for his parents' sustenance. (At the eastern side of Jinling City, Lady Qian, the wife of Gu Cheng, was once at her mother’s home. At that time, an epidemic was raging;

it spread rapidly until there were families where every member had died, and no more than a few people remained in entire alleys. Relatives dared not visit those who were ill. Gu Cheng fell ill first;

his parents, sons, and wife—eight people in all—lay prostrate on their pillows awaiting their fate. When Lady Qian heard this, she wished to go and see them. Her parents resisted her with all their might. Lady Qian said: "The life and death of my elders is a momentous matter. To bear such a heart and not return—is this no different from being a beast? If I go, I shall surely die, but..."

She ventured to hope that her parents would visit her. As she traveled alone along the road, she saw spirits and ghosts conversing with one another, saying: "All the gods are guarding us; the filial wife is returning! If we do not flee quickly, the reprimand will not be small. Thus, all eight people were saved.

This was an event from the third month of the Jiawu year, the eleventh year of the Shunzhi era of our dynasty. (The wife of County Magistrate Gu Deqian, Zhang, dreamed that a deity told her: "Due to your past karma, you shall be struck by a thunderbolt tomorrow. Upon waking, Zhang heard the thunder and knew she would surely die.

She thought silently to herself: "Death is unavoidable, but what of my aged mother-in-law’s terror? She then changed her clothes and went outside, standing at a distance beneath a mulberry tree. Suddenly, she heard a voice from the air saying: "The Supreme Lord already knows this thought of yours. He has specifically—" )

"I declare that you shall die. Shortly thereafter, the sky indeed cleared and brightened, and Lady Zhang remained unharmed. This was precisely a manifestation of her moving Heaven and Earth. △ 7. Comparing Filial Piety with Engratitude.

If a son or daughter of good family, in order to repay their mother’s kindness, were for the duration of an eon to cut the flesh from their own bodies three times every day to nourish their parents, they would still not have repaid even one day’s debt of gratitude. Why is this?

Because while all sons and daughters are dwelling within the womb, they suckle at the root of the breast, drinking and consuming their mother’s blood; and once they have emerged from the womb, [they continue to do so] during their infancy.

Before [the child] was weaned, the mother drank one hundred and eighty *hu* of breast milk; she ensured that her son received the finest flavors, and it was the same with her exquisite and wonderful garments.
Though he was foolish and lowly, her affection for him remained undivided.
The following section on repaying the kindness of one's mother describes matters that do not exist in the world;
they are all but hypothetical comparisons. A child exerts its utmost sincerity, yet nothing surpasses this [in its intensity].

That even so one cannot repay the kindness of a single day may be said to mean that casting away one’s body is insufficient to repay great benevolence, and sacrificing one’s life is hardly enough to repay profound grace. Alas for the kindness of a mother! O Heaven!

The kindness of heaven is boundless. This is why the following scriptural explanation is given: while the child is in the mother’s womb, it sucks at the root of the breasts and drinks the mother’s blood.
How can such kindness ever be repaid? Furthermore, from the time of birth until childhood, the amount of breast milk consumed is beyond human calculation;
only a Buddha knows this through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as it accumulates day by day and month by month.

"One hundred and eighty *hu*. For such an act of kindness, how could it ever be repaid? When obtaining food of the finest flavor, he could not bear to eat it himself; he would set it aside to give to his son.
When obtaining exquisite clothing, he likewise could not bear to use it for himself; he thought only of his son. Rather than endangering his own person, he sought to establish his son in safety.
Once the son had grown to maturity, he instructed him in benevolence and righteousness. To speak of them in general terms, they encompassed all that is noble in the world."
There is no kindness that surpasses that of one’s parents; though a child may exhaust their sincerity, they can never fully repay it. Such a debt of gratitude—how can it ever be requited?
Those who are ignorant fail to understand the principles of things, and those who are base and vulgar are not even counted among the ranks of men.
Yet, within a mother’s heart, her affection remains singular and undivided. Alas! If anyone who is a son or grandson fails to be sincere and filial, [they are truly lost].
They are not even equal to birds and beasts. To call them "human" by reason alone should cause them to die of shame. △ Eighth: Compassionate Love Leads to Rebirth in Heaven.
Long ago, there was a woman who traveled far to another country. Carrying her infant son in her arms, she crossed the Ganges River. Suddenly, the waters rose in a violent flood.
Though she could not advance further due to her physical strength, she could not bear to abandon her son out of maternal affection; thus, both mother and son perished together.
By the power of these roots of goodness born of such loving-kindness, they immediately attained rebirth in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven as Great Brahmā Kings.

This citation from antiquity illustrates the nature of gratitude. Regarding "crossing the river": because there were no boats or rafts and she had no companion, she carried her child alone as she waded through the water;
hence, it is called "crossing the river. As a woman, her physical strength was weak, and moreover, the waters were surging and overflowing;
thus, she lacked the power to move forward. Had she abandoned her child and let go of his hand, she might have felt somewhat stronger and perhaps not died; yet, due to her love—

The son could not bear to abandon her; thus, both mother and son perished together. By the power of the roots of goodness from his compassionate heart, he was reborn at the summit of the Form Realm as a Brahmā King.
This account speaks only of the mother’s kindness—how she would rather die than bear to abandon her child.
Because of their love, their feelings of deep gratitude are so profound that they are moved to be reborn in heaven. How great, then, is the kindness of one’s mother!

Other sutras also state that there was one who, by practicing filial piety and supporting his parents throughout his life, attained rebirth in the Brahma Heaven; this also demonstrates the gravity of the debt owed to one’s parents.

The *Āgama Sūtra* says: "Suppose there were a person who placed his father on his left shoulder and his mother on his right shoulder, carrying them for ten million years, providing them with clothing, food and drink, bedding and furniture, and medicine for their illnesses and infirmities—even while discharging excrement from their shoulders..."

Even after discharging urine, one still cannot repay the kindness of one’s parents. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: As clarified in the sūtras, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "You should know that even if there were a filial son who carried his father on one shoulder and his mother on the other for a hundred years, traveling everywhere, this would still not be a true repayment of the kindness of his parents.

If there is a filial son who can exhort his parents toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and toward the principles of cause and effect—causing those who have no faith to believe, those who already believe to increase in their faith, those without pure precepts to be encouraged to receive and uphold them, those with stinginess and greed to be encouraged to practice giving, and those without superior wisdom to be encouraged to cultivate it and dwell securely therein, thereby achieving self-discipline—this alone is called the true repayment of the kindness of one’s parents."
△ Ninth, a detailed explanation of the ten virtues.
For these reasons, the mother possesses ten virtues. The first is named "Great Earth," because within the mother’s womb, she serves as the foundation.

The second is named "Capable of Producing," because she is able to produce [the child] while undergoing manifold sufferings. The third is named "Capable of Correcting," because she constantly uses her hands to attend to the five sense organs.
The fourth is named "Nurturer," because she is able to nourish and raise [the child] according to the requirements of the four seasons. The fifth is named "Wise Woman."
Sixth, it is named "Adornment," because it can produce wisdom through skillful means (upāya) and is thus adorned with exquisite garlands.
Seventh, it is named "Peaceful Abiding," because it provides rest within the mother's embrace. Eighth, it is named "Instruction," because of its skillful means (upāya-kauśalya).
Ninth, it is called "Instruction," because by means of virtuous speech, one causes others to abandon all evils.
Tenth, it is called "Entrusting Affairs," because one is able to entrust the family business to one's children.

Regarding the great earth: the *Tāi jīng* (Womb Sūtra) states that for those with merit, while in the mother’s womb, it is like a multi-storied pavilion or palace, a realm of successive wonders where they experience joy;
for those without merit, it transforms according to their karma, such that what they perceive differs.
Therefore, the mother’s womb is regarded as the great earth; it possesses the virtue of being the support upon which the child relies.

Second, regarding the virtue of being able to give birth: the child originally has no form, yet emerges from the mother; thus, she possesses the virtue of being able to bring the child forth. Third, regarding the virtue of being able to nurture:
the mother loves her child, tending to them at all times, stroking them with her hands, and ensuring that the child’s eyes, ears, nose, and tongue [develop properly].
The body shall not suffer injury or damage; this is the virtue of being able to correctly rectify the five faculties. (Question: What of those who currently possess incomplete faculties?)

Answer: This child lacked virtue in a previous life, and this retribution has manifested in the present life; or perhaps it was due to his own lack of self-regulation that he suffered injury. It was not the mother who caused him to be incomplete.
Fourth, as for "nurturing," this refers to adjusting food and clothing according to the four seasons to provide support and care, ensuring that exposure to cold and heat is appropriate.
That the child gradually grows and prospers is due to the virtue of the mother’s nurturing. Fifth, she is called "the wise" because of her maternal love.
Fearing that her son might be dull or base, she employed various methods as the occasion required to stimulate his development and cause him to give rise to wisdom.
Thus, even the son’s own brilliance and acuity are virtues stimulated by the mother. Sixth is the name "Adornment."
Because a mother loves her child, she adorns and embellishes them with necklaces, precious jewels, and fine silks, not sparing any expense;

this is the virtue of a mother’s adornment out of love for her child. (Question: Families of wealth and status can easily provide such adornments, but how shall those of poverty and low station adorn their children? Answer:)

This statement shows that a mother’s virtue and love for her child reach everywhere; even in poor households where these [material things] may be lacking, such a heart still exists. Seventh is "providing security":

by holding the child in her arms, nursing it with milk, and moving it from dry places to moist ones, she causes the child to rest and attain peace; this is the virtue of a mother. Eighth is "instruction":
"teaching" (jiao) means training and admonishing, while "bestowing" (shou) means explaining and imparting; through a mother’s love for her child, she employs skillful means...
He then instructs and admonishes them, causing them to follow his words and emulate his learning; this includes the intent to request teachers, provide for their studies, and so forth.
This constitutes the virtue of instruction and guidance. The ninth is called "admonition" (*anuśāsanī*), which differs from the former.

Whereas the former involved teaching various kinds of wholesome matters such as ritual, music, and literature, this involves teaching them to cease evil, guard against wrongdoing, and remain far removed from it.
These various faults are, in fact, virtues that serve as sincere warnings. Tenth is "entrusting with the family business":
this means that once the son has reached maturity and mastered both practical affairs and underlying principles, the father entrusts the family estate to him, charging him with its responsibility.
This constitutes the virtue of ultimate entrustment. "Fu" (付) means to hand over; "zhu" (嘱) means to exhort or admonish. △ Tenth, the comparison of poverty.
"O son of good family, among all those in the world, who is the wealthiest and who is the poorest? One who has a compassionate mother living in the house is called wealthy;
one who does not have a compassionate mother living there is called poor. When the compassionate mother is present, it is called midday."

When the mother dies, it is called the setting of the sun; while the compassionate mother is present, it is called the brightness of the moon. When the compassionate mother has passed away, it is called the night of darkness.
When parents reside in the hall, one has someone to rely upon and is wealthy; when parents have departed this world, the child has no one to rely upon and is destitute.
When poor, yet with parents living in the hall, they teach their children wisdom and open their intelligence so that it shines like the sun at its zenith, illuminating everything without exception.

When the parents have passed away, one no longer hears their virtuous words; it is as if the sun has already set. When parents provide warnings and admonitions, one does not become foolish or ignorant;
it is like the brightness of the moon. When parents are no longer present, one acts according to one's own whims and follows one's impulses; thus, through folly, one fails in one’s affairs.
It is like the dark of night. The detailed analysis and differentiation are hereby concluded. III. Conclusion and Exhortation to Practice Filial Piety:

Therefore, you all should diligently cultivate the practice of filially supporting your parents; the merit of such a person is equal to that of one who makes offerings to the Buddha, with no difference between them.
One should repay the kindness of one's parents in this manner.
Therefore, the two characters [preceding] receive the special grace mentioned above. From "You all" onwards, there is an exhortation to filial piety;

that is to say, one must apply oneself diligently and not be indolent, and one must practice cultivation without negligence. Regarding filial piety, one should attend to them morning and evening; regarding nourishment, one should serve them...
Delicious and savory foods, served with reverence and offered with sincerity, can eliminate calamities, increase blessings, and prolong life;
therefore, they are equal in merit to making offerings to the Buddha, without any difference. Furthermore, it says "one should":
The conclusion consists of earnest exhortations and reminders. This refers to the natural affection between mother and child, the greatest of human relations;
it is not an external or forced exhortation, but rather that which ought to be done spontaneously. The section on the kindness of parents is hereby concluded.
II. The Kindness of Sentient Beings (three parts): 1. Mutually being one another’s parents.

Good son, as for the debt of gratitude owed to sentient beings: since beginningless time, all sentient beings have transmigrated through the five realms of existence for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Throughout many lifetimes, they have mutually served as one another’s fathers and mothers.
Because they have been each other’s parents, every man is a compassionate father and every woman is a merciful mother; in every previous birth, they possessed great compassion.
Therefore, it is just like the kindness of one's present parents; they are equal and without distinction.
All noble ones and ordinary beings are identical in their *dharmakāya*, yet they each have differences according to the retribution received through karma.

Because they take birth among the various classes of beings, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*). As for "kindness," since beginningless time, all have been each other's parents; thus, [this kindness] exists.

Great is the grace [of the Buddha]. Because beings transmigrate through the five realms, their heads and faces are changed; the physical eye cannot see them, and deluded consciousness is difficult to clarify.

They harm one another and lose their original debt of gratitude. Only the World-Honored Buddha, with the vision of the Buddha-eye and the clarity of primordial wisdom, knows their origins and endings and examines their causes and effects.
Sentient beings, shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, stubbornly oppose this truth. Thus, the Tathāgata...
Having clarified this, I cannot bear not to speak of it. I respectfully exhort the gentlemen who study the classics: do not claim that these matters are trivial and thereby incur public censure;

it would be a great fortune if you were to believe them. As for the five paths, they are: the path of devas, the path of humans, the path of hell-beings, the path of hungry ghosts, and the path of animals.
Asuras are concealed within the realm of devas; thus, they are called the five destinies.

As for "revolving," it is because sentient beings follow their karma without fixed destination—suddenly ascending and suddenly descending, suddenly dying and suddenly being born—like the turning of a wheel. This has been so since beginningless time.
For hundreds of thousands of kalpas, there has been no rest; yet, since we have mutually served as fathers and mothers, all men are thus compassionate fathers and all women are thus merciful mothers.
Because of the great compassion exercised in past lives, they are no different from one's present parents. II. Turning Kindness into Enmity.
Such past kindnesses have yet to be repaid. Yet, due to deluded karma, various conditions of opposition or compliance arise; because of attachment, one instead becomes their enemy.

Why is this? Shrouded by ignorance, the clear knowledge of past lives fails to perceive that in former births they were one's parents—those to whom one owes gratitude and from whom one received mutual benefit—and thus such a person is called unfilial.
Regarding those whose past kindness has not yet been repaid: even without the Buddha’s teaching, one would still be unable to recognize it, so how could one possibly repay it?
Or, as some say, "not only is it unrepaid, but one further binds new grudges. As for "deluded karma," this refers to the conditions of daily life.

As for "conformity and opposition," these refer to the union and separation of such circumstances. For example, regarding the affairs of daily life, those that accord with one's mind are considered... [favorable].
"Conformity. That which is not in accord is contradiction. It is like two people who both desire the same beautiful thing;
when one obtains it, the other feels resentment, and when the other obtains it, the first feels resentment. This leads to mutual strife and slander, accumulating until they become sworn enemies.

Through kalpas and even unto the end of kalpas, their enmity cannot be resolved. The two characters "attachment" (*zhi-zhu*) are precisely the mark of self (*ātman*). Because of this mark of self, [conflict arises].
The arising of those characteristics and the very root of saṃsāra both emerge from this. Why is this so? [The text] interrogates:
"Since there has been the debt of mutual parentage in past lives, why is it that they now, on the contrary, contend and harbor resentment toward one another? The explanation states:
Because ignorance obscures the wisdom and clarity of past lives, they are unable to clearly perceive that in their previous births they were mutual parents.
This is the gratitude one ought to repay. Since we have all been each other’s parents, it is only logical that we should mutually benefit one another;
yet now, not only do we fail to repay this kindness, we instead harbor enmity toward one another. Therefore, the Buddha condemned this behavior, naming it "filial impiety.

Furthermore, because sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance which obscures their wisdom, and enveloped by afflictions which cloud their minds, they are unable to perceive the sublime and sacred clarity of the Sages.
Seeing that there are no sages who possess penetrating insight, such that they have come to harm one another, this constitutes the realm of the Tathāgata’s compassion;

unable to bear it, he does not fail to speak. As for those with the karmic affinity to personally encounter the Buddha’s intent, it would be unfilial if they did not cleanse their hearts, repent their errors, and contemplate repaying his grace.
△ Third, the conclusion and exhortation to repay the debt of gratitude.
For these reasons, all classes of sentient beings have also bestowed great kindness upon us at all times, and it is truly difficult to repay them.
Such matters as these are called the "kindness of sentient beings."
The first phrase承接 (carries forward from) the preceding discussion on the causal conditions of being mutual parents. "At all times" refers to the three periods of time.
Since sentient beings are said to comprise "all classes," they do not consist of only one type, namely the human realm, but include all ten categories of sentient beings.
Which class does not possess Buddha-nature? Which class has not undergone birth and death? [They have] truly bestowed great kindness. Truly...
"It is difficult to repay. Thus concludes the section below. The section on the kindness of sentient beings above is finished. △ Third, the kindness of kings, in three parts:
first, a general indication of their superior virtues.
As for the king’s benevolence: his merit is supreme; though born among humans, he has attained sovereignty.

A "kingdom" (*rājya*) refers to a bounded territory, and its ruler is the "king" (*rājan*), whose position is the "nine-fives" (the apex of authority). He rules over the four quarters of the world; thus, he is called the "King of the Kingdom. Regarding "benevolence":
by means of his blessings he covers the world and benefits the people with virtue; this constitutes the king's benevolence. Consequently, the borders are at peace.

Quiescence is called "blessing" (*puṇya*); the vast and surging breeze of benevolence is called "virtue" (*guṇa*). When the virtue and blessings of a single person surpass those of the entire world, it is therefore called "supreme.
Although born in a lowly station, he truly embodies the principle of a king. Another sutra states:

"A Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) becomes a king of Jambudvīpa, teaching and transforming the world, with his rank reaching down to the human realm. However, since he is already a Bodhisattva, he ought not to remain among ordinary humans.
He became a king of the world. By the power of his great compassionate vows, he governed all under heaven and transformed the human realm.
His descent into this world was not like that of ordinary men; acting according to his own will, who would dare not obey?
Therefore it is said: "Though born among humans, he attained sovereignty. II. Specifically Explaining His Superior Virtues (eleven sections). 1. Protected by the Various Heavens.

Yù. Because the devaputras of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven constantly provide him with their power and perpetually protect and uphold him, everything within his realm—from the mountains, rivers, and great earth to the very limits of the ocean—belongs to the king; the merit of this single person surpasses that of all others.
By virtue of the merit of sentient beings, this Great Holy King transforms them through the True Dharma, enabling all sentient beings to attain complete peace and happiness.

The Heaven of the Thirty-three, that is, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, is situated at the summit of Mount Sumeru. Therein dwells the Honored Deva Śakra, who presides over the thirty-two surrounding heavens;
together they number thirty-three. Among these various sons of gods, the son of gods serves as their king. Thus it is.
The ministers and assistants of his domain constantly provide him with strength; "strength" here refers to the two kinds of power: merit and wisdom.
"Providing" means being empowered by celestial forces. Because the sovereign possesses the Way, the myriad people rely upon him, and the heavenly deities protect him;

therefore, it is said that he is "constantly guarded and sustained. Below this, the scene of Great Peace is revealed. Since he transforms the world through the True Dharma, he is thus called a Sage King.
Because the merit of a single person universally benefits others, it is able to cause all sentient beings to attain peace and happiness;
this is entirely due to the great benevolence of the King, whose blessings extend even to distant regions. △ Second, the actual metaphor for the nature of the state.
For example, in the world, pillars are the foundation of all halls and palaces; the king is the foundation of the people’s abundance and happiness, for it is by depending on the king that they exist.
Just as the Brahmā King is able to give birth to the myriad things, so too can a noble king (cakravartin) give birth to the laws for governing the state.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he is like the Sun Deity who can illuminate the world; the Holy King likewise can survey the realm so that people may dwell in peace and happiness.
He is like the central pillar, which serves as the foundation of a hall or palace and upon which all other timbers depend; thus, the King is to his people.
It is the root of all things and that upon which the myriad people rely; therefore, it is said that the abundance and joy of the myriad people are all moved by the King’s virtue.

As for the claim that the Brahmā King creates all beings, this is a tradition of the non-Buddhist teachings of the Western Regions, asserting that at the beginning of the kalpa, the Brahmā King was able to produce the ten thousand things.
The Buddha now employs this as a metaphor, just as a king produces the laws for governing a state. People...
They obtain the benefit of peace and happiness and attribute this grace to the King; thus it is said, "for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.

Just as the Sun Deity illuminates the four continents, so too can a person accomplish all matters—there is no greater grace than this. This serves as a metaphor for the King’s virtue of overseeing and presiding over his realm:
whether he tours abroad or conducts investigations within, he is able to understand the customs of the people and discern between the heterodox and the orthodox.
Distinguishing truth from falsehood and weighing good against evil, it ensures that the wicked and devious do not seize power and that upright people do not lose their positions.
Thus, the national character naturally flourishes and the people attain peace and happiness; hence it is said, "Because the people are peaceful and happy.

As for the statement that the Brahmā King can give birth to all things: (The heterodox practitioners of India who smear ashes on themselves, as well as the various Brahmins, collectively maintain that Maheśvara is the cause of all things, asserting that this deity possesses four attributes: first, substantiality.)

[They hold that this deity is] secondly, all-pervasive; thirdly, eternal; and fourthly, capable of producing all things. Furthermore, they calculate that this deity has three bodies: first, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), whose essence is eternally all-pervasive and whose magnitude is equal to empty space, capable of producing all things; second, the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), which resides above the heavens of form (*rūpadhātu*);

and third, the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which assumes forms according to the six destinies to teach and transform sentient beings. Therefore, they cling to this deity as being eternal, as being one, as the cause of all things, and as the cause of *nirvāṇa*. However, although non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) maintain these attachments, in reality, it is not so.
△ The auspicious response to the transformation of the Three Virtues:
When a king loses correct governance, the people have no one to rely upon. If he governs with correctness, the eight great terrors will not enter his kingdom.

That is to say, because the eight calamities cannot invade them: foreign nations attacking and pressing upon them; internal rebellions within their own borders; afflictions from evil spirits and diseases;
famine within the land; unseasonable winds and rains; excessive winds and rains; eclipses of the sun and moon;
and the portents of the stars and constellations—none of these can prevail against a king who governs with righteousness for the benefit of his people.
The King constitutes the very body of the state; his fortune and misfortune are intimately linked, and thus he is that upon which the myriad people rely.

This is because the sovereign alone serves as the standard for the world: when the superior honors the aged, the people are inspired to filial piety; when the superior honors the elders, the people are inspired to fraternal respect.
Since the King has lost the way of rectitude, the hearts of the people have become scattered, even to the point that some have failed to observe the prescribed norms. Therefore—

It is said that people have nothing to rely upon. One should know that although the Buddha fundamentally spoke of a ruler who possesses the Way (*dharma*), he first clarified those who lack the Way for the sake of contrast and to make it known to others.

If one transforms the subordinates through correctness—meaning the ruler possesses the Way, rectifies the fundamental social norms, establishes customs and transformations, and spreads benevolence and righteousness throughout the world—this is called "transforming through correctness."
Thus, the spirits and deities will naturally provide assistance, and the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) will not invade. When it says "fear" rather than "difficulty," it refers to this.
If these eight matters prevail within a state, calamity will surely befall the people; one who seeks to avoid fear cannot achieve it.
What is called "inferior things appearing" means that other states will invade and press upon it—whether from foreign lands or neighboring territories.
Regarding the state: when an aggressor’s troops press upon its borders, the common people cannot avoid fleeing and hiding; this is the first of their terrors. Regarding "within the realm":
this refers to one's own country. Regarding "rebellion": this refers to high ministers or military commanders of one's own country who turn their backs on gratitude and rebel against the state.
These constitute the second category of terrors. Evil spirits, diseases, and the prevalence of various epidemics and pestilences are truly great terrors.

The three matters concerning famine in the land and so forth are easy to understand. Furthermore, there are solar and lunar eclipses, as well as the anomalous transformations of the stars and constellations.
These are all omens of calamity. It is said that when Heaven displays such portents, humans will inevitably face disaster;

they serve as a warning and exhortation to the human heart, so that one dares not commit what is wrong. Regarding these eight kinds [of difficulties]: if a king lacks the Way, then depraved matters will encroach upon him;

if a king of men governs with rectitude, the people will find peace. Naturally, the people will rejoice and the spirits will show reverence; thus they move and respond to Heaven and Earth. Such are the eight hardships.
Therefore, they cannot be harmed. △ Fourth, loving the people as one's own children:
It is like an elder who has only one son, whose love and remembrance for him are beyond compare; he cherishes and benefits him, constantly bestowing peace and happiness.
Day and night he does not abandon them. So too is it with the Great Holy King of the land;
he regards all living beings equally, as if they were his only son, and his heart of protection never ceases, day or night.
A householder loves his children, bestowing his kindness upon them alone; a king loves his people, extending his benevolence to all under heaven.

To love the people as one loves one's own children is truly the mark of sagely virtue. With every thought fixed upon the people, he never ceases day or night. △ Five: The Interrelation of Good and Evil.
Such a king of men who causes others to practice the ten wholesome actions is called a "King of Merit. If he does not cause them to practice them, he is called a "Lord of Non-merit.
Why is this? If within a king's realm even a single person practices goodness, the merit produced by that act is divided into seven portions.

Those who perform virtuous deeds receive five parts [of the merit]. Of that, the king constantly receives two parts, because he shares in the welfare resulting from the king’s cultivation of wholesome causes.
It is the same for the commission of the ten non-virtuous actions, as they share in the same undertaking throughout the entire kingdom.
Fields, gardens, groves, and all things produced therein are likewise divided into seven parts.

The ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) do not transcend the three types of karma; namely, the three of body, the four of speech, and the three of mind. (Wholesome means the sense of conforming to principle;

it refers to practicing these ten dharmas because they all accord with principle. Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, restraint (*saṃvara*), and second, cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Restraint means ceasing one’s own evil and not afflicting others. Cultivation means practicing superior virtues to benefit and bring peace to all. (1. Non-killing)

1. To refrain from taking life means not to harm the lives of any sentient beings; this is the virtue of abstaining from killing. Having ceased killing, one should practice the virtue of releasing captive creatures. 2. To refrain from stealing means not to pilfer the property of others;

this is the virtue of abstaining from theft. Having ceased stealing, one should practice the virtue of giving. 3. To refrain from sexual misconduct means not to engage in improper sexual desires; this is the virtue of abstaining from lust. Having ceased sexual misconduct, one should practice the virtue of the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).

(4) Abstinence from false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). This means not giving rise to deceptive words to delude others; it is the virtue of ceasing false speech. Since one does not speak falsely, one should practice the virtue of truthful speech. (5) Abstinence from divisive speech (*paiśunya*).

This means not speaking of this person’s virtues to that person or that person’s faults to this person to cause them to quarrel; it is the virtue of ceasing divisive speech. Since one does not engage in divisive speech, one should practice the virtue of promoting harmony and benefit. (6) Abstinence from harsh speech (*pāruṣya*). This means not uttering coarse, violent, or evil words.

To refrain from reviling others is the virtue of ceasing harsh speech. Since one does not engage in harsh speech, one should practice the virtue of gentle and soft words. (7. Not engaging in frivolous speech means not using words that are artificially embellished or flowery, yet intended to please the listener.)

This is the goodness of ceasing frivolous speech. Since one does not engage in frivolous speech, one should practice the goodness of straightforward and correct speech. (8) Non-attachment to sensual desires means not being greedily attached to the objects of the passions. This is the goodness of ceasing greed.

Since one does not harbor attachment to sensual desires, one should practice the goodness of the pure *brahmacarya* life. (9) Non-ill will means not giving rise to a mind of anger or resentment toward others. This is the goodness of ceasing ill will.
