Since one does not harbor ill will, one should practice the goodness of loving-kindness and patience.

(10) Non-perverted views means not holding biased, heterodox, or divergent views, nor clinging to what is wrong as being right. This is the goodness of ceasing perverted views. Since one does not hold perverted views, one should practice the goodness of right faith and right view. (11) To act contrary to these is...
[They] commit the ten evils). If a king can instruct his people to cultivate the ten wholesome dharmas, he is truly a virtuous and benevolent ruler possessed of merit.

Conversely, if he does not cause them to practice self-restraint, the people will follow their own impulses and will inevitably commit the ten evils. Since he permits the people to act wickedly, he is called a non-meritorious king.
Therefore, the following explanation is provided: one who teaches people to cultivate goodness is a meritorious king; one who does not cause them to so cultivate is not.
Why is it that even for a king who does not perform merit, [merit is still acquired]? The commentary explains:

If a single person within the kingdom practices virtue, the resulting merit is divided into seven parts. The person who performed the virtuous deed receives five parts, while the king of that country constantly receives two parts.
This is because the virtuous act of this person was cultivated precisely through the king’s instruction; therefore, it belongs to the king as well.
It is shared for mutual benefit. Furthermore, while one person may perform a virtuous deed and receive its merit, the King obtains two shares of it.
If the people of the world practice virtue, the King’s merit becomes immeasurable. Since this is the case with good deeds, it is likewise for evil acts.

Therefore, it is said that when ten [shares] are produced—such as from fields, gardens, and groves—all things produced shall be divided into seven parts, and two of these parts shall be given to the King, because the King provides governance.
Because the people engage in sowing and reaping, it is said that whether a king possesses fortune or misfortune depends solely upon his teaching of the people to do good or not to do good.
△ Sixth, the Good Dharma is Equal to Heaven.

If there is a king who possesses right view and transforms the world in accordance with the Dharma, he is called a "Lord of Devas," because he transforms the world through the wholesome dharmas of the devas.
Consequently, the various celestial deities and the World-Protecting Kings constantly come to provide protection and guard the royal palace.
Although dwelling among humans, he practices the deeds of the devas; because his mind regarding reward and punishment is free from partiality, the laws of all noble kings are thus.
A sovereign such as this is called a King of Righteous Dharma (Dharmarāja).
One who possesses right view perceives correctly. To transform the world in accordance with the Dharma is the virtue of a king.

To transform conduct through the ten wholesome paths of action, being as impartial and upright as heaven, is called the "Heavenly Wholesome Dharma. One is named a "Lord of Heaven" because, although existing among humans, [one acts as such].
Because they share the same virtue as the heavens, their rewards and punishments are free from partiality; this is the rectitude of the legal code.
Furthermore, it is a natural necessity that a ruler who possesses the Way is assisted by the hundred spirits.

Therefore, it is said that the various heavens take one case as an example for the rest, and thus it is said that "the laws of all sage-kings are likewise. The final two phrases conclude [the section] by identifying them as sage-kings. △
The seventh is the accomplishment of the ten virtues.
By these causes and conditions, one accomplishes the ten virtues. The first is named "Able to Illuminate," because one illuminates the world with the eye of wisdom.
Second, it is named Adornment, because it adorns the kingdom with great merit and wisdom. Third, it is named Bestowing Happiness, because it bestows great peace and happiness upon the people.
Fourth, it is named Subduing Enemies, because all adversaries are naturally subdued. Fifth, it is named Freedom from Fear.
1. Able to ward off the eight difficulties, for it causes one to be free from terror. 2. Named Abiding in Worthiness (*Bhadra-vāsa*), for it assembles all worthy men to deliberate on state affairs.
3. Named the Source of Dharma (*Dharmamūla*), for the myriad subjects abide in peace by relying upon the king.

4. Named Sustainer of the World (*Lokadhara*), for by means of the royal dharma, he sustains the world. 5. Named Master of Karma (*Karmādhipati*), for all karmas, whether good or evil, belong to the king. 6. Named Man (*Puruṣa*).
Lord, because the king is the sovereign of all the people, all kings, through the merit of their previous lives,
achieve these ten kinds of supreme virtues.
The first phrase follows from what precedes it. It is by means of the causes and conditions of rewarding the good and punishing the evil that the ten virtues are accomplished;

this is the general heading. What follows is the specific explanation. In each case, the first phrase states the name, and the second phrase explains its meaning. Regarding "being able to illuminate":
it means that the affairs of the world do not fall into obscurity, because the King possesses wisdom as his eyes, enabling him to examine Heaven.
...the affairs of the lower [realms]. Thus it is said that he "illuminates the world. In all such cases, the character *gu* (hence) serves as the concluding particle of the sentence.

Regarding the two types of adornment (*vyūha*): because the King possesses vast merit and wisdom, his great merit brings peace and stability to the world, so that the people enjoy a time of great tranquility.
His great wisdom enables him to investigate and discern; thus, the wicked and corrupt dare not incite rebellion. He possesses great...
Wisdom is able to establish the laws; the myriad people then follow their regulations. When this is so, all evils are eliminated and the ten thousand virtues are fully manifested.
Is this not because virtue constitutes a great adornment for the state? As it is said: "The State of Chu has nothing with which to be adorned as a treasure;
it takes only virtue as its treasure. Third, regarding those who possess joy: this refers to a ruler who possesses the Way.
Because he shares his joy with the people, by virtue of the King’s merit and wisdom, the eight remote regions do not invade one another, and the four classes of the people do not fall into disorder.
The abundance of the five grains and the flourishing of ritual and music ensure that the myriad people obtain peace and happiness;
all this is brought about by the King’s power. Thus, they attribute their gratitude to the King, which is why it is called "sharing joy. Fourth is "subduing resentment. As for resentment—
"Enmity" (*chou*) refers to hostility. "To lie low" (*fu*) means to crouch; to humble oneself and follow another is called "lying low.
Although the King possesses the Way, there are those who do not forget ingratitude—some who were enemies in a previous life leading to resentment in this present life.
"Foes" (*di*) refers to the unruly hordes of foreign lands who intend to invade; even if they raise rebellious arms, because the King possesses sagely virtue, [they shall be subdued].
Furthermore, that which is inspired by great wisdom and grand strategy cannot be undertaken recklessly; it skillfully causes [others] to turn their hearts toward [the Way].
Because there is no need for the use of weapons or military conquest, it is said that they submit naturally. Fifth, as for the name "Free from Fear":
since one is a ruler who possesses the Way, the hundred spirits naturally provide assistance; therefore, the eight difficulties cannot be imposed upon him.
What cause for fear could there be for the state? Sixth is named "Abiding in the Worthy. This means that when a ruler employs the worthy, the worthy will surely gather.
Some, admiring his reputation, will come from beyond a thousand li; others, looking up to his virtue, will not decline the hardships of travel to arrive.
Now, employing worthy men to assist the state is the great principle for governing the world.

Those who evaluate state affairs refer to the deliberation and discussion of the administration of the nation—namely, harmonizing the cauldron of statecraft and regulating the yin and yang—thereby bringing about the great order of the world;
this constitutes the sovereign’s great virtue. Regarding the seventh title, "The Foundation of the Law" (*fǎběn*): "Foundation" refers to the essence of the state, while "Law" refers to...
The standard of conduct is that by which the myriad people rely upon the sovereign. The sovereign is taken as the substance and the people as the function;

since the function does not depart from the substance, they dwell relying upon the sovereign. This is why ritual, music, military expeditions, and punishments all proceed from the Son of Heaven, so that the people may obtain their proper laws.
This is what it means to abide in peace. Regarding the eighth, "sustaining the world": the world refers to the realm under heaven. "Sustaining" means to maintain and preserve.
Although the realm under heaven belongs to all people of the world, its security or peril depends upon the sovereign.
If the ruler is upright, there is peace; if not, there is peril. This refers to a ruler who possesses the Way, who preserves [the realm] through the laws of the Heavenly King.

Furthermore, the Heavenly Kings refer to the Four Great Heavenly Kings (*catur-mahārāja-kāyika-deva*). They are able to suppress the heterodox and support the orthodox, each protecting one quarter of the world.

The preservation of the state by the sovereign is likewise so. Ninth, regarding the term "owner of karma" (*karmasvāmī*): "karma" refers to the various activities performed within the world, whose nature as good or evil is not fixed;
all these belong to the king. It is like how a straight form produces a straight shadow, or how deep roots result in lush fruit. This means:
When the king is virtuous, the people are virtuous; when the king is evil, it is likewise so. Therefore, it is said that all wholesome and unwholesome karmas belong to the king.
The tenth [title] is "Lord of Men. "Men" refers to the myriad subjects. When the people obtain their lord, they do not fall into disorder, just as a net has its main cord.
This means that the world cannot be without a ruler for even a single day; hence it is said, "all the people..."
Because the king is the sovereign, the following provides a summary: that one king is thus, so too are all kings; hence it says "all. "Previous lives" refers to former births.
Because merit was cultivated in previous lives, the fruits thereof have brought about the accomplishment of these ten virtues in this life.
This demonstrates that the causes and effects of good and evil are never in vain. △ Eight hundred spirits provide secret protection.
Mahābrahmā and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven constantly assist the king of men, enabling him to experience supreme and wondrous bliss.
Although the various rākṣasa kings and deities do not manifest their forms, they come secretly to provide protection. When the king and his retinue look upon the people, [they see them as follows].
When they commit various unwholesome deeds and are unable to restrain themselves, all the celestial deities and others will distance themselves from them.
If they see them practicing virtue, they will rejoice and praise them, all proclaiming: "Our Holy King! The dragons and devas are delighted; they shall pour down the rain of ambrosia."
The five grains ripen; the people are prosperous and happy.
The king possesses the Way, being impartial and selfless. The celestial deities love and revere him, and it is fitting that they provide protection and aid.
As for a ruler who cannot restrain the people from committing evil, this is described as another kind of unrighteous king. Since the king lacks the Way, the people—

Furthermore, there is no path [of righteousness]. They commit various unwholesome deeds, and the king is unable to restrain them. Thus, there is neither governance nor order; he allows the people to act with evil.
Therefore, it is only natural that the celestial deities are displeased and have all departed from him.

If one sees those who cultivate goodness—[referring back to the preceding text concerning] a king who possesses the Way—there is a missing passage therein which should be supplemented as follows: "If the various people..."

"Seeing that the King cultivates goodness, which accords with the words and accords with the meaning, they rejoice and offer praise," and so forth—this refers to the joyful shouts of the myriad people.
Therefore, it is said that "all together cry out: 'Our Sage King! This is the joy of humans;
below them, the spirits are delighted, and thus the dragons and devas rejoice, raining down the nectar of immortality. Consequently, the five grains [flourish].
They were brought to maturity. The people enjoyed abundance and happiness. △ Ninth, neighboring states all submitted.
If one does not associate with various evil persons and so forth, one will extensively benefit the world, and all shall follow the transformation of the Right Dharma, like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
The kingdom will surely manifest [prosperity]. All neighboring kingdoms will come to submit and serve; among humans and non-humans alike, there will be none who do not offer praise.

The first two lines are a negative illustration (*pratiṣedha*) of those who associate with evil persons, such as the six heretical teachers of the Western Regions (India), all of whom served as the king’s preceptors and deluded the king with false teachings—wherein "false" is precisely what is meant by "evil. Now, it is said that [the king does not do so]...
As for "those who draw near," they do not associate with the followers of the six heretical teachers, but rather transform and govern the world through the True Dharma;
hence it is said that they bring universal benefit to the world and all follow the correct transformation. As for "the wish-fulfilling jewel will surely appear in the king's realm," it means:
This is precisely what Heaven sends down as an auspicious omen (*śakuna*). Because the state obtains this treasure, all matters proceed according to its wishes.
However, auspicious omens do not necessarily consist solely of the descent of a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*);

whenever the phoenix arrives in ceremonial grace, the qilin appears in the world, or when a star of virtue manifests in the heavens, or a numinous *lingzhi* fungus grows upon the earth—all such occurrences constitute auspicious omens.
Furthermore, the statement that he must appear in the royal kingdom is because he is well able to move Heaven; thus, the path of resonance and response is naturally so.

Within the realm of the king—that is, amidst the mundane dust—he acts as the sovereign and transforms those who come from beyond as guests. Therefore, the neighboring states submit and serve him out of being moved by the king’s virtue.
Whether they be humans or spirits and deities, those who offer praise do so to celebrate the excellence of the king’s Way.
Furthermore: △ Ten: Evil Persons Punished by Gods and Spirits.
If there is an evil person within the kingdom who conceives a rebellious mind, even for a mere moment, such a person—
His merit will naturally decay and vanish; at the end of his life, he shall fall into hell and pass through the realms of animals, undergoing all manner of suffering.
Why is this? Because the Holy King failed to recognize kindness and gave rise to various acts of malice and rebellion, he receives such retribution.
Good and evil, sages and ordinary beings, are all created by the mind alone. The retributions of the three miserable realms are summoned by one's own karma.

Within the realm of a virtuous king, if one does not comply with the royal transformation, turns one's back on kindness and forgets righteousness, or suddenly gives rise to rebellious intent, one will be dragged away by one's own karma and punished by devas and nāgas.
Thus, when blessings decline and calamities arrive, one cannot escape the retribution of the three miserable realms. This is why [the following] is cited as evidence.
[Question: Why is it that for a single thought of evil, one must necessarily pass through the three miserable realms (*trāya*), such that the karma is light yet the retribution is heavy?
[Answer: It is because [the person] was ignorant of the grace of the Sage-King; it was not the Sage-King who caused it to be so.
Because they themselves gave rise to wicked rebellion, they receive such retribution. [Judgment: Since it was initiated by a single individual at the outset, it will necessarily...
There were many who assisted him from behind; there was no improper act he would not commit. He ruined the Way of the Benevolent King and injured the purity of social customs and transformation.
He created it himself, experienced it himself, and received its consequences himself; the retribution is like a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound.
Should those who observe this not have their hearts stirred with alarm? △ Eleven: The Virtuous Obtain Blessings.

If there are people who can practice a virtuous mind and respectfully assist a benevolent king, honoring him as they would a Buddha, those people will enjoy peace, security, abundance, and happiness in this present life;
whatever they seek or desire shall not fail to accord with their wishes. Why is this? Because all kings—
In the past, he observed the pure precepts of the Tathāgata and was constantly a king of men, living in peace and happiness.

This clarifies that those who follow the way of kings receive virtuous retribution, which is like a shadow following a form or an echo following a sound. Thus, one who is able to practice a virtuous mind [reaps such results].

This means that when wholesome mindfulness arises in the mind and wholesome deeds are practiced outwardly, one who can simply follow the Dharma is thereby honoring the king and assisting in rectitude.
If a benevolent king obtains virtuous people and employs them in office to assist the state, it is like a chariot obtaining its wheels.
When a bird gains its wings, it is certain that the True Dharma can be practiced.

Furthermore, if one honors the King as one honors the Buddha, this person will enjoy peace and security in the present life, and their aspirations will surely be fulfilled. Therefore, the single phrase of inquiry asks:

why is it that being able to practice a virtuous mind and respectfully assisting the benevolent King is not only what is required of the human way, but also results in the attainment of peace in the present life? And so...
Why is it that even their requests are fulfilled according to their wishes? The commentary states:

Because all kings in past lives have received the Buddha’s precepts; since a king who receives the Buddha’s precepts is a disciple of the Buddha, when these virtuous people revere the king, they are as if revering the Buddha.
Moved by the power of the Buddha’s influence, they obtain such a reward. △ Third, a summary of these superior virtues.
For these reasons, the retributions for both opposition and compliance are like echoes responding to sounds. The benevolence and virtue of the Sage-King are as vast as this.

This single phrase connects with the two preceding sections: "opposition" refers to the aforementioned evil persons being punished by the spirits, while "compliance" refers to the aforementioned virtuous persons obtaining blessings.
Opposition and compliance are like the sounds; the retributions are like the echoes. Cause and effect are thus clearly manifest—who could deny them?
How could I dare not believe it? The final two lines summarize the King’s kindness. △ Fourth, the kindness of the Triple Gem, in two parts. First, the general designation of the Triple Gem:
"Good son, the kindness of the Triple Gem is called inconceivable; it brings benefit and happiness to sentient beings without ceasing."
The Three Jewels are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. "En" (恩) refers to their benevolent grace. The term "inconceivable" briefly clarifies the meaning of "Jewel.

The two phrases concerning "benefit" and "happiness" briefly clarify the meaning of "grace. This means that they are called gracious because they benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings without ceasing.
Since they benefit living beings without rest, their minds must necessarily be unfathomable. Thus it is said:
It cannot be expressed by words; therefore, it is called "inconceivable. △ Second, the specific explanation and broad demonstration has two parts.
First, the Tathāgata’s direct revelation of the Three Jewels has three parts. First, the Jewel of the Buddha has two parts. First, the direct clarification of the Jewel of the Buddha has three parts.
First, the general indication of the Buddha’s virtues has two parts. First, the towering majesty of the merits of cultivation and realization.
These bodies of the Buddhas are truly wholesome and untainted, realized through causes cultivated over countless great eons.
The karmic fruits of the three realms of existence are forever exhausted without remainder; they are mountains of precious merit, towering and peerless, which all sentient beings cannot know.
His merit is profoundly deep, like the great ocean; his wisdom is unimpeded, equal to empty space; his supernormal powers and transformations fill the world;
and his radiance shines universally throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
These characters are terms that point toward the Dharma. "The bodies of all Buddhas" refers to the True Body (*dharmakāya*).
"True, wholesome, and without outflows" is a brief indication of the meaning of the body. The two lines beginning with "innumerable" explain the two characters "true" and "wholesome.
It means that this is the actual fruit realized through the cultivation of causes over the long duration of innumerable great eons; it is not like a phantom or an illusion, and is therefore "true."
This is the body of goodness. The final two phrases of the third existence explain the term "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). "Outflow" (*āsrava*) means to fall or to lose.
This refers to how all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) possess the afflictions of the five abodes and have their various physical and verbal karmas complete;

thus, the cycle of birth and death with distinct segments does not cease. Having lost the wealth of the Dharma and fallen into birth and death, they are called "outflows. Since the Buddha has already [transcended] karma and its fruits...

Because they are forever exhausted, they are called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). Regarding the "three existences" (*trai-dhātuka*): this refers to the non-extinction of cause and effect within the three realms.
Since there must be an effect for every cause, it is named the "three existences. Regarding "karmic effects": karma refers to the activities and functions performed by sentient beings.

Although these differ as wholesome or unwholesome, because the two attachments (*dvaya-grāha*) have not been extinguished, they all belong to the outflowing category. Furthermore, karma is invariably accompanied by afflictions (*kleśa*), which serve as the conditions for [rebirth].

The cause of the fruit. Birth and death follow accordingly as the fruit that repays the cause. That which is "permanently exhausted" is severed by the Buddha through true, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
When the cause is exhausted, the fruit perishes, and there is no further rebirth; hence it is called "permanent exhaustion.

"Without remainder" distinguishes this from "with remainder," meaning that while the practitioners of the Two Vehicles exhaust only the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), their ignorance (*avidyā*) is not yet exhausted; therefore, it is said to be "with remainder."
"Remainderless" (*anupadhiśeṣa*): Only the Buddha has exhausted all afflictions of view and thought, as well as ignorance, such that nothing remains; hence it is called "remainderless.

Regarding the two phrases concerning "merit" (*guṇa*) below: while the previous statement that "karmic fruits are eternally exhausted" was intended merely to show the absence of faults, the present statement regarding "merit" and so forth [indicates the presence of positive qualities].

This further clarifies the possession of virtue: cultivating the causes is the merit, while realizing the fruit is the virtue. "Majestic" (*weiwei*) describes a lofty appearance; "Jewel Mountain" (*baoshan*) is used as a metaphor.

It means that because there are jewels within a mountain, it is called a Jewel Mountain; this serves as a metaphor for the Buddha’s true body (*dharmakāya*), which is richly endowed with myriad virtues and possesses boundless oceans of marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
How majestic! No among the multitude of spirits can equal it; hence it is said to be "without peer. (1)

"Cutting off all" (*qie xia*) reveals the Buddha’s self-realization. Since "all sentient beings" (*yǒuqíng*) is mentioned, this includes not only ordinary beings (*fánfū*) but also those of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas;
as their afflictions and delusions are not yet exhausted, they are all collectively termed "sentient beings.

As for those who do not understand, they claim that even one on the first stage (*bhūmi*) does not know the realization of the second stage, let alone the Buddha. The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can [truly]..."

This exhaustively investigates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, manifesting that it cannot be measured by others. Regarding the two phrases on merit: the ocean serves as a vertical metaphor for its depth being unfathomable.
Regarding the two phrases on wisdom: space serves as a horizontal metaphor for its breadth being inexhaustible.

Wisdom possesses both the provisional and the ultimate; through ultimate wisdom one realizes principle, and because the realization of principle reaches its consummation, it is called "unimpeded. Through the provisional...
Born in Chile, he was exceptionally adept at seizing upon the essential point; this is also called "unimpeded. Because it is unimpeded, it is equal to empty space. "Equal" means identical.

Thus, the Buddha-body’s true goodness and non-outflowing purity represent the Greatness of Essence (*dharmatā-mahattva*). Its profound merit and virtue represent the Greatness of Characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*).
Its supernatural powers and transformations represent the Greatness of Function (*kāritra-mahattva*). "Spiritual" (*shen*) refers to its void and numinous nature, which is unfathomable.
"Penetration" means that response and resonance are without fixed direction; "transformation" refers to manifesting bodies according to the various classes of beings.
Because this resonance is like ten thousand rivers reflecting the moon, it is said to be "pervasive and full. The second couplet regarding "light" concludes both the essence and the function:

the Reward Body takes wisdom as its essence and illumination as its function. Internally, it illuminates the true Dharma-realm with the light of wisdom; externally, it illuminates with the light of the body.

It reflects throughout the ten directions; thus, horizontally, it pervades everywhere, with no place that it does not illuminate. Throughout the three periods of time, it exhausts all eternity, with no moment that it does not illuminate.
How could sentient beings possibly fathom such merit? △ Second, admonishing the common masses for their lack of awakening.
All sentient beings, through their afflictions and karmic obstructions, remain entirely unaware; they sink into the sea of suffering, transmigrating through birth and death without end.
When the Triple Gem appears in the world, it acts as a great captain, able to cut across the current of craving and transcend to the other shore. All those who possess wisdom—
All gaze up [at them] with reverence.
Although sentient beings generally encompass those of the Two Vehicles, for now we shall focus on ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Afflictions (*kleśa*) refer to the two delusions of views and thought, which can obstruct the true nature and thus constitute the affliction-obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Karma refers to the karma-obstruction (*karmāvaraṇa*); all outflowing karmas (*sāsrava-karman*) are likewise able to obstruct.
"Regarding the Way, 'not being aware at all' clearly explains that which is obstructed. This means that ordinary beings are obstructed by afflictions and karma;
they do not know that Buddha-nature exists, nor do they know that the spontaneous creation of karma is the cause of suffering. Consequently, they sink [into saṃsāra].
The following two phrases reveal that the retribution itself is also an obstruction. Because they create karma through non-awakening, it becomes the cause of birth and death."
Thus there is falling and no rising; hence it is called "sinking and wandering. It is like a person falling into the sea and suffering the pain of drowning;
being born again and dying again, with birth and death never ceasing, it is therefore called "endless. All of the above refers to the delusion and obscurity of sentient beings.

From the section on the Three Jewels below, the great kindness is clearly revealed: since a person fallen into the sea of suffering cannot emerge by their own power, they must rely upon [the Three Jewels].

Boats and rafts are used to ferry one across. "Able to cut off the stream of craving" (*tṛṣṇā-srotas*): "cutting off" (*chid*) means severing and belongs to wisdom (*jñāna*); "craving" refers to emotional attachment and belongs to delusion (*moha*).
Taking the Dharma as the boat, with the Buddha as the boatman, one is thus able to cut off the stream of craving and transcend to the other shore.

Suffering (*duḥkha*) is a metaphor for the ocean of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); the water is a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*); the other shore is a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, there are the Three Jewels (*triratna*).
Like a boatman, the teaching of the Dharma is like crossing a torrent by cutting through the current.

If people rely upon the teachings to practice and realize them, they will be like those who board a boat or raft to cross the ocean of suffering and the stream of craving, ascending to the other shore. The final two lines provide a concluding exhortation:
since the Triple Gem possesses such grace, the wise must not neglect it; all should look up to them and follow their transformation, lest they fail the Buddha’s kindness.

Thus ends the general summary of the Buddha’s virtues. △ Second, the detailed exposition of the three bodies (trikāya), in two parts: First, the general summary of the great significance of the three bodies;
second, the specific designation of the single essence as the three bodies. First, the designation of the single essence as the three bodies.
"O sons of noble family, the single Buddha-jewel possesses three kinds of bodies: first, the self-nature body (*svābhāvika-kāya*); second, the enjoyment body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*);
and third, the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*). II.
A brief explanation of the great meaning of the three bodies has three parts. First, the primary Buddha-body."
The first Buddha-body possesses the virtue of great abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), which is manifested by the two kinds of emptiness. All Buddhas are entirely equal in this regard;
this is the Dharma-body Buddha (*dharmakāya-buddha*). "Virtue of abandonment" refers to *nirvāṇa*. "Abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) means to eliminate and to exhaust.

Because it is the virtue manifested when all afflictions have been purified and exhausted, it is called the "virtue of abandonment. The phrase "manifested by the two kinds of emptiness" explains its meaning.

The two emptinesses refer to the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). This means that by severing the two attachments to self and phenomena, one manifests the emptiness of self and the emptiness of phenomena.
The *tathatā* (suchness) manifested by these two emptinesses is free from the two kinds of birth-and-death;

it is inherently pure and constitutes the essence of the merit of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). The term "Great" serves to distinguish this from the Lesser Vehicle, as the Lesser Vehicle also possesses the merit of cessation. All...
The latter two phrases are interpreted together. "Equality" means that it reveals the body of the Buddhas' Dharma-nature is non-dual.
△ Second, the second Buddha-body:
this second Buddha-body possesses great wisdom, is truly eternal and untainted, and all Buddhas are of one mind with it.
This is precisely the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya) Tathāgata. Possessing great wisdom and virtue, it is itself bodhi.
Being truly eternal and untainted (anāsrava), this is the meaning of "Śākya. "True" means free from delusion; "eternal" means non-extinguishing.

Because the afflictions of the five abodes have been exhausted, its essence is perfected and it no longer falls back into birth and death; therefore, it is called "untainted. All who agree with this [share] the same intent. Intent...
The character "字" (zi) is likely an error for "智" (zhì). This is because the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya) Tathāgata takes wisdom as its essence.
The character "大" (dà), meaning "great," distinguishes it from the "small," as explained previously. △ Third, the Buddha-body of the third [category].
The third Buddha-body possesses great benevolent merit. Its meditative concentration, supernatural powers, and transformations are shared by all Buddhas;

this is the benevolence of the Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body). It possesses great benevolent merit, which is precisely the saving of sentient beings. Regarding the explanation of "meditative concentration, supernatural powers, and transformations":

it means that from the power of meditative concentration, one exercises supernatural faculties to manifest hundreds, thousands, and billions of emanations, transforming according to the capacities of beings in various ways.
They are not the same. That sentient beings obtain benefit is what constitutes great grace. That all Buddhas perform the same work means that they manifest their bodies and preach the Dharma;
these are all the activities performed by the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body). △ Second, the detailed explanation of the distinctions between the three bodies has three parts.
First, regarding the Buddha of the Svabhāvakāya:
"Good son, that svabhāvakāya is without beginning and without end; it is free from all marks and transcends all conceptual proliferation;
it is all-pervasive and boundless, remaining eternally and immutably."
The Dharmakāya Tathāgata takes self-nature as his body; therefore, it is called the Svabhāvakāya (Self-Nature Body). This phrase indicates the essence.
From the words "without beginning" (*anādi*) onwards, all serve to explain its meaning. That is to say, because its origin cannot be measured in the past, it is said to be "without beginning.

Because its limit cannot be fathomed in the future, it is said to be "without end. Since it has neither beginning nor end, it is without arising or ceasing, and is thus the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).
The essence. The two subsequent phrases, "detached from all," reveal that the essence itself is free from fault. "All characteristics" encompasses an immense range;
this refers to the Reward Body and Transformation Bodies of the Buddha, which possess all the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa* and *anuvyañjana*), whereas this Dharmakāya does not.

Furthermore, it is entirely empty of the two kinds of birth-and-death, the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra-kleśa*), the causes and effects of the noble and the ordinary, and the realms of defilement and purity. Therefore, it is said:
It is free from all marks. Because all names, marks, and linguistic discriminations are illusory, false, and unreal, they are all mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Since these do not exist even within the essence of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), it is said that [the nature] "transcends all. The following two lines concern its pervasive perfection.

This reveals the virtue of being pervasive, eternal, and all-encompassing. To be filled throughout the *dharmadhātu* is called "circumferential" (*zhouyuan*). To be free from all measure and limit is called "boundless" (*wujie*).

Being unchanging and steadfast means that from the beginningless past it has fundamentally existed without omission; being eternally abiding means that until the end of the future it will ultimately never perish.
Part Two: The Enjoyment Body Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya-buddha*) has two sections. First, the general presentation of the two bodies.
The Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) has two aspects: first, the self-enjoyment; second, the other-enjoyment. II.
The specific names of the two bodies. A. First, the self-enjoyment body, in five parts. 1. First, when practice is perfected and one is about to attain enlightenment.

Regarding the body of self-enjoyment: having cultivated the myriad practices over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings, and having reached the fulfillment of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), he transports his body directly to the Heaven of Ultimate Purity (*Akaniṣṭha*), transcending the pure and wondrous realm beyond the triple world (*tridhātu*).
He sits upon a great jewel lotus flower of immeasurable magnitude.
The first phrase serves as a heading. Regarding the "three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*," this refers to the duration traversed while cultivating the causes.
The character *saṃgha* (僧) is missing its initial character *a* (阿); this omission was made by the translator so that the four characters would form a complete metrical line. Flower.
Regarding the expression "incalculable time" (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*): these three *asaṃkhyeyas* refer, for the time being, to the duration of Śākyamuni’s cultivation of the bodhisattva path.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* asks: "If it is called 'incalculable,' why then say 'three'? It answers:
"The term 'incalculable' indicates that which cannot be counted; it does not mean 'non-existent' (or 'zero'). As for the first *asaṃkhyeya*, it refers to when the Tathāgata first began...
From the ancient Śākyamuni Buddha up to Śikhin Buddha, he encountered seventy-five thousand Buddhas;

this is called the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa. (The *Śāstra* states: "In a previous life, Śākyamuni Buddha was a potter named Mahāprabha. At that time, there was a Buddha named Śākyamuni who came to the potter’s house to stay overnight. The potter offered three things—a grass seat, a lamp, and rock honey—to the Buddha and made a vow, saying:

'May I become a Buddha in the future, with a name no different from this Buddha's. Therefore, when he now became a Buddha, he was also titled Śākyamuni. In Sanskrit, *Śikhin* is also called *Śikhi*; in the language of China, it means 'Fire'. )

Regarding the second *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa: this refers to the period from when the Tathāgata followed after Śikhin Buddha until he encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha, during which he met seventy-six thousand Buddhas;
this is called the second *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa. As for Dīpaṃkara Buddha, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When the Buddha was first born, his bodily radiance was like a lamp;

later, upon attaining Buddhahood, he was thus named Dīpaṃkara. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha was known as the Youth (Māṇava). He presented five stalks of lotus flowers to the Buddha and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. Seeing that the ground was damp and muddy, he immediately took off his deerskin garment to cover it, but it was insufficient to conceal the mud.

He then untied his hair and spread it upon the ground, commanding the Buddha to tread upon it as he passed. The Buddha thereupon made this prediction: "From this point forward, after ninety-one kalpas—during which the eon shall be named Bhadra—you shall become a Buddha, titled Śākyamuni. Regarding the "three asaṃkhyeyas":
this refers to the period from when the Tathāgata followed Dīpaṃkara Buddha up until Vipaśyin Buddha, during which he encountered seventy-seven thousand Buddhas;
this is called the third asaṃkhya (Sanskrit: *Vipaśyin*, also known as *Vaiśvāsika*, translated here as "Victorious"). It was during this time that he cultivated the ten thousand practices.

The final three phrases clarify the fulfillment of the causes. (The "ten thousand practices" are said to be numerous; they do not merely refer to ten thousand. From the expansion of the six perfections, they reach into the infinite. Speaking in terms of a general total, they are briefly termed "ten thousand practices.

All acts of relinquishing what is difficult to relinquish and enduring what is difficult to endure are collectively categorized as the ten thousand practices. Regarding "benefiting and bringing peace and happiness," the following clarifies the methods for altruistic practice within the causal stage:

one brings peace by uprooting suffering through the power of compassion, and one brings happiness by bestowing joy through the power of loving-kindness. This constitutes the fulfillment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

As for the "mind," it refers to the practice from the initial generation of the bodhicitta. Whenever one abandons a portion of delusions and realizes a portion of the Truth, there are fifty stages from the stage of the Ten Faiths up to the Ten Grounds.
Together with the four preparatory practices prior to the Grounds and the Dry Wisdom prior to the Faiths, these constitute the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi.
Upon reaching the Dharma-Cloud Ground, one is shaded by the compassion of the Dharma.
When the clouds cover the ocean of *nirvāṇa*, the mind is thereby fulfilled. Regarding "moving the body downward":

this means that once the mind is fulfilled and one is about to attain Buddhahood, one exercises supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), enabling the body to proceed directly to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven (the *Qixin lun* states:

"manifesting a body of supreme height and magnitude throughout all worlds, attaining Buddhahood in this heaven"). There are two reasons why one must necessarily attain Buddhahood in this heaven. First, regarding the primary school...
The *Xinshu* states: "By entrusting [the stages] to the Ten Kings, one manifests the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*). Now, the Bodhisattva of the Tenth Ground is entrusted to this heaven;

therein, within that very body, he manifests the attainment of *bodhi*. This has two meanings: first, it signifies that the practice of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* is complete and the fruition is about to be realized;
second, it signifies that he must attain *buddhahood* in a place of supreme height and nobility, thereby manifesting the exalted and noble status of the Buddha-position."
This is because it is remote from them. "Transcending the three realms" means that although one is in those heavens, one is nonetheless not of those heavens;

that is to say, while remaining within the three realms, one is detached from the three realms. Hence, it is called "transcending. "Pure and wondrous land" refers to the Land of Real Reward Adornment (*vipākaphala-saṃbhoga-vyūha-bhūmi*).
Because it is the locus upon which the Reward Buddha relies, it is called a "land. It is thus both within the realm and yet detached from it.
Because it is a realm, it is called "pure and wondrous. Regarding the phrase "sitting upon countless [lotuses]" below:

since he has manifested a body of supreme height and magnitude, that upon which he sits must necessarily be a great flower of immeasurable number. Ultimately, the reason for sitting upon a flower is that the flower symbolizes the cause, while the Buddha symbolizes the fruit.

The Buddha sitting atop the flower signifies that the cause is capable of producing the fruit; for the fruit must necessarily rely upon the cause. Thus, the word "flower" implies the absence of... [limit].

Regarding "number": it signifies that both cause and effect are beyond all calculation. Regarding the fact that the flower must be called a "lotus": it signifies that cause and effect are fully manifested.
Furthermore, the reason the flower is large and necessarily beyond calculation is to signify that it is not within the scope of intellectual deliberation, thereby revealing its inconceivability.
△ Second, the assembly at the ocean-like gathering offers respectful offerings.

Furthermore, an unspeakable ocean-like assembly of bodhisattvas surrounded him from front and back, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising him by binding stainless silk ribbons upon his head; this is called the benefit of future retribution.
"Inexpressible" refers to the ultimate limit of great numbers. "Ocean-like assembly" refers to the vastness of the multitude;

that is, a gathering of many people is called an "assembly," and a multitude of many people is called an "ocean. The bodhisattvas serve as their supporting companions, surrounding them from front and back, like the host of stars encircling the North Star.
As for "tying a stainless silk cloth upon their heads," this is an offering made to the bodhisattvas.
"Silk" (*zēng*) refers to silk and cotton-wool; that is, types such as *zhòu*, *bó*, *líng*, and *luó*. "Stainless" (*wúgòu*) means white. "Hanging" (*xì*) means suspending;
that is, like plain white silk, either made into banners and streamers (*chuángfán*) or into jeweled canopies (*bǎogài*), and suspended above the Buddha’s head.
Banners and streamers symbolize the crushing of heterodoxy and the manifestation of the orthodox; the jeweled canopy symbolizes the true compassion that provides shelter from above. Stainless—
That which represents what the Buddha has realized is the pure and white Dharma (*śukla-dharma*). That which is bound upon the Buddha represents the honored, supreme, and most excellent path.
That offerings must be accompanied by reverence signifies the sincerity of the offering. That one further adds praise with deep respect is to extol his virtue.
Such as these are called "benefits of subsequent retribution," for by means of these two— [the realization and the path]— [one attains such results].

"Character" (*zi*) refers to the perfection of the practices of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and the fulfillment of the mind of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Surrounded by Bodhisattvas, one is about to attain Buddhahood;
such supreme events constitute the benefit of the subsequent retribution (*paścātkarma-vipāka*). This subsequent retribution is spoken of in contrast to the preceding causes.

The preceding cause consists of the Bodhisattva’s practice, while the subsequent retribution constitutes the fruit of the Tathāgata. △ Third: The exhaustion of delusions and the ultimate attainment of Buddhahood.
At that time, the Bodhisattva entered the Vajra-samādhi, severed all subtle cognitive afflictive obstructions,
and realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
One who enters the Vajra-samādhi possesses a power of concentration so firm and sharp that it is likened to a vajra.

By giving rise to a single moment of wisdom corresponding to this state, ignorance is suddenly severed, and one enters wondrous enlightenment to become a Buddha. This constitutes the equipment for the realization of the Way.

Regarding the phrase "all subtle objects of knowledge" (*jñeya*) and so forth, this encompasses all afflictions and the two obstacles; however, the two characters for "objects of knowledge" (*jñeya*) [are used here] specifically to... [text ends].

This is an obstruction. Fundamentally, it is the principle manifested by the emptiness of both self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-śūnyatā*). Since it is called "the known" (*jñeya*), there must necessarily be a "knower.
Because the knower is wisdom (*jñāna*) that knows the known, as long as the knower and the known have not yet ceased, it is termed an "obstruction.
This is because it obstructs the principle. It is not that the known itself is the obstruction; rather, the obstruction is that which obstructs the known. Furthermore...

It is called the obstacle of principle (*dharmāvaraṇa*), also known as the obstacle to wisdom (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), because it is most extremely subtle. As for the various afflictions (*kleśa*), they refer to the delusions of the five stages;

since the afflictions themselves are obstacles, they are called the obstacle of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*). They are also called the obstacle of phenomena (*vastvāvaraṇa*), because they can obstruct the superior, wondrous, and excellent matters of humans and devas.
Because these two obstacles are eliminated, the two deaths are exhausted, the two emptinesses are perfected, and the two virtues are fulfilled.
Only upon the ultimate realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does one first attain its actual *sambhogakāya*.
△ Fourth, elucidating the lifespan of the true body:
Such a wondrous fruit is called "manifest benefit" and is the true *sambhogakāya*. It has a beginning but no end; its lifespan lasts for the duration of kalpas.
There is no limit. From the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment until the end of the future, his faculties and marks of excellence pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
These two characters [“thus” and “attained”] are words used for specific designation. "Sublime fruit" refers to the fruit of sublime awakening, which is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Manifesting benefit" means that having already become a Buddha, he manifests his body to bring benefit.
This refers to the true *saṃbhogakāya*. "True" means it is not illusory; "recompense" means it is the reward for causes.

It is accomplished through actual practice and is the genuine fruit of retribution, not something manifested according to the needs of those to be transformed. Regarding "having a beginning but no end": this means that because one attains Buddhahood when the causes are fulfilled, there is a beginning;
because it is ultimately imperishable, there is no end. Its lifespan, measured in kalpas, is without limit.
Regarding this phrase, there are two interpretations of the character *yù* (欲). First, it may originally have been the character *liàng* (量, measure), which was later miscopied as *yù*.
Second, it is not a miscopy; rather, it refers to the "fruit of reliance" (*yīguǒ*) that is desired. For the sake of consistency with the current text, we shall proceed based on the reading *yù*.
For example, "measure of life" (*shòuliàng*) refers to the Reward Body Tathāgata (*bǎoshēn rúlái*), who, by means of the wisdom of suchness (*rúrú zhì*), accords with...
The realm of suchness (*tathatā*) gives rise to wisdom based upon that realm; with wisdom illuminating the realm, the realm and wisdom merge in profound unity.

This is precisely the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body). Now, regarding "life span" (*āyus-pramāṇa*): since the realm is immeasurable and boundless, eternally abiding and never ceasing, and since wisdom likewise conforms to the realm, eternally abiding and never ceasing, wisdom is taken as the life span.
"Desire" refers to the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*)—that which is relied upon according to one's desire. This is the fruit of reliance.
Furthermore, the adorned realms that serve as the basis for the fruition are likewise immeasurable. The first four lines clarify the magnitude of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Regarding the "faculties," this refers here to the six sense faculties. "Marks" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the general physical form and appearance, which are supremely wondrous and extraordinary;

there are ninety-six kinds of marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*). "Subsidiary marks" (*anuvyañjana*) refer to the secondary features that follow the primary form. These follow the... [text truncated]
Beautiful, radiant as blossoming flowers. Another sutra states: "A single body possesses infinite marks; a single mark possesses infinite secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*);
a single secondary sign possesses infinite radiance. The supporting fruits upon which it rests are likewise infinite.

The phrase "pervasive and omnipresent" refers to the realm that is illuminated, which is none other than the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena). Because the *dharmatā* is pervasive and omnipresent, all the characteristics of the sense faculties [are likewise so].
Excellent. All are able to accord with their nature (*dharmatā*) and pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*. Regarding the *dharmadhātu*, there are two explanations.

First, "dharma" refers to the *dharmatā* (the true nature of phenomena), which vertically exhausts all time and horizontally pervades all space; it exists nowhere not and at no time not. "Dhātu" (realm) refers to a delimited boundary.

Here, although it is not a delimited realm, it is called a "realm"; the nature itself is the realm, a name established based on its own essence. Second, "dharma" refers to the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*), as well as the holy ones...
All things have their respective rules; taking these rules as the Dharma, each has its own limits which constitute its boundaries, such as the ten realms of existence (*dharmadhātu*).

Although there are two types [of realms], for now we speak in terms of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Since the characteristics of the various faculties and the marks of excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are all able to accord with this nature, it is said that they are "pervasive and omnipresent.
V. Differentiating the Transformation of Consciousness into Wisdom (2 sections). First, the actual explanation of the four wisdoms.
The distinctions are twofold. First, a general indication of the four wisdoms:
the perfection of the four wisdoms is the true *saṃbhogakāya*, which experiences the bliss of the Dharma.
△ Second, a detailed explanation of the four wisdoms, in four parts. First, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).
The first is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). By transforming the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*), one attains this wisdom.
Just as a great round mirror manifests all forms and images, so too within the Tathāgata’s Mirror Wisdom can the various wholesome and unwholesome karmas of sentient beings be manifested.
For this reason, this wisdom is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. Relying upon great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), it constantly takes sentient beings as its object; relying upon great wisdom...

Therefore, it is always in accordance with the dharma-nature; it simultaneously contemplates the ultimate and the conventional without interruption, and is constantly able to sustain the untainted faculties and body, serving as the basis for all meritorious qualities.
The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is so named by way of analogy; it is the wisdom that is transformed.

Its nature is pure, perfect, and luminous, capable of illuminating all phenomena, and thus it is likened to a round mirror. "Transforming the ripening consciousness" (*vipākavijñāna*) refers to the consciousness that performs the transformation, meaning that wisdom arises from the transformation of consciousness.
"Ripening" (*vipāka*) is an alternative name for the *ālayavijñāna*. From beginningless time until the eighth [stage]...
The ground is named *ālaya*; this is translated as "storehouse. A "storehouse" (*kosa*) means that which stores. Because it contains seeds, it possesses three meanings:
the capacity to store, that which is stored, and being clung to by the attachment to self. From beginningless time until the path of liberation, it is called *vipāka*;
this is translated as "ripening. Some say that prior to the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), the store-consciousness is termed "equanimity" (*upekṣā*).
It subsequently becomes the *vipāka* (ripening result). It is called *vipāka* because it ripens through transformation (*pariṇāma*), ripens at a different time, and ripens as a different category.
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, the *vipāka* is transformed into the immaculate consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*);

the mental complex associated with the eighth consciousness is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). Therefore, it is said that the Great Perfect [Mirror] and the Immaculate arise simultaneously.
It universally illumines the lands within the dust motes of the ten directions. This sutra speaks directly of the transformation of consciousness into wisdom;

those scholars who cling to the school of characteristics need not engage in debate. What is here called "transformation" (parāvṛtti) is precisely "alteration. This means that when the cause alters, the fruit ripens.
As in the six lines following [the word] "great," the dharma is used as a metaphor to explain the meaning. The first two lines are the metaphor: like a great, perfectly round mirror suspended...
Within this very hall, all forms and appearances manifest therein. Thus, it is joined with what follows below:
that is to say, within the Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) of the Tathāgata, the causes and effects of good and evil of all sentient beings are all able to appear, just as they do in a mirror.

This concludes the definition of the name. Regarding "Based on the Great [Compassion]" and so forth: it correctly clarifies the meaning of the mirror; because it relies upon great compassion, it constantly takes [all beings] as its object.
"Sentient beings" refers to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), for the cycle of birth and death resulting from the karmic fruits of sentient beings is an object of compassion.

"Abiding eternally according to the dharma-nature by relying on great wisdom" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); it is like a mirror possessing light, wherein the light reflects back upon itself.
Thus, there is the sense of compassion and wisdom mutually guiding one another through the simultaneous contemplation of these two truths; that is, wisdom guides compassion, so that although—

Observing conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one does not fall into the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); guiding wisdom with compassion, although one observes ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one does not lapse into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
By observing and guiding through these two in mutual interdependence, one reaches the end of the future limit, abiding eternally without extinction; hence it is said that there is no interruption.
The phrase "constantly able to" below clarifies the capacity for sustaining the untainted faculties and body, which refers to the various faculties of the Buddha-stage.

The marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), and all other merits, are also inherently present by nature. Because it maintains these myriad virtues—the wealth of the Dharma—without loss, it is called "untainted" (*anāsrava*).
Regarding its being the "basis," this means that if this wisdom did not exist at the stage of Buddhahood, the root-body and its merits would have nothing upon which to rely.
Thus, maintaining the seeds during the causal stage and maintaining the virtues during the resultant stage both manifest [this function].
This is the Great Function. △ Second, the Wisdom of Equality.
By transforming the consciousness of self-view (*ātmadṛṣṭi-vijñāna*), one attains this wisdom.
Because of this, one is able to realize the nature of non-dual equality between self and others. This is what is called the Wisdom of Equality.
The wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) is so named because it is that which is realized; it is the wisdom that undergoes transformation.
It contemplates all phenomena such that oneself and other sentient beings are entirely equal, and thus this name is established.

The "view of self" (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) refers to the seventh consciousness, the *manas*, which is the root of self-clinging and serves as the consciousness that performs the transformation. The character "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) signifies conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*); in ordinary beings...

The state [of delusion] arises from this discrimination, whereby one conceives of "self" and "what belongs to self," distinguishing between self and other among all phenomena and forcibly establishing boundaries.
Because of this discrimination, one fails to attain equanimity and remains constantly associated with the four afflictions, such as craving and so forth.

Now, when these are transformed into wisdom, the two attachments to self and phenomena no longer exist; the nature of wisdom is all-pervasive and free from discrimination, and thus [equanimity] is attained.
It is equality. Regarding the equality of self and other: this is the principle to be realized. That is to say, the principle is fundamentally equal, being without self and without other.
Wisdom is that which realizes; if wisdom were to possess discrimination, it would likewise not be equal.
Only by attaining non-discriminative wisdom can one realize it. Therefore, it is said: "By attaining this wisdom, one is thus able to realize non-duality."
Regarding "the nature of self": there are two kinds of self, namely the self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*).

When the consciousness of the view of self has not yet been transformed, one clings to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as being a sovereign self, and regards all property, wife, children, and so forth as belonging to that self;

hence they are called "what belongs to the self. The word "non-" (*a-* or *an-*) is that which dispels [this clinging]; it refers to the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*) that is attained through transformation. (2)
I have been sent here. However, since consciousness (*vijñāna*) can be transformed into wisdom (*jñāna*), the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) are suddenly emptied.

This nature (*svabhāva*) is that which is realized; therefore, it is called "the non-dual self-nature" (*advayātmatā*). Thus concludes the title below. [Question: The Dharma-character school (*Faxiang zong*) asserts that the seventh consciousness merely cogitates upon the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as the self, and does not speak of "discrimination" (*vikalpa*), as it lacks a separate function.

Yet, in the present commentary, it is stated that the character "seeing" (*dṛṣṭi*) is itself discrimination, calculating "self" and "what belongs to the self" (*ātman-ātmīya*), which is similar to the sixth consciousness. I fear this may contradict the Dharma-character school. How is this to be distinguished?

[Question: Is there a distinction? [Answer: "Discursive thought" (*santīraṇa*) refers to the subtle aspect of discrimination; it merely functions spontaneously and belongs to the innate afflictions of volition (*cetanā*), which is the function of the seventh consciousness. "Discrimination" (*vikalpa*) refers to the coarse aspect of discursive thought;

it belongs to the defiled habitual tendencies, namely the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi*), which is the function of the sixth consciousness. Here, the coarse is used to explain the subtle for the sake of clarity. However, since the Sūtra states that self and others are equal and that both lack the nature of self, one knows from this that if one clings to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as the self, how could one not cling to its image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as "mine"?

Students who study the Sūtras must not be like those who fix the strings of a zither (i.e., remain rigid); although it is called "discrimination," it ultimately is not the sixth consciousness. △ Third, Sublime Contemplation.

Investigating wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Third is the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*); by transforming the discriminating consciousness (*vikalpavijñāna*), one attains this wisdom.

It is able to observe the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena and, before assemblies of beings, preach the sublime Dharma, enabling sentient beings to attain non-retrogression. For this reason, it is so named.
This constitutes the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (wisdom of wondrous observation).

The first phrase provides the name; it is established based on its grasping and maintaining all objects of observation. Qingliang says: "Its spiritual power is unimpeded, hence it is called 'wondrous' (*miao*);
it takes both specific and general characteristics as its objects, hence it is called 'observation' (*guan*). This is the wisdom that results from transformation."

Discriminating consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*) is the consciousness capable of transformation; it is precisely the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). It is able to observe below [the five sensory objects]. "Able" refers to the wondrous function of wisdom (*jñāna*).

Regarding "all phenomena" (*sarva-dharma*), this encompasses everything, including the environments and inhabitants of all sages and ordinary beings, as well as their defiled and pure causes and effects. As for "specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*"):

specific characteristics refer to the distinct characteristics possessed by each phenomenon, such as form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). Common characteristics refer to that which is one... [The text continues with the definition of the universal characteristic of emptiness.]
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) within the realm of form are identical in being impermanent, suffering, empty, selfless, and impure.

Since every phenomenon is identical in this way, it is called the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, it is said that the "perfected nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is termed the common characteristic because all phenomena share the same essence;

whereas the "dependent nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is termed the "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) because each possesses its own distinct essence. In the following section, this is precisely elucidated.
"The function of the subtle observation of wisdom" refers to the teaching of various sublime dharmas; that is, the teaching that accords with the capacities of beings.

First, one employs sublime wisdom to observe whether the faculties of sentient beings are sharp or dull, whether their afflictions are thick or thin, and whether their wisdom is shallow or deep, and so forth.
Thereafter, he preached the Dharma according to the capacities of beings. Because the Dharma can adapt to the specific needs of each individual, it is called the "Sublime Dharma" (Saddharma).
That which bestows great grace upon sentient beings resides entirely therein. The phrase "is able to cause" and following clarifies the benefits obtained by sentient beings upon hearing the Dharma.
There are three kinds of non-retrogression: first, non-retrogression in stage, which means not being born in the three miserable realms and so forth;
second, non-retrogression in practice, which means not being born in border regions and so forth; third, non-retrogression in mindfulness, which means knowing past lives and so forth.

It is said that from the eighth stage onward, by means of the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*), one flows spontaneously into the ocean of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); this is the stage of non-retrogression. This is because [the following] is below...

The Name of the Bond (The one who teaches the Dharma according to the capacities of beings: that is, teaching the Small Vehicle to those of small capacity, such as through the Four Noble Truths and Dependent Origination; and teaching the Great Vehicle to those of great capacity, namely through the teachings of the Sudden and Perfect [Vehicles] from beginning to end.
As for the Self-Enjoyment Body being able to preach the Dharma, this will be discussed in the subsequent section). △ Fourth, the Wisdom of Accomplishing What is to be Done.

Fourth is the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). By transforming the five types of consciousness, one attains this wisdom, which is able to manifest all manner of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) to bring sentient beings to maturity in their wholesome karma. For these reasons, it is called the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done.
This name is established based on its functional activity (*kāritra*). That is to say, it accomplishes the deeds that the Tathāgata ought to perform for the sake of liberating sentient beings.

Regarding the transformation of the five kinds of consciousness and so forth: the "five kinds" refers to the first five consciousnesses, namely, the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*).

The nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness—consciousness acts as the transformer and wisdom acts as that which is transformed. The phrase "capable of manifesting all things below" clarifies the great function of this wisdom:

it manifests bodies according to the capacities of beings, transforms the three karmas, fulfills the power of original vows, accomplishes all tasks that ought to be done, and employs all supernatural powers and wondrous functions to subdue demons and adversaries through skillful means (*upāya*).

This causes all those below [to attain realization]. It clarifies the efficacy of manifesting the body to deliver sentient beings. "Maturing" means causing those who have not yet resolved to generate that resolve;
increasing it in those who have already resolved; encouraging the indolent to advance; and enabling the diligent to attain the fruit.

That is to say, bringing to completion what is not yet complete, and maturing what is already completed. "Karma" refers to the various daily activities of sentient beings, by which [they are brought to completion].
Matured. All are transformed into wholesome karma, as well as untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) and so forth; thus, these are the names of the lower summations.
△ Second, the summation revealing that the merits are immeasurable:
These four wisdoms serve as the primary leaders, fully possessing eighty-four thousand gateways of wisdom. All such [wisdoms] are...
All these meritorious qualities are called the Tathāgata’s body of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).
This clarifies that, with the four wisdoms as the primary basis, when expanded, they fully comprise eighty-four thousand gates of wisdom.

Regarding these eighty-four thousand, there are two explanations. One is as previously stated in the commentary on the *Dazhi duoluo jing* (The Sūtra of the Great Aspiration) by the Elder [Vasubandhu].
Regarding the enumeration: that [tradition] refers to them as "perfections" (*pāramitā*), while here they are called "gates of wisdom.
Those are the causal practices of a bodhisattva; these are the resultant wisdom of a Tathāgata. They cannot be considered entirely identical. Now, I shall provide another interpretation.
Furthermore, a person has eighty-four thousand pores, and upon reaching the state of fruition, all of these become gates of wisdom. There is yet another explanation: generally speaking...
Now, there are eighty-four thousand gates of affliction (*kleśa*); yet upon attaining Buddhahood, these are all transformed into eighty-four thousand gates of wisdom.
This teaching is even more subtle. The enumeration of afflictions remains the same as before; thus concludes the naming [of the previous section]. II.
The Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*). Part One: Explaining the body, land, marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), and the preaching of the Dharma.
Good sons, second is the Tathāgata’s Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*).

It is endowed with eighty-four thousand marks and minor signs, dwells in the truly pure land, and teaches the Dharma of the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*), causing all bodhisattvas to enjoy the subtle and wondrous Dharma-bliss of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*): "self" refers to oneself, while "other" refers to another person; thus, the ten-stage Bodhisattvas are the intended recipients.
It is called "enjoyment" because it causes others to receive and obtain benefit; "body" refers to the Buddha-body.

This refers to the Reward Body Tathāgata manifesting as a supreme Emanation Body to preach the Dharma, enabling other Bodhisattvas of the ten stages to receive the Buddha-dharma and enjoy the bliss of the Dharma.
Because it is designated according to its function of benefiting others, it is called the "Body of Enjoyment for Others.
The phrase "endowed with" and so forth clarifies that its marks and signs differ from those of the Transformation Body, which possesses only the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs.
This body is fully endowed with eighty-four thousand marks and signs of excellence. These are likewise equal in number to the pores of the skin.
This is because the ordinary person’s minute body has a limited capacity, possessing eighty-four thousand pores;

now that one has attained the Buddha’s sublime and extraordinary body, its magnitude is exceedingly vast, such that every pore becomes a mark of excellence, a sign of excellence, and a radiance of light. Truly.
The Pure Land is also the land of true recompense and adornment. "True" means it is substantially real, manifesting that it is not an illusory realm.
"Pure" means it is adorned, manifesting that it is free from dust and defilement. It is the dwelling place for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage;

others do not perceive it, and thus it is called the "True Pure Land. That which is taught as the Dharma of the One Vehicle is the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground, serving as the capacity to be covered [by the teaching].
This is the teaching. The various bodhisattvas are the specific capacities (the *adhikāra*) for whom it is intended.

Phrases such as "causing the various bodhisattvas to partake" correctly explain the term "other-enjoyment" (*parasaṃbhoga*), because the name reveals its underlying reality. The Mahāyāna is itself the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Sometimes it is called "wondrous" when it is taught that all phenomena are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*); sometimes it is called "sublime" when it is taught that the triple world is mind-only (*cittamātra*). The Mahāyāna serves as the capacity...
The explanation: the subtle and wondrous Dharma is that which is explained. When Bodhisattvas grasp the essential meaning, they enjoy the bliss of the Dharma.
△ Second, clarifying the ten bodies’ exposition of the ten stages (bhūmis), in two parts: first, the general heading.
All Tathāgatas, in order to transform the assembly of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages (*bhūmi*), manifest ten kinds of bodies for the enjoyment of others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*).
Appearing in accordance with the capacities of those on the ten stages, they manifest ten types of bodies, each subsequent one being superior to the preceding. This is merely a general designation;
next follows the explanatory text. △ Next, there are two parts to the detailed enumeration. First, the separate explanation of the first three stages.
The first Buddha-body sits upon a hundred-petaled lotus flower and expounds the "Illuminating Door of the Hundred Dharmas" for Bodhisattvas of the First Ground.
Having attained awakening, the Bodhisattvas manifest great supernormal powers and transformations that fill a hundred Buddha-worlds, bringing benefit, peace,
and happiness to countless sentient beings.

This is the first Buddha-body, which transforms for Bodhisattvas of the First Ground. The varieties of flowers are most numerous; the necessity of sitting upon a lotus has a symbolic significance in the Dharma.
It takes its place in the mud yet remains unstained, emerging from the water with fragrance and purity. This is because the Buddha has now attained enlightenment.

Like a lotus flower emerging from the water, the fragrance of the Way permeates everywhere; pure and white, it maintains itself. Furthermore, the flower represents the cause, while the Buddha represents the fruit.

The fruit necessarily relies upon the cause, as when the Buddha sits upon the flower. As for the hundreds of petals of the flower, these also have their symbolic significance, corresponding to the categories of names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Whenever a single thing or a single name is mentioned, there are ten aspects. The Master of the Commentary says: "Ten..."

It serves to complete the number, thereby expressing the meaning of perfection. This case is likewise: all numbers such as one hundred, ten thousand, or one million are used to complete the count and also signify the sense of perfection.
"For" (wei) refers to that which is below the first stage (bhūmi). "For" (wei) signifies "to give. This is the compassionate vow-mind of the Tathāgata.
The first stage is the objective capacity for whom [the teaching] is intended. This Bodhisattva proceeds from the position of the foremost among ordinary beings prior to the stages. One.
It is associated with mindfulness (*smṛti*). By severing all conceptualization and the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), one attains the realization of pervasive *tathatā* (suchness);

this constitutes the true Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) and is termed "Joy" (*pramuditā*), for one rejoices because of being able to see the Path. As for the "Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas" (*dharmāloka-mukha*), it refers to the teaching that serves as the means [to attain this];

the categories of dharmas therein number one hundred, namely: eleven material dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*) (the five sense organs and the six objects), eight mental dharmas (*citta-dharma*) (the eight consciousnesses), and so forth.

The King (the mind) has fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*). (In total there are six categories: namely, the five omnipresent (*sarvatraga*), the five object-specific (*viniyata*), the eleven wholesome (*kuśala*), the twenty-six unwholesome roots and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the four indeterminate (*aniyata*).

These are the dharmas that are employed by the eight types of mental kings; therefore, they are called mental factors. There are twenty-four dissociated (*viprayukta*) dharmas. (From acquisition (*prāpti*) to the nature of non-concordance (*aprāpti*);

because they do not correspond with the king [mind] or its factors, these together constitute ninety-four dharmas, which are mundane dharmas. There are six unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas. (From the unconditioned of space (*ākāśa*) to the unconditioned of suchness (*tathatā*); these are supramundane dharmas.)

The "total" refers to the hundred dharmas. Regarding the "gate of illumination" (*vidyā-mukha*): "illumination" (*vidyā*) is wisdom (*prajñā*), and "gate" (*mukha*) has the sense of a passage; it refers to the teaching (*dharma*).
