The next three lines are the metaphors, and the final four lines are the application of the dharma. The supreme jewel is like a *vimalaprabhā* (dust-warding) pearl, which does not combine with dust; the Three Jewels are also thus.

Thus, because the Buddha is free from the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*), the Dharma is fundamentally free from desire, and the Saṅgha maintains pure precepts, they are far removed from dust and defilement;

therefore, they are called "Jewels. (Regarding the simultaneous presentation of both metaphor and dharma: it is like designating them as "stainless"; since both the metaphor and the dharma are stainless, they are presented together.)
Third is the bestowing of happiness. Just as the celestial vase (*devaghaṭa*) is able to bestow peace and happiness, so too are the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha;
they are likewise able to bestow upon sentient beings both mundane and supramundane happiness.

This [concept] takes virtue and happiness as its treasure. A "divine jar" (*devakumbha*) has not yet been seen recorded in extant texts; I shall now explain it according to the meaning of its characters.
"Jar" (*kumbha*) is the name for a vessel. "Divine" (*deva*) refers to the heavens. This means there is a jar in the heavens, and that jar possesses virtue.
It is named for its dwelling in virtue, called the "Vase of Celestial Virtue" (*devaguṇakalaśa*). Since it is said to possess virtue, it must also necessarily possess both merit and majesty;

thus, it can eliminate misfortune, ward off malevolent influences, dispel calamities, and prolong life. If people obtain it, they attain peace and happiness, and they attribute this success to the vase;
therefore, it is said to "bestow bliss. The Three Jewels are likewise so: by relying on the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action, people attain worldly [happiness].

Regarding "intermediate happiness": by taking the six perfections and so forth as objects of contemplation, one attains supramundane happiness; thus, one attributes this grace to the Dharma, which is why it is given the name "Jewel.
Fourth is "difficult to encounter": just as an auspicious jewel is rare and hard to obtain, so too are the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
Sentient beings hindered by karma find it difficult to encounter this [teaching] even in hundreds of millions of eons.
This takes auspiciousness as its treasure; the treasure is named "Auspiciousness" and is also called "Difficult to Encounter.

It is not a treasure that is commonly found in the world. If one encounters it through a karmic affinity, it will surely bring about auspiciousness. The Three Jewels are likewise; they too are not... of the world.

They have always existed in the interim. For example, even if one does not encounter a Buddha’s world for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, the Dharma is what the Buddha taught, and the Sangha are the Buddha’s disciples;

thus, when difficult, all are difficult, and when encountered, all are encountered. Furthermore, as it is now, although the Buddha has entered nirvana, the Three Jewels remain in the world and exist everywhere.
They expound the Dharma according to conditions, and Chan and Vinaya are both practiced. Yet for sentient beings of meager merit—
Karmic obstacles make [the encounter with] them difficult; yet, if even the Three Jewels residing in the world are thus, how much more so the Three Jewels of distinct characteristics (*betsō sanbō*)!
As for what is called "auspiciousness," it is as stated in the *Praise of the Three Jewels* (*Sanbōge*): "Where a Buddha dwells, dragons and devas rejoice;

where there is no Sangha, they grieve for the Dharma, and ghosts and spirits lament. How could these not be the Jewels? That which is most revered is the Three Jewels of distinct characteristics (the Dharma, Reward, and Transformation bodies).

The Buddha is the Jewel of the Buddha. The teachings, principles, practices, and fruits are the Jewel of the Dharma. The Bodhisattvas and Arhats are the Jewel of the Sangha (this definition also includes those who preach the Dharma and possess right view among ordinary monks).
Fifth is the ability to destroy. Just as a wish-fulfilling jewel can destroy poverty, so too are the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha;
they likewise destroy all the poverty and suffering of the world.

This takes the relief of poverty as its treasure; like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), it produces all manner of precious wealth according to one's desires and is able to destroy a person's poverty.
The Three Jewels are likewise: if a person seeks them, they produce all manner of Dharma-wealth and are able to destroy a person’s cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Because people lack wisdom, they fall forever into birth and death and fail to obtain the wealth of the Dharma.
This is what constitutes poverty. If a person draws near to the Triple Gem, they transform ignorance into wisdom and become endowed with all virtues;
this is the wealth of the Dharma.

Sixth is majestic power (*pratāpa*): just as the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*) possessed by a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) is able to subdue all enemies, so too are the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
It is likewise so. Possessing great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he subdues the four māras;
thus, the subduing of māras is his treasure. As for those who are enemies—whether they be vengeful neighboring states or rebellious feudal lords—[he likewise subdues them].
Those who do not submit and commit aggression are the enemies. At such times, the Wheel-Turning King may either display his majesty to warn them or take up his halberd to strike;
wherever the Wheel-Treasure turns, the enemy rebels lose heart and immediately submit. The Three Jewels are likewise:
they subdue the Maras and their enmity through supernatural powers and wisdom, and thus they are called "Jewels. As for the four Māras, they are [the Māra of] afflictions...
The māra of affliction, the māra of the five aggregates, the māra of death, and the celestial māra.
Seventh is the fulfillment of wishes: like a maṇi jewel, it can rain down all manner of treasures according to whatever is sought by the mind—the jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
It is likewise so. It can fulfill the virtuous aspirations cultivated by sentient beings.
"Maṇi" is the Sanskrit term for "wish-fulfilling. This is largely the same as the fifth [jewel], with only slight differences:
while that refers to it as a treasure because it dispels poverty, this refers to it as a treasure because it fulfills aspirations.
Eighth is adornment. Just as such precious jewels adorn the royal palace, so too do the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha adorn the Bodhi-jewel palace of the Dharma King.
This takes adornment as its treasure; just as a royal palace is adorned with precious jewels, so too is bodhi adorned by the Three Jewels.
The Dharma King is the Buddha. Bodhi is the fruit of the path realized by the Buddha; the Buddha abides by means of the path, just as a king dwells in his palace.
This means that the Buddha takes awakening (*bodha*) as his adornment, and the Dharma takes guidance and preservation (*dhāraṇa*) as its [adornment].
Adornment: the Sangha takes harmony as its adornment.
Ninth is the most exquisite: like the wondrous jewels of the heavens, which are the most subtle and refined, so too are the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
It surpasses all worldly things as the most supreme and wondrous jewel.

Since it is called a "celestial wondrous jewel," it must be perfectly harmonious and translucent, its radiance illuminating the heavens, its spiritual efficacy penetrating everywhere, and excelling all other categories;
it is treasured for its subtle, wondrous, and preeminent excellence. The Three Jewels are likewise so: since they are said to transcend the world, [they possess these same qualities].

Thus, through seeing, hearing, reading, or reciting [the Triple Gem], sins are extinguished as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; through prostrating, recollecting, and taking refuge, merit increases immeasurably.
It is for this reason that they are regarded as treasures because of their supreme excellence.
Tenth is immutability: just as pure gold does not change when placed in fire, so too are the Treasures of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
The eight winds of the world cannot cause it to waver;
this is because it takes the eternally abiding as its treasure. Just as pure gold does not fear being smelted by fire, how could the Triple Gem fear the shifting of circumstances?

The "eight winds" refer to praise and blame, suffering and pleasure, gain and loss, and defamation and fame. [Question: If the Buddha-dharma is truly eternal and thus inherently incapable of change, and if the noble monks who have attained the Way are likewise incapable of change, then [how can there be transformation]?

There are two kinds of ordinary monks. With the heaps of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) upon their heads, they forcibly perform Buddhist services; yet as they pursue objects and encounter conditions, it is not necessarily that they do not flow [with the mundane]. Why then do they not transform? Answer: A monk of right view dwells in the world’s conditions with his body, but his mind abides beyond the dust [of defilement].

He follows along without flowing; how could he be moved or turned? As for ordinary secular monks, they are not discussed here. △ Third, concluding by revealing the immeasurable spiritual transformations.
The Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha possess immeasurable supernormal powers and transformations, benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings without even momentary rest.
For this reason, the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha are called "Jewels."
The ten metaphors explained above are by no means exhaustive; if one were to fully elucidate them, they would be immeasurable.

As for supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), one manifests in the form of a Vidyārāja to crush and subdue demonic adversaries. As for transformations (*nirmāṇa*), one manifests bodies according to the various classes of beings to gather and guide sentient beings.
Although ordinary monks lack such supernatural powers and transformations, they are nonetheless able to subdue demons through wisdom and eloquence. All...
O heterodox practitioners, this seamless integration and lack of obstruction, wherein skillful means accord with what is appropriate, is itself a spiritual transformation. It brings benefit and joy;
that is to say, ordinary minds receive advantage without ceasing, and they may forever look up to it for reliance. Its fame is manifested based on its virtue; it is truly a great treasure.
The preceding section, which separately elucidates the four debts of gratitude, is hereby concluded. △ Third, the exhortation to practice.
"Good sons, for your sake I have briefly explained these four kinds of objects of gratitude, both mundane and supramundane.
You should know that when practicing the bodhisattva path, you ought to repay these four kinds of kindness."
These four debts of gratitude are so profound that they cannot be repaid even by the practices of a Bodhisattva who has generated the bodhicitta.

Although this is spoken as an exhortation regarding these debts, it is in fact intended to rouse and awaken [the listener], causing them to turn away from the Lesser Vehicle and toward the Great Vehicle;
this is the essential point. The extensive explanation of the four debts of gratitude that ought to be repaid is hereby concluded. △ Third, the Elder’s Request.
Questioning on Repaying Kindness:
At that time, five hundred elders addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, these four kinds of kindness are extremely difficult to repay.
What practices should one cultivate to repay such kindness?"
Having heard what the Buddha taught, the elder understood that there are four debts of gratitude. He then reflected: "If there were no parents, who could nourish and raise us?
If there were no king, the world would not be at peace. If there were no Triple Gem, there would be none to deliver and transform us."
Although sentient beings may have no kindness toward one in the present life, they do possess kindness from the past.
If one is unaware of it, that is one thing; but if one knows it, one must certainly repay it. Now, wishing to repay them, I do not know what practice would be appropriate. Therefore, I ask.
△ Fourth, the Tathāgata’s instruction to resolve the Great Mind, in three parts. First, the enumeration of the three kinds of ten practices.
The Buddha addressed the elders, saying: "Sons of good family, for the sake of seeking bodhi, there are three kinds of ten pāramitās:
first, the ten kinds of dāna-pāramitā; second, the ten kinds of upasthāna-pāramitā;
and third, the ten kinds of bhūta-pāramitā."
This is the Buddha’s answer regarding the householder’s practice of repaying kindness.

The Buddha’s intention was that to repay the four debts of gratitude, one must rely upon seeking supreme enlightenment above and transforming sentient beings below; apart from these, there is nothing else by which one may repay them.
Within the sutra, for the sake of seeking even a single phrase, there is the mind that initiates the aspiration, followed by the three types of ten *pāramitās* as the practices to be performed.

Regarding the *pāramitās*, there is the heading but no commentary; as for merely presenting the general names, it is because the Buddha knew there were ten [types], yet fearing prolixity, he did not enumerate them, but instead presented the general meaning to lead people to resolve their minds. *Pāramitā* means "reaching the other shore," as explained previously.
As for the first, *dāna* (generosity), the root sūtra does not list ten specific names; they should be understood according to the ten types in the *Avataṃsaka*.

The Treasury of Giving (*dānagañja*). 1. Giving with partial reduction: (If one obtains delicious food, one must first give it to sentient beings before eating it oneself; the same applies to other things. 2. Exhaustive giving:

(According to what one possesses, one gives everything away to benefit others, without stinginess even unto the end of one’s life. 3. Internal giving: (Giving one’s body, life, hands, feet, head, eyes, and so forth, in order to save the sick. 4. External giving.

(One gives away the royal throne, and even all manner of external wealth, bestowing them entirely upon others. Five: The Internal and External Giving. (The body and the royal throne are both impermanent;

one gives them to those who seek them. Six: The Universal Giving. (Kingdoms, marrow, brains, wives, and children will inevitably be separated from us; one gives these all away without stinginess. Seven: The Giving of the Past. (All phenomena of the past, when sought throughout the ten directions, are ultimately unobtainable.)
8. Ultimate relinquishment of future giving: observing that all future phenomena are unobtainable, one ultimately relinquishes them all without forming conceptual constructions. 9. Present giving.

(Contemplating all conditioned phenomena as dreams and unreal, one has no attachment. This is the tenth, ultimate giving. (This body is precarious, fragile, and not solid; one should relinquish it to fulfill their aspirations. There are ten kinds of "approaching" (*upaniṣad*);
they do not go beyond the categories of the original sūtra’s analysis, and are also called "giving.

The current explanation still relies on the previous ten kinds of giving, but by not clinging to signs (*animitta*), one approaches the principle. This constitutes the ten kinds of approaching. Regarding this:

There is no contradiction in principle. (Question: This interpretation states that if one merely does not cling to appearances (*nimitta*), one approaches the principle. If so, can it be said that the Bodhisattvas of the *Dānapāramitā* in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* all cling to appearances? Answer:

As in the "Inconceivable Realm" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka*, the Bodhisattvas of the *Dānapāramitā* certainly do not cling to appearances. However, what is emphasized there is the *pāramitā* of giving, which refers specifically to generosity. Here, the focus is on the forgetting of appearances to illustrate the approach to the principle. To unify the two while opening them as distinct is not contradictory to the principle;

why should there be any doubt? Regarding the ten kinds of reality, even numerical categories do not exist. As explained in the commentary of this very sutra, it also simply says: "To give rise to bodhicitta..."
Focus the mind and exhort the assembly to together resolve to recite even a single four-line verse for the sake of a single sentient being, leading them toward Bodhi;
this is called "the true. Now, since it is said to be "for a single sentient being," it remains a Dharma-gift (*dharma-dāna*) among the various forms of giving.
One should know that this Dharma-gift is the Dharma-gift within the *dāna-pāramitā* (perfection of giving) among the ten perfections of a Bodhisattva. Thus, since the Tathāgata—

Regarding these ten kinds, one should logically revere and be sincere in the giving of Dharma. When the ten perfections are fully realized: when the teaching of the Dharma is free from defilement, this is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*);

when encountering adverse conditions with a mind of emptiness, this is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); when instructing others without weariness, this is the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*);

when speaking while remaining non-speaking, this is the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*); and when reflecting upon oneself in accordance with what is taught—this is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
That which skillfully demonstrates according to the capacities of beings is the *upāya-pāramitā*. That which desires for all to achieve the Way is the *praṇidhāna-pāramitā*.
That which causes others to give rise to understanding is the *bala-pāramitā*. That which possesses unimpeded eloquence is the *jñāna-pāramitā*.
All these flow forth from the mind of bodhi and are spoken in accordance with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). There is no...
It is not real. △ Second, a brief exposition of three meanings to distinguish [the four]. First, clarifying giving to distinguish the real:
If there are good sons or good daughters who resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and are able to...

If one fills a trichiliocosm with the seven precious jewels and bestows them as alms upon immeasurable impoverished sentient beings, such giving is merely called the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*); it is not called the true perfection.
"Good sons" refers to those who have resolved their minds [to attain enlightenment], encompassing both lay and ordained persons, as well as men and women.

"Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" and so forth refer to the path toward which one is directed; "mind" refers to the thought of being directed toward that path. One must necessarily possess the three minds and four vows.
"Below" refers to the wealth that is given as a gift—the seven treasures, namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and so forth, the most precious of rarities.
"Filled with" means that the place below is filled with these seven treasures. "Giving to those below" refers to the person who receives the gift.
Now, the mind that can be thus aroused is called *bodhi*; the wealth that is given is called the seven treasures; and the place to which it is given is called the Great [Vehicle].

A thousand [times]. One who practices giving calls it "immeasurable. Although this is merely a provisional designation, for a Bodhisattva possessing supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), it would not be difficult.
Within the practice of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), this is indeed praiseworthy;

yet, when distinguished by name, such giving, though a sublime practice, belongs entirely to the category of material giving (*āmiṣadāna*) and is not called "true. That which is truly real, however, is the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
Furthermore, one must exercise discernment because material giving benefits living beings but not those who have died; it can alleviate poverty but cannot save one from the suffering of karma.
According to the subsequent text, although such acts constitute sublime practices, they do not constitute repaying kindness.
△ Second, clarifying the proximity of those who are genuine.
If there are sons or daughters of good family who give rise to the mind of great compassion and, seeking unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
give away their own wives and children to others without any sense of stinginess, as well as their own flesh, hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow, and brain.
Even giving up one's body and life to those who come seeking it—such a form of giving is merely called "approximating" the pāramitās;
it is not yet called the "actual" pāramitās.
Within this giving, it may be called "exhaustive giving" and "all-encompassing giving," wherein one disregards body and life;

it is truly the ultimate limit of a bodhisattva’s perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*). Yet, even while distinguishing it as merely "approaching" (*upaniṣad*), it means that by disregarding body and life, one takes only the Way as one's kin, drawing near to the correct principle;
this is indeed a sublime practice. Nevertheless, it is still distinguished as not yet being "true" (*bhūta*), meaning as follows:
This practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) merely serves to break one’s own stinginess and to free oneself from the two attachments;

it cannot benefit others and thus is not called "repaying kindness. However, what is here emphasized is that only the teaching of the Dharma to deliver sentient beings is permitted as the true repayment of kindness.
△ Third, clarifying the true [repayment] by distinguishing it from the previous two.
If a son or daughter of good family gives rise to the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta while abiding in the state of non-apprehension,

and exhorts all sentient beings to likewise give rise to this mind, bestowing even a single four-line verse of the true Dharma upon a single sentient being so that they may be directed toward unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment— this is called the true pāramitā. The two preceding types of giving have not yet [attained this status].
This is called "repaying kindness.
This is identical to the previous two types of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) in that it is directed toward the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood for one’s own benefit;

however, while the former two emphasize the aspect of self-benefit, their altruistic activity is not beyond the scope of giving (*dāna*). Regarding the statement here that this stage is "without attainment," it still remains [within the realm of conceptualization].
An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), though not yet having attained the rank of a sage, is able to exhort the multitude to collectively resolve upon the Great Mind;
such is the "flesh-body bodhisattva" who manifests their mind in the world. From the phrase "By means of the True" (*zhen*) onwards, the text correctly clarifies the Dharma being expounded.

"True" (*zhen*) refers to *tathatā* (Suchness), which is neither delusory nor subject to change. "Real" (*shi*) refers to the *bhūtalakṣaṇa* (Ultimate Reality); all phenomena return to this Truth. If one bestows grace upon people at this very point, even a single...
The verses are few; they consist of a mere four lines. As for their benefit, it is bestowed upon but a single person, causing that one person to incline toward Bodhi.
Because this alone is what is most weighty, it is used as the title.

Only then is it truly a *pāramitā*. The first two [verses] are set aside, stating: "Those two types have never yet taught the Dharma; they are not called 'repaying kindness. It should be understood thus.

Knowing that this person remains still among the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), to speak even a single word of the true Dharma and deliver a single individual is the most inferior form of benefiting others;
yet it is still a repayment of their kindness. How much more so, then, for one who has entered the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*) and extensively expounds the Dharma?
The salvation of the many multitudes goes without saying. △ Fourth, truly being able to repay the four debts of gratitude:
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family can cultivate this third true *pāramitā*, they are then said to be truly able to repay the four debts of gratitude.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, Kāśyapa and others said: "The Buddha's kindness is vast and great. Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, who could ever repay it?
Even by providing for him with hands and feet, prostrating with head and crown, and making every kind of offering, none can repay it. If one were to carry him upon one's head..."
Carrying [the Buddha] upon their two shoulders, they would serve him with the utmost devotion throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Furthermore, they would offer exquisite food, immeasurable precious robes, various bedding and seats, diverse medicinal decoctions, ox-head sandalwood, and all manner of rare jewels;
they would construct stupas and temples, and spread precious garments upon the ground—performing such acts of worship throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Even so...
It cannot be repaid. Now, this sutra is that which was spoken from the golden mouth of the Buddha.

To speak even a single phrase or four lines of the True Dharma, exhorting a single sentient being to turn toward Bodhi—this alone is called "truth," and it is capable of repaying the four debts of gratitude. Alas!
The Dharma-propagating śramaṇa ought to value this highly. △ Third, the inquiry and explanation regarding the reason for the true recompense, in two parts. First, the inquiry: "For what reason?
The intent of the inquiry is as follows:
regarding the two previous forms of giving—one filling the great trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and offering them to immeasurable multitudes—[why is this not considered the true recompense?].

Now, as for that which the entire world is unable to practice: to offer one’s head, eyes, marrow, brain, body, flesh, hands, and feet—disregarding even one’s own life—is the most difficult form of giving.
Yet such acts are surpassed by even a small portion of the teaching of the Dharma.
For even if one were to speak of True Suchness (*tathatā*) or point toward the Limit of Reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), this remains easy for one who understands the Dharma. Why is this so?
Such is the distinction between the superior and the inferior; truly, one does not know why this is so. △ Second, the explanation:
The first two types of giving involve a mind that grasps at attainment. The third giver possesses a mind of non-attainment;

by means of the true Dharma, they bestow gifts upon all sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, great Bodhicitta. When such a person attains the realization of Bodhi, [they will realize the fruit].
To extensively deliver sentient beings without end, and to perpetuate the lineage of the Three Jewels so that it is never severed— for these reasons,
it is called "repaying kindness.
As for the former two types involving a mind of grasping, this refers to those who have resolved their minds [for enlightenment] but are not yet like a treasure that fulfills the world.
One who is not ungrudging regarding wealth, as well as marrow and brain, cannot fulfill their own *dānapāramitā*.
Such a person, wishing to fulfill their own *dānapāramitā* and attain realization of *bodhi*, only then gives rise to the mind of giving; this is a mind that grasps at attainment.
The third, the mind of non-apprehension, is established by the heading and explained as follows. "True Dharma" refers to the teachings proclaimed in accordance with ultimate truth.

To bestow this upon all sentient beings, causing them to generate the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta, acting solely for the benefit of others without any other ulterior motive—this is the mind of non-apprehension. Furthermore, it is correct...
When teaching, one does not cling to the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*), nor does one cling to the mark of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*). The three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are empty in essence;

this is also called the mind of non-attainment (*anupalambha-citta*). Regarding the two characters "this person" (*ayaṃ puruṣaḥ*), there are two explanations. First, they refer to the assembly of sentient beings (*sattva-rāśi*).

Having heard the wondrous Dharma and having generated the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), they then awaken according to what they have heard, practice according to their awakening, and realize according to their practice.

This constitutes their own self-benefit and is further capable of benefiting others; hence it is said, "extensively delivering [beings]," and so forth. Second, this still refers to the individual themselves:

since they are already able to benefit others by preaching the Dharma, how could they not also practice it themselves and realize it for themselves? Moreover, even while at the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), one is already able to benefit others.
How much more so when they have realized *bodhi*, being able themselves to teach and transform sentient beings everywhere and at all times in an unfathomable manner;
therefore it is said that "they extensively deliver sentient beings without end.

Regarding "succeeding the Three [Jewels]," this clarifies the transmission from one to another, where transformation follows transformation infinitely; thus it is said that "they succeed the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it shall not be severed. By means of...
To cause the lineage of the Buddhas to flourish is the true repayment of kindness. Both explanations are valid.
△ Fifth, the elders resolve their minds and obtain benefit.
At that time, five hundred elders heard from the Buddha this teaching on repaying kindness, which they had never heard before; with these thoughts in mind...

They leaped for joy, having attained what they had never before experienced; they resolved their minds to seek and advance toward unexcelled bodhi, attained the samādhi of patience, entered inconceivable wisdom, and became forever non-retrogressive.
This was the efficacy of the elder’s hearing the discourse on repaying kindness.
Previously, when the five hundred elders heard the Buddha preach the Mahāyāna Dharma of cultivating the mind-ground, they conceived feelings of aversion and did not wish to hear it.
They thought that only after enduring long-term hardship could one achieve success; thus, they intended to realize the lesser fruits as a means of acknowledging their debt of gratitude.
On Repaying Kindness. At that time, the Buddha took pity on his ignorance, yet rejoiced in his intention to recognize and repay kindness.

Not wishing to bypass the student's capacity but rather to meet him with the appropriate means and administer medicine according to the ailment, he spoke of the four debts of gratitude that ought to be repaid.
Upon hearing it said here that nothing short of the bodhicitta can repay such kindness, [the man] was suddenly filled with the joy of the Dharma; thus it is said, "his heart leaped with joy."
"Leaping up" is the ultimate expression of joy. "Attaining what has never been attained before" refers to the teaching on repaying kindness;

although one had not previously failed to hear such things, they had never been so intimate and detailed. Consequently, inferior thoughts were suddenly stilled and great aspirations began to flourish;
thus it is said, "the mind is aroused," and so forth. As for "the samādhi of patience," it means to adjust, shift, and turn away from [delusion] to achieve liberation.
The essence is great awakening. However, the principle thus awakened is a dharma known only to oneself; that one ultimately cannot express it to others is *kṣānti* (patience).
That the single mind remains unmoving is *samādhi*. Note that the character "辱" (*ru*) is merely a particle used for emphasis.
It is also another name for the "Dharma-patience of Non-arising. Having realized this dharma, not even the slightest dharma arises. Not even the slightest...
"The extinction of dharmas" refers to that which is realized through patient acceptance and silent resonance. "Entering the inconceivable wisdom" means that wisdom is itself bodhi;
"entering" signifies harmonious accord. Because one accords with the Way through numinous awareness, it transcends speech, deliberation, and mental thought;
hence it is called "inconceivable wisdom. This constitutes the partial attainment of the Buddha-wisdom. "Never again falling back" refers to ascending to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). △ Six.
Having gathered together, they heard the Dharma and obtained benefit.
At that time, within the assembly, eighty-four thousand sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and attained firm faith, as well as this samādhi.
The great multitude gathered like an ocean all attained the Vajra-patience Samādhi, realized the patience of non-arising, and [attained] gentleness.

[They attain] the patience of conformity (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*). Or they realize the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) and obtain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Immeasurable sentient beings resolve their minds on enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) and abide in the stage of non-retrogression.

Regarding the bodhicitta, as stated in the *Awakening of Faith* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*), there are three kinds: first, because of right mindfulness of the dharma of suchness (*tathatā*); second...
First, because one delights in gathering all wholesome dharmas; second, because one desires to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings.

For a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva, these constitute the foundation for attaining Buddhahood. If one does not give rise to this mind, then even if one were to sacrifice one's life and body, it would all be the work of Māra.
One of firm and resolute faith immediately hears and understands the four debts of gratitude, and gives rise to the aspiration to...
The response: "One faith is eternal faith; it never regresses again, and is therefore called 'firm and solid. This samādhi also refers to faith;
that is to say, because faith is firm and solid, nothing can turn it back—this itself is samādhi.
As for the term 'assembly like the ocean' used by the great multitude: the ocean is the general gathering place of waters. Thus, all the myriad streams under heaven flow back to the ocean."

It is able to gather and contain; the ocean takes its meaning from "great. Using this as a metaphor, the present Dharma assembly of the Tathāgata—where all holy ones and ordinary beings from other directions and this world have gathered here like the waters of the ocean—is therefore called a "Ocean Assembly" (*sāgara-melāpaka*).
As for "Vajra Patience," patience is explained according to the preceding section; "Vajra" takes the sense of "solidity," meaning that one has attained these three.
Obscure. "One forbearance and eternal forbearance" means that external things cannot turn one's mind, for it is as firm as the substance of a vajra.

"The realization of the forbearance of non-arising" refers to thoroughly understanding that all phenomena are fundamentally without arising or ceasing; having investigated with truth and attained patient acceptance, deluded thoughts are suddenly stilled.
"The forbearance of pliancy and compliance" means being able to accord with both principle and phenomena; being able to penetrate the fact that both phenomena and principle are entirely one reality.

Because one thoroughly examines, accepts with patience, and does not oppose [the dharmas], it is called "patience of compliance" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*). Alternatively, regarding "patience of non-arising of the lower":
this is stated in contrast to "arising. That is to say, prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*), there still exist the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) of conceptualization;

since these are taken as "arising," upon reaching the first stage, the two obstacles have already been abandoned, and thus it is called "non-arising. Because one realizes this through silent, intuitive penetration of reality, it is called... [patience].
Patience. Below [the section on] the Immeasurables, there are three stages of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). First is non-retrogression in stage (*bhūmi-avaivartika*):

this refers to Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*) who, from the first dwelling (which corresponds to the first faith of the Perfect Teaching), sever the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). From the second dwelling up to the seventh dwelling, they sever the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*), whereby they never again fall back from the supramundane rank;
this is called non-retrogression in stage. Second is non-retrogression in practice (*caryā-avaivartika*): this refers to the Separate Teaching from the eighth [dwelling]...

Having so abided, one proceeds to the stage of the ten practices (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*), where one suppresses and severs the delusions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, never again falling back from the bodhisattva conduct;
this is called "non-retrogression in practice" (*pratipatti-avaivartika*). Third is "non-retrogression in mindfulness" (*smṛti-avaivartika*):

this refers to bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-vyākhyāna*) from the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*) onward, who, having shattered the delusions of ignorance (*avidyā-kleśa*), never again fall back from the right mindfulness of the Middle Way; this is called "non-retrogression in mindfulness. Now...
The sūtra merely states that he "dwells in the stage of non-retrogression. Alternatively, there may be differences in depth;
generally speaking, these two preceding sections are both texts arranged by the compiler of the sūtra. This concludes the five hundred major sections in general.
△ Second, the conclusion and exhortation to receive and uphold [the teaching], in two parts. First, the formal exhortation to cause it to spread widely:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the five hundred elders:

"In future ages, if any sentient beings hear this 'Chapter on Repaying the Four Debts of Gratitude' from the *Cittabhūmi-parivarta*, and receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, copy, and cause it to spread widely..."
"Receiving and upholding" (śīla-dhāraṇa) below refers to the practice of circulation. Combined, there are only four; expanded, they become eight. These are:
"receiving" means to accept with faith and compliance; "upholding" means to shoulder the burden and carry out the practice; "reading" means to master the text and understand its meaning;

"studying" means to engage in learning so that it permeates the spirit; "explaining" means to analyze and commentate; "preaching" means to lecture and differentiate the teachings; and "recording the text as a book."
"Transcribing" refers to copying by hand; it also includes printing. Collectively, these are termed "the practice of dissemination.
△ Second, clarifying the merits for the present and future, in two parts. First, increasing and prolonging blessings and longevity in the present life.
For such people as these, merit and wisdom increase; they are protected by the devas. In their present lives they are free from illness, and their lifespans are extended.

Auspicious signs constitute their merit, and spiritual discernment constitutes their wisdom. Through the empowerment of the Dharma and the protection of the devas, so-called "hundredfold blessings" arrive in abundance and spiritual discernment becomes ever more flourishing.
Being free from illness, the body is at peace; with the extension of life, longevity is attained.
All these are what people desire; they also arise from the application of the power of the Dharma and the protection of its spiritual efficacy.
Such are the benefits for this present life. △ Second, the realization of Bodhi as the fruit in the future, in three parts. First, rebirth in the Inner Court at the end of life.

At the time of death, one will immediately attain rebirth in the inner palace of Maitreya; beholding the mark of the white tuft between his brows, one will transcend birth and death, and at the three assemblies under the Dragon Flower tree, one shall surely attain liberation.

This refers to the merit for future lives. It means that those who cause [the teaching] to spread widely, each according to their own aspirational mind and power of wisdom—whether by receiving, upholding, understanding, or explaining it—and who dwell therein with single-minded steadfastness, shall accordingly attain rebirth in accordance with their vows.
The inner palace is the inner court. This, too, is rebirth according to one's vows. Maitreya has both an inner and an outer court;
while those dwelling in the outer court are ordinary beings who may still fall back, those in the inner court belong to the stream of the sages and are free from birth and death.

One should know that such a person must have been reborn while still carrying afflictions (*kleśa*), for they were only able to uphold, recite, and study [the teachings], but had not yet reached [full realization].

The severing of delusions constitutes a practice characterized by signs (*sanimitta*). By virtue of the power of the Dharma’s transformative influence and one's own aspirational force, one is born directly into that palace.
Those who behold the mark of the white tuft (*ūrṇā-kośa*) seem as though they have not yet seen the Compassionate One’s countenance; they see only the mark of the tuft.

As for those who transcend birth and death, it means that once born within the inner court, although they have not yet personally beheld the Compassionate One’s countenance, they are nonetheless sustained by the gathering-in of his compassionate power.
This leads to falling away; that is, it transcends [the cycle]. Regarding "under the Dragon-Flower tree," the *Maitreya’s Descent into the World Sūtra* states:

"On the very day Maitreya Bodhisattva leaves the household life, he immediately attains Buddhahood. He sits beneath the Dragon-Flower tree in the Flower Forest Garden and preaches the Dharma in three assemblies.
Hence, it is called the "Three Assemblies under the Dragon-Flower. In the first assembly, he delivers ninety-six [thousand disciples] across the river of birth and death.
The assembly of koṭis (in the language of China, "one hundred billion") of śrāvakas—within the True Dharma of Śākyamuni—are able to perform the work of a Buddha.

Whether they plant roots of goodness themselves or instruct others to do so; whether they fashion images of the Buddha from the seven precious substances, copper, iron, clay, wood, or other materials;
or whether they create painted images and stūpas, large or small, and offer them incense and flowers—it is by virtue of these roots of goodness that [they attain their results].
By the power of this merit, when Maitreya attains Buddhahood, they will obtain a human body with great excellence.
In his first assembly, they will shave their heads and leave the household life; by virtue of the power of their past vows, they will immediately attain nirvana.
In his second assembly, he will deliver ninety-four koṭis of śrāvakas, including kings, ministers, and commoners. This refers to those who, during the present True Dharma of Śākyamuni Tathāgata—
In this world, they are able to perform Dharma activities regarding Mahāyāna sūtras, Vinaya, or Śāstras— whether by reading or reciting them,
or by reverently making offerings to them, or by adorning the volumes with various colored silks. By the power of these roots of goodness,
when Maitreya Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, they will successfully obtain a human body in the second [eon].
In that assembly, he shaved his head and left the household life; by the power of his past vows, he immediately attained *nirvāṇa*.
In the third assembly, he delivered ninety-two *koṭis* of *śrāvaka* disciples. He said:

"If there are sentient beings who, within the true Dharma of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, are able to perform monastic duties, plant roots of goodness for themselves, or teach others to plant them, on the first day of every month..."
On the eighth day, the fifteenth day, or the first day of the month, they establish a vegetarian feast to make offerings to bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs;
or they make offerings to those practicing dhyāna-concentration; or they make offerings to various preachers of the Dharma; or they give gifts such as sitting mats to make offerings to the Saṃgha.
By the power of these roots of goodness, when Maitreya attains Buddhahood, they shall shave their heads at his third assembly.

Having left the household life, by the power of his past vows, he immediately attained *nirvāṇa*. One should know that this present sutra merely states that at the end of his life he was reborn in the inner palace;
as for those who behold the white tuft (*ūrṇā*), if one compares this with that other sutra, it appears they have not yet beheld the Buddha’s face.
Furthermore, by relying on the inner court of the Bodhisattvas for nourishment and cultivation, one shall descend together with them at the time of their descent.

At the first assembly where the Dharma is preached, one shall attain liberation. There are two kinds of liberation (as stated in the *Ratnagotravibhāga*): first, liberation through intrinsic purity (*prakṛtiviśuddhi-vimukti*).
This means that the nature of sentient beings is fundamentally pure and devoid of the characteristics of bondage or defilement; therefore, it is called liberation through intrinsic purity.

The liberation through the exhaustion of the two hindrances means that sentient beings possess the delusions of afflictions which obstruct the noble path, preventing them from attaining transcendence.
If one is freed from these hindrances, one immediately attains mastery; this is called liberation through the exhaustion of hindrances.

Thus, it is known that when the root sūtra speaks of "attaining liberation," it refers precisely to liberation through the exhaustion of hindrances. This is because [the practitioner] previously upheld and explained [this teaching].
By virtue of this merit, according to their aspirational power, they are reborn while still carrying their karmic burdens.

Although it is said that they transcend birth and death, in reality, they receive the guidance and protection of Maitreya and do not fall into the lower realms. They must wait for his descent to earth, where by hearing the Dharma they sever their delusions;
only then will their obstructions be exhausted and they attain ultimate liberation. This description applies to those of duller faculties; as for those of sharp faculties—
The details of the lower grade are shown separately below. △ Second, seeing Buddhas and hearing the Dharma according to one's wishes:
one is reborn at will in the pure lands of the ten directions, where one sees the Buddhas, hears the Dharma, and enters the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

This also relies on the previous [discussion]. Regarding the merit of causing [the teachings] to spread widely, one has not yet severed the afflictions (*kleśa*). Thus, according to one's inclination, one is reborn in a pure land of the ten directions while still carrying one's karmic burdens.
Therein, one is able to see the Buddhas of the ten directions, hear the True Dharma from those Buddhas, and enter the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Once one has entered this meditative concentration (*samādhi*), that concentration can give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*); and through wisdom, one will surely realize the Path. This is the comparison.
Previously, for those of sharp faculties: △ Third, swiftly realizing the seed-wisdom of Bodhi;
swiftly accomplishing Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
This text was already established in the preceding section; that it is now treated as a separate section is for the purpose of clarifying the three grades of spiritual capacity.
Specifically, those of dull faculties, due to their firm faith, will be born in the Inner Court and must await rebirth below.

Only at the three assemblies under the Dragon Flower Tree will they finally attain liberation; because the duration of time required is long and they have not yet attained swift realization, they are judged to be of dull faculties.

The next category has somewhat sharper faculties; they also attain rebirth in the pure lands of the ten directions through the power of their karma, where they are able to see the Buddhas and hear the Dharma.
This differs from the former group, who merely beheld the white tuft between the eyebrows without yet being able to see or hear [the Buddhas] directly; this person’s faculties are sharp.

The vow is profound; therefore, one attains the vision of the Buddha and hears the Dharma. Having entered right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), one will surely be able to give rise to wisdom and swiftly realize [enlightenment].
Nevertheless, even though realization is swift, it still relies upon the Buddha’s empowerment. This third section is for those of the sharpest faculties;

merely by being able to receive, uphold, read, and study [the teaching], with a single thought it permeates the spirit, all delusions are suddenly emptied, and perfect enlightenment is established. Therefore, it is said:
"Quickly attaining [enlightenment]," etc. "The wisdom of the Tathāgata" refers to the attainment of the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience). Question:

Since "quickly attaining," etc., originally belongs to the preceding section, to now establish it separately might misrepresent the Buddha’s intent. Answer: From the perspective of the logical flow of the treatise, it indeed belongs to the preceding section and should not be established separately.
However, with respect to the specific point of "quickly attaining," establishing it separately is also appropriate. Why? Because of the subsequent text.

In the *Shuzhang* (Excerpts from Special Chapters), this sutra was judged to belong to the Sudden Teaching (*dunjiao*). Now, although the text follows the preceding [sections], it is established separately according to its specific meaning.

Thus, the commentary states: "When the defiled spirit is purified in a single thought-moment, all delusions are suddenly emptied, and one establishes perfect enlightenment; therefore, it is called 'swift accomplishment' (*suncheng*)."
Thus we know that those of sharp faculties who encounter the sudden teaching are like a bird flying over a mountain: by spreading its wings, it reaches its destination immediately.

Therefore, while the first category involves those of dull faculties achieving success gradually, and the second category involves even those of sharp faculties still awaiting rebirth, this [third] case achieves completion instantaneously in a single thought-moment.
This still does not require waiting for rebirth. An ancient worthy said: "Follow the meaning, not the letter; thus there will never be even one error.

Those who have attained the meaning need not be like those who fix the strings of a zither and refuse to tune them. [The student] asks again: "If it is called the 'Sudden Teaching,' why must you further divide it into three grades, including those that are 'gradually accomplished'?

[The Master] answers: "The 'Sudden' refers to the teaching (*dharma*); the 'Gradual' refers to the capacity of the practitioner (*yogin*). How can you use the capacity of the practitioner to challenge the teaching?"
The Sutra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground Based on the Mahāyāna Jātaka, Volume Two, with a Light Commentary;
The Sutra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground Based on the Mahāyāna Jātaka, Volume Three, with a Light Commentary.
Light Annotated by the Śramaṇa Lai-zhou of Zhantan Monastery in the Capital of Qing III.
A Separate Commentary for Zhi-guang, Part Two Chapter Title:
Chapter on Repaying Kindness, Second, Lower Section.
Originally this was a single volume, which was divided into two; hence there are the upper and lower parts. △ Second, the text of the sutra has four sections.
First, Jñānaprabha’s reverent request for the Dharma. 1. First, the introductory narration by the scribe.
At that time, eighty yojanas to the northeast of the great city of Rājagṛha, there was a small kingdom named Puṇyavardhana.
In that country lived an elder named Jñānaprabha, who was advanced in years and had only one son.
His son was of a wicked nature and did not obey his parents; he could not follow any of their instructions.
From afar, he heard that the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings in this defiled and evil world.

He proclaimed the Mahāyāna, the Dharma for repaying kindness. Then the parents, the son, and all their retinues, in order to hear the Dharma, brought various offerings and came to where the Buddha was;
there they made offerings and paid him respect.
This passage provides an account of the origins and details of the four debts of gratitude as set forth in the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*.

The Elder Jñānaprabha is the person who, being the appropriate recipient, requests the Dharma. Below the section on Rājagṛha, the text describes the Elder’s native village; he is a man of that country who has come here from there.
"Jñānaprabha" is the name of the Elder. "Decrepit" describes the Elder’s old age, indicating his advanced years.
This passage reflects a state of mind marked by a sense of decline and frailty. Only the final five lines truly recount the origins and circumstances of the matter.
An elder possesses a natural affection for his son;

since the son is of a wicked disposition and refuses instruction, even if he were brought before the authorities and disciplined with legal punishment, it would still likely wound that innate bond of parental compassion. Now, from afar...
I have heard that the World-Honored One is at Vulture Peak Mountain preaching the Dharma on repaying the four debts of gratitude.
Therefore, leading my entire household and carrying offerings, I have not shunned the toil of over three thousand *li* to come see the Buddha and seek the Dharma.
Not only has this caused my wicked son to reform his evil ways and follow the good, but it has further inspired him to resolve upon Bodhicitta and attain patience.
[The Buddha said: "Excellent! Householder, you may truly be called a compassionate father; you may truly be called one who teaches his children well.
(One *yojana* is forty *li*). In the sutra, there are the two characters "parents. Either the householder, though advanced in years, still has parents;

or the householder and his wife serve as the parents for their children. [Question: "Householder Jñānaprabha, hearing the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma from beyond eighty *yojanas*—is this hearing it directly?"

Is it hearsay? Moreover, there are three grades of *yojana*: the superior is eighty *li*, the middling is sixty *li*, and the inferior is forty *li*. Even by taking the inferior measure, the distance remains over three thousand two hundred *li*; how could one arrive in a single day?

Why, as soon as the preceding passage concludes, does the text proceed to describe the Elder’s invitation to hear the Dharma? How easy it was for him to hear, and how swift his arrival! The answer is: The Tathāgata possesses the three secrets. Regarding the secret of speech (*vāg-guhya*), a single utterance is heard simultaneously throughout the sands of all worlds, as if sitting right before Him.

How much more so for a distance of merely three thousand *li*—how could he not have heard? Observing the Elder’s most sincere demeanor, he must surely share a karmic affinity with the Buddha; had he lacked such affinity, the force of his own karma would have turned away from him.

This is right before his seat, yet you have not even heard of him; how much more so from three thousand *li* away? As for those who arrive so swiftly, they must surely have a karmic affinity with the Buddha and possess roots of goodness from past lives.

Moved by their own sincerity, the Buddha will certainly bestow his grace from afar. Relying on the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), they can arrive in a mere instant. This mutual resonance between the response and the stimulus is inconceivable—what cause for doubt is there? (The "three mysteries" refer to the mystery of body, the mystery of speech, and the mystery of mind.
II. Zhiguang’s Request for the Dharma. Part One: First, stating the purpose of the visit.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying, "I have a son whose nature is wicked and evil; he does not accept any instruction from his parents.
Now, having heard the Buddha speak of repaying the four kinds of kindness, he has come to the Buddha's presence for the sake of hearing the Dharma."
"Bài" (pãi) means "vile" (lòu). It signifies being "unbearable. To speak of "evil" as "bài" refers to the evil of base vulgarity; it is utterly unbearable.

According to what the Elder said, although there may be karmic conditions from the past, they are still relatively light when considered for oneself, yet they are truly grave when considered for one's child.
Because they did not accept the instructions of their parents, they wish to rely upon the Buddha’s compassion to receive his revelation and guidance.
Since parental kindness is included among the four kinds of gratitude, they have come to listen and receive [the teaching] so as to reform their evil ways.

In this way, not only will they not lose the affection between father and son, but they shall also carry upon their heads the great grace of the Tathāgata’s transformation and never forget it. △ Second.
We beseech you to proclaim it.
We pray that the World-Honored One will, for our sake and that of our retinues, expound the profound and wondrous meaning of the four debts of gratitude,
so that those wicked sons may give rise to hearts of filial piety and obedience, and may attain peace and happiness in this life and in future births.
I pray that you will grant my earnest plea: let the first four lines below be for the sake of the entire family, and let the latter four lines be specifically for the sake of this wicked son.

Furthermore, based on the final two lines, one can perceive the extent of the compassionate father’s grace—the ultimate limit of a father’s love for his son—such that even for one who is unfilial and rebellious, he ensures they are loathed by others in this life, or [punished] by devas and nāgas.

If executed, after death one will surely fall into the three miserable realms and suffer immeasurable pain. Now, having received the Buddha’s transformation, they wish to turn their rebellious and perverse hearts back into hearts of filial piety and obedience;
thus they are respected by people in the present life and will be reborn in heaven in future lives. Therefore it is said:
"In this life they shall be born [in virtue], attaining peace and happiness. Alas! This may truly be called "desiring to repay profound kindness, though the vast heavens are boundless."
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s praise of the good exhortation, which has two parts. First, praising the good exhortation and urging them to listen:
At that time, the Buddha addressed Jñānaprabha: “Excellent, excellent!
For the sake of the Dharma, you have come to my presence to make offerings and pay respect, desiring to hear this teaching. Listen attentively and reflect upon it well.”
"Praising the good" does not refer solely to praising his sincerity, but also praises his compassion, for his purpose in coming was originally for the sake of his son.
"Listen attentively" is a word of admonition; yet if the elder had come, it would have been sincere even without such an instruction.
Yet, regarding your faults, you must still issue a warning: do not act with haste before speaking;
you must examine and contemplate with precision, delving deeply into the meaning so that you do not initially fail the intent of those who have come to you. Contemplate this well.

These are words of exhortation and entrustment. "Good reflection" (*samyak-cintā*) is precisely "right reflection. This means that the Tathāgata speaks in accordance with the correct principle, and you must reflect in accordance with that principle;
do not misinterpret the Buddha’s intent. "Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is an instruction that one must not forget.

(In general, for those who lecture, these words of "good reflection" should not be interpreted too deeply regarding their ultimate meaning; this is merely to restrain the arrogance of those whose natures are wicked and deluded.)
△ Second, the account of truly obtaining the retribution [of merit], in two parts. First, a general account of attaining the fruit of a Wheel-Turning King:
If there are good sons or good daughters who resolve upon Bodhicitta and, for the sake of hearing the essential Dharma, lift their feet and set them down—
According to the distance and the number of atoms in the ground he treads upon, by these causes and conditions, he attains the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin).
When the retribution of the Sage King is exhausted, he becomes a Heavenly King of the Desire Realm. When the retribution of the Desire Heaven is exhausted, he becomes a Brahmā Heavenly King.
Upon seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, one swiftly realizes the sublime fruit.

The phrase "if there are those of lower [capacity]" generally refers to all people; even those who merely give rise to the aspiration and come specifically to hear the Dharma will all receive the retribution of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) and so forth.
Regarding the "essential Dharma" (*dharmāyāsa*): the Buddha’s intent is the Dharma, and that which cuts through directly is the essential. Furthermore, it refers to the Buddha’s words.

Although there are many [explanations], taking the "mind-ground" (cittabhūmi) as the essential point: to lift the step is called "raising"; to set the foot down is called "lowering"—this refers to walking.
A long path is "far"; a short path is "near. To tread upon the earth with the feet is called "stepping on" (kramaṇa); to obtain blessings by relying on the earth is called "following" (anugama).
However, the two phrases following "even a minute speck of dust" are unclear; one should know that the earth is merely an accumulation of various particles.
It is accomplished. The Buddha’s intention must be that he considers the number of dust motes on the ground traversed by his footsteps;
as the distance of each step varies, so too does the quantity of those dust motes. This serves as the cause for raising the mind to listen to the Dharma.
Through the conditions of the hardships endured during one's travels, one will surely experience the retribution of being born as a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) and so forth.
Comparing a single lifetime to a single mote of dust, according to the number of such motes, one obtains the retribution of a Wheel-Turning King and so forth, proceeding from one birth to the next.

It is also like the varying number of motes of dust. However, as for the fact that their retributive fruits successively become increasingly superior, it is because their sincere hearts increase twofold, and thus their retributive fruits become twofold more excellent.
Regarding the passage "seeing the Buddha" and below: furthermore, it does not stop at the retribution of celestial fruits;
one continues to obtain the great retributive fruit of seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, and swiftly realizing Bodhi. One should know this further.

There is a profound meaning here. For instance, if one practices the mundane discipline of ordinary meditative concentration in the human realm, even if one attains the retribution of a Wheel-Turning King or a Brahmā deity, one will be captivated by celestial pleasures and have no leisure to see the Buddha or hear the Dharma; how much less could one swiftly realize Bodhi?

Nevertheless, as for those who have come here, considering the sincerity of their resolve, the hardship of their journey, and the great distance they have traveled—they listen to the Dharma with such a sincere heart that they infuse their spirits with the Buddha-dharma and cultivate the seeds of holiness (*ārya-bīja*). Even with the retribution of the Brahma-heaven, they will not be bound by pleasant realms;
thus, moment by moment they see the Buddha, and from time to time they hear the Dharma. When these holy seeds are activated, then—
Having traversed *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one can attain the path to Bodhi in a single lifetime; this demonstrates that it is the Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna.
△ Second, clarifying the karmic retribution of Prajñāprabha.
Great Householder, you and the rest of this assembly have come to me for the sake of the Dharma, traveling eighty yojanas.
For every single atom of dust along the way, you shall each receive the karmic fruit of being a Wheel-Turning King among gods and humans.
Having heard the Dharma, you shall in the future realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The first phrase refers to the Buddha as Jñānaprabha (Light of Wisdom). The second phrase refers to the retinue he governs. Below this, it clarifies the resulting retribution:
"For the sake of the Dharma, you set out from your own home and came to where I am. Thus [it is said].
With every step taken and set down, one passes over as many particles of dust as there are in eighty *yojanas* of the great earth.

For each and every particle of dust, one is able to experience a corresponding karmic retribution; from one life to the next, in birth after birth, one receives the rewards of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) and so forth, as numerous as those particles of dust.
The above has merely described the retributions experienced by that which is brought forth by raising the mind from afar.

The retribution is as described above. "Having heard" and so forth means that once one has reached the Buddha’s presence and personally heard the Dharma being preached, the retribution one receives will not be limited merely to the realms of humans and devas;
rather, one will certainly realize Bodhi in the future. Part Three:
The Tathāgata Speaks Verses to Reiterate the Teaching, in Two Sections. First: Accepting the Previous Promise to Speak.
Although I have previously explained the profound and subtle meaning of the four debts of gratitude, I shall now once again proclaim this same meaning for you.
Thus, he speaks in verse.
△ Second, the actual exposition of the verses has two parts. First, the praise of the Buddha’s noble virtues has three sections. First, the supreme virtues of the Honored One among men.
The Most Victorious Dharma King, the Great Holy Lord, is peerless among all humans and devas.
As a Son of Heaven among men, he attains sovereignty over humanity and becomes a king of men; as a Buddha, he attains sovereignty within the Dharma and becomes a Dharma King.

"Lord" (*jǔ*) signifies leadership and governance; "holy" (*shèng*) refers to the ultimate person; "great" (*dà*) is a term of supreme honor. Thus, [he is called] the "Great Holy Lord. These two—[the title and the description]—...

Those who ride upon the vehicles from the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the fourth fruit are all called noble ones (*ārya*). Among them, the *pratyekabuddha* is foremost; yet all are but small noble ones.
In the Mahāyāna, those from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the stage of *samāpatti-bodhi* (equal enlightenment) are all Mahāyāna noble ones.
However, the Buddha stands above even equal enlightenment; only the Buddha is the Great Noble One (*mahā-ārya*). Thus, the "Masters" [refer to] the small and great noble ones and sages.
All are his retinue; only the Buddha is the sovereign lord. "Most Victorious" (*zuishèng*) is a term for transcendence—the ultimate state of victory.
The subsequent phrase "equal in peer" (*lún*) refers to a match or counterpart. Throughout all the realms of humans and devas, there is none who can equal or rival the Buddha.
As it is said: "In heaven above and on earth below, I alone am supreme. △ Second.
The virtues of the marks and signs and supernormal powers:
endowed with all the marks and signs to adorn the body, the ocean of wisdom is like space, immeasurable; the practices for the benefit of self and others are all perfected;
your fame is heard throughout all lands; you have forever severed the afflictions along with their residual habitual tendencies; you skillfully maintain secret conduct and provide protection.
With all faculties perfected and the one hundred and forty kinds of unique qualities complete, the vast ocean of merit is entirely fulfilled;

endowed with all samādhis and supernormal powers, he constantly sports in the palace of the eight masteries. Among the humans, devas, and non-Buddhists of the ten directions, there is none who can challenge the Teacher, the Subduer.
The first phrase is easy to understand. The second phrase praises the Buddha’s two wisdoms—expedient and ultimate—which are as profoundly deep as the ocean and as immeasurable as space;

this explains the meaning of his previously mentioned "supreme and peerless" nature. The two phrases concerning self and others refer to the manifestation of causal virtues through the fruition [of Buddhahood].
Because he benefits both himself and others, his virtues are honored and his fruition is perfected; thus, throughout the lands of the ten directions...
The people heard his name and revered him; they looked up to his virtue and took refuge in him. Who would not follow his transformation?

The first line praises the virtue of benefiting both self and others. "Forever severing" (永斷) refers to the next two phrases, which praise the virtue of abandoning faults and maintaining protection. "Forever severing" (永斷) in the single phrase [of the next line] refers to the exhaustion of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*).

This is the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). As for "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*): although the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) and seeds have been exhausted, what remains is the habitual tendency. It is like a vessel that once held poison; though the poison has been completely drained out, there still remains a residue.

Wash it again with water. Although the dregs have been removed, the odor has not yet vanished. Here, the jar represents the human body; the poison represents active afflictions (*kleśa*); and the fine residue is like the seeds [of these afflictions]. One must eliminate them further through profound wisdom.

Yet, although the seeds have been removed, the residual perfuming (*vāsanā*) is not yet exhausted, just as the odor within the jar has not yet disappeared. In Arhats, the seeds and manifestations of the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) are both exhausted, yet residual habits (*vāsanā*) still remain—such as the anger of Śāriputra or the pride of Piṅgala.

Only in the Buddha are the seeds and manifestations of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*) both exhausted, and the residual habits also eliminated; therefore, he attains ultimate Buddhahood. "Skillfully upholding even a single phrase" reveals the upholding of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*). [This is] the esoteric [meaning].

Regarding "conduct" (caryā): it refers to the Buddha’s three secrets (*triguhyaka*). "Secret" means profound, mysterious, and unfathomable; "conduct" means acting with mastery according to the capacities of beings. First is the secret of body (*kāyaguhyaka*):
among all humans and devas, what is perceived differs according to their individual capacities. Some see a large body, some see a small body; some perceive him as compassionate, others as majestic;

some perceive him as virtuous, others as non-virtuous, and so forth. Second is the secret of speech (*vāgguhyaka*): from a single sound, he speaks out in ways that reach both the distant and the near.

"Hearing together" (*sahāśravaṇa*) means that each understands according to their respective capacities, and so forth. "Secret of Intention" (*manomaya-guhya*) refers to the simultaneous illumination of both self and others, such as the unity of the provisional and the real, and so forth.
However, the Buddha’s three karmas (*trikarma*) are unknown to the nine realms; only the Buddha knows them himself, and thus they are called the "Three Mysteries.

Because of his wisdom and virtue, he protects them so they are not lost; hence, it is said he "skillfully maintains" them. Regarding "the various faculties" (*indriya*): they are called "various" because they are numerous.
The Way has its root; this refers to the roots of goodness accumulated through the three mysteries for the benefit of sentient beings. The character "good" (zen) runs through what follows:

namely, skillfully upholding the secret practices and skillfully guarding the sense faculties. Regarding the one hundred and forty kinds of unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), there is a heading but no explanation, and their numerical categories do not appear here.
However, since they are called "unique," they must be those attained by the Buddha alone. Only the Buddha and...

"Buddha" (Bhagavān) refers to ultimate realization and penetration, which is not shared with those of provisional or limited capacities; this is an exaltation of the Buddha’s unique, distinguished qualities.
The single phrase "vast and great" (*vipula*) extols the Buddha’s merit (*puṇya*); it is called "vast and great" because it accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and is all-pervasive.

It is "profound and unfathomable like the great ocean" because he cultivated merit during the causal stage and is fully endowed with it in the resultant stage; hence, it is called "perfectly complete. (3)
The phrase "Mysterious One Sentence" praises the essence and function [of the Buddha-nature]. Samādhi is the essence of the concentration of the nature;
supernatural powers (abhijñā) are the function of spiritual transformation. Since essence and function are not lacking, they are said to be "complete.

The phrase "Eight Sovereign Powers" praises the four virtues of Nirvāṇa. A palace is that which a king dwells in; it serves as a metaphor for the dharma-nature of Nirvāṇa, which constitutes the eight sovereign powers.
This is that upon which I rely and in which I dwell. Being by nature unstained and unclouded is the virtue of purity; possessing the eight masteries is the virtue of selfhood (*ātman*);

"self" carries the meaning of mastery, as well as the two characters for permanence and bliss. Thus, all four virtues are fully realized. In summary, it is said that there is the Great Samādhi and Great Supernatural Power and Wisdom;
therefore, one is able to manifest according to the capacities of beings. Since essence and function do not lose their integrity, [the Buddha] is able to appear in various forms.
It is said that all are fully possessed. There are eight meanings of sovereignty: first, the ability to manifest a single body as infinite bodies;
second, manifesting a body the size of a single atom filling the great trichiliocosm; third, the great body rising lightly and traveling afar;
fourth, manifesting in infinite forms while always dwelling in a single land; fifth, the mutual functioning of the sense faculties; sixth, attaining all dharmas without the notion of dharmas.
Seventh, expounding the meaning of a single verse for immeasurable eons; eighth, the body pervades all places like space—these are the eight.

"Constantly sporting in joy" refers to the power of mastery (*vaśitā*). Since it is called "mastery," it signifies true play (*vihāra*), wherein one enjoys the bliss of the Dharma, remaining indestructible throughout eternal kalpas;
this constitutes the two virtues of permanence and bliss. [The following two lines] begin with "the ten directions."
This phrase praises the virtue of the Buddha’s transcendent wisdom and eloquence. It means that because the Buddha possesses supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he subdues all Māras;

because he possesses great eloquence (*pratibhāna*), he refutes all non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthika*); and because he possesses skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), he transforms and benefits humans and devas.
Therefore, among all humans, devas, non-Buddhists, and celestial Māras, who would dare to challenge the Buddha in debate? He is the Teacher who Tames and Guides.
"Buddha" is a title for one who can harmonize and guide humans and devas, preside over ordinary beings and sages, and serve as a model for all.
△ Third, the virtue of the wisdom and eloquence in preaching the Dharma:
His golden mouth can proclaim unimpeded eloquence; even without anyone to question him, he speaks spontaneously, like the ocean tide that arrives at its appointed time.
It is lost. Furthermore, just as the celestial drum accords with the will of the gods, such sovereignty belongs only to the Buddha;

it does not belong to those with the five supernatural powers, nor to sages, Māras, or Brahmās. Through the cultivation of vows over inconceivable oceans of kalpas, one realizes such great supernormal powers.
Entering the chamber of the great tranquility of samādhi, I observe the faculties, medicines, and diseases of all beings.
The Buddha possesses four kinds of eloquence (*pratibhāna*). Following the Dharma and its meaning, it flows like a cascading torrent of water without any obstruction;

hence it is called "unimpeded eloquence" (*asaṅga-pratibhāna*). Regarding "speaking spontaneously without being questioned": because the Buddha is able to discern the capacities of sentient beings, he speaks whenever it is appropriate to do so.
There is no need for formal inquiry; yet, if it were not appropriate to speak, even a question would be improper. This simply reveals the Buddha’s knowledge of the capacities and timing [of beings].

As in the passage below, this is a metaphor for the sovereign power of the Buddha’s wisdom, correctly explaining unimpeded eloquence (*anāvaraṇa-pratibhāna*): because there is a stimulus, there is a response.

The first two lines, "Like the ocean tide" and "Preaching the Dharma without partiality," are like the celestial drum (which sounds spontaneously without being struck, able to express the meaning of the Dharma in an inconceivable manner, serving as a metaphor for the Buddha’s impartial preaching of the Dharma;

yet, since the celestial drum accords with the will of heaven, the Buddha-Dharma must likewise accord with the capacity and resonance of sentient beings). These two lines conclude that these qualities belong inherently to the Buddha.

The next two lines, "Inconceivable," and so forth, reveal the source and development of his penetrating wisdom. The final two lines, "I enter," and so forth, eulogize his observation of the capacities of sentient beings.
He expounds the Dharma like a skilled physician treating an illness. "The chamber of great tranquility" (*mahāśānti-gṛha*): "great tranquility" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
