Wisdom abides by relying upon concentration, just as a person enters a room. *Samādhi* is the name for concentration; "great tranquility" is the definition of concentration.

The various faculties refer to the differences in the roots of goodness planted by sentient beings in the past, such as those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*). "Illness" is a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*); "medicine" is a metaphor for [wisdom].
Regarding meditative concentration and wisdom: illness is that which is to be treated, and medicine is that which treats it. Because illnesses vary in depth and severity, medicines likewise differ.
One must observe the color of the illness and examine its underlying pulse patterns so that it may be cured with a single dose. The Buddha is also like this;
observing sentient beings, he sees that their delusions vary in thickness and their wisdom varies in depth, and thus he teaches methods suited to their specific needs to bring them liberation.
If one practices that way, one can suddenly sever the afflictions and suddenly transcend birth and death, just as a disease is cured by taking medicine.
△ Second, the verse reiterates the preceding text in two parts. First, the verse reiterates the Buddha’s discourse on the cultivation of the mind-ground.
Having emerged from meditative concentration, he offered praise to the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The first four characters of the verse describe arising calmly from samādhi; "emerging" means to arise.

While the prose is detailed, the verse provides only a brief summary. This is because the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground is the method universally cultivated by all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The reason for this praise is explained according to the long prose section in two fascicles. △ Second, the verse on the arousal of the four debts of gratitude that ought to be repaid.
Part one: the verse on the elder’s disparagement of the great and seeking of the small.
At that time, the various elders withdrew from their great resolve and took pleasure in dwelling in the self-benefiting practices of the two vehicles.
The interpretation is as explained in the long prose. △ Second, the verse on the Tathāgata’s extensive praise of the four debts of gratitude has two parts.
First, the verse on the profundity of the Buddha’s wisdom has two parts. First, the verse on the general indication of the Buddha’s wisdom as its source.
I have opened the teaching of great wisdom and skillful means to lead [beings] into the three gates of liberation through emptiness.
This clarifies that the Tathāgata reveals the provisional by means of the real. "Wisdom" refers to provisional wisdom; "skillful means" refers to provisional teaching.

By relying on this provisional teaching, one is led into the gates of the three emptinesses. The provisional teaching—namely, the extensive praise of the four debts of gratitude—is that which serves as the means of guidance.

The three liberations of emptiness are the path that leads one in. One should know that these liberations share the same names as the three gates of liberation of the two vehicles, yet their meanings differ.
Since they are called the "three emptinesses," they must refer to the simultaneous emptiness of both the self and phenomena.

Emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*) is the nirvāṇa realized by severing the afflictions of clinging to a self. Emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is the nirvāṇa realized by severing the afflictions of clinging to phenomena.

Emptiness of both is the supreme nirvāṇa realized by abandoning the cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa), which involves neither clinging to persons nor phenomena nor even adhering to the principle of emptiness itself.
These "gates" serve as the means for reaching the path; that is, by means of these three types of emptiness.
The gateway through which one enters unsurpassed *nirvāṇa* and attains great liberation. △ Second, a specific verse on the fact that the provisional and small [vehicles] cannot fathom it:
"The intentions of the Tathāgata are immeasurable; only a Buddha can know the true secret. Even those with sharp faculties among the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*..."
Even all the Bodhisattvas who diligently seek awakening without regressing, deliberating together for twelve eons, would be unable to know even a small fraction of it.
Even if the wisdom of all ordinary and holy beings throughout the ten directions were bestowed upon a single person to make him wise,
such wise people, as numerous as a grove of bamboo, could not measure even a small fraction of it.

This is largely identical to the praise of wisdom in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. "Intention" (*abhiprāya*) refers to great wisdom; "secret" (*guhya*) refers to the teaching of skillful means (*upāya*).
This means that the Buddha’s intention is directed such that he can manifest three while being one, and can be one while manifesting three; to speak of three is itself to speak of one.
Reaching the point where both negation and affirmation are simultaneous—negating and affirming at once—such is the supreme and wondrous skillfulness of expedient means. Toward...
What people speak of is none other than the Buddha’s true secret gate; only the Buddha can know it, while all others are unable to fathom it.
"Those of dull faculties" below refers to those who cannot measure it; although *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* are sharp, they are still unable to do so.

These are still the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna). The non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas are the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). Over the long duration of twelve kalpas, they collectively attempted to fathom and measure it;
yet they not only failed to obtain even the full portion of its secrets, but were unable to know even a slight fraction thereof.
This is spoken merely in reference to the worthies and sages of their own lands; were one to further extend this to include those of the ten directions...
All the wisdom of every ordinary person and sage is bestowed upon a single individual, such that the wisdom of one person may become the incomparable wisdom of all throughout the ten directions.
Furthermore, such incomparable wise ones are not limited to just one;
they may be as numerous and immeasurable as a dense grove of bamboo. Even if all these many people were to exhaust their thoughts in attempting to measure it, [they could not fathom it].
One cannot even fathom a small portion of it; thus, the unfathomability of the Buddha’s wisdom may be known. Why is this so?
It is because the Buddha’s wisdom is provisional yet ultimate; it values direct realization rather than measurement.

Measurement belongs to the path of the conditioned mind, where the conscious intellect attempts to gauge and calculate; the more one thinks, the further one strays. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "It is not through thought..."

This is what can be understood through the discrimination of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). One should know that the Buddha taught the four debts of gratitude (*catvāra upakārāḥ*) as a timely medicine suited to the illness [of sentient beings].
This is intended for those who have regressed from the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), so that they may realize these four debts must be repaid;
they must resolve to generate the Great Mind, cultivate the Great Path, and perform Great Deeds. Only by benefiting oneself and others can one realize Bodhi. Thus it is possible...
Repaying kindness. How could such skillful means be measured? △ Second, the verse on the four debts of gratitude to be repaid, in two parts.
First, refuting the delusions and backsliding of ordinary fools regarding the objects of gratitude.
Ordinary worldlings lack the eye of wisdom; deluded regarding the source of their kindness, they lose the wondrous fruit.
The sentient beings of this degenerate age of five turbidities do not awaken to profound gratitude and constantly turn their backs on virtue.
This criticizes the human condition. Ordinary beings possess only the physical eye; when covered by it, they are obscured, and when touched by it, they are harmed.
They can only perceive sensory objects, thereby inducing consciousness to create karma. Lacking the wisdom-eye, they fail to see that the four debts of gratitude must be repaid.

There are two meanings of "sublime fruit" (*miāoguǒ*). First, it refers to being able to be filial toward one's parents; the retribution for this lies in the Brahma Heaven, and thus the Brahma Heaven is taken as the sublime fruit.
Second, it takes unsurpassed *bodhi* as the sublime fruit. This means that because of a lack of the eye of wisdom, one does not even know how to repay kindness;
how then could one perceive the Path? Without perceiving the Path, how could unsurpassed *bodhi* ever be attained? Therefore, [the former] is entirely rejected.
Below the section on the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), the reasons for delusion and confusion are set forth.

Because the obstacles of the five turbidities are heavy and evil karma flourishes, sentient beings in the world merely know how to discriminate based on sensory objects and create karma through greed and anger; thus, they do not awaken to profound kindness and constantly turn their backs on its virtue.
II. Explaining the four debts of gratitude (*catvāra upakāriṇaḥ*) to give rise to right view, in two parts: A. First, a general enumeration of the four debts of gratitude.
I shall reveal the four debts of gratitude to lead you into the path of enlightenment through right view.

The Buddha taught the four debts of gratitude primarily to induce the arising of right view; right view is the eye of wisdom, enlightenment is the fruit of Buddhahood, and the "path" refers to the way.
Thus, it means that the Buddha taught the four debts of gratitude in order to trigger the realization of right view and the attainment of enlightenment.

This is merely the path [to understanding]. △ Second, the detailed explanation of the four debts of gratitude has five parts. First, the debt of gratitude to one's parents has two parts. First, the general presentation of the names and meanings:
"The compassionate father and merciful mother have the grace of nurturing; all sons and daughters thereby attain peace and happiness. The grace of the compassionate father is as lofty as a mountain."

O King, the debt of gratitude owed to one's compassionate mother is as deep as the great ocean. Even if I were to remain in this world for an entire kalpa, I could not exhaustively describe the kindness of my compassionate mother.
What I have now spoken is but a small fraction, like a mosquito or a gadfly drinking from the great ocean.
He who first gives birth to me is called the father. He whose affectionate concern is deep is called the compassionate one (*maitrī*).
"Mother" (*mātr*) means nursing. A child emerges from the body; "nursing" (*payaḥ*) means to feed, and it also implies longing, for it is that which an infant longs for.
The grace of nurturing and raising will be explained in the subsequent text. Because parents possess the grace of providing reliance and support, sons and daughters obtain peace and security.
This is joy. The father’s kindness is like a mountain; the mother’s kindness is like the ocean—this speaks of their being immeasurable.
The two lines beginning with "If I" are words that transcend measure, for they directly manifest the gravity of their kindness.
The section beginning with "I now" states that while one generally cannot fully express it, this is merely a brief account of a small portion. This is like a single line of a metaphor, namely:
The kindness of one's parents is as vast as the ocean; it cannot be measured.
What I have described is but a small fraction, like a mosquito or a gadfly drinking from the ocean water—the waters of the great sea remain unmoved.
By this analogy, although I have spoken thus, the magnitude of their kindness remains untouched. Since even the World-Honored One, the Great Sage, has uttered these words, we know that...
The kindness of one's parents is truly immeasurable. How could the gentlemen of this world fail to practice filial piety?
△ Second, the extensive manifestation of profound kindness, in three parts: first, verses comparing coarse [benefits] with [immeasurable ones].
Suppose there were someone who, for the sake of merit, made offerings to pure-practicing brahmins, to ṛṣis possessing the five supernatural powers and mastery,
to great wise teachers and virtuous friends; providing them with halls and palaces made of the seven precious gems,
as well as chambers of gośīrṣa sandalwood, and medicinal decoctions that cure ten thousand ailments, all contained within vessels of gold and silver— thus making such offerings.
To perform worship for even a small portion of a single moment toward one’s compassionate mother—the field of great kindness—is superior to doing so three times a day for as many as a hundred kalpas;
its merit is boundless and immeasurable, such that no calculation, fraction, or analogy can compare to it.
This is entirely identical to the prose section of the two-volume [text]. As for the phrase "not as [great as]," it means "does not equal.
This refers to the brevity of the time—a single thought-moment—and the insignificance of the object—a small portion of an offering.

Yet, because the field of merit consisting of a compassionate mother’s kindness is immeasurable, even if a child offers a small portion for a single moment, the merit obtained is likewise immeasurable; this is due to the compassionate mother’s...

The weight of the field of gratitude (*kṣetra*) bestowed is thus profound. "Calculated divisions" (*gaṇanā-bhāga*) refer to the methods of calculation, the proportions from the smallest to the largest.
"Metaphorical divisions" (*upamāna-bhāga*) refer to the ultimate of similes and analogies.

"All are incomparable" means that even when one offers the world’s most precious treasures to a seer possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), or to teachers and virtuous friends, for a hundred eons—
"Venerable One, if one were to compare the merit obtained from even a small portion of a single moment's offering to one's mother with the merit obtained through calculation,
through the greatest of fractions, and through the most exhaustive of analogies,
that vast amount of merit would still not equal even a small fraction of the merit from offering to one's mother. Such words of exceeding measure truly manifest the nature of gratitude."

Profound and difficult to repay. Alas! For any who are children, even if they encounter this sacred scripture and exert all their strength to practice filial piety, they still cannot repay even a small fraction of this debt of gratitude.
△ Second, the verse on the detailed distinctions (eleven parts).
First, the verse on the grace prior to physical formation.
The compassionate mother of the world conceived her child; for ten months she carried the fetus, enduring constant suffering.

She had no attachment to the pleasures of the five senses, and likewise remained moderate in her food and drink at all times. Day and night she constantly harbored a heart of compassion, undergoing various hardships whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
"Pity" refers to compassion; "womb" refers to pregnancy. The five desires constitute the realm of pleasure for sentient beings.

To say one is "unattached" does not mean being entirely unattached, but rather that the mind's inclination toward sensual pleasure is slight. Because there is a child within the womb, one fears potential danger;
therefore, one is not deeply attached. As time passes, even if one encounters the finest food and drink, one does not crave them excessively.

Because of his grief for his son, he has been filled with such sorrow and compassion day and night [regarding the five desires—namely, wealth, beauty, fame, food, and sleep; or alternatively, form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch].
△ Second, a verse on the kindness of giving birth:
When the child in the womb is actually being born, it is as if sharp blades were being driven into one’s limbs and joints;

one is bewildered, unable to distinguish east from west, and suffers such pervasive bodily pain that it is unbearable. Some may even lose their lives because of these difficulties, leaving their six types of kinsmen and relatives all [in mourning].
Grief and distress. All such manifold sufferings arise from the child; the intensity of sorrow and lamentation cannot be fully expressed by words.
"Giving birth" (*dàn*) refers to the act of delivery. "The child in the womb" (*tāizàng zǐ*) refers to the child contained within the womb and abdomen.
"A hundred joints ache as if being dismembered by sharp blades"—this collectively describes the agony of approaching childbirth. Or, due to the labor...
There are many instances where [the mother] has died; consequently, the entire family wails in grief and the six relations are filled with sorrow—all because of their son.

It is for this reason that the Buddha describes it with such great effort, wishing for people to recognize the profound weight of the compassionate mother’s kindness, so that they may repay her with sincere filial piety.

(Regarding the "six relations": there are three types. One's own six relations are one's parents, brothers, and sisters. One's father's six relations are one's paternal uncles, brothers, sons, and grandsons. One's mother's six relations are one's maternal uncles, brothers, sons, and grandsons.)
Relatives (referring to paternal and maternal aunts, brothers, children, and grandchildren). △ Third, a verse on the kindness of nursing:
"If one recovers and the body finds peace and joy, it is like a poor man finding treasure—the joy is immeasurable.

Gazing upon their countenance, one never tires; the heart of compassionate concern is not abandoned for even a moment. The affection between mother and child is always thus; they do not leave each other's chests whether going out or coming in."
Before her breast, the mother’s milk is like a spring of nectar; it nourishes [the child] at the proper time and never fails.
This is largely the same as the prose section. △ Fourth, a verse on the grace of compassionate love.
The grace of her compassionate mindfulness is truly difficult to compare; the virtue of her nurturing care is likewise immeasurable.

The great earth is called the heaviest thing in the world, yet the heavy kindness of a compassionate mother exceeds it. Mount Sumeru is called the highest thing in the world, yet the height of a compassionate mother’s kindness exceeds it.
The swift wind alone is the swiftest in the world, yet raising her mind for a single thought-moment exceeds it.
The innate compassion of a mother, the thought of affectionate attachment, and the grace of nurturing and raising—truly, the great earth is insufficient to compare with their weight;
Mount Sumeru cannot match their height; even a violent wind can hardly serve as a metaphor for their swiftness.
That the violent wind is used as a metaphor for swiftness merely speaks to the intensity of her longing for her child. △ Fifth, a verse lamenting that her son has fallen.
If there are sentient beings who practice filial impiety, causing their mother to give rise even briefly to a heart of resentment or for even a slight portion of words of grievance to arise,
the child shall consequently encounter suffering and hardship; neither all the Buddhas nor the Vajra-devas, nor the secret dharmas of the ṛṣis,
can save them.

Regarding the preceding section on the metaphor of the fierce wind: this prose passage originally belongs to that section. However, if applied according to the specific wording, there are two meanings.
If it is used in the preceding section, it serves as a metaphor for the intensity of longing for one's child, as swift as a fierce wind.

If it is assigned to this section, it states that the fierce wind possesses the power to break and snap, serving as a metaphor for the power of the resentment held by parents. [This is] the secret method of the immortal.

This is a matter of skillful means. It is simply because you were unfilial that your parents harbored resentment; they suffered distress with every word [you spoke], and neither Buddhas nor immortals could save them.
It was not that they were unable to save them, but rather that Buddhas and immortals do not save rebellious children.

(Wang Si, a native of Linchuan County in the Song dynasty, was unfilial toward his father. His father, unable to endure his indignation, intended to go and lodge a complaint with the authorities. Wang Si took two hundred coins, overtook his father, and called out urgently, saying, "Use this as payment for paper and ink. He threw the money into his father’s bosom. Before his father had traveled half a *li*,)

A violent thunderstorm broke out. He hurriedly sought shelter in a house. When the rain ceased, he went outside and heard that his son had already been struck dead by lightning. He ran to look at him; the coin was found beneath the boy’s ribs, still attached to the flesh. Yet when he searched inside the boy’s chest, it was already gone.
This is proof of how the power of resentment leads to suffering). △ Sixth: A Verse on Receiving Blessings through Filial Piety.

If there are sons or daughters who rely upon their mother’s teachings, obeying her countenance and never opposing her, all calamities and misfortunes will be entirely eliminated, and they will be protected by the devas, always dwelling in peace and joy.
If one can obey and comply with a compassionate mother, such sons and daughters are by no means ordinary;
they are Great Compassionate Bodhisattvas manifesting in the human realm, demonstrating various skillful means for repaying kindness.
To receive and comply with [the teachings] without opposition is the way of a filial son.

As for being moved by the Buddha’s and the devas’ protective grace, it is intended to assist people in practicing filial piety. Regarding the four phrases that follow—"not ordinary" and "bodhisattva"—these are words of praise.

This was because there was nothing other than his exhortation for people to practice filial piety. (Zhao Juxian of the capital city: his father was ninety-one years old and his mother ninety-four. Both were stern and impatient by nature. Juxian and his wife served them with diligence and care;

their filial conduct was perfectly harmonious. Every evening they burned incense and prayed for their parents. The Three Shis deities reported this to the Heavenly Emperor, who dispatched the Great Flying Deity to supervise them daily. Seeing that their hearts were single-minded and their intentions focused, [the deity granted them protection].)

He bestowed upon his seven sons and three sons-in-law official positions; all attained the fruit of immortality in their previous lives. This may indeed be called a testimony of the extraordinary. △ Seventh: A verse comparing filial piety with grace.
If there were men or women who, in order to repay their mother’s kindness, practiced filial piety by cutting their own flesh and drawing their blood to provide for her constantly,
doing so for as many as one entire kalpa and diligently cultivating every aspect of the path of filiality— even then, they would still be unable to repay even a moment’s worth of her kindness.
The first five lines describe the pinnacle of filial conduct; the final line provides a comparative evaluation, stating that even this is insufficient to repay [the debt].
This expresses, to the utmost, how profound the kindness is and how difficult it is to repay. All of this follows the prose section. △ Eighth, a further verse on compassionate love and mindful pity.
For ten months dwelling within the womb, constantly sucking the root of the milk-vein and drinking the blood of the fetus;

from the time one is an infant until childhood, the breast-milk consumed amounts to more than a hundred *hu*. As for food, drink, medicine, and fine clothing, it is the constant rule that the child comes first and the mother second.
Even if a child is foolish and detested by others, the mother still regards them with compassionate affection and does not abandon them.
The first two lines refer to the kindness [shown] within the womb; the next two lines refer to the kindness of nursing.
An "infant" (*yinghai*) refers to the period of swaddling; a "child" (*tongzi*) refers to the time after leaving the swaddling clothes.

From the moment one emerges from the mother’s womb until leaving the swaddling clothes, the milk and food consumed amounts to more than a hundred *hu*. Alas! That the body itself emerges from the mother is like the birth of heaven and earth.
All things are again nurtured by their mothers, just as the dews and rains nourish the hundred varieties of excellence.

As for the sequence of providing food and clothing, the depth of their affectionate concern is such that even Mount Sumeru cannot compare to its height, and the vast void can hardly match its breadth.
Truly, when one wishes to repay such profound kindness, it is as boundless as the great heavens. 9. A Verse on Compassionate Love Leading to Rebirth in Heaven.
In the past, there was a woman who, while carrying her child, was crossing the Ganges River during a torrential flood. Because the water was so deep, she could not advance;

unable to abandon her child, she and he both drowned. By the power of the roots of goodness from this compassionate thought, at the end of her life she ascended to be born in the Brahma Heaven, where she long enjoyed the bliss of Brahma-samādhi.
There she encountered the Tathāgata and received a prophecy from the Buddha.
The first seven lines are identical to the prose section; only the eighth line is absent from the prose and is supplemented in the verse.
This means that because the mother’s kindness and compassion are profound and her heart is like the Buddha’s heart, she would rather sacrifice her own life than bear to abandon her child.
Such a person will not only enjoy bliss in the Brahma Heaven, but shall also encounter the Tathāgata, who will bestow upon them the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.
Since the mind is already identical to the Buddha, the mind itself is the Buddha; the mind itself acts as the Buddha.

Regarding the methods of cultivation and realization from the stage of cause to the stage of fruition, the Tathāgata has explained them and bestowed his prediction of enlightenment upon me. I personally recall and receive this teaching, upholding it firmly without forgetting.
This is the reception of the Buddha’s prediction. △ Ten verses extensively clarify ten virtues:
first, the Great Earth; second, the Ability to Produce; third, the Ability to Correctly Guide; fourth, Nurturing; fifth, Bestowing Wisdom; sixth, Adornment;
seventh, Peace and Security; eighth, Instruction; ninth, Admonition; tenth, Bestowing Karma. No further benefits exceed these.
The Mother’s Kindness.
Beyond the ten virtues, there are further aspects that cannot be fully expressed in words; these constitute the "remaining kindnesses. All should be understood according to the prose section.
△ Eleven: Comparing Poverty and Wealth.
What is the greatest wealth in the world? What is the greatest poverty in the world? When one’s mother is present in the home, that is the greatest wealth;
when the mother is no longer there, that is the greatest poverty. While the mother is alive, it is midday; when the compassionate mother passes away, it is sunset.
While the mother is alive, all things are complete; when the compassionate mother passes away, all is utterly empty and void.
The first two lines pose the inquiry; the next two lines (the third and fourth) explain it. The final two lines (the fifth and sixth) concern the grace of illuminating and presiding over all;
these should all be understood according to the prose (*gadya*). One should know that between the verse (*śloka*) and the prose, there is a mutual interplay of concealment and manifestation.

In the prose, the simile of the moon is present as a manifestation, while the absence of emptiness is concealed. In the verse, the absence of the moon simile is concealed, while [the presence of] perfection and... [is manifested].

"Empty and void" is used to illustrate this: when the mother is present in the hall, she manages the family estate so that it does not waste away, and she disciplines the household members so that they do not become estranged;
therefore, it is called "complete. When the mother passes away, one gains the upper hand for oneself;
wealth and goods may then be dissipated, and family members may become alienated; therefore, it is called "empty and void. Nevertheless, this is still...
A Brief Discussion. According to principle, parents are the heaven and earth for their descendants. Not only can they give birth, but they can also provide shelter and support.
If they were absent for even a single day, would it not be the case that all things would have nothing to rely upon?
Thus, for a child who has no parents, it is like the myriad things having no heaven and earth; their eyes do not behold the kin who gave them life.
Their ears do not hear the words of my instruction; having no reliance and no support, they are empty and void. △ Third, the verse concluding the exhortation to practice filial piety, in four parts:
first, the direct exhortation to practice filial piety.
All good sons of the world, the kindness of one's parents is as heavy as a mountain; one should always keep filial piety and respect in one’s heart.

To know gratitude and repay that kindness is the path of the sages. One should serve them with delicious food, not sparing even body or life, never for a single thought failing in the care of their physical needs.
Yet, when one's parents suddenly pass away, though one wishes to repay their kindness, it is truly beyond reach.
The first phrase is the Buddha’s summons to the assembly present before him, while also encompassing all sentient beings of future worlds;
though he addresses "men," this likewise includes women. The second phrase is intended to awaken them.

The two characters for "heavy kindness" (*ēnzhòng*) should follow the word "parents" to demonstrate that the parents' kindness is as immense as a mountain or a hill. This should be placed immediately below.

These are the words of the Buddha’s exhortation and instruction. He states that since the kindness of one's parents is as heavy as a mountain, a child ought to be profoundly sincere, attending to them morning and evening and serving them with bowed body; this is what is naturally right, hence it is said "one should.

"Filial" (*xiao*) refers to performing good service, being in accord with the Way and not contravening the principles of human relations. "Reverent" (*jing*) means not daring to be disrespectful or negligent. Thus says the text.
It is said: "Even dogs and horses can be provided with nourishment; how then can they be distinguished from [human] children if there is no reverence?

Therefore, one must certainly be reverent in order to fully fulfill the way of a filial son. Furthermore, he instructed that this should always be kept in mind, meaning it must not be forgotten for even a single moment, whether in wind or rain, or in leisure or busyness.
To practice in this manner is to recognize kindness and repay it; this is—
It is subsumed within the Noble Path. Indeed, among the great filial piety of the Confucians, none surpasses that of Shun;
Shun is a sage. Among the great filial piety of the Buddhists, none surpasses that of the Buddha; the Buddha is a sage. As the Sūtra says: "The Great Filial One is Śākyamuni.
"Delicious flavors" refers to exquisite tastes, namely the food and drink one offers. "Not sparing body or life" means that a person—

It is not that you do not love your own body; it is because there are parents who are worthy of reverence. Even if it requires driving a carriage or performing manual labor, or even if it means losing your life and perishing in body, you would not dare to decline.
"Never falling short" (*wei xia*) means to be deficient or lacking. "A single thought-moment" (*yi nian*) refers to the brevity of time.
As for "appearance" (*se*), there are two meanings: first, observing the countenance of one's parents, such as their joyful expression.
The child should rejoice in this, reflecting that they have served with propriety.

If the parent’s countenance shows signs of illness or anger, the child should feel fearful and remain deeply vigilant, considering that they have failed to serve them well. "Nourishment" refers to the delicious foods provided;
as for the second, the quality of what is served, one should select the finest items to offer to the parents and keep the coarse ones for oneself.

"Never having done so" (*mùzēng*) means "never having failed to do so. This refers to the ancient sages and former worthies who served their two parents with filial care and nourishment appropriate to their needs;
they kept this in mind at all times, never for a single thought-moment falling short. These two phrases serve as an even greater exhortation:
it means that among those born into this world, there is none who attains longevity or immortality. [Yet] one's current parents are still living.
Hall. If one does not serve with careful diligence, should an unforeseen event occur and the time of sudden death arrive, one will wish to repay [one's parents], yet it will truly be too late.
"Sudden death" refers to dying unexpectedly. △ Second, citing oneself to exhort filial piety, in two parts.
First, the actual citation of one's own experience, in three parts. First, practicing cultivation for the sake of one's mother.

In the past, the Buddha practiced for the sake of his compassionate mother, thereby attaining a body of golden hue adorned with the marks and signs of excellence. His fame is vast and pervasive throughout the ten directions;

all humans and devas bow their heads in reverence, and both humans and non-humans pay him homage. This is because he has personally repaid the kindness of his mother through the fruits of his former deeds.
The term "former" does not refer exclusively to this present life; it generally refers to many past lives as well.

To say that one must practice cultivation specifically for the sake of one's mother refers to the filial piety of a Buddha, which is not the same as the filial piety practiced by worldly people. As for the filial piety of worldly people:
It is not that there is nothing in the present life; to bring peace and happiness to the bodies of one’s parents is considered appropriate.
Yet, if this cannot support their spirits or aid them on the Path, such filial piety is insufficient to be called "great filial piety.

If, however, one practices the Way until enlightenment is attained, one not only frees oneself from suffering but also enables one’s parents to leave suffering behind; one not only achieves the Way for oneself but also enables one’s parents to achieve the Way. Therefore it is said:
To practice cultivation as one’s compassionate mother is what constitutes true great filial piety. "Moved to receive... and so forth clarifies that this is a retribution for filial piety.

That is to say, by raising a single thought and practicing cultivation as a mother, one subsequently moves [the Buddhas] to manifest marks and signs, a golden complexion, a name renowned everywhere, and offerings from humans and devas.
Compared to filial piety in the human world, how does this measure up? This concludes with the phrase "due to conditions" (zìyuán), which refers to conditions.
This is due to such conditions. "I myself" refers to from the very first moment of generating the aspiration for enlightenment.

It means that since the distant past, I have cultivated various practices through a single thought of aspiration in order to repay the kindness of my compassionate parents. It is because of these conditions that I have now attained retributions such as a golden complexion.
△ Second, preaching the Dharma for his mother.
I ascended to the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and for three months preached the True Dharma to my mother.
Seven days after the birth of the Buddha, Queen Māyā passed away; her spirit was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. When the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, [I descended].

Reflecting on his mother’s profound kindness, he ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and preached the Dharma for three months, desiring that his mother hear the teaching and attain a high realization, thereby liberating herself from birth and death.

(Although born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, compared to the human realm, its joy and longevity still do not exempt one from the birth-and-death of the segmented nature; when the retribution is exhausted, one falls back again.
Therefore, the Buddha taught the supramundane Dharma, which is called the True Dharma, so as to cause her to be forever liberated. △ Third, the Mother realizes non-arising.
I cause my mother to hear the Dharma and return to the Right Path, awakening to the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) so that she never regresses.
All this is done to repay her compassionate kindness; yet, though the repayment is profound, it remains insufficient.

Those with the capacity for the Mahāyāna, upon hearing the true Dharma of the Mahāyāna once, awaken to and enter the dharma of non-arising and the path of true permanence, never regressing thereafter;
this is like attaining the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*).

Regarding the latter two phrases, it is said that although the Mother has obtained benefit, the Buddha’s mind is not yet satisfied, because her kindness is so profound that it is difficult to repay. Now, as for what the Buddha...
He preached the Dharma, causing his mother to leave behind birth and death and attain the Noble Path. Yet, even this was not yet sufficient;
how then do the gentlemen of the world compare themselves to the Buddha? △ Second, he additionally cites Maudgalyāyana.
Maudgalyāyana, foremost in supernatural powers, had already severed all afflictions of the three realms.

Using his supernormal power, he observed his compassionate mother and saw that she was suffering among the hungry ghosts. Maudgalyāyana went in person to repay his mother’s kindness, rescuing his compassionate parent from her suffering and causing her to be reborn among the hosts of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, where they dwelt together in pleasure within a celestial palace.
Maudgalyāyana was an Arhat endowed with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). Among the disciples of the Buddha, all those of the rank of Arhat or above possess such powers;

this Venerable One is the foremost among them, and is therefore called "the first. The afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms do not exceed the two delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*).
That which involves conceptual discrimination is called "view"; it is a coarse delusion, referring to [afflictions] arising from false teachings and false teachers.
This does not accord with correct principle; it is a false and erroneous discrimination. Altogether, these constitute the eighty-eight *anuśayas* (proclivities).
The term *anuśaya* carries the meaning of "driving and employing"; they are able to drive and employ all sentient beings, causing them to transmigrate through birth and death.

As for what is called "delusion of views" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), it refers to the various discriminations arising when the faculty of mind (*manas*) encounters mental objects (*dharmas*). Therefore, because they consist of discrimination, they are termed "views. There are ten kinds of such deluded thoughts.

1. The view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). (This refers to the false calculation that the five aggregates—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are one's own body. 2. The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). (Based upon the view of a self-body, calculating either annihilation or permanence.)

1. Adherence to one extreme; hence it is called a "view of extremes. 2. View-grasping (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*): This refers to mistakenly perceiving what is not truly supreme as *nirvāṇa*, thereby giving rise to a mind of attachment and grasping.

3. Precept-and-vow-grasping (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): This refers to mistakenly regarding what is not a true precept as a precept, and adopting it as a practice for progress. 4. False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*): This refers to failing to understand due to ignorance, and thus apprehending reality with a distorted mind. 5. Greed (*rāga*): This refers to the insatiable drawing toward and grasping of various objects of desire. 6. Hatred (*pratigha*):

This refers to the arousal of various forms of anger toward objects that oppose one's feelings. 7. Delusion (*moha*): This refers to being confused and lacking understanding regarding all phenomena and principles. 8. Pride (*māna*): [This refers to] relying on oneself...
Because one treats others with contempt due to [one's] talent, virtue, wealth, or status; (10) doubt (*vicikitsā*), which means the deluded mind deviates from principle and wavers indecisively.

These ten proclivities (*anuśaya*), when traversing the four truths of the three realms, differ in their increase and decrease, collectively forming eighty-eight proclivities. Specifically, under the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) in the desire realm...

The ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) are fully present [in the truth of suffering]. Under the two truths of origination (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*), there are seven proclivities each, excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

(These three proclivities are established based on the truth of suffering; since they do not exist under the truths of origination and cessation, they are excluded. Under the truth of the path (*mārga*), there are eight proclivities, excluding the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes.

(These two proclivities also arise based on the truth of suffering; since the truth of the path is devoid of suffering, they are excluded. Thus, the four truths together comprise thirty-two [proclivities].
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). In the four truths of the form realm and the formless realm, they are all as in the desire realm;
furthermore, from each truth, one instance of hatred (*pratigha*) is excluded. Thus, there are twenty-eight latent dispositions in one realm, and fifty-six when the two realms are combined.
Together with the thirty-two latent dispositions of the desire realm, they total eighty-eight in number. As the verse says: "Suffering..."

In the lower realm (*kāmadhātu*), all [afflictions] are present. In the [realms of] origination and cessation (*samudaya* and *nirodha-satya*), three each are excluded. Weeping, he hurried back to inform the Buddha, recounting everything in detail. The Buddha said, "The roots of your mother's transgressions are deeply entangled;

"On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when the *pravāraṇā* ceremony of the monastic community takes place, you should, for the sake of your parents of seven generations past as well as your parents of the present life, [offer to the assembly of monks in the ten directions]."

For those in the midst of calamity and distress, one should prepare food of a hundred flavors and the five fruits, vessels for drawing and pouring water, fragrant oil, lamps and candles, couches, mats, and bedding—

Inheriting the Way of the multitude of sages, his virtue is vast and boundless. He causes his parents of the present life to enjoy blessings and happiness for a hundred years;

This is the source and sequence of Maudgalyāyana’s salvation of his kin. △ Third: A Comparison of the Two Merits.
One should know that the kindness of one's parents is the deepest; all Buddhas and sages repay this virtue.

If a person makes offerings to the Buddha with a sincere heart, and another person diligently practices filial piety and support—there is no difference in the merit of these two individuals, and the rewards they receive throughout the three periods of time will likewise be inexhaustible.
This verse applies not only to Śākyamuni and Maudgalyāyana, but to all Buddhas and the noble ones of the Three Vehicles;
there are none who do not repay the kindness of their parents. If one were to compare their merits: suppose one person makes offerings to a Buddha and another person makes offerings to their parents.
The merit obtained by these two individuals would be equal and without difference. As for those who receive the retribution, they receive the reward of that merit.

Furthermore, there are two interpretations regarding the "three generations. First, the merit that is elicited does not terminate within a single lifetime, but extends through three generations, reaching even to infinity.

bestowing it upon one's descendants constitutes the second generation; together they form the three generations. There may even be more beyond this.

The merit is bequeathed to future generations; therefore, it is said to be "inexhaustible. △ Fourth, being cautious at the end and honoring the distant past. Part five: First, regarding how children fall into suffering.
People of the world commit various sins on behalf of their children, causing them to fall into the three miserable realms and suffer for a long time.
"To act for them" means to be single-mindedly desirous; it means to cherish them with affection. This refers to how, in the world, there is nothing parents will not do for their children.
Some commit every kind of transgression for the sake of their children's food and drink, such as cooking sheep and slaughtering livestock.

Others commit every kind of transgression for the sake of their children's clothing and bedding, such as raising silkworms and boiling cocoons. Still others commit all manner of evils for the sake of seeking fame and achievement for their children.
All grave offenses—such as harming others for one’s own benefit—are such that the preceding phrase indicates the cause and the subsequent phrase indicates the retribution.

This refers to those who know only to cherish their children, yet remain ignorant of the future retribution. The three miserable realms are as previously described. 2. The Child’s Delusion and Ignorance.

Section Two on Merit. First, it clarifies how the Golden Light removes suffering and brings about awakening.

The "arousing of the thought" constitutes the first phrase. It follows upon the preceding discussion regarding the causes and conditions for being unable to rescue one's parents. "You" refers to Jñānaprabha, as well as the wicked sons and others.

Relying upon and receiving the Buddha-dharma, you dedicate these merits to them—whether by prostrating to the Buddha and performing repentance, or by offering food in the *Lanpen* (Ullambana) ceremony, or by constructing Buddha images and stupas, or by reciting mantras and reading sutras.

"Benefit. "To pursue" (*zhui*) means to follow after. This refers to the fact that the souls of one's parents are so profound and obscure that ordinary people cannot see them;

One deeply receives the power of the Dharma, such that it can move the Buddha to emit golden light that shines downward upon the hells. The light...
This is the middle and lower [grade]. It is the Golden Light preaching the Dharma. He may preach on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, impurity, and so forth;
or he may preach on the Six Perfections of the Mahāyāna, the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, and so on.

As for "profound and wondrous voice," it means that within a single sound, many kinds of Dharma-gates are fully contained, such that according to what each being understands, there is individual awakening. "To cause" (令) means to enable; that is, the Dharma.
It is by the power [of the Buddhas] that they are so moved. "To give rise to the intention" (*cittotpāda*) is precisely "to give rise to the mind.

This means that once one has attained awakening, one will inevitably resolve to cultivate the mind—whether it be the mind of a *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*, or the mind of *bodhi*. Such a person is a filial son or daughter.

By cultivating various meritorious virtues, the repayment of kindness and the deliverance [of the parents] are as described above. (The Dharma-preacher of the *Golden Light Sūtra* manifests not only the great filial piety that moved the son, but also reveals the vastness of the Buddha’s compassion.
△ Second, clarifying that a single thought of repentance removes all transgressions.
"Recalling the sins committed throughout past lives, a single thought of repentance completely extinguishes them all.
This means that although the souls of one's parents may be in hell, by hearing the teaching of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, they suddenly come to know the sins committed during their past existences.
"Recalling" (*yǐ*) refers to the sense of suddenly bringing something to mind. "Throughout past lives" (*xī suǒ shēng*)...

At that time, even the transgressions will vanish; this is the meaning. The above has merely clarified how one deeply receives the superior power of the Buddha-dharma and is thus able to extinguish transgressions.

By reciting "Namo to the Buddhas of the Three Times," one shall be liberated from the body of suffering and hardship in the states of no-leisure, and be reborn among humans and devas to enjoy long-lasting bliss.

Having been extinguished from suffering and liberated from transgressions, one recognizes this as the Buddha’s power; therefore, one recites the Buddha’s name with the mouth, desiring to seek rebirth there.

This means to be suddenly liberated from suffering and hardship. "Without leisure" (*akṣaṇa*) refers to having no interval of respite while undergoing suffering; that is, being without interruption or rest, which is called the Avīci Hell.
This means that by receiving the compassionate salvation of the Buddha, one attains liberation from the body of suffering.
"Rebirth below" refers to rebirth according to one's vows. Human and celestial realms constitute the pleasures of the mundane world; furthermore, one is able to see the Buddha and hear [the Dharma].
The Dharma must certainly be practiced in accordance with the Dharma; one shall thereby attain Buddhahood in the future. Furthermore, it is the supreme bliss that transcends the world.
Or, for those who aspire to the pure lands of the ten directions and wish to be born by transformation within a lotus flower, their resolve shall likewise be fulfilled.

The Buddhas of the ten directions have awakened to and entered the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena) and serve as companions to the non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas.

To "study together" means to study the Buddha-dharma together. Since they are fellow students, they must necessarily exhort and remind one another so that ignorance is suddenly opened up and spiritual powers become sovereign.

Therefore, it says "attaining entry," and so forth. Filial piety:
these are all Bodhisattvas who, as sons and daughters, manifest among humanity through the power of their great vows. This is called truly repaying the kindness of one's parents.
You sentient beings, cultivate and learn this together.
This is what the Buddha called a filial son. Having extracted his parents from suffering, he further attains rebirth according to his vows and enters into Bodhi;

This is true requital of gratitude, and it serves as a model for the descendants of the human world. Therefore—
Appearing as men and women, the final line offers a solemn exhortation to practice and study. The two characters "you all" refer to the rebellious son and his retinue led by Jñānaprabha.

In this world, parents are one's kin. Without a father, one is not born; without a mother, one is not nurtured. Thus, one is entrusted to the mother’s womb;

for ten months the child is carried within her. When the years are complete and the months fulfilled, both mother and child emerge together. Upon birth, the infant falls onto the grass; parents nourish and raise them.
Lying upon a cradle, the child is held in their embrace; smiling yet unable to speak, they make soft, playful sounds when hungry.
When hungry, one requires food; it is not without a mother that one is fed. When thirsty, one requires drink; it is not without a mother that one is nursed.

When a child is hungry, they swallow what is bitter and spit out what is sweet, pushing away the dry and seeking the moist; it is not without a father that one is cherished, nor without a mother that one is nurtured.

A compassionate mother nourishes her child even at the cost of leaving behind a cart that blocks the way, and from within her ten fingernails, she consumes the impurities of her child. When the child drinks the mother’s milk, eight *hu* (bushels) are consumed.
Four *dou* [of grain]. Calculating and deliberating upon the mother’s kindness, it is as vast as the great heavens and has no limit. Alas, compassionate mother! How can it ever be repaid?

As for my coming and going to the neighboring households to the east and west, or to the wells, hearths, mortars, and mills, when I do not return home at the proper time, my mother suddenly feels her heart tremble with alarm.
As her two breasts flowed with milk, she immediately recognized her son; remembering me at home, she returned to her dwelling.

It is further said that when her son saw his mother approaching from afar, he would either lean against the carriage, shaking his head and wagging his rump, or else drag his belly along as he followed her.
"Alas, O Mother! For the sake of her child, the mother bends her body downward; she stretches out both hands and rubs away the dust. Alas, her mouth!

As she grew up, she was accompanied by friends; she combed her hair and smoothed her locks, desiring fine garments to cover her body.

As they grow old and their beauty fades, they become rife with fleas and lice; unable to sleep day or night, they sigh and lament longingly: "By what sin or past transgression was this life born?"
"This is unfilial. At times he would call out to her, staring with angry eyes and full of indignation, yet she never complied.

When her husband and children scolded her, she would lower her head and smile. And so on. The commentary says: Filial sons and virtuous grandsons certainly exist in this world, yet those who are unfilial are many, following the common stream of worldly custom.
Among a hundred people, there may be one whose mother does not act as described above, or one whose son does not act as described below.
There is not a single one. This is truly because, since beginningless time, they have been deluded regarding the truth and have clung to the false, acting with inverted views.
Since the root has become inverted, every branch and detail is likewise so. Because of the profound kindness of their parents, children often act in opposition to them.
Therefore, I cannot help but cite [these examples] so that people may understand them; they remain somewhat entangled in complications. I trust you will not weary of this prolixity.
The section on the "Enlightenment of Parents" is concluded. △ Second, the "Enlightenment of Sentient Beings," in three parts: first, the actual verse on their indebtedness.
Sentient beings transmigrate through the six realms like the wheel of a chariot, without beginning or end. From time to time, they become parents or children;
in life after life, they have mutual debts of kindness. To see them as no different from one's own parents is impossible without realizing noble wisdom.
All men have been one's fathers, and all women have been one's mothers.

"Sentient beings" refers to living creatures, because all such creatures possess consciousness and feeling. The analogy of "saṃsāra" to the six realms is used because all sentient beings revolve according to their karma:
those who perform wholesome deeds follow their wholesome karma and thus receive wholesome retributions in the heavens or among humans, like the upward rotation of a wheel;
those who perform unwholesome deeds follow their unwholesome karma and thus [fall into the lower realms].* *Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete at the end.*
In the hells and the three miserable realms, one undergoes evil retribution like the downward-turning of a chariot wheel.

When the evil retribution is exhausted and one encounters favorable conditions, one is reborn among humans or devas. When the good retribution is exhausted and an evil thought arises, one falls again into the three miserable realms. Alas!
Since beginningless time, if all sentient beings have not encountered the Buddha-dharma, or if they have encountered it but are deluded and do not believe or accept it, or...
There are those who believe and accept [the teachings] yet are unwilling to practice; or there are those who do practice, but are diligent in the morning and indolent by evening.

For those who have not yet realized the Way, even if they were to continue until the end of the future, there would be no time of cessation. Therefore, it is likened to a wheel, which has neither beginning nor end.
These two lines merely clarify the cycle of birth and death within the six realms; they have not yet spoken of the existence of [Nirvana].

"En" (gratitude) refers to the latter two lines, which clarify that beings are mutually parents and mutually children, from one lifetime to a hundred lifetimes, and from one world-age to a hundred world-ages.
Since there is already the debt of gratitude between father and son, how could there not be the affection between siblings?
Therefore, it is said: "mutually perceiving gratitude. The phrase "as if seeing" [the Buddha] is the teaching of the Buddha and our own single essence.
Contemplate them as equal, seeing all sentient beings as being like one's own parents, identical and without distinction.
Not realizing even a single phrase is what the Buddha laments. Since you have never yet realized the untainted noble wisdom (*anāsrava-āryajñāna*), you still harbor the delusion of causing abortions;
though they may change their heads and faces, and though they mutually possess kindness, it cannot be recognized by the common sentiments of the fleshly eye. All...
The final two lines are the Buddha’s most earnest exhortation that one must not make discriminations. One should universally regard all men and women as having been one's own parents;
within one's heart, one should reflect: "In birth after birth, there has never been a life I have not received from them.
Thus, it is only right that one should always maintain a mind of gratitude toward them. △ Second, the admonition not to harbor resentment or disdain.
How can one fail to repay the kindness of previous lives, yet instead give rise to heterodox thoughts that breed resentment and jealousy? One must always repay kindness and mutually benefit others;
one should not strike or revile them so as to cause resentment and aversion.
The two characters "How can" (如何) are words of reproach and lamentation. They state that sentient beings possess the delusion of falling into the aggregates (陰).
Although they have been their parents over many successive lifetimes and thus owe them a debt of gratitude, in the present life they have changed their heads and faces and do not recognize this;

therefore, they are unable to repay it. Furthermore, a single phrase arises stating that not only do they fail to repay it, but they even turn that kindness into enmity. This is because— [text truncated]
They may become harmonious, yet they may also harbor divergent thoughts, leading to resentment or the arising of jealousy. Therefore, the Buddha sighed in lamentation, saying, "How [can this be]?

This phrase is always intended as an exhortation, urging people to repay one another's kindness and benefit each other, so that they do not fail their past debts of gratitude. The phrase "should not" is a solemn admonition; whether in the home...

Regarding domestic servants: whether they be those who perform manual labor and exert physical strength, or fellow villagers and neighbors, or even guests from distant lands—since it has already been stated that one transmigrates through the six realms of existence, including even the species of camels and mules—one must not whip or beat them, nor must one insult or humiliate them.
Furthermore, one must not harbor resentment, malice, or contempt, but should always maintain the awareness of their kindness and strive to repay it.

how could I dare to give rise to anger? Alas! If the gentlemen of the world truly followed the words of the Buddha, there would be no matters of mutual strife or killing in this world, and all would enjoy eternal peace.
As for those people of the world who denounce the Buddha as a heretic, I— [do not...]
One knows this by attaining it. △ Third, exhorting one to make vows:
"If you wish to further cultivate the gates of merit and wisdom, you should make vows during the six periods of day and night.

May I, in birth after birth throughout immeasurable kalpas, attain the great supernormal power of the knowledge of past lives, so that I may know hundreds of thousands of past existences and mutually recognize one another."
My parents, who have cycled through the six realms and four modes of birth, may I always reach them in a single thought to preach the wondrous Dharma for them to abandon the causes of suffering,
so that they may constantly enjoy the bliss of humans and devas. May I inspire in them the firm aspiration for Bodhi and lead them to practice the gateway of the Bodhisattva’s six perfections,
forever severing the two kinds of causes for birth and death, and swiftly realizing the unsurpassed path of Nirvana.
The first two phrases mean: Having already received the Tathāgata’s instruction, how could one fail to recognize and repay that kindness?
The Buddha taught that if a person wishes to increase their cultivation of merit and wisdom, those who find the gateway to it must generate vows day and night to assist their resolve.
This is because the term "cultivation" (xiū) used here signifies "increase" (zēng), meaning to become more flourishing. That is to say, one cultivates merit from previous lives.
One cultivates wisdom. Having now been born into the human realm and further having faith in the Buddha-dharma, one cultivates again in this life;

thus, as cultivation progresses, it becomes increasingly superior. This is the fruit of increased merit and wisdom. A "gate" (mukha) is that which enables passage; by taking the cultivation of causes as the gate.
One realizes the fruit by means of the cause, just as a person must enter through a door before reaching the inner sanctum of a hall. The causes of merit consist of practices such as giving;
the causes of wisdom consist of listening to the teachings and investigating them. Following the phrase "day and night," this is a formal exhortation to make vows.

It is said that to practice without a vow leaves one with no destination, while to have a vow without practice leaves one with no foundation. Thus, one knows that to repay the debt of gratitude, one must certainly resolve to make vows.

"Vow" (praṇidhāna) means that although sentient beings have already received kindness in the past, they generally do not recognize it; therefore, one diligently cultivates merit and wisdom to seek its realization through vows.

Regarding the "six periods": for example, practicing the Way and making vows during the hour of Zi (11 PM–1 AM), resting in quiet meditation during the hour of Chou (1 AM–3 AM), and likewise during the hours of Yin and Mao, and so forth.

Throughout the vast duration of immeasurable kalpas, may I not fall into the delusion of the aggregates.

May I attain the wisdom of past lives—“past lives” being synonymous with “past destinies”—and the great supernormal powers, namely the six abhijñās, such as the celestial eye that perceives from afar and the celestial ear that hears from afar.
By means of these two subsequent lines, it is shown that through the attainment of the wisdom of past lives and the supernormal powers, one is able to know hundreds of thousands of births.
Within this cycle, beings act as parents to one another; they remember and do not forget, recognizing the kindness received.
"Circulating downward" refers to how this vehicle universally rescues those from suffering. "Huan" (環) means an iron ring; "xun" (循) means to revolve around.
This is a metaphor for the transmigration through the six realms, like an ant moving along a ring, circling back and forth without end. "Qu" (趣) means to head toward or incline towards.

Within the six realms, one undergoes birth repeatedly and death repeatedly; because the retributions of these six realms serve as the destinations one pursues, they are called the "six destinies" (*ṣadgati*).
Regarding the "four modes of birth": one undergoes birth within the four categories of womb, egg, moisture, and transformation;
therefore, they are called the "four births. "May I [go] below" means that once supernatural powers have been attained, one constantly arrives [there] in a single moment of thought.
Among those within the six realms of existence and four modes of birth, he expounds teachings suited to their individual capacities; hence it is called the "Wondrous Dharma.

As for "leaving behind the causes of suffering," once they have heard the Dharma, they reform their evil ways and cultivate goodness, refraining from committing the karmic deeds of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying.
This is the cause for severing suffering. Since one has already departed from the causes of suffering, one will certainly not fall into the bitter fruits of the three miserable realms.
This phrase merely speaks of departing from suffering; the subsequent phrase then speaks of attaining happiness. However, having heard the sublime Dharma, one must practice various virtues.

It serves as the cause for the happiness of humans and devas. By relying on this cause, one experiences the fruit, thereby attaining the wholesome fruits of birth among humans and devas and enjoying their pleasures.
"Exhorting and inspiring" (in the following section) means encouraging others to realize the Way. "Arousing the vow for Bodhicitta" refers to the truth of the mind.
"Firmly established" refers to the decisiveness of one's resolve; it is by means of this that one practices the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s Six Perfections. [End of previous section]

The first four stages cultivate merit, while the final two stages cultivate wisdom. Through these two stages of meditative concentration and wisdom, one eternally severs the afflictions of the two attachments and eternally transcends the two kinds of birth-and-death.
The cause consists of the two attachments to self and phenomena; Nirvana is the fruit of the complete severance without remainder;
and the Unsurpassed Way is the fruit of Bodhi-wisdom. Because of the sincerity of such exhortation, success is swiftly achieved.
Therefore it is said: "The signs of illness, etc. This, moreover, is an exhortation from among humans and devas to arouse the aspiration for enlightenment and cultivate the path to attain Buddhahood.
The way to repay this kindness can be called ultimate and exhaustive. For indeed, sentient beings possess great kindness toward us, yet people do not perceive it;
how then could they repay it? What is truly important is to make vows to seek spiritual penetration and to receive wisdom in order to preach the Dharma.

To cause those sentient beings to realize the Way based upon these words is to repay their kindness. (Regarding the two kinds of birth and death: they are the birth and death of分段 [fen-duan, segmented] for ordinary worldlings.)
The section on the kindness of sentient beings above the two vehicles’ *pariṇāmanika-cyuti* (death through transformation) is concluded. △ Third, the kindness of kings has three parts.
First, a verse summarizing their supreme virtues:
All kings throughout the ten directions, who transform people through the True Dharma, are holy sovereigns. The merit and virtue of these kings is supreme.
"Victorious. One who possesses mastery over their actions is called a "deva" (heavenly being).
While the prose version refers only to the king of a country, the verse encompasses all [kings] throughout the ten directions; thus, the former is concise while the latter is detailed.
This means that if the merit and sovereign power of a single king are such as this, the same applies to all kings. The first line establishes the subject, while the second line clarifies it.
"En" (Gratitude). Benevolence, righteousness, and moral virtue constitute the True Dharma (*saddharma*). To transform people through benevolence and righteousness is to be a sagely sovereign.
Regarding the second and third lines: it means that having transformed people through the True Dharma, the resulting merit and virtue are most supreme and sovereign;
thus, such a ruler may be called a "Heaven among men. Why? Because the king possesses the Way, he acts according to the Way; because he possesses virtue, he [acts] with virtue.

Employing the people according to the seasons, the fundamental social order remains undisturbed, and the hearts of the people find peace. Naturally, Heaven assists them and the people turn toward them;
they feel gratitude as if toward Heaven itself. △ Second, the verse separately clarifying the supreme virtues in eleven parts: first, the verse on the various heavens obtaining protection.

The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three and other celestial beings constantly employ their power of merit to assist the king’s governance; the various devas protect him as if he were their only son.
It is for this reason that he is entitled to the name "Son of Heaven."
The first two lines correspond to the prose explanation; the third and fourth lines are not present in the prose but are supplemented here in the verse.

The various devas protect the king as a father protects his son, because the king’s mind accords with the mind of the heavens; thus, like father and son being of one body, he is called a "Son of Heaven.
△ Second, the verse on the primary metaphor for the nature of the state.
The world takes the king as its foundation; all the people rely upon him.

Just as all dwellings in the world are established with pillars as their foundation, so the king transforms the people through the True Dharma (*saddharma*), just as the Great Brahmā King gives birth to all things.
If the king practices what is contrary to the Dharma and lacks governance, he is like King Yama, who destroys the world. Whatever the king permits or receives...
A person of wicked and depraved intent is no different from an elephant trampling a lotus pond. Just as the Sun Deity illuminates the world, so too does the king transform the world.
Although the sunlight does not shine during the night, it enables sentient beings to obtain peace and happiness.
The first two lines constitute the *dharma* (the subject), while the subsequent lines are all metaphors. The house represents the kingdom; the pillar-base represents the king.
This means that just as a room cannot stand without pillars, so too the people have no support without a king. The king is described by two lines:

having instructed the people with the True Dharma (*saddharma*), the people emulate his conduct and give rise to roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). This is likened to how the Brahmā King is able to bring forth the myriad things.
"Things. The Brahma King is likened to the king; the myriad things are likened to the roots of goodness of the myriad people.
This says that when the superior acts and the inferior emulates, the world is at peace. The following four lines concerning the king serve as a counter-example:
it means that if the king lacks the Way and practices what is unlawful, losing his governance of the state and failing in principle, he is like King Yama crushing [the realm].

It threatens human life and prevents people from living long; therefore, it is said that it "extinguishes the world. "Unrighteousness" (fǎ) refers to the disordering of the social order and the loss of ethical principles;
it denotes the failure of the royal way to be upright. The first two lines describe the lack of the Way in one's own conduct.
Statecraft has already declined. The following two lines further allow the treacherous and wicked to assist in governing the state, causing the regular order of things to become increasingly chaotic.

Unable to avoid mutual deception between superiors and subordinates, the fundamental integrity of the state falls into great disorder. This is like Wang Mang usurping the throne or Cao Cao deceiving the sovereign;

all such instances arise because the ruler loses the grand principle of governance, allowing depraved persons to enter. The phrase "an elephant treading" is a metaphor for chaos, referring to the lotus.
Within the flower pond, there are jade lotus roots below and blooming lotuses above. The azure waves are clear and still, and their fragrant scent assails the senses.

If a mad elephant enters the pond, trampling and rushing about, it is a pity that both the flowers and the roots are destroyed. This is a metaphor for how a treacherous and wicked person throws a state into chaos;
it is just like this. Furthermore, the four lines concerning "the sun" serve as a metaphor for the grace of the Sage King’s illuminating presence.

Just as the sun shines upon the vast heavens, able to dispel the darkness of the world and enable all people under heaven to accomplish their various tasks, so too is it with the ruler who oversees the realm.
He illuminates and inspects from time to time, ensuring that the wicked do not enter and that no evils are practiced.
Thus, the world enjoys peace and the myriad people delight in their vocations. Therefore, it is said that the king’s transformation of the world is also like this.
This refers to the two lines following "Sunlight. They serve as a metaphor for the appropriateness of movement and stillness.

This means that when the Son of Heaven occasionally tours and inspects the realm, it is like the sun illuminating the day. When he does not tour at other times, it is like the sunlight not shining during the night;
yet people still obtain peaceful sleep and enjoy themselves. Altogether, this metaphorizes a ruler who possesses the Way, under whom the world is secure and tranquil.
...Thus. △ Third, the verse on the auspicious responses to the transformative power of virtue:
When a king governs the world through unrighteousness, all his subjects have no refuge. Yet, whatever terrors exist in the world cannot arise due to the power of the king’s merit.
One should know that the peace and happiness achieved by the people are the result of the king’s merit.
[It reaches] all that exists in the world. All the most excellent and wondrous flowers in the world bloom by the power of the king’s merit.
All the wondrous gardens and groves in the world flourish through the power of the king’s merit. All the medicinal herbs in the world cure various ailments by the power of the king’s merit.
All the hundred grains and crops in the world bear fruit through the power of the king’s merit. [In the world...]
The people enjoy abundance and happiness; by the power of the king’s merit, this occurs spontaneously and constantly.
The first two lines serve as a metaphor for a ruler who has lost the way of government.

Although these originally constitute the concluding passage for the previous section on the failure of governance, they are placed here because they are presented in contrast to the "King of Merit. Since he does not transform the world through the Dharma, the people have no refuge.

By manifesting the True Dharma to transform the world, the people have something upon which to rely. "In this world below," it is because the Sage-King possesses merit that the myriad subjects depend upon him.

As for those who are terrified—such as when foreign nations invade and press upon them, or when rebellions arise within their own borders—it is because the King possesses the Way and is shielded by his merit and virtue that none of these calamities can arise. (This concludes the preceding verse.)
The prose section describes eight kinds of terrors. The twelve lines beginning with "the people" open the verse by extolling the grace upon which all things depend.

Taken as a whole, these speak of the security of the people, the excellence of the flowering trees, the lushness of the gardens and groves, and the ripening of the hundred grains—all of which are signs of abundant joy resulting from the sovereign’s added power of merit and his great benevolence toward humanity.
None can repay it. △ Fourth, the verse on loving the people as one’s own children:
"Suppose an elder has an only son, wise and dignified, peerless in the world. His parents’ affection for him is like that for their own eyes;
day and night they constantly give rise to a mind of protective mindfulness. The Great Sage King of the land is likewise; he loves and cherishes all sentient beings as..."
Regarding his only son, he nurtures the elderly and rescues the orphaned and solitary; in his heart, his principles of reward and punishment are ever consistent.
Such a benevolent king is a sagely sovereign, revered by all living beings as equal to a Tathāgata.

In the analogy, even having only one son is already a cause for affection; how much more so when he is endowed internally with the capacity for wisdom and externally with the appearance of physical excellence—such a person is a marvelous son.
Therefore, his parents bestow special favor upon him, loving him as they do their own eyes.
To constantly give rise to a heart of protective mindfulness is the universal sentiment of parents throughout the world. This principle accords with the great laws of the state:
the King is likened to the elder, and sentient beings to his only child. To nurture the elderly is to love the aged; to rescue the solitary and the orphaned is to pity the widowed.
One who is young and fatherless is called an orphan (*gu*); one who is old and sonless is called solitary (*du*). Since he is thus able—
To provide rescue and relief is the benevolence of a king. To reward the good and punish the evil is the Way of a king. To maintain a mind that is always undivided is the impartiality of a king.
The general principles of benevolent kings throughout antiquity and the present are all thus. Thus, he is concluded as a sage ruler at the end of the passage.

Therefore, it is only natural that the multitude of living beings revere him as they do a Buddha. (Question: In the parable, the one son possesses the endowment of wisdom and dignified appearance; for this reason...)

"Paternal love. [Objection: According to the Dharma, sentient beings have not yet attained complete virtue; what is there to love? [Answer: The karmic retributions of sentient beings differ, but their Buddha-nature is not different; thus, they are one with one's own child. Although their retributive conditions, habitual tendencies, and outflows differ, their nature contains all virtues and is no different.
