Therefore, the Buddha contemplates that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and are endowed with all virtues; this is why he regards them as one body. (5) Verse on the Interrelation of Good and Evil.
When a benevolent king transforms and governs the state, there will be no calamities; the myriad subjects will be respectful and diligent, always dwelling in peace and security.

If a king lacks the Dharma to transform the world, pestilence will spread and afflict sentient beings. Thus, for all such humans and non-humans, their sins and merits are manifest and cannot be concealed.
Within the laws of good and evil, the fruit is divided into seven parts: the perpetrator receives five, while the king obtains two. [This applies to] gardens, groves, fields, and houses.
It is exactly so for all things. The same applies to taxes and equal shares. When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears, the realm is divided into six parts:
the King receives one part, while the people receive five parts. It is likewise with the retribution of good and evil karma.

The first two lines describe how you, O Benevolent One, possess the complete virtues of a king: above, you hold the way of governing the state; below, you ensure the peace of those who follow the law.
"Respectful" means to honor and comply with the clear teachings; "diligent" means to maintain mindfulness and carry them into practice.

It is for this reason that the kingdom is free from calamities and epidemics, and always enjoys tranquility. The second pair of lines (the third and fourth) are the opposite of this; since there is no governance of the world...
The Dharma. When the people have nothing to fear or dread, benevolent deities do not bestow their protection, and calamities swiftly arrive.
Epidemics arise as various maladies, accompanied by both warfare and famine. This is what is meant by "calamity will surely reach the person.
These two phrases follow from the preceding, stating that good and evil are clearly manifest and leave nothing hidden or concealed. This applies to all humans and non-humans alike.
"Those who are human" refers to the myriad people who are reverent and diligent; "those who are not human" refers to the reckless ruffians who create karma.
To the reverent and diligent, Heaven bestows blessings; to those who are not human, Heaven bestows calamities.

This is manifest and cannot be concealed or hidden—what is called "blessing for those who follow the path of wisdom, and misfortune for those who follow the path of rebellion. The subsequent lines concerning good and evil clarify that these matters are directly related to the king.

All is in accordance with the prose section of the two-volume [text]. Regarding the three phrases following "the wheel-turning king" (*cakravartin*), it further cites the wheel-turning monarch as proof for the king.

That is to say, when a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, he transforms people solely through the path of goodness; since he receives one-sixth [of their merit], the people receive five-sixths.
How could this not also be the case for worldly kings? Although there are slight differences between the six and seven [divisions], the king’s merit remains [intact].

Second. The final line provides the concluding summary: Although the retribution for good and evil karma is the cause and effect of all the people, when its origins and developments are investigated, it all depends upon the king’s virtuous governance or his lack thereof. Therefore, it says, "it is likewise for all.
This section serves as a warning for the king to reflect upon his own mind. △ Sixth, the verse on how virtuous laws are like those of heaven.
If there is a king who cultivates right view and transforms the world according to the Dharma, he is called a Lord of Devas; because he transforms the world by relying on the celestial dharma,
King Vaiśravaṇa will constantly protect him, as will the other three deva kings and the hosts of rākṣasas, all of whom shall guard the palace of that noble king.
The first two phrases mean that having already cultivated right view, his conduct accords with the Dharma;

because he teaches and transforms the world through the path of accordance with the Dharma, he receives the title of "Lord of Heaven" (*devendra*). This may be like the teachings of the Three August Ones (*sanhuang*), which were simple and plain;
or like the teachings of the Five Emperors (*wudi*), which were detailed and refined; or like the teachings of the Three Kings (*sanwang*), which were profound and solemn.
It is certain that what the superior does will be emulated by those below, and the people will listen to it without opposition; thus, all shall transform the world according to the Dharma.
The three or four phrases explain the title "Lord of Heaven" (*Devendra*). He is named Lord of Heaven because he transforms the world in accordance with the laws of heaven.

This is because heaven possesses the virtue of circulating, transforming, generating, and completing through the four seasons, while the king possesses the merit of teaching and transforming by rewarding the good and punishing the evil. Thus...

He embodies the virtue of Heaven and practices the Way of Heaven; thus he obtains this name. "Vaiśravaṇa" (毗沙), here below, means that when a sovereign possesses the Way, there are spiritual beings who assist him.
Vaiśravaṇa is translated as "Much-Hearing" (多聞); he is the name of the Heavenly King of the North.
As for the other three heavenly kings, they are Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the East, Virūḍhaka of the South, and Virūpākṣa of the West.
[This refers to] the eyes. As for the "hosts of rākṣasas," they are the groups such as the *pūlas* governed by the Heavenly Kings; "guarding" means protecting.
△ Seventh, the verse on accomplishing the ten virtues.
When a Sage-King appears in the world to govern the nation, he benefits all sentient beings and accomplishes ten virtues:
first, the ability to illuminate the realm; second, the adornment of the land; third, the ability to bestow all forms of peace and happiness;
fourth, the ability to subdue all enemies; fifth, the ability to ward off all terrors; sixth, the cultivation and assembly of all sages and worthies; seventh, [the mastery of] all dharmas...
He is the fundamental basis. Eighth, he is named the Protector and Sustainer of the World; ninth, he is named the One Capable of Performing the Work of Creation;
tenth, he is named the Sovereign of the Realm and its People.

These phrases are identical to those in the prose section (*dīrgha-pada*), with the sole exception that the ninth is there called the "Lord of Karma" (*karmādhipati*), referring to all virtuous and non-virtuous karmas. To him they belong.
Because it concerns the king, this verse is titled "The Power of Creative Transformation. It is also said that its distinct meaning is the same:
namely, that the power of creating and transforming the world does not transcend the two categories of good and evil, all of which belong to the king. The commentary follows the prose section.
△ Eight verses: A hundred spirits secretly provide protection.

If a king accomplishes the ten supreme virtues, Brahmā, Śakra, and the various devas, along with the kings of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and ghosts, will constantly come to protect the realm while remaining hidden from view.
The dragon kings, filled with joy, will send down sweet rain, causing the five grains to ripen and all things to flourish.
His clan name was An. Precious jewels were produced everywhere throughout the kingdom; its people and horses possessed great strength, and there were no enemies.
A wish-fulfilling jewel appeared before the king.
All the verses are identical to the prose, with the exception that two lines concerning the kingdom—which are absent from the prose—are supplemented here within the verse.

This refers to the production of jewels in various places, which has two meanings. First, it means that when a sovereign possesses merit, there are instances where the deities of wealth present him with jewels.
Second, it means that when a king transforms the world through the wholesome Dharma, all people become virtuous; as everything becomes virtuous everywhere, virtue alone is considered a jewel.
Regarding those who possess great strength in both men and horses: even under the transformation of a sage-king, one must still guard against unforeseen dangers.
Therefore, one should maintain people and horses. Because they are empowered by the force of merit and assisted by devas and nāgas, the army becomes strong and its power formidable.
Even if there are hostile enemies, their courage fails upon hearing of this, and they do not dare to even entertain the thought of rebellion; thus, the borders naturally become peaceful and tranquil.
Therefore, there are no enemies. △ Ninth verse: All neighboring countries submit.
The kings beyond the borders submit as guests.
"Beyond the borders" refers to outside one's own country. "Guests" (賓) means they address themselves as subjects; "submit" (伏) means they come to prostrate and surrender. △ Tenth [verse].
The verse says: The wicked person destroys himself.

If one gives rise to unwholesome thoughts within the kingdom, and a single moment of thought produces manifold evils, that person will fall into hell at the end of life, suffering for eternal kalpas with no time of release.

When a ruler who possesses the Way has already transformed the world through the Correct Dharma, it is only natural that the common people and the myriad subjects should embody the king’s heart, follow the king’s teachings, and practice the king’s Way. If every person can become a Yao or a Shun, why worry that the world will not be at peace?
This may be called knowing gratitude and repaying kindness. Suppose, however, there are those who turn their backs on kindness and lack righteousness; if—

When there is a single matter that offends the mind, one immediately gives rise to an evil intent and adds slander. Although this arises in the brevity of a single thought-moment, it does not prevent ten thousand evils from following in its wake.
This extends even to those who do not intend to rebel against their country; as it is said, "Sin originates from the mind."

Retribution manifests from the mind; therefore, when life ends and one falls into suffering with no prospect of escape, it is not something sent down by Heaven or surged up from the Earth, nor is it the addition of spirits or the attachment of ghosts.
It is entirely the result of one’s own actions as the cause and one’s own experience as the fruit.

Nevertheless, when people in the world often encounter those who harbor resentment toward their sovereign, they should take heed of this and guard their minds. Verse Eleven: The Good Person Attains Blessings.

If there are those who diligently receive the assistance of spirits and deities, and are protected by the various heavens so that their honor and fortune increase—these are people who understand gratitude and repay kindness. "Diligence" means earnest application; "spirits" refers to one's mental vigor.

It means that having recognized the King’s grace, one must apply oneself with earnest effort and maintain a spirit of clarity and alertness to assist in the Way of the King, just as Xiao He and Cao Cao did.

Fu Han assisted the Han dynasty; Fang and Du assisted the Tang. Ruler and subjects were of one body, moving Heaven through their resonance. Naturally, the various heavens protected and remembered them;

they received honors of enfeoffment and rank, enjoying a stipend of a thousand *zhong*. (Question: Those who hold official positions may assist the king, but what about the common people of the world? Answer:

Although not in office, if they can give rise to this mind, it also constitutes repaying the debt of gratitude. △ Third, the concluding summary of virtues in eight parts. First, clarifying the permeation of precept-virtue.
Cultivation.
Elder Jñānaprabha, you should know that all human kings are produced by the power of karma. No phenomena whatsoever are established without causes and conditions.
If there were no causes and conditions, there would be no phenomena; thus, one cannot speak of rebirth in the heavens or in the evil realms. Such a person [does not exist].
The "revealing cause" (parijñā-hetu): To hold that there is no cause and no effect is a great false view. Not knowing of sin and merit, one gives rise to false conceptualizations.
The various blessings and pleasures Your Majesty now enjoys were summoned by the cultivation of the virtue of the three pure precepts in the past.
Having attained the wondrous fruit of humans and devas, you have obtained this royal body.
This clarifies that the noble virtues manifested by a human king in the present life all derive from his observance of the precepts in previous lives.

Because the precepts are supreme, they induce a corresponding excellence in the resulting fruit; thus, it exhorts people to give rise to faith. The first phrase calls out the title to provide instruction; the second phrase clarifies that the cause is capable of inducing the fruit.
Regarding the term "all," there are two interpretations: one refers to all human kings, and the other refers to all [beings].
Regarding cause and effect: although a king is most exalted, he too is subject to what is induced by karma. Karma may be good or evil, and its retribution may be refined or coarse.

This has been stated in general terms; it has not yet specified which particular karma is meant. If this is true for one king, it is so for every king; therefore, it is said that "all" [kings] are thus.
The phrase following "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*) expands upon and indicates this point: it means that this applies not only to the single case of a human king, but indeed...
This extensively encompasses all phenomena, none of which are established without causes and conditions; it precisely demonstrates the existence of causes and conditions.
For example, the seed of rice or wheat is the direct cause for the production of a sprout, while plowing, sowing, water, and soil are the auxiliary conditions that facilitate its growth.

Therefore, sprouts grow. This is also like the sons and disciples of men: when there is the internal cause of intelligent capacity and the external condition of instruction in the *Shi* and *Shu*, then success and renown are achieved.
The second phrase reveals the opposite: if there is no condition, even with a cause, success cannot be achieved;
if there is no cause, even with a condition, it likewise cannot be achieved. Such is the nature of all phenomena.
All phenomena are thus. Therefore, it is said that there are no phenomena. The four lines below, which speak of "non-existence," serve to refute erroneous views.
These "speakers" are those of *icchantika* who lack faith; they claim that heaven is a natural vapor, and that what is pure and ascends becomes heaven.

How could there be any principle by which a person who performs good deeds would, upon death, attain rebirth in heaven? As for the evil destinies, they are the three miserable realms (*trāya*). Furthermore...
Lacking faith, they perform evil deeds; the principle that they will fall into the miserable realms after death is thus [stated].

In this way, he first rebukes their ignorance. Regarding "not understanding causes": this means they are unable to clearly comprehend how wholesome and unwholesome causes bring about wholesome and unwholesome fruits.

Regarding "being without cause" and so forth: this points out the reason for their lack of understanding; namely, since these individuals deny the existence of cause and effect, they constitute a great false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Those who do not understand give rise to false views; that is, because these people have fallen into false views, they do not know that sin is the cause of evil and merit is the fruit of goodness.
Those who give rise to false conceptualizations (parikalpa) mean that since such people do not believe in sin and merit, what could they possibly attain?

They take false attachments and false conceptualizations as attainment. As for "false conceptualization," it refers either to clinging to the view of a self-body (satkāya-dṛṣṭi) or to the view of extremes (antagrāha-dṛṣṭi).

To hold that there is neither annihilation nor permanence is collectively termed a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). These first four lines were spoken because the King possesses wholesome karma capable of inducing a noble fruit;
fearing that people might not believe this, [the Buddha] thus offered this critique. The subsequent four lines below correctly clarify the existence of cause and effect.
The first line points to the present fruit; the second line points to the past cause; and the third line clarifies the virtue of his precepts.

The seeds perfumed [by practice] act as the cause; the practitioner’s actual observance of the precepts acts as the condition. The precepts are that which brings about the result, and the result is that which is brought about.
By pointing to the result to clarify the cause, it is said "that which is summoned and brought about. The fourth phrase refers precisely to the sublime result thus brought about.
Regarding the two categories of humans and devas, there are two meanings: first, a king is a "deva among humans," and thus it is said...
"Human and Celestial. Second, by virtue of the aforementioned cause of observing the precepts, one is not only a king among humans, but can also be born in the heavens as a celestial king.
Whether in the heavens or among humans, all who are kings possess wondrous fruits. Because these are manifested in contrast through the categories of high and low, it is called "human and celestial.
△ Second, explaining the exhortation for people to observe the precepts, in two parts: first, the actual explanation of the precepts.
Chapter Three. First, the Supreme Grade of the Dharma-King Precepts:
If a person gives rise to the bodhicitta, and through the power of their vows accomplishes the unsurpassed fruit, they maintain the supreme grade of pure precepts;
dwelling and moving with mastery as a Dharma King, their supernatural transformations fill the ten directions, universally saving all beings according to conditions.
Regarding the various classes of beings:

this is not present in the prose version, but is supplemented in the verse. That is to say, by generating a superior mind, one attains superior precepts and realizes the superior fruit of a Dharma King.
Taking the bodhicitta as the cause, maintaining the precepts as the practice, and aspiration as the guide.
The Guide. By means of three kinds of power, he assists in the realization of the fruit. As for this "unsurpassed fruit," it refers to the fruit of Buddhahood;

hence it is said that his "rising and reclining are sovereign," and so forth. "Rising and reclining" refers to movement and stillness. This means that in movement he accords with the Way, and in stillness he unites with the Spirit.
He does not fall short in his mind, remaining in profound resonance with principle; thus, he acts with sovereignty as appropriate, serving as the King of the Dharma.
The Dharma King is none other than the Buddha. This refers to attaining the essence (tǐ). The phrase "supernatural powers (shéntōng) arise below" refers to the manifestation of function (yòng):

manifesting bodies according to the various classes of beings and preaching the Dharma in response to their capacities; hence it is called "transformation" (biànhuà). Appearing in all lands throughout the ten directions without exception, it is therefore called "supernatural power."
He must possess the marks of compassionate majesty and the gates of subduing and gathering; thus it is said he "follows conditions.

That which he teaches consists of the precepts, goodness, the truths, dependent origination, the six perfections, and other such dharmas; that which he benefits is vast, and thus it is said he "universally saves all classes of beings.

This statement—that he is currently a king—is because he came from having maintained the precepts in a previous life; in this present life, he again proceeds from the superior grade of preceptual vows.
Through these provisions, one will certainly attain Buddhahood; moreover, it does not stop at becoming a human king. △ Second, the wheel-turning kingship of the medium grade of precepts:
One who upholds the Bodhisattva precepts of the medium grade becomes a Wheel-Turning King with sovereign merit and virtue; whatever they do according to their will, all is fully accomplished.
Accomplished. Immeasurable humans and devas all revere him.
This clarifies the middle-grade mind, which attains middle-grade precepts and brings about the fruit of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).

Although these individuals uphold the Bodhisattva precepts, they have not yet eliminated the notion of self (*ātman*) and have not attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*); they merely receive the retribution of a Wheel-Turning King. △ Three: Lower Grade.
In this chapter on the Great Ghost Kings of the Lower-Superior Grade, there are three sections.
First, regarding the Great Ghost King of the Lower-Superior Grade who upholds the precepts: all non-human beings submit to him.
Although he may have deficiencies or transgressions in his observance of the precepts, because his adherence to the precepts is superior, he has attained the status of a king.
In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, regarding those who practice dhyāna and maintain the precepts while harboring a murderous intent, the resulting retribution is described as follows:

"If the murderous intent is not eliminated, one cannot transcend the realm of dust. Even if much wisdom and meditative concentration manifest before them, if they do not sever their killing, they will inevitably fall into the path of spirits.
Those of superior grade become powerful ghosts; those of middling grade become flying yakṣas."
The various ghost generals and their like, in their lower grade, shall become earth-walking rākṣasas. Their commentary states:
"The powerful ghosts are the honored emperors and sovereign kings of the Five Peaks and Four Rivers; these are the 'great ghost kings' mentioned in this sutra.
As for the "non-humans" in the subsequent phrase, they refer to the various ghost generals and earth-walking rākṣasas from that [other] sutra; these are the ghost kings.
Regarding those who are led [as subjects]: this is concluded by the second and third lines of the verse.

It means that although one may have committed transgressions and fallen into the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), by virtue of the excellence of their power of precepts (*śīla*), they still obtain the status of a king. △ Second, the lower-middle grade kings of birds and beasts.
Those who maintain the lower and middle grades [of precepts] become kings of birds and beasts; all that flies and runs submits to them.
Although they may have lapses or transgressions regarding the pure precepts, they attain the status of king by virtue of the excellence of their discipline.
The Brahmajāla Sūtra also states: "Even if one who has received the Bodhisattva precepts should violate them and fall among the various classes of beings, they shall always become a king:
among those that fly, they become the King of Birds; among those that run, they become the King of Beasts. The King of Birds is the phoenix; the King of Beasts is the lion. 3.
The King Yama of the Lowest-of-the-Low Grade.

Those of the lowest-of-the-low grade uphold [the precepts] before King Yama; though they dwell within hell and constantly exercise power there, even if they violated the prohibitions and were born in evil realms, it is because their adherence to the precepts was superior that they have become kings.
*Yama*, or *Yamala*, is translated as "Tranquil Rest" (*ching-hsi*). This is because he can bring to rest the unwholesome karma of those who commit evil;

thus, it is an alternative name for King Yama. Since one would fall into hell and undergo immeasurable suffering due to breaking the precepts after having received them, it is precisely because his adherence to the precepts was superior that he attained the status of a king and, conversely, governs the offenders. Therefore, it is said: "By oneself... [the self].
[Section] Two: Conclusion on Excellence and Exhortation to Uphold.
For this reason, all sentient beings should receive the pure precepts of a bodhisattva and be able to guard and maintain them well without deficiency or transgression.
Wherever they are born, they shall become kings of men. If there are those who do not receive the Tathāgata’s precepts, they will not even be able to attain [the state of] a wild beast.
Drying the body.

The first four lines exhort one to uphold [the precepts]. Although they are called "pure precepts," if the grasping at a self has not been eliminated, they belong to the category of tainted (*sāsrava*) precepts and merely result in the retribution of a human king.
What is emphasized is that one must be able to protect and maintain them well; they must not be deficient or violated. If, furthermore, one adds [the following]...
Regarding the outflows, meditative concentration, and wisdom: while in the stage of a bodhisattva, one does not merely serve as a king.
"If there were those of lower [capacity]" and so forth—although this is an indirect illustration (*paryudāsa*), it is also a comparison of the light with the heavy.

If one were not to receive the pure bodhisattva precepts, even the attainment of the body of a jackal would be impossible; this speaks of how one would fall into hell and undergo immeasurable suffering. Although the jackal...
Even those in the evil realms do not yet endure such various painful punishments; compared to the hells, this [human state] is already difficult to obtain.
How much more so is it to become a king among humans and devas? One should know that the Tathāgata praised the Dharma of precepts as supreme, for they are the foundation for entering the Path.
What is called "arising of concentration from precepts" and "arousing of wisdom through concentration" is termed the Threefold Training in the Outflows-free (*anāsrava-śikṣā*).
For this reason, one earnestly exhorts others to uphold the precepts; it is not because the precepts are superior that one causes people to violate them. Let those who study be cautious of this.
The jackal (*śṛgāla*) is a mountain beast that travels in packs and howls at night. This statement requires clarification: for example, among ten thousand people in the world...
Not even one or two people have ever received the precepts. Is it not the case that all people throughout the world are destined to fall?
You should know that the Buddha-dharma is a living word; those spoken of in the sutras are the most wicked people in the world.
Those who are rebellious and hold heterodox views—those who fall and do not rise, with no place to escape—yet fortunately have the Three Jewels upon which they can rely.
If they turn their hearts toward the Way and receive the Great Precepts of the Buddha, they may avoid hell; if they do not receive the precepts, [they shall not].

It is certain that there is no escape; this does not mean that everyone in the world falls [into such a state]. (Question: The sutra states that by upholding the pure precepts of the Buddha, one receives the retribution of being born as a human king. This statement is questionable.)

"Why is this? Let us set aside for a moment the śramaṇas and bhikṣus who uphold the precepts in the world today; even among laypeople living at home who have received the Buddha’s precepts, they are likewise beyond counting. If every person who has received the precepts were to become a king, would there not then be an incalculable number of kings in the world?

Answer: "Those who receive the precepts are indeed many, but those who can uphold them are few. Even among those who can uphold them, those who do so for a long duration are few. Even among those who maintain them for a long duration, those who uphold them with precision are few. Does the Sūtra not say:

'One who is skillfully able to protect and uphold [the precepts] without deficiency or transgression'? Furthermore, consider that while those who uphold the precepts may be infinite, how many are truly without deficiency? One should know that the Buddha’s words are skillful means (*upāya*), none of which fail to manifest excellence and encourage upholding. If it were truly as the Buddha said—that one remains without transgression for the rest of one's life—then the future result would be...

[The Buddha] replied: "Even if they do not become kings, they may still be born into royal families as members of the king's retinue, or be born into the families of great ministers and officials as members of the nobility; why must they all necessarily be kings?
△ Third, the verse concludes by clarifying the causes for becoming a king.
Therefore, a king is not without cause; through the diligent cultivation of the karma of ethical discipline, he achieves sublime fruits.

As a king is the sovereign of his people, he should cherish them with compassion as a mother nourishes her infant. Such a ruler of men possesses great kindness, and the heart that nurtures and protects them is difficult to repay.
For this reason, if all sentient beings can cultivate and realize Great Bodhi, [they shall act] toward all living beings...
One should give rise to great compassion and receive the Tathāgata’s threefold aggregate of precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*).

As for the phrase "therefore," it refers back to the preceding passage concerning how upholding the precepts brings about the state of a king; "not without cause" precisely clarifies that there is indeed a cause.
Diligence in the practice of the precepts is the cause for kingship, and the sublime fruit is the royal throne. The following section concerning the king reveals the sovereign's supreme benevolence:
having become the lord of the myriad people, one must employ a heart of compassion and kindness to pity and cherish the common folk, just as a mother nourishes her child.
To "pity" and to "nurture"—there is no measure to which this does not extend. These two characters [“pity” and “nurture”] refer to...
The grace of compassionate pity and the virtue of nurturing and raising cannot easily be repaid.

For this reason, one should follow from below and encourage from above to uphold [the precepts], considering that the benevolent kings of the world attained their status through the causal conditions of obtaining the fruit by means of the precepts.

Should all sentient beings be able to give rise to the mind of great bodhi and practice the categories of Great Vehicle morality, concentration, and wisdom, they will certainly realize unsurpassed [enlightenment].

The fruit of Bodhi is that which constitutes self-benefit. Regarding those below [the aforementioned], if one were to again give rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and the thought of delivering sentient beings, this cannot be achieved without taking the precepts as the foundation.
Therefore, it is exhorted: "One should receive the Tathāgata’s threefold aggregate of precepts (*trisaṃvara-śīla*).
As for "should receive," during the time when the Buddha was in the world, whenever all kings and ministers assumed their offices, they would first receive the [Bodhisattva] vows.

Upon receiving the Bodhisattva precepts, one is protected and aided by benevolent deities; only then may one assume office, which will surely bring great auspiciousness. As for the three clusters [of precepts]:

the cluster of the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) consists of refraining from all evils, because body and mind are thereby purified. The cluster of the morality of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) consists of practicing all virtues;
furthermore, within that pure body and mind, one accumulates all merits and plants the roots of manifold virtues. The cluster of... [the morality of benefiting sentient beings].

The precepts of birth arise because they bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings. Since they thus benefit both oneself and others, they also serve as the foundation for attaining Buddhahood in the future.
(A "cluster" [聚] refers to a comprehensive category; that is, within each cluster many meanings are contained, such as various evils, various virtues, or bringing benefit and happiness to all.
4. Verse on the Teaching for Cultivating the Method of Repentance (in two parts): First, clarifying the offenses to be repented.
If one wishes to receive the precepts in accordance with the Dharma, one should repent of one's transgressions so that they are extinguished.
This merely exhorts that karmic offenses should be repented; "receiving the precepts in accordance with the Dharma" refers to the highest grade of mind.
"Should" is a term used to instruct or command. The Sanskrit term *kṣamā* is translated here as "repenting of offenses. These offenses pertain to many lifetimes.
If the various transgressions and faults of the present life are not confessed and eliminated, they will hinder one's observance of the precepts and cause a deficiency in one's virtues;
therefore, it is said that one "should confess."
There are ten conditions that give rise to transgressions: the three of body, the four of speech, and the three of mind. Birth and death have no beginning, and transgressions are endless.
The great ocean of afflictions is deep and bottomless; the steepness of karmic obstructions is like Mount Sumeru.

The commission of karma arises from two kinds of causes: namely, active manifestation and seeds. The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) maintains all conditions and seeds, following them like a shadow follows a form.
It does not depart from the body; at all times it obstructs the Noble Path.
This explains that the seeds and the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of transgressions both possess causes and conditions.

That is to say, whether in the mundane or supramundane realms, no phenomena can be established without causes and conditions. There are two explanations: the general and the specific. The specific refers to the primary cause and the auxiliary conditions.

Regarding "conditions" (*pratyaya*): this has already been explained in the preceding text. As for the general explanation, as the present sutra states: "There are ten conditions that give rise to offenses;
that is to say, the cause is itself the condition, just as one relies upon conditions. This first phrase establishes the topic, while the subsequent phrase explains it.
Regarding the three of the body: there are three types of karma performed by the physical person—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
Regarding the four of the mouth: false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech. Regarding the three of the mind: namely, greed, hatred, and delusion.

Due to the causal conditions of these ten karmas, from time immemorial, birth and death have continued in succession as one commits various transgressions; therefore, they are said to be "without end."
The afflictions do not exceed the ninety-eight *anuśayas*. They disturb the ground of the mind and vex the nature and temperament; they are deep and bottomless, like the great ocean.
Their seeds and manifestations mutually perfume and incite one another; the power of karma obstructs the Path, being as lofty and steep as Mount Sumeru.
"The creation of karma" below clarifies the continuity of karmic results. Regarding the phrase "arising from two kinds of causes," it further states:
This is the causal basis of the ten conditions. Specifically, it clarifies two types below.

"Active manifestation" refers to the activities that arise in the present moment, namely the ten types of karmic deeds such as killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. "Seeds" serve as the cause for these active manifestations.
That is to say, the karma created in previous lives, once it has been perfumed and formed, serves as the seed.

As for the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), *ālaya* is a term translated as "store" or "repository. "Store" (*zàng*) means to contain; it refers to the containing and storing of seeds, deriving its name from this function.

"Holding" (*chí*) signifies the meaning of containing and maintaining [the seeds] without loss. "Conditions" (*yuán*) refers to the conditions such as the body and so forth—the ten types of karmic conditions. The seeds flourish by virtue of these conditions.

Therefore, it is called "sustaining conditions. One repents of transgressions based on the teachings; while this refers primarily to unwholesome seeds, its meaning extends to wholesome seeds as well, which is why it says "all.
As stated below, "like a shadow": this means that seeds and their manifestations depend upon one another, just as a shadow follows a form and does not depart from the body itself.
In this way, at all times, they are able to obstruct the Noble Path.
It closely obstructs the excellent fruits of happiness for humans and devas; it distantly obstructs the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi. Remaining at home can bring about the causes of affliction;
leaving home likewise destroys pure precepts.
This reveals the profound faults that obstruct the Path. The wondrous fruits of humans and devas must arise from the goodness of the precepts.
If there is the karma of killing, it can obstruct compassion; the karma of stealing can obstruct liberation; and the karma of sexual misconduct can obstruct the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Furthermore, greed obstructs generosity, hatred obstructs patience, and delusion obstructs wisdom. These are able to hinder the excellent and sublime matters of humans and devas.
Since there is no longer the cause of such excellent matters, how could one obtain the sublime fruits of humans and devas? Therefore, it is said that they are "proximate obstructions" (*upakleśa*).

Unsurpassed Bodhi must involve the simultaneous abandonment of both seeds and manifest activity; only when even the nature of abandonment itself is absent can one truly attain correspondence [with enlightenment]. Now...
Once the seeds have been sown and manifested through perfuming, they continue uninterruptedly from time to time; how then could the sublime fruit of Bodhi be attained?
Therefore, it is said that "hindrances are distant" and so forth. The latter two lines explain the meaning of the former two:

that is to say, lay men and women constantly engage with worldly affairs and conditions, thereby gathering afflictions which become the cause of birth and death; thus, they are able to obstruct the Path. (Worldly affairs and conditions)

They immediately manifest and assemble, and are thus perfumed to form seeds. Those who leave the household life to receive the precepts but fail to bring them to completion do so because their seeds and habitual tendencies have not been severed;
when they encounter conditions, these tendencies are activated, leading them to break the precepts. Once the essence of the precepts is destroyed, how can concentration and wisdom arise?
Therefore, that unsurpassed bodhi is not achieved is due to being obstructed by this. The above clarifies the offenses to be repented.
[The preceding section] is concluded. △ Second, explaining the method for performing repentance:
"If one can perform repentance according to the Dharma, all afflictions will be completely eliminated.

This merely provides a general indication of the method of repentance. A separate sutra states: "When the retribution of karma arrives, it is not found in the void, nor in the midst of the ocean, nor..."
Even if one enters among the rocks of the mountains, there is no place where one may escape and avoid receiving retribution; only through the power of repentance can it be eradicated.
Now, if one wishes to attain the wondrous fruits of the human and celestial realms, as well as unsurpassed *bodhi*, one must eliminate the causes of afflictions and karma.
Yet, in wishing to eliminate these karmic causes, there is no other excellent remedy than the single practice of repentance.
Regarding the Dharma: furthermore, that which is most important is the two characters "according to the Dharma" (rúfǎ).

This means to cleanse one's mind with earnest supplication before the Triple Gem, revealing all faults with total sincerity and without concealment. Thus, past transgressions are extinguished through repentance, and future transgressions are not dared to be committed again.
If one can truly act in this manner, it is "according to the Dharma. Therefore, the Sūtra says, "If one can... and so forth.
Just as the kalpa-fire destroys the world, burning away Mount Sumeru and the vast oceans, so too does repentance burn the fuel of afflictions.
Repentance enables one to travel the path to the heavens; repentance allows one to attain the bliss of the four dhyānas.

Repentance rains down precious maṇi-jewels; repentance can prolong the adamantine life-span. Repentance enables entry into the palace of eternal bliss; through repentance, one may emerge [from suffering].
The prison of the three realms: through repentance, one can cause the flower of Bodhi to bloom; through repentance, one beholds the Buddha’s Great Perfect Mirror;
through repentance, one can reach the Precious Abode.

These are extensive metaphors for the method of repentance. Specifically, the method of repentance is likened to the kalpa-ending fire, while afflictions are likened to Mount Sumeru and the vast ocean.
In the analogy, when the fires of the kalpa arise, all that exists in the world—the Mount Sumerus and the great oceans—is utterly consumed by the flames.
In the Dharma, washing the mind through repentance causes all afflictions, fetters, and karmic deeds to be completely cleared away until they are empty.
This is because the arrogance of sentient beings is as high as Mount Sumeru, and their craving and desire are as deep as the vast ocean. Since they themselves...
It can be eliminated; repentance (*pratideśanā*) can eliminate it, and thus it is likened to the kalpa-fire.

The third phrase refers to afflictions (*kleśa*), which encompass both seeds and manifestations, serving as the cause of birth and death within the three realms. The ninth phrase refers to the prison of the three realms, which is the fruit of birth and death.

This refers to being confined within the cage of the three realms, which is like a prison. If one can perform repentance, afflictions (*kleśa*) become empty, and one will not return to the three realms to undergo the fruits of birth and death;
therefore, it is said that one "can escape. Afflictions are like firewood, and the method of repentance is like fire.
The method of repentance extinguishes transgressions, just as fire burns wood. These four lines all serve as metaphors for the great power of repentance in extinguishing transgressions. Its...

The remaining eight metaphors all illustrate the generation of goodness, the cultivation of causes, and the realization of fruits. That is to say, because repentance can eliminate obstacles, the wondrous fruits of the human and celestial realms are within reach;
thus, it is likened to the path leading to rebirth in heaven. Once one is able to be born in heaven, one attains the bliss of the four dhyānas.
With the conditions for obstruction gone, what is sought is fulfilled according to one's wishes, like a mani jewel brought by rain. When delusions and karma have been repented, [the results follow].
Not creating the causes of birth and death, one does not receive the retribution of arising and ceasing. One attains the lifespan of the Dharmakāya;

therefore, it is metaphorically likened to a vajra, eternally abiding and indestructible. Having realized the Dharmakāya, one possesses the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, which serve as its support;
therefore, it is metaphorically likened to a palace. Since obstructive conditions have been exhausted and sublime practice is unimpeded, it is metaphorically likened to opening [a door].
The Flower: The light of the mind shines forth, illuminating the entire Dharma-realm; thus it is like a great mirror.

Because one attains the realization of the fruit through repentance that extinguishes transgressions, it is likened to reaching a treasury of precious jewels. Alas! The power of repentance not only extinguishes transgressions but can also lead to the realization of the fruit.
Worldly gentlemen ought not to fail to practice this. This is because royal virtue arises from the precepts; if one wishes to attain [it]...

Regarding the precepts, one should seek repentance; this is why the exposition has been extended to this point. △ Fifth, the verse on the instruction to cultivate the two contemplations, in three parts:
first, the general indication of the two contemplations.

If one is able to perform repentance according to the Dharma, one should practice by relying on two types of contemplative gates: first, the gate of extinguishing offenses through the contemplation of phenomena;
second, the gate of extinguishing offenses through the contemplation of principle.
The first two lines establish the subject; the following two lines state its name. △ Second, the specific explanation of the two contemplations (divided into three parts):
First, the general indication of the three grades; Third, the contemplation on phenomena that extinguishes transgressions. First, the general indication of the three grades.
There are three ways to observe phenomena to extinguish transgressions, categorized into three grades according to the superior, middling, and inferior faculties.
II. A detailed enumeration of the three grades has three parts. First, the method for extinguishing transgressions for those of superior faculties.
If there are those of superior capacity who seek the pure precepts, they shall give rise to a mind of great diligence without retreat.
With tears of compassion flowing like blood, they shall always remain earnest and sincere; their bodies shall be moved by such grief that blood appears all over them.

Fixing their mindfulness upon the Triple Gem of the ten directions, as well as all sentient beings of the other six realms, they shall kneel for a long time with palms joined and undisturbed. They shall confess and cleanse their hearts, seeking repentance, and pray: "May the ten directions..."
The Buddhas of the three periods of time, out of great compassion, take pity on me. I dwell in saṃsāra without any refuge; throughout the long night of birth and death, I am perpetually unawakened.
As an ordinary being, I am bound by all fetters; my crazed mind is inverted and wanders everywhere in pursuit of objects.
I dwell within the burning house of the triple world; deludedly stained by the six sense-objects, I have no protector. I was born into a poor and lowly family; I do not...
Having attained mastery [over my life], I constantly suffer; I was born into a family of parents with false views, and I committed sins by relying on evil associates.

I only pray that the Buddhas, the Honored Ones of Great Compassion, will look upon me with pity and mindfulness as if I were their only child. Having repented once, I shall never again commit any sin;
may the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time bear witness to this. One who repents with such vigor is called a superior seeker.
Pure precepts:
The first phrase identifies the person; the second phrase instructs them to apply diligence, meaning a refined mind free from distraction and tireless progress on the path.
This constitutes the foundation for a practitioner entering the Way. If there is even a single thought of retreat or rest, then all matters [will fail].
This is not established; therefore, one must not allow the mind of faith to regress. As for the manifestation of tears and blood, this is the expression of sincere and earnest devotion.

"Sorrow" (*bi*) refers to a sense of shame and deep emotional distress; "tears" (*lei*) arise from the eyes due to the pain of the heart and mind. As for the shedding of tears until blood appears, it signifies the ultimate limit of such grief.
This is the height of sorrowful grief. To fix one's mindfulness upon the Triple Gem and extend it to the six realms of existence is because the Buddha-nature is the same;
it is the contemplation of them as a single essence and equality. This is the firm dignity of the Buddhist teachings and the Triple Gem, yet the six realms are no less so.
One does not form thoughts of saint or ordinary person, thoughts of high or low, nor thoughts of defilement or purity; this is what belongs to me.
He is my field of merit, my teacher’s family, and the place where my transgressions are extinguished; therefore, I turn toward him to seek repentance.
Thus, with knees long drawn out and palms joined, I focus the mind without distraction. To reveal one's faults, both heavy and light sins are all emptied;
to wash the heart, even the most subtle habitual defilements are all purified. Alas! When one seeks repentance in this manner, what sin remains unremoved?
Extinction. What merit would not arise? I only pray that you will further show compassion. "I dwell below" expresses my earnest intent.
"Without a lower [refuge]" means to rely; it means to be at peace. One relies on a body so as to find peaceful rest.
Because one is caught within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), there is no basis for the Noble Path. The metaphor of birth and death as a "long night" means that although one possesses...
The Buddha-nature is shrouded by ignorance, like one dwelling in the long night of darkness who cannot see the three luminaries.
Since they possess neither the divine clarity of a sage nor the penetrating illumination of a sage, they treat birth and death as ordinary occurrences and remain unaware of it themselves.
Those bound by all fetters are like silkworms spinning cocoons around their own hearts.
Madness is like a monkey leaping from branch to branch. The three realms are likened to a burning house: the delusory defilement of the six sense objects is like the fire;

the conditioned environment of the three realms is like the house; and the self is like the person within that house. Because one’s thoughts are bound by the six sense objects, one is able to evoke birth and death and rely upon the three realms, being oppressed by the suffering of karma.
How is this any different from a great fire burning down a house? Since there is no rescue, [one is lost].
O Protector, one may say that [the state of] being solitary and destitute is extreme indeed. Poor, one lacks the wealth of the sages’ concentration and wisdom;
impoverished, one lacks the rank of the noble ones’ stages. Fallen into the lowly and base household of the outflows, one constantly undergoes manifold sufferings;
therefore, one does not attain sovereignty. Generally, those who do not realize that all is mind-only are of the school of false views. Those who do not give rise to...
The Bodhicitta is universally accompanied by evil associates. I only pray that you will conclude this section by requesting the Buddha’s empowerment, saying:
"Consider me as one without refuge; protect me through the long night. Have compassion for me who am bound by fetters; have pity on me who am deranged.

Since all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, just as a single child is cherished without partiality, cause me to turn away from false views and achieve right view, so that I may suddenly awaken to the True and Eternal."
Leaving behind evil associates, one gains virtuous companions; refraining from all transgressions, one escapes poverty and meanness to possess the wealth of the Dharma.
There is now a prospect for the Noble Path. Escaping the burning house, one mounts the white chariot, wandering at ease and with self-mastery.

Severing the defilement of delusion, one harmonizes with the six sense objects and beholds the protection of all Buddhas. Transforming birth and death, one realizes nirvana—this alone constitutes greatness.
The Compassionate Honored One awakens [the practitioner]. The two lines following "one confession" state that one shall not commit further transgressions, requesting the Buddha to bear witness.
The final two lines provide a summary. The two characters "thus" (rúshì) refer generally to the preceding text:

being able to exert oneself with diligence and earnestness, washing the heart and reforming one's faults, such a person is a courageous man and a true repentant; this may be called the superior grade of seeking.

Regarding the person who observes the precepts (one should know that the two characters "courageous" and "bold" refer to what a great man must do with resolute daring. It is like a great general breaking through a heavy siege; if one possesses even a slight bit of timidity, one will be captured by others.

Likewise, since beginningless time, all accumulated transgressions and past karma have been immeasurable and boundless. If one does not rely upon courageous and diligent effort to cleanse the mind and seek repentance, these offenses cannot be eliminated).
△ Second, the method for eliminating offenses of medium grade.
If tears flow profusely and crosswise, and one is unaware of them, with sweat streaming over the entire body, one should beseech the Buddha.

One should confess the karma of birth and death from beginningless time, praying that the waters of great compassion may wash away the dust of afflictions. May the obstacles of sin be cleansed and the six sense-faculties purified.

Grant me the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Aggregate Precepts; I vow to uphold them firmly without regressing, diligently practicing to deliver suffering sentient beings. While I have not yet attained liberation for myself...
First, one delivers others, continuing without interruption throughout the limits of the future. One who is thus diligent and courageous seeks Bodhi without sparing body or life.
The streaming tears and profuse sweat are outward manifestations of fear; yet because there is sincere faith, one knows that karmic entanglements are cumulative.

Having accumulated such profound merit, one knows that once a human body is lost, it will not be regained for ten thousand kalpas; the bitter retribution of the three miserable realms is certainly impossible to escape.
One’s liver and gallbladder ought to shatter with grief—how could one dare to fear anything beyond this? If one does not rely on the Buddha’s power to pull one up and save one, [what can be done?]
In the blink of an eye, I have been overcome; thus, with tears mingling with sweat, I beseech the Buddha. I now confess my transgressions as follows, praying that the Great One will cleanse my heart.
I say: from beginningless time, I have accumulated the habits of worldly toil, which have defiled my Buddha-nature.
I pray that within the Great Compassionate Heart of the Buddha, you will bring forth the nectar-water of the Dharma to wash away the dust and grime of my mind.
(This refers to the afflictions. "To wash away" below: "to wash" (*di*) also means to cleanse. "Karmic obstacles" (*zuì zhàng*) are also the dust of worldly toil (*chén láo*).
To purify the six sense faculties means that if the afflictions and deluded thoughts of the mind are removed, one will not commit various transgressions.

Once the roots of transgression are eliminated, there will be no conditions that obstruct the Path. Thus, the eyes will not be deluded by dark or yellow, crimson or purple, nor by the beautiful forms of men and women. Then...
When the faculty of the eye is pure, and so on up to the mind not being defiled by mental objects, then the faculty of the mind is pure.

If the six faculties are pure, this constitutes the requisite for receiving the Way. The three groups of precepts are explained as before. Because one returns the grace to the Buddha, it is said that "the Buddha bestows them upon me.
From "I vow" below is the generation of the aspiration; that is to say, since the Buddha has already bestowed the three precepts upon me, my mind is firm.
"Maintaining non-retrogression" is the vow for one's own benefit. "Diligently practicing below" refers to further generating the vow for the benefit of others.

"Before oneself has attained [liberation], etc. is as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "One who seeks to deliver others before having themselves been delivered is a Bodhisattva who has resolved their mind;
one who, having realized their own perfection, can awaken others is a Tathāgata appearing in the world. Although I have not yet been delivered, I vow to deliver and liberate them."
It is the same for all sentient beings. As long as they have not all been delivered, it is according to the vow of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva:
"Only when all sentient beings are saved shall I realize Bodhi; until hell is emptied, I vow not to become a Buddha.

Therefore, it is said that [the practice] is "ever-continuous," meaning the perpetual salvation of beings. The concluding sentence following these words may be understood accordingly. How magnificent! Although this is...

Who would dare to conceive such [a thought] unless taught by the Tathāgata? This is not for those who lack the faculties for the Mahāyāna. △ Third, the method for extinguishing offenses of the inferior grade:
If there are those of inferior faculties who seek pure precepts and give rise to this unsurpassed bodhicitta, with tears of sorrow and their body hair standing on end...
Standing upright, one should feel deep shame and remorse for the transgressions committed.

Before the Triple Gem of the ten directions and in the presence of all beings of the six realms, one should with utmost sincerity confess all instances of having disturbed and troubled sentient beings since beginningless time.

Arousing the heart of unimpeded great compassion, one should disregard even body and life to repent for the three karmas. One must confess all sins already committed and [vow against] those not yet committed.
"I shall not commit further offenses.
This section is largely identical to the preceding one; there is no need for an elaborate explanation. As for "the hairs on his body stood on end," it signifies the height of terror.
△ Third, the conclusion that clarifies the three grades.

Thus, these three grades of repentance for all transgressions are all called the foremost pure precepts. Using the water of shame and remorse to wash away the dust of affliction, both body and mind become categories of purity.
O sons of good family, you should know that although the various repentances through pure contemplation have been explained, there is no difference in their underlying principle;
it is only because of differences in faculties and conditions that they appear distinct.
These two characters [“first”] are terms used to designate the preceding three categories. They are all called “first” because their essential nature (*śīla-tattva*) is largely the same.
The following two phrases provide the explanation: just as water can wash the body, so too do shame (*hrī*) and remorse (*apatrāpya*) wash the mind;

thus, shame and remorse are metaphorically compared to water. Since persons belonging to these three categories have all washed away their defilements and afflictions (*kleśa*) with the water of shame and remorse...
Body and mind: the body is pure and does not perform defiled actions; the mind is pure and does not give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*).

Since both the internal and external constitute the category of purity, they are both supreme. Regarding "all virtues" and below: this is intended to cause understanding, hence it says, "one should know.

At that assembly below, one pours forth sincerity to seek repentance. That which manifests externally is called "matter" (*vastu*); the category of pure precepts is the Way, which is darkly harmonious.

That which pertains to the mind is called principle (*li*). In this assembly, phenomena and principle are largely identical; therefore, it is said they are "without difference. However, this is distinguished by what follows:

since phenomena and principle are identical, yet the three capacities (*indriya*) are still differentiated, this is due solely to the conditions of the superiority or inferiority of one's innate nature and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Because they are determined according to these capacities and conditions, they must necessarily differ. Furthermore, there is another interpretation: "capacity" refers to...
The *dharmatā-nature* (正因佛性) is possessed by all three types of persons and serves as the fundamental basis for attaining Buddhahood.

The "conditions" (*pratyaya*) refer to the *pratyaya-buddha-nature* (緣因佛性), which differs among the three types of persons. This refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) formed through the influence of virtuous conditions encountered throughout successive lifetimes;

this constitutes the *pratyaya-buddha-nature*. Consequently, even if one seeks repentance and the like with a sincere mind in this present life, [the results will differ according to these prior conditions].

All of these are triggered by seeds and habitual tendencies; thus, their severity differs. Nevertheless, the Buddha’s division into three grades is likewise determined according to these seeds. Regarding what is emphasized in the first section:
although there are no words about saving others, the meaning is encompassed by the manifestation of tears and blood.

Regarding what is emphasized in the middle section: tears flow profusely and sweat is produced, along with the discourse on the two benefits (self-benefit and benefit for others). [The latter] has not yet...

Furthermore, because blood appears, it is inferior to the first [instance]. The mind that seeks both self-benefit and the benefit of others surpasses the latter. Although this section likewise involves the arousal of the bodhicitta, the vow for the dual benefit is not yet seen;
though there is a heart of shame and trepidation that makes one's hair stand on end, [it lacks the aspiration for the welfare of others].

There is nothing other than reforming the past and cultivating the future; therefore, they are judged as those of inferior capacity. Thus, while the phenomena and principles are identical, their categories and qualities differ.
Furthermore, one sees that within identity there is difference. △ Second, the contemplation of principle for extinguishing transgressions has three parts.
First, the explicit explanation of the contemplation of principle.
If you wish to cultivate the contemplation of correct principle and distance yourself from all distractions, put on fresh, clean robes and sit in the full-lotus posture.

Gather the mind with right mindfulness and remain free from all external objects. Constantly contemplate the wondrous Dharma-body of all Buddhas, whose essential nature is like space and cannot be apprehended.
The nature of all transgressions is likewise so: they arise from the deluded mind through the causal conditions of inversion. Such is the characteristic of these offenses.

Originally empty, within the three periods of time there is nothing to be attained. It is neither internal, nor external, nor in between. Its nature and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*), entirely unmoving.
The wondrous principle of true thusness transcends names and words; it can only be penetrated by the wisdom of the sages.

It is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent; it is neither not-existent-and-non-existent, being free from names and marks. Pervading the entire dharma-realm, it is without arising or ceasing. All...
The Buddha is fundamentally of one and the same essence.
The first phrase establishes the state of being "far removed" (*viveka*), and all that follows constitutes the practice to be performed.
"Far removed" means to cease distraction and enter stillness, so that the six sense organs do not flow outward but instead turn back to shine inwardly. "Donning new clothes" symbolizes...
This means being pure both internally and externally. As for sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), it involves crossing the two legs with the soles of the feet facing upward;

in common parlance, this is called the "double-knee-locked" meditative form. When the mind is gathered, delusions do not arise; when one is detached from conditions, the sensory dust does not disturb.
Because one contemplates the ultimate truth exclusively, it is called "right mindfulness. "Constantly contemplating below" means that one's practice must not be interrupted.

Regarding the "Dharma-body," the Dharma-nature constitutes the body; this means that while the two bodies of all Buddhas—the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) and *nirmāṇakāya* (response body)—are distinct, their Dharma-bodies alone are identical.
Because they are identical yet distinct, they are called "all Buddhas"; because they are distinct yet identical, they are called the "wondrous Dharma-body. Below...

This passage correctly explains the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). It states that the essence and nature of the Dharma-body is perfectly luminous and pure through and through, leaving no room for anything else within it;
therefore, like space, it is ungraspable. The section beginning with "All" brings delusions back to the True.

One must necessarily observe with true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) that the nature of all offenses is fundamentally empty; as everything is *tathatā* (Suchness), this is itself the extinguishing of offenses. [The section on] "Inversion" follows.
Because they give rise to offenses, sentient beings who currently commit offenses do so because they lack true wisdom and thus are deluded regarding reality;
they grasp at phenomena as existing outside the mind and thus pursue the false. This delusion regarding reality is termed "perversion," and this pursuit of the false is termed "inversion."
This is the causal condition for such inversion; thus, the deluded mind creates offenses. "Arising" refers to the manifestation of the deluded mind as it discriminates sensory objects.
The following passage explains that the nature of offenses is entirely like [the nature of reality]: "nature" refers to the essence, while "characteristics" refers to its manifestations.

Since the essence is identical to reality (*tathatā*), its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) cannot be manifested; therefore, it is said to be "originally empty. One should know that the word "empty" is a term for the negation of characteristics.
It simply means not clinging to the characteristics of sin; all characteristics are entirely the nature (*dharmatā*), and the essence is *tathatā*.

The passage beginning with "the three periods of time" provides a further explanation of this original emptiness: it means that when observing the past, the characteristics of sin have already ceased; when observing the future...

Before the characteristics of offenses have arisen, when one observes them directly, the characteristics of offenses are immediately suchness; therefore, it is said that "nothing is to be found in the three periods of time.

This does not refer to a place within or below where they are dispelled. "Internal" refers to the sense faculties (*indriya*); "external" refers to the sense objects (*viṣaya*); and "middle" refers to the space between these two poles of faculty and object.

This means that when one contemplates the six internal sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), they are merely the "seeing portion" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the mind alone; thus, the characteristics of sin are utterly non-existent.

When one contemplates the six external sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), they are likewise merely the "image portion" (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the mind alone; here too, the characteristics of sin do not exist. When one contemplates the space between the faculties and their objects, there is nothing at all to be indicated;
how, then, could the characteristics of sin exist? Therefore, one knows that the nature and characteristics of sin are entirely empty; its very substance is suchness (*tathatā*).
It is thus: fundamentally it is unmoving. To speak of true suchness (tathatā) as being "thus" is merely to dispense with words;

for since the nature and characteristics of offenses are all suchness, and the wondrous principle of true suchness transcends all names and expressions, in its reality there is no delusion, and in its suchness there is no movement.
The wondrous is empty and harmonious; in principle, there is no duality of substance. Therefore, one is free from the mark of names and free from the mark of speech.
All that is provisionally designated by names and words is merely deluded thought; it is neither true nor suchness. Thus, they are eliminated by means of the transcendence of characters.
[The text] below provides further profound meaning. Question: Since names and words are transcended, there is no representation. How, then, can one enter the Way?
Answer: It is solely through noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) that one contemplates without giving rise to conceptual discrimination; thus, one is able to penetrate [reality] without obstruction.

It is not by means of negating the characteristics of mental objects through lower [levels of understanding]. That is to say, when true wisdom illuminates the principle: "non-existence" negates the conventional; "non-emptiness" negates the ultimate;
"neither existence nor non-existence" negates both existence and non-existence; and "neither non-existence nor non-non-existence" furthermore...
To eliminate that which is neither existent nor non-existent may be called departing from the four propositions and severing the hundred negations.

When one reaches the point where there is nothing further to be eliminated, one is free from all names and characteristics, and every phenomenon is entirely true. Furthermore, there is another interpretation; both meanings are valid.
"Neither existent nor non-existent" is the same as before. The three characters "neither existent nor non-existent" (*naiva san naivāsan*) are terms that establish a definitive seal.
That is to say, "neither existent nor non-existent" is a door of negation (*pratiṣedha-mukha*), while "not not existent nor non-existent" is a door of affirmation (*vidhi-mukha*).

The word "not" (*na*) in this phrase is identical to the word "neither" (*na*) in the preceding phrase; furthermore, the "neither" (*na*) above it is a term of exclusion (*apavāda-śabda*). This means that "neither" is not a definitive negation of existence.
It is not non-existent; therefore, it is said that it is "neither non-existent nor existent. This means it is neither "not existent" nor "not non-existent.

Generally speaking, the preceding negation of existence is the gate of exclusion (*pratiṣedha*), while this negation of non-existence is the gate of affirmation (*vidhi*). If there were only exclusion and no affirmation, one might fall into the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of the view of nihilism.
If there were only affirmation and no exclusion, one might fall into the conceptual proliferation of the gate of eternalism. What is meant here is that exclusion and affirmation occur simultaneously.

The non-obstruction of principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*). Furthermore, regarding the phrase "departing from names and marks" (*li ming-xiang*): this means that through the gate of negation (*zhe-men*), one departs from attachment to the names and marks of existence;

through the gate of affirmation (*biao-men*), one departs from attachment to the names and marks of non-existence. Departing from both existence and non-existence is the subtle contemplation of the Middle Way (*zhongdao miaoguan*).

The two lines following "pervasive" (*zhou-bian*) signify the convergence with the Buddha-body (*fo-ti*). Thus far, principle and phenomena are non-obstructive; principle and phenomena are perfectly interfused. [End.]
It pervades and harmonizes with the *dharmadhātu*. Being without birth or extinction, it is the definitive meaning.
It is the fundamental essence of all Buddhas, and likewise the Buddha-nature of all sentient beings. Therefore, it is said to be "all-pervasive" and so forth. Alas!

Since the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is identical in substance to that of the Buddhas, it is only logical that one should initiate cultivation in accordance with this nature and realize the Way by awakening to this nature. In this way, not only does one avoid failing the Buddha’s teaching, but also—

Furthermore, I shall not betray my own spiritual nature. I hope that there may be fellow practitioners with whom I share this path; it would be a blessing to practice together. (Question: That which belongs to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) has names and forms, so it can be discarded.

But the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is nameless and formless; why should it also be discarded? Answer: One speaks of the "ultimate" in contrast to the conventional, yet even the ultimate is not truly ultimate. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "To speak of the false in order to reveal the true—falsehood and truth are both equally false.
This is like gold dust: though precious, once it falls into the eye it becomes a speck of grit. Therefore, all such [distinctions] are discarded. △ Second: Further Entreaty for the Buddha’s Blessing.
I only pray that all Buddhas will grant their protective grace, enabling me to extinguish all inverted minds.
May I swiftly awaken to the source of true nature and quickly realize the unsurpassed path of the Tathāgata.

"May the Buddha grant his protection": Although the above includes the contemplative gates of both phenomena and principle (*dharmatā*), one may still fear that due to the profound power of karma accumulated since beginningless time, one will spontaneously give rise to notions of right and wrong, preventing the contemplation from reaching fruition.
Therefore, one prays for the Buddha’s power to provide protection, so as to extinguish the mind of perversion and awaken to the source of true nature;
this is precisely the realization of the Path (*darśanamārga*). The final phrase means that through such awakening, one accomplishes the Path.

Furthermore, if one relies upon the Buddha’s teachings, one can achieve success within a single lifetime; thus it is said that "enlightenment is swiftly realized," and so forth. [Question: Previously, it was stated: "Before one has attained deliverance oneself, one first delivers others, continuing until the end of the future, forever without interruption. The commentary further states that this is like the vow of Kṣitigarbha: "Only when all sentient beings have been delivered will one realize Bodhi. This is the ultimate limit. Furthermore, regarding what is called "the swiftness of realizing the Way": this refers to those who, while still carrying afflictions (*kleśa*) as they save sentient beings, have not yet perfected their wisdom and supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); thus, those saved by them are limited. If one further vows to achieve realization swiftly, they will possess great supernatural powers and bestow great wisdom and eloquence;

they will divide their forms and disperse their shadows, manifesting bodies according to the species [of beings], preaching the Dharma in response to their capacities, so that those saved become limitless. Therefore, the vow to save sentient beings is as it was described before, while the vow to achieve realization is as described here. Moreover, saving sentient beings does not obstruct the achievement of realization—it is the truth within phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Achieving realization does not obstruct saving sentient beings—it is phenomena within the truth. This is the lively style of the house; why must one be bound by fixed rules? △ Third, the ability to extinguish all sins.
If there is a virtuous son of noble faith who is able to contemplate the wondrous principle of emptiness day and night, all karmic obstacles will naturally be eliminated;

this is called the supreme upholding of pure precepts. If a person contemplates and realizes the emptiness of the true mark (*dharmatā*), they can extinguish all grave sins, just as a great wind blows upon a fierce fire that consumes immeasurable grasses and trees.
"Pure believer" refers to a refined and pure lay practitioner (*upāsaka*). "Able to contemplate day and night" means that one must not allow for interruption.

Because there is no interruption, one is able to subdue delusive thoughts. What is emphasized here is the two characters "able to contemplate" (*kuan*); this refers to the very moment of contemplative observation.
Do not cling to dullness; do not give rise to discursive thoughts. Contemplate *tathatā* (suchness) with right wisdom, like light merging with space.

There is no mind of discrimination, nor the characteristics of subject and object. When one’s practice accords with the effort in this way, "wondrous principle" (*miaoli*) is another name for *tathatā*, and "emptiness" (*kong*) is the wondrous principle of *tathatā*.
"True" (*zhen*) means being without delusion; "as-it-is" (*ru*) means not...
Movement. Departing from delusion and severing all marks, there remains only the single true emptiness (*tathatā*).

Since it is only true emptiness, within it all seeds and active manifestations of karmic hindrances are eliminated of their own accord, without the need for deliberate eradication. Thus it is said, "all," and so forth.
This is called the concluding summary that returns to the observance of the precepts. For pure observance of the precepts serves as the foundation. And...

Precepts can give rise to meditative concentration; concentration can bring forth wisdom; and wisdom can illuminate the principle. Within this wisdom and the principle, karmic offenses and hindrances are utterly unfindable;
therefore, it is said that they are "spontaneously eliminated. If one were to cite the preceding metaphor to explain this, it refers to what was previously called the "sublime principle."
This is called "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); while the names differ, their essence is the same. It is as follows below:

visualization is like fire, vows are like wind, and all grave offenses are like grass and wood. Through the two types of contemplation—of phenomena and of principle—one can extinguish grave offenses, just as fire burns wood until the smoke vanishes and the ashes fly away;
hence the phrase "just as," etc. △ Third, the admonition not to speak lightly.
"Good sons, this true contemplation is called the secret and essential gateway of all Buddhas. If you wish to explain it extensively for others, do not proclaim it among those who lack wisdom;
for when ordinary, foolish beings hear it, they will inevitably give rise to doubt and lack faith.

However, if there are those with wisdom who give rise to faith and understanding, observing and realizing *tathatā* (suchness) in every thought-moment, the Buddhas of the ten directions [will protect them]."
All shall manifest before them, and the wondrous fruit of Bodhi will be realized spontaneously.

Good son, after my parinirvāṇa, those of pure faith in future ages who constantly perform repentance through these two gates of contemplation shall receive the Bodhisattva’s threefold aggregate precepts.
