"O sons of good family" is a general address to the great assembly gathered for the Dharma. Regarding "true observation": if it is treated as a single category, it is the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*);
if it is treated as two categories, "true" refers to the contemplation of principle and "real" refers to the contemplation of phenomena (*shi-guan*).

This means that earnest supplication and repentance are all matters of actual practice. Regarding "the secret essentials": "secret" means transmitting mind-to-mind; it is not [disclosed] to those who are not suitable vessels.
The *Chuan* (Transmission) states: "The essential point is that by realizing the emptiness of the single thought-moment (*ekacitta*), one swiftly attains Bodhi.

The 'Gate' refers to the two contemplations of principle and phenomena as the thorough path to Buddhahood. The passage beginning with "If you wish... expresses the intent of earnestly entrusting [the teaching] so that it may circulate.
It means: "This is the heart-essence of all Buddhas; how could you receive it for yourselves alone without transmitting it? You must expound it extensively to others."
Discrimination requires the necessary discernment of whether a person is a suitable vessel or not. For instance, one who lacks wisdom is simply not a suitable vessel;

as the saying goes, "yellow river water does not pour into a clay jar. Therefore, it is prohibited by stating, "Do not proclaim this. All subsequent explanations are for the sake of those of inferior capacity.
This refers to those of little wisdom who have long been deluded; upon hearing [the teaching] even once, they will inevitably fall into hesitation.

They may doubt that the Buddha is not a sage, or doubt that the Dharma is not true, or doubt that they themselves are not worthy persons. Since they do not give rise to faith, they will ultimately resort to slander.
This is not merely a loss of words; it causes sentient beings to fall into suffering. Rather than being beneficial, it is harmful. Not so.

It would be improper not to speak [of this]. The above instructions must not be transmitted to those who are not of the right capacity. If there are those below [who are suitable], it is clear they are of the right capacity and should be taught.
Since they possess wisdom, they will surely give rise to faith upon hearing it once; they will certainly be able to understand the meaning.

Within every thought-moment, they will observe and reflect upon themselves, awakening to and clarifying True Suchness (*tathatā*). Not only will such persons not be lost, but the Way will find its place in them.
The Transmission states: "A person gains something of benefit. Why is this? At the moment of that person's single awakening, all the Buddhas of the ten directions appear before them.

Through their spiritual power and protection, they cause that person to naturally and personally realize the wondrous fruit of Bodhi. This concludes the exhortation for the virtuous sons and daughters;
it means that while the Buddha was in the world, he was able to teach and transform beings, but after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the future...

In this world, everything depends entirely upon you. Regarding those with pure faith through their capacity for speech: purity means the mind is free from distracting thoughts, while faith means right mindfulness is free from doubt.
These constitute the prerequisites for receiving the Way; therefore, you should bestow upon them two types of contemplative gates.

Within the contemplation on phenomena, one should constantly perform repentance to first purify the three karmas. One shall then receive the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Pure Precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*).
This meaning encompasses the realization of truth and the attainment of the Way through principle-contemplation. △ Sixth, the verse for requesting a Precept Master has three parts;
first, the formal request for the holy master as an external protector.
If you wish to receive and uphold the superior grade of precepts, you should invite the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as your preceptors.

I, Śākyamuni Buddha, shall serve as the Upādhyāya for the Bodhisattva precepts; the Honored King of Pure Wisdom of the Dragon Race (Nāga-jāti-viśuddha-jñāna-rāja) shall serve as the Acarya for pure morality;
and the Future Guide, Maitreya Buddha, shall serve as the Teacher of Purification. [To those] currently in the ten directions...

The Honored One among Two-Legged Beings shall serve as the preceptor for the purification and realization of the precepts; all Bodhisattvas of the ten directions shall serve as companions for the practice and study of the precepts;
and Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and Vajrapāṇi shall serve as the assembly of external protectors for the study of the precepts.
Thus, I reverently invite these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

The first phrase identifies the person; the second phrase identifies the teacher. This means that a wise person who wishes to receive the superior grade of precepts should invite a teacher of the superior grade.
This must necessarily be one of two kinds: either a sage or an ordinary person. A "sage" refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Please grant me your consent to be designated as the preceptor. Within this great trichiliocosm, all are those whom I, Śākyamuni, have transformed;

it is therefore appropriate that you invite me first. I shall serve as the *upādhyāya* for your reception of the Bodhisattva precepts. (The Sanskrit *Śākyamuni* is translated here as "Capable Benevolence and Silent Realization. "Capable Benevolence" is his clan name, derived from his ability to practice kindness and compassion.

"Silent Realization" refers to the principle realized, the path of silent and tranquil realization. The Sanskrit *upādhyāya* is translated here as "Power-Born," meaning that the disciple's path arises from him. From... [the disciple's path... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment. The translation provided reflects the extant portion and the context of the passage regarding the invitation of Śākyamuni as a preceptor for the conferral of Bodhisattva precepts.)

The Master is born from the power of oral instruction. Regarding the "Dragon-Species" (Nāga-jāti) section below: it is requested that the Ācārya be invited. "Dragon-Species Pure Wisdom Honored King" (Nāga-jāti-viśuddha-jñāna-rāja) is the name of the Buddha already realized by the Great Being Mañjuśrī.

In Sanskrit, *ācārya* means "standard" (*kai-koku*) or "right practice" (*shōgyō*). The *Nanshan Chao* states: "Because he is able to correct the conduct of his disciples. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* clarifies five kinds of *ācāryas*: first, the *pravrajyā-ācārya*, upon whom one relies to receive ordination;

second, the *upasaṃpad-ācārya*, who performs the *karma* for the full ordination; third, the *anuśāsaka-ācārya*, who instructs one in the rules of decorum (*iryāpatha*); fourth, the *śruta-ācārya*, from whom one receives the sūtras... [and so forth].

Regarding the Sūtras: if one explains the meaning of the Sūtras, even as little as a four-line verse; regarding the five *niśraya-ācāryas* (teachers of dependence), including those upon whom one relies for even a single night—these are performed by the *upādhyāya* and other teachers who have already completed ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*).

The aforementioned four types of teachers are all performed by those who have already completed five years of seniority (*pañcavarṣa*). This refers specifically to the *śīla-ācārya* (preceptor). Regarding "the future" below: he requests the *śikṣācārya* (teacher of instruction). Maitreya is currently at the stage of a Bodhisattva;
since he will only attain Buddhahood when he descends to be born in the future, he is called the "Future Buddha. Because...
Because he guides sentient beings through the three assemblies at the Dragon Flower (*Nāgapuṣpa*), he is called the "Teacher.

Regarding the section on the present: one invites the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions to serve as witnesses to the precepts; this refers to the Honored Witnesses. "The Honored One Among Those with Two Feet":

"feet" means fulfillment—namely, the fulfillment of merit and the fulfillment of wisdom. As for the fulfillment of merit, one is venerated by both the holy and the ordinary; as for the fulfillment of wisdom, one transforms and benefits all beings.
"Generating [the resolve]... Below 'the ten directions,' he invites the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions to serve as fellow students and companions.
Since sentient beings who receive the Buddha-precepts immediately enter the rank of the Buddhas, their virtue will not be solitary; there must surely be neighbors.

Therefore, he invites the Bodhisattvas to constantly serve as companions—those who shall provide mutual critique and refinement, correcting one's practice. Although they are all holy teachers and holy companions,"
If there is no external protection, there is fear that Māras or heretics may cause disturbance;

therefore, one requests Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and Vajrapāṇi to serve as external protectors to prevent demonic affairs. The final phrase provides a summary (the term "Vajra" is also used for "Heavenly Beings," as it applies to the twenty deities).
△ Second, the request for the presiding preceptor.
As for the preceptor who transmits the precepts in person,
these aforementioned noble masters are none other than those who provide protection through their supernormal powers and assist in the generation of wisdom,

causing one to give rise to resolute conviction and receiving secret guidance to accomplish the essence of the precepts (*śīlaskandha*). That upon which one relies is still the ordinary preceptor present before one.
The teacher of the precepts must personally instruct the disciple in the Dharma of the precepts, as well as in proper conduct and dignified demeanor.

Tiantai said: "The teacher possesses the capacity to mold and perfect; the disciple possesses the virtue of being a worthy vessel. As for the 'vessel,' it means that the disciple leaves his father to follow the teacher, revering the teacher as he would his father.
The teacher, in his humility, treats the disciple as an elder brother. Nanshan said: "The increase of the Buddha-Dharma..."

This is truly due to the mutual support between teacher and disciple, their earnest encounters with one another, and their dual provision of material goods and the Dharma. Thus, day by day their practice deepens and their path becomes profound;

that their conduct endures long and their virtue remains firm—all depends upon this. Therefore, those who seek the precepts must choose as their teacher one whose precept-virtue is pure and whose heart is devoted to others.
By receiving the precepts from such a person, the essence of the precepts (śīla-skandha) will certainly be attained. From them, one should study the Vinaya.
The restraint will certainly be established, for that teacher provides wholesome instruction.

Now, if the teacher lacks the intention to guide and lead, while the student lacks the resolve to practice, and the two abandon one another to wander falsely into base circumstances, how can one hope for the precepts to be firm and the light of the Way to shine?
In principle, the position of a precept-teacher at the stage of an ordinary person should not be limited to the single office of the *upādhyāya*; it must necessarily...
The ten masters must all be complete. △ Third, the exhortation to receive the precepts as a repayment of gratitude:
In order to universally repay the four debts of gratitude, one should give rise to the pure bodhicitta and receive the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Aggregate Precepts:
the precept of benefiting all sentient beings, the precept of gathering all wholesome dharmas, and the precept of subduing all transgressions.
The precepts of ritual conduct. These three aggregates of pure precepts are protected and remembered by the Tathāgatas of the three times;
sentient beings who have not heard of the Dharma and act contrary to it have neither heard of nor seen them throughout immeasurable eons.
Because these four debts of gratitude are so profound that they cannot be repaid, one is urged to resolve upon bodhicitta and seek the bodhisattva precepts;
for through the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*), all such debts may be repaid. [The following] explains the three clusters in detail.
As previously stated, the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint) comes first; it means not committing any evil and maintaining the precepts accordingly, which is also called "cessation" (*samvara*).
"Upholding. Because it can cease all unwholesome deeds, the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) follows next;
that is, the practice of performing all manner of good. It is also called "active upholding," because it can perform all wholesome deeds.

Next, what is called the "precept of benefiting sentient beings" (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*) is that which brings abundant benefit to all sentient beings. This refers to one's own observance of the precepts, which is also described as follows:
Through the Dharma they exhort others to receive the precepts; having personally realized the Noble Path, they are also able to inspire others to awaken to that Path.
Having personally developed spiritual understanding, they extensively study the Buddha-Dharma and likewise cause others to do so.
They are those who propagate the fundamental tenets, establish the teachings, and raise the banner of the Dharma. What was previously explained follows this sequence. Now...
The Sūtras place the precepts for benefiting sentient beings first because the mind of repaying kindness is so urgent and because the task of solely benefiting others is so pressing.
Whether it be the transmission of the precepts, the transmission of the lineage, or the transmission of the teachings, benefiting others is the foremost practice.
How could one not repay the four debts of gratitude? How could there be anything that is not supported by the three jewels? Therefore, these are placed at the beginning.

This is precisely for that reason. Regarding "wholesome dharmas being next": the wholesome dharmas of a Bodhisattva take the six perfections, such as giving, and expand them into the ten thousand practices;
by extensively practicing these wholesome dharmas, one repays the four debts of gratitude. Regarding "the code of discipline (*vinaya*) being last":

this means that when a true person receives the precepts, how could there be any possibility of transgression? It is natural that they do not wait to maintain them [only after having committed a fault].
This is because one does not commit transgressions. It is truly because the Threefold Pure Precepts (tri-śikṣāpada-śīla) enable such repayment:
my parents gave me life, and the king governs me; both expect me to practice goodness, and I ought to repay them with wholesome dharmas.
Although sentient beings have bestowed kindness upon me, their appearances change and they may be reborn in the human realm or among other species; I must not fail to [repay them].
To bring peace and security to those who have committed many evils is already an act of repaying their kindness; how much more so for those who possess extensive virtue?

To rescue their spirits and consciousness, causing them to increase in merit and obtain benefit, is the very place where one performs the greatest repayment of kindness. The Triple Gem has bestowed grace upon me, yet there is no way to repay it fully.
I shall uphold the Buddha’s pure precepts, raise the banner of the Buddha-dharma, practice the wondrous path of the Buddha, and transform and enlighten all sentient beings.
"One may repay [the Buddha's grace] by benefiting all beings. Thus, the latter two lines conclude with an exhortation, meaning:
"These three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*) are protected and remembered by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time; how could you not receive them?
Regarding the two characters "wu wen" (無聞) [in the phrase "wuwen xia," etc.], there are two interpretations. One is that it refers to those who have not heard [the Dharma].
Monks, there are those born in the Heaven of Non-perception who maintain themselves through the concentration of emptiness; even if a Buddha appears in the world, they are unable to see or hear him.
Or there are those in the world who are deluded and confused, entangled by worldly affairs, such that they have no leisure to see the Buddha or hear the Dharma.
They are also called "those who have not heard. Those who do not follow the Dharma are those with false views and non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).

Because their paths differ, even if the Buddha were to preach the Dharma, they would not wish to see him, let alone hear him. Thus, throughout immeasurable kalpas, they have lived and died in vain, never having attained hearing or seeing [the Truth].
The Tathāgata uses this as an admonition, desiring that virtuous people with whom he has a karmic affinity receive the Buddha’s [teaching].

Maintaining pure precepts, hearing the Buddha’s True Dharma, and giving rise to the thought that it is difficult to encounter, one should do so with a heart of reverence and a firm desire to practice;
only then will one not fail the Tathāgata’s earnest exhortation. △ Seventh, the verses extensively cite exhortations to uphold [the precepts], in three parts.
First, praising how the Tathāgatas of the three periods attained their fruits through the precepts, in three sub-sections. First, the actual clarification of how the Buddhas obtained benefits.
Only the Buddhas of the ten directions in the past have already received the pure precepts and constantly upheld them;

having forever severed the two obstacles and the afflictions, they attained the fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi. All World-Honored Ones of the future will likewise guard the treasure of the three clusters of pure precepts;
having severed the three obstacles along with their habitual tendencies, they shall realize equal and great Bodhi. Those of the present in the ten directions...

All Sugatas have together cultivated the causes of the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*), forever severing the suffering of the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and attained the fruit of the enlightenment of the three bodies (*trikāya-bodhi*).
The passage "From the past... and below means that all Buddhas have come from among ordinary beings; this is used to cite the Buddhas as an exhortation for the assembly.

Regarding "guarding and maintaining" (*ārakṣaṇa-dhāraṇa*): to preserve and not lose it is called "guarding"; to uphold and not depart from it is called "maintaining. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"One who maintains pure precepts with diligence is like one who guards a bright pearl. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Just as one crossing the sea cherishes a life-preserving float, so too is the guarding and maintaining of the essence of the precepts.
Because of this guarding and maintaining, [the precepts] are as clear as ice and frost, and [so are] concentration and wisdom.
It manifests spontaneously; thus, the two obstacles—the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—are forever severed without remainder.
With the power of ethical discipline (*śīla*) as the cause for severing these obstacles, and with ethical discipline as the cause for realizing the Path as the fruit:

as it was for all Buddhas of the past, so it is for those of the future and the present. The following section specifically explains the benefits obtained in the present, which are mutually consistent with those of the two previous periods.
There is a distinction between the manifest and the hidden. The first two [stages] clarify only the severing of obstacles along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Since they exclude only the causes of birth and death, they do not yet clarify the severing of the suffering of birth and death; thus, while the cause is manifest, the result is hidden. Why is this? Because once the cause has been removed, the result will necessarily not arise.
This stage merely clarifies the departure from suffering without yet manifesting the cause, because the precepts (*śīla*) contain meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Wisdom is the cause for severing hindrances, whereby the fruit of suffering is prevented from arising.

Regarding the realization of the three bodies (*trikāya*), this is explained in terms of the Dharma-body, Enjoyment-body, and Transformation-body; all are realized through the pure observance of the precepts.
(The three hindrances refer to the hindrance of karma, the hindrance of retribution, and the hindrance of afflictions. 2. An analogy clarifying the superior benefits of the virtue of the precepts.
The pure precepts of a bodhisattva serve as a boat and raft for crossing the deep, vast ocean of birth and death.

The pure precepts of a bodhisattva serve as a sharp sword for severing forever the fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion. The pure precepts of a bodhisattva serve as a dwelling place for quelling all fears on the perilous paths of birth and death.
The pure precepts can act as a wish-fulfilling jewel that eliminates the causes of poverty and low status, and [liberates those] possessed by malevolent spirits.
For all diseases, the pure precepts of a bodhisattva serve as the excellent medicine. As kings among humans and devas, they attain sovereignty;

the three clusters of pure precepts act as the favorable conditions. Furthermore, for the bodies of kings throughout the other four realms of existence, pure precepts serve as the condition for obtaining the supreme fruit.
Birth and death are boundless, like a great ocean. The pure precepts of a bodhisattva are like a boat or raft;

just as a boat or raft can cross the great ocean, so too can pure precepts ferry one across birth and death. The next two lines concern the three poisons, which are like ropes that bind sentient beings;
pure precepts are like a sword, capable of severing those bonds. The fifth and sixth lines concern birth and death.
The metaphor of the perilous road having many terrors illustrates that impermanence does not guarantee even morning or evening, and that the human body is easily lost and difficult to regain.
Pure precepts are like a dwelling because they can give rise to concentration and wisdom; if a person relies upon them, it is like finding a house on a perilous road, whereby fear does not arise.
The seventh and eighth lines mean that if one has birth and death but lacks the wealth of the Dharma, then...
The poor and lowly suffer much affliction. That the precepts are like a wish-fulfilling jewel means that whatever is sought will surely be granted, according to the wishes of sentient beings.
This is because the wish-fulfilling gem can produce rare treasures; once the suffering of poverty is eliminated, great wealth is attained.
By analogy, when the precepts give rise to concentration and wisdom, the suffering of birth and death is necessarily eliminated, and then—

"Ordinary beings attain Buddhahood. Regarding the two lines on "ghosts and demons": this refers to the various illnesses of sentient beings' false views, which are likened to being possessed by ghosts and demons.
When people can take the excellent medicine of the Tathāgata’s pure precepts, they are able to effectively expel the ghosts and drive away the demons, returning from evil to the right path.
Regarding the four lines on "humans and devas": this refers to the two realms of humans and devas, where kings exercise sovereign power.
Their nobility all arises from having observed the precepts in previous lives as a causal condition; thus, they attain the status of king in this life.
This clarifies that being among humans or devas is the fruit, while pure morality is the causal condition.

As for the other four realms—namely, the asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—even those within these classes can become kings provided they are able to receive the precepts. Among each respective category, one becomes a king...

Because it is superior, it is called the "superior fruit" (*viśiṣṭa-phala*). One should know that the two paths of humans and devas are the causes for those who are able to receive and uphold [the teachings];
however, as they have not yet given rise to untainted noble wisdom (*anāsrava-ārya-prajñā*) and have not yet severed the afflictions (*kleśa*), they experience [this state] and become kings.
As for the other four destinies, these are those who were able to receive the precepts but subsequently broke them; because of that breaking, they fell into the four destinies.

Because their original possession of the precepts was superior, they are still able to become kings. This reveals the excellence of the virtue of the precepts, with the intention of encouraging their observance.
△ Third, the exhortation to the king to respect the precepts by receiving their benefits.
Therefore, by being able to cultivate the causes of mastery, one shall become a king and receive noble honor.

One should first pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions and increase the cultivation of pure precepts day and night. Protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas, one should uphold them; these precepts are like adamant, indestructible.
The devas of the three realms and all benevolent deities shall guard the king’s person as well as his retinue from all enemies.

All submitted and bowed in reverence; the myriad people rejoiced, moved by the King’s transformation. Therefore, one should uphold the Bodhisattva precepts to evoke the unconditioned fruits of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
The Three Jewels abide eternally, transforming the world; their benevolence and virtue are vast, inconceivable, and beyond thought.

Through the kalpa-oceans of the past, future, and present, their merit benefits sentient beings without ceasing. The Buddha-sun, with its thousand rays, constantly illuminates the world, bringing benefit.

He benefits the multitudes and delivers those with whom he has a karmic connection; those without such a connection do not behold the Buddha’s compassionate light, just as a blind person sees nothing.
Therefore, these two characters follow from what precedes: because one is able to cultivate pure precepts, this serves as the cause for sovereign kingship;
one shall become a king and thus receive the fruit of noble dignity. These two lines follow the preceding and initiate what follows, and should be placed first, namely:
This present noble status has arisen from the observance of precepts in previous lives. Now that one has attained the position of a king in this life, one ought to pay homage to the Buddhas:
first, out of gratitude and a refusal to forget; second, to further seek their protection. Regarding the phrase "day and night":
it means that because one observed the precepts in a previous life, one has now become a king; and in this life, one is again able to receive the precepts. This is...
This is the superior practice. Regarding the passage beginning with "The Buddhas," it further clarifies the benefits of receiving the precepts.

It means that those who uphold the precepts are protected and mindful of by all the Buddhas. This is because the precepts are the foundation of meditative concentration and wisdom, and the cause for attaining Buddhahood.

When one raises the mind to receive the precepts, the mind becomes identical to that of a Buddha; thus, through the mutual resonance of cause and effect, the Buddhas protect and cherish them. For this reason, the King...
This principle should be upheld. Because it is protected and maintained, there is no corruption of the precepts.
"Equal to a vajra" means that just as a vajra object cannot be destroyed, the purity of the precepts cannot be disturbed by corruption.

Regarding the passage "In the three realms," because the king’s essence of the precepts is firm and his virtue is so profound that the spirits revere him, he moves the various devas and benevolent deities of the three realms to... [not to harm him].
It is solely by protecting the person of the king that the queen, the court ladies, and the entire retinue attain peace and happiness.
As it is said: "When one person possesses merit, many people depend upon it.

Because he possesses virtue and provides protection, all enemies, bandits, and rival states, hearing that the king maintains the precepts and follows the Way, are able to submit their offerings and surrender. Within his own realm, the myriad...
Those surnamed Huanyu were moved by the grace of the King’s transformation. Therefore, following the previous section, the benefits are now revealed:
through the power of moral discipline (*śīla*), one can bring about both mundane and supramundane unconditioned fruits (*asaṃskṛta-phala*).

Now, these unconditioned fruits are the *nirvāṇa* realized when both afflictions and birth-and-death are entirely empty; because there is no further activity or conditioning, it is called "unconditioned. [End of] Worldly [Section].
The intermediate retribution lies precisely within the midst of birth and death; how could it be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
It was spoken thus in a muddled manner because the translators wished to form seven-character lines. The intent lies in the totality of the words while their meanings remain distinct:

that upholding impure precepts results in becoming a king among humans or devas, which belongs to conditioned fruit; whereas upholding pure (*anāsrava*) precepts causes both the cause and the fruit of the three realms to perish.
The high realization of *nirvāṇa* belongs to the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*). The subsequent lines below demonstrate that the Three Jewels are eternally abiding and their grace is great.
Because the duration of the three periods of time is vast, they are called "oceans of kalpas. Within these oceans of kalpas, they remain eternally to benefit sentient beings;
therefore, there is no rest. Regarding the "Buddha-sun": while the sun can illuminate the day but cannot illuminate the night, the Buddha’s wisdom [illuminates] the profound...
It manifests universal illumination; therefore, it is called the "Buddha-sun. The phrase "thousand rays" refers to the excellence of its light.

Because the Buddha’s light shines universally, remaining constantly bright day and night, it is able to destroy the darkness of birth and death for sentient beings; hence, it is said to "benefit the multitudes of living beings."
Although the Buddha is a Great Sage, he must deliver those with whom he has a karmic affinity; those who lack such affinity do not see him even when face-to-face.
Though the Buddha possesses compassionate light that shines universally, their own karmic power acts as an obstruction, so they are like blind people who see nothing.
It is not only the case with the blind; consider, for example, the old woman to the east of the city, who was born at the same time as the Buddha, yet could not [see him] for an entire lifetime.
They saw the Buddha. Furthermore, among the nine hundred million households in the city of Śrāvastī, three hundred million saw the Buddha and heard the Dharma;
another three hundred million heard that there was a Buddha but had not yet been able to see him in person; and another three hundred million had neither seen nor heard of him before.
Alas! It is not only in the age of a Buddha that one fails to see the Buddha; even now, while the teachings of Chan, the doctrinal expositions, and the Vinaya pervade the heavens...

[The Buddha] descended and dwells eternally in the world. When the Good Spiritual Friend opens the hall and takes his seat each day, those who lack the karmic affinity and do not believe shall neither see nor hear him.
This is not because the Spiritual Friend lacks compassion, nor is it because his voice and teachings fail to reach them;

rather, it is due to their own self-obstructions and self-concealment, for which there is nothing that can be done. Those who encounter this sutra should deeply admonish themselves. II. [Second Section]
Praise for the Dharma Jewel: Of one flavor, it is understood differently according to individual capacities.
The Dharma Jewel is of one flavor and undergoes no change; what the Buddhas of the past and future preach is identical. It is like rain, which is of one flavor yet universally moistens all;

though plants and trees flourish, there are distinctions between the large and the small. Sentient beings each attain understanding according to their faculties, just as plants and trees receive the moisture.
Regarding the distinction:
the term "Dharma" is called a "jewel" because it serves as a model for humans and devas, provides a guide for the worthy and the sages, and acts as the mother of all Buddhas;
thus, its supreme excellence constitutes its jewel-like nature. "Of one flavor" reveals that the Dharma is pure and unadulterated, being solely the One True [Reality].
Just as the flavor of the Dharma is, its essence is eternally abiding; therefore, it undergoes no transformation or alteration.
"The former Buddha" refers to the Buddhas of the past, and "the later Buddha" refers to those of the future; the intention here also includes our own Buddha, who is spoken of as being in the present.
"Their teachings are the same" means that the various Buddhas are not distinct, for there is but one path and one Dharma. "Like rain falling" refers to the Buddha and his listeners.

This is to dispel doubts. Fearing that there may be those who harbor doubts—asking why it is that what we currently perceive as the Tathāgata’s teachings appear inconsistent—the Buddha therefore dispelled their doubts, saying:
"The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma originates from a single voice that universally reaches all. It is like a single rain that falls everywhere equally;
yet because the faculties and capacities of sentient beings differ, their hearing and understanding vary accordingly. It is not that there is any discrepancy in the Buddha’s teaching."

They are distinct; indeed, sentient beings possess their own inherent differences. This is also like how grasses and trees, according to the size of their roots and stems, receive moisture and grow, yet each species remains distinct.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Though they are born from the same earth and moistened by the same rain, the various grasses and trees possess their own distinctions.
Yet this is not the partiality of Heaven and Earth, but rather [the nature] of the grasses and trees themselves."
This is selfishness. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "When the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind.

Those with the faculties of humans and devas hear and realize the Dharma of precepts and wholesome deeds; those with the faculties of the two vehicles hear and realize the Dharma of the Truths and Dependent Origination;
and those with the faculties of Bodhisattvas likewise hear, according to their respective capacities, the Dharma of the sudden and perfect [enlightenment] from beginning to end."
Because their differences are not uniform, it is said that "each understands differently. Question: For what purpose is this taught? Answer: The Buddha is fundamentally one mind;
the Dharma is fundamentally one flavor. With a single voice, the Buddha teaches the one flavor, universally desiring that all sentient beings see their nature and achieve Buddhahood.

This statement was made to manifest the profound gravity of the Buddha-Dharma’s grace. △ Third, praising the Sangha Jewel: the concurrent practice of provisional and ultimate teachings through transformation and edification.
Part one: directly manifesting the transformation and edification of the noble Sangha.
Bodhisattvas and śrāvakas transform sentient beings; like the flow of a great river, it is inexhaustible. Yet when sentient beings lack faith, they cannot be transformed;
like being in deep darkness where the sun finds it difficult to shine, even the Tathāgata’s moonlight—so exceedingly cool and refreshing—is likewise unable to dispel the many obscurations.
Just as the moon does not shine upon an overturned basin, so too are deluded sentient beings [inaccessible]. The Dharma-treasure is nectar.
This is a wondrous and excellent medicine capable of curing all diseases of affliction (*kleśa*). Those with faith who take this medicine realize *bodhi*;
those without faith fall into evil realms according to their conditions.
The first two lines mean that in the world there are always holy monks (*āryasaṃgha*) providing instruction, continuing without interruption, like a great river.
This is like water. Its waves succeed one another, flowing constantly day and night without ever being exhausted. "Exhausted" means dried up; it means ended.
The Bodhisattva is likened to water; their continuity is like the waves. Regarding the passage on sentient beings below: it clarifies that those without faith cannot enter.

Those who possess faith encounter the Way (the "Channel") at every turn and are constantly graced by transformation and enlightenment. Those without faith are precisely the icchantikas, who lack [the seeds of Buddhahood].
Regarding the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*): although there may be noble Saṃghas who provide instruction and transformation, they cannot reach those who lack it.
Yet, the noble Saṃgha universally reaches all capacities for awakening, like the sun illuminating the vast heavens. Those who lack the faculty of faith are like those dwelling in deep darkness;

though the sun possesses light that shines everywhere, it cannot illuminate such obscure places. Therefore, it is said that they are "difficult to illumine. [The passage] beginning with "The Tathāgata... follows below.
It is said that the teaching and transformation of the Sages do not pertain solely to Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas; the Tathāgata is likewise able to manifest transformations within the human realm.
This is like the moonlight illuminating the world. The moon provides two benefits: first, it can dispel darkness; second, it can provide coolness.
For example, during the height of the scorching summer heat, when the warmth is unbearable, once the moon rises, it can dissolve the vapors of heat, thereby bringing about clarity and coolness.
"Cool. The preceding phrase serves as the metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*), while the subsequent phrase serves as the teaching (*dharma*). Therefore, it says: "It can likewise dispel all darkness.

One should know that within the teaching and the metaphor, there is mutual concealment and manifestation. In the metaphor, the dispelling of heat is more manifest, whereas the breaking of darkness is more concealed;

in the subsequent phrase, which applies the teaching by analogy, the opposite is the case. This is like the following: the moon is able to shine universally, yet it does not illuminate the space beneath a covered basin.

This is a metaphor for the Buddha’s light being universally pervasive, yet not reaching sentient beings who are deluded. Because the delusion of sentient beings is like an overturned basin covering the ground, it is said, "it is also thus.
Furthermore, this is identical to the previous statement that the holy Sangha does not save those who lack faith.
Below the section on the Dharma Jewel: "Amṛta" is translated here as the "Medicine of Immortality," hence it is called the "Sublime and Excellent Medicine.
Although it possesses the power to raise the dead and restore life, it cannot cure those who are destined to die. The Dharma Jewel is likewise:
it can cure all the maladies of afflictions and birth-and-death. Those with faith who hear, understand, and practice it may realize Bodhi. As...

If a person takes medicine, they will surely attain longevity. However, if there is one who lacks faith, such as an icchantika, and upon hearing this fails to believe it and instead slanders it, they will surely fall into the evil realms.
This is because when the Dharma meets those with the faculty of faith, it is like a pool of cool water that can be entered from all four sides;
yet when the Dharma meets an icchantika, it becomes a pit of fire—not only does one fail to find coolness, but one is even scorched by contact.
If one touches it, one is burned; if one enters it, one dies. Alas! Is it not necessary to be cautious? (The Sanskrit term *icchantika* means "one who lacks faith.
△ Second, explaining how sentient beings receive grace and obtain benefit.
Bodhisattvas and śrāvakas always remain in the world, delivering sentient beings through countless skillful means.

If there are sentient beings with hearts of faith and joy, each shall enter the secure and blissful state of the three vehicles. If the Tathāgata did not appear in the world, all sentient beings would enter onto deviant paths;
forever deprived of the nectar of immortality, they would drink poisonous medicine, long submerged in the sea of suffering with no time of escape. Then the Buddha-sun appears.
Throughout the three thousandfold world system, he emits great radiance that illuminates the long night. Sentient beings, like those asleep, do not perceive it;

yet, receiving this light, they gain entry into the chamber of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Before the Tathāgata had preached the Dharma of the One Vehicle, the lands of the ten directions were entirely empty and desolate.

Having resolved their minds and practiced cultivation, they attained perfect enlightenment, and all Buddha-lands became adorned and pure. The Dharma-treasure of the One Vehicle is the mother of all Buddhas. Three...

The Tathāgatas of the world are born from this; through the uninterrupted cultivation of *prajñā* and skillful means (*upāya*), the path of liberation is perfected and one ascends to wondrous enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).
If Buddhas and Bodhisattvas did not appear, the sentient beings of the world would have no guide; they could find no way to pass beyond the perils of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
How then could they reach the precious abode? By the power of great vows, they act as virtuous friends, constantly preaching the sublime Dharma so that—
They practice the path, advance toward the ten stages, and realize bodhi. They skillfully enter the state of nirvana and bliss.
These sages transform beings by perfectly conforming to the conditions of time and opportunity; their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and vibrant Dharma gates are immeasurable in number.
Their sole purpose is to deliver sentient beings. If sentient beings possess a heart of faith and aspiration, then according to their...

The faculties and natures [of practitioners] differ, and thus there are the fruit-positions of the three vehicles. Although these positions are indeed distinct, the principle realized within them is the same:
peaceful bliss. It is "peaceful" because the pervasive afflictions of views and thought have been severed, leaving nothing further to disturb the mind;
it is "blissful" because one has departed from birth-and-death through segmentation and is no longer subject to oppression. (The "three vehicles" refers to the śrāvakas...)

[The teaching of] the Pratyekabuddhas, the provisional teachings, and the Buddha-vehicle—this is how sentient beings receive grace and obtain benefit. The following four lines of the Tathāgata’s verse reveal this by contrast:
for while it is indeed natural that the Tathāgata appears in the world, when he does not appear, sentient beings all enter into deviant paths.

(For example, the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders—such as those who serve fire or venerate water—each establish their own systems of practice. Their irrational and erroneous calculations deny cause and effect; because their paths are not upright, they are called "heterodox paths. All people in the world who have not heard the True Dharma fall into the net of these heterodox paths.

Nectar is a metaphor for the Buddha’s teachings, which can bring one out of birth and death. Poisonous medicine is a metaphor for the heterodox doctrines of the outsiders, which can cause one to fall into the realms of suffering.
This means that if a Buddha does not appear in the world, one will not hear the Buddha-Dharma, just as...

They are forever deprived of the ambrosia [of the Dharma]. Since there is no holy teacher in the world, sentient beings will inevitably turn toward heterodox paths and accept false teachings, like drinking poisonous medicine;
this may be called "passing from darkness into darkness.

They shall never again hear the name of the Buddha, and thus it is said they are "perpetually submerged in the sea of suffering" with no time of escape (the sea of suffering is birth and death; "time" refers to a fixed limit). When the Sun of the Buddha descends, they are once again enlightened.
"From the Buddha, one emerges from suffering. This means that once the Buddha has appeared in the world, he is like the sun shining brightly in the sky, illuminating heaven and earth.
Within the three thousandfold world system, he radiates great light, enabling sentient beings to abandon error and return to the right path, thereby allowing them to escape the realm of suffering.
The "long night" is a metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*); because people are obscured by the veil of ignorance, they give rise to delusions and create karma.
They revolve through birth and death, like those dwelling in the long night who do not see the three luminaries.

The Buddha illuminates the world with the light of his body, illuminates the mind with the light of wisdom, and instructs with the light of his speech; thus he is able to illuminate the long night of ignorance and birth-and-death for sentient beings.
The passage beginning with "sentient beings" states that sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance, as if in a deep sleep during the long night.

People are in a state of profound ignorance and do not realize it. Once they are bathed in the Buddha’s light, which pierces through the darkness of *avidyā* (ignorance), they finally come to know that the dream of birth and death is entirely empty.
"Entering the chamber of non-action" (*asaṃskṛta*) means that once the great dream of birth and death is realized as empty, one attains the realization of non-active *nirvāṇa*.
This is like a person entering a room and having a place to rely upon. From the words "The Tathāgata" onwards, the preceding [section] is distinguished and clarified.

This is indeed so. What was previously explained refers to the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles, which cause people to realize the nirvana of the Three Vehicles. However, the true Dharma of the One Vehicle has not yet been taught.
Although one may realize the nirvana of the Three Vehicles, it remains provisional rather than real; therefore, it is described as "empty and hollow.

The mention of "generating the aspiration" (*cittotpāda*) and so forth refers to the period when the Buddha was still on the causal path. It is from the very beginning that the Buddha generated the mind of the One Vehicle and practiced...
The practice of the One Vehicle is that by which the fruit of perfect enlightenment is realized. All things are equal:
as it is said in the *Avataṃsaka*, where one attains the Way in a single place, one can attain the Way in every place. Even all minute dust motes and pores are Buddha-lands;
therefore, it is called "all. By adorning one place, all places are adorned; by purifying one place, all places are purified.

Therefore, it is said that they are all "adorned and pure. This is because the Dharma-treasure of the One Vehicle can produce wondrous fruits and lead to ultimate Buddhahood, just as a mother gives birth to a child;
thus, the Dharma-treasure is called the mother of all Buddhas. Hence, it is said that they are "equal throughout the three periods of time."

*Prajñā*, Part Two. This assembles the Buddha’s three virtues. There are three aspects of *prajñā*: namely, the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), contemplative illumination (*vipaśyanā*), and words and letters (*vyañjana*).
Through words and letters, one awakens contemplative illumination; from contemplative illumination, one attains the true mark.

The Sanskrit term *prajñā* is here translated as "wisdom. Wisdom serves as the expedient means for entering the Way. By turning the light inward to illuminate, one applies oneself with single-minded diligence.

Because one abides [in this state], it is called "uninterrupted cultivation" (*anantara-bhāvanā*). It serves as the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the Mahāyāna, which is precisely the *prajñā* of contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā*).

As for the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), by entering into principle through contemplative insight, all afflictions become empty and the two types of death are exhausted; like a bird escaping from a cage, it is therefore called "liberation.
"Sublime Enlightenment" (*miao-jue*) refers to the fruit of Buddhahood. "Ascending" (*deng*) means to realize or attain it; that is to say, as soon as liberation is attained.
One immediately enters wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*) and attains Buddhahood. Now, wondrous enlightenment is the merit of the Dharma-body of original enlightenment (*ben-ju*);

this is the Greatness of Essence (*ti-da*). Liberation is the emergence from the entanglements; this is the Greatness of Characteristics (*xiang-da*). Prajñā is the power of contemplative observation; this is the Greatness of Function (*yong-da*).
This means that by relying on the essence to give rise to function, and by uniting function with the essence, one attains liberation. Thus is the realization of the ultimate stage of fruition.
The passage beginning with "If the Buddha... further employs reductio ad absurdum to clarify that when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not appear in the world, people lack a guiding teacher;
how then could they attain the path of cultivation? The section beginning with "Birth and death... means that it is like a person who resolves to travel to a place of precious jewels to seek them:
they must have a guiding teacher to avoid the treacherous and traverse the level paths before finally reaching the site of the jewels.
If one were without the guidance of a teacher, one would not even know how to avoid the perils and difficulties; how then could one reach the place of jewels?

The Buddha is likened to the venerable teacher, sentient beings to those seeking the jewels, the perils and difficulties to birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and the place of jewels to the fruit of Buddhahood.
By using these analogies to clarify the Dharma, one knows that the Buddha’s grace is vast and great. This concludes the section on "The Greatness [of the Buddha]."

This reveals the Buddha’s grace. It means that the Buddha possesses great vows by which he sustains all beings; engaging with the phenomenal world from the perspective of ultimate principle, he acts as both teacher and friend to the people of the world.
He expounds the Dharma to guide them, leading them to practice so that they may advance toward the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and realize supreme enlightenment (*bodhi*).

He skillfully enters *nirvāṇa*. (The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage manifest their most exalted and vast bodies at the summit of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, thereby attaining ultimate Buddhahood. *Bodhi* refers to the virtue of wisdom; *nirvāṇa* refers to the virtue of cessation.)
Virtue (takes the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* as the place of peace and bliss). △ Third, the concealment of the superior and the manifestation of the inferior through great compassion:

Greatly Compassionate Bodhisattvas transform the world, using skillful means to guide sentient beings; they secretly maintain the true practice of the One Vehicle within, while outwardly manifesting as Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas.
Those of dull faculties and small wisdom, upon hearing of the One Vehicle, feel fear and resolve their minds [to practice]. Through the Sūtra...
Throughout many kalpas, they do not realize that their own bodies possess the *tathāgatagarbha*. They only delight in nirvāṇa and loathe the defilements of saṃsāra.

Yet the seeds of bodhi originally inherent in sentient beings all reside within the *ālayavijñāna*. If they encounter virtuous friends and resolve upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), they will undergo the threefold refinement and cultivate sublime practices.
Thus, they will forever sever the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), realizing the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding body—bodhi.
The wondrous fruit is not difficult to achieve; a true spiritual friend is indeed difficult to encounter.

The first four lines clearly explain the concealment of the superior and the manifestation of the inferior, skillfully bringing about transformation and edification. "Internally concealing" refers to self-concealment.
The actual practice of the One Vehicle is the great virtue of the Bodhisattva. As for the external manifestation, it displays the characteristics of the Lesser Vehicle;

its intent is to lead those of provisional capacity toward the ultimate reality. The following section explains the meaning for those of dull faculties: because sentient beings have long endured birth and death, their wisdom is small and their practice inferior.
Upon suddenly hearing the Great Dharma of the One Vehicle, they give rise to fear, thinking that this refers to the initial resolve of a Bodhisattva.

One must deliver sentient beings throughout long kalpas and undergo diligent suffering for a long time before finally attaining the Way. It is for this reason that those of small wisdom necessarily give rise to fear.

Therefore, the Bodhisattvas of Great Compassion humble their dignity to conform to the lowly, manifesting as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas to associate with them, gather and transform them, and lead them to resolve upon the Path, causing them first to realize the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle. Intending to...
Having thus enticed them, he then causes them to turn from the small toward the great, so that they may realize Bodhi.
This reveals that the expedient mind of the Sage reaches everywhere. "Not knowing," etc., explains the reason for fearing the Great [Vehicle].
It means that those of small wisdom do not know that there is a Tathāgatagarbha within their own bodies, and thus they only delight in the quiescent fruit of the Small [Vehicle].

(This refers to the nirvana of the two vehicles, which is characterized by the severance of defilements like ashes. They loathe worldly toil and the cycle of birth and death; thus, they take the lesser path.
Regarding the phrase "sentient beings inherently possess [it]," this means that one gradually causes them to enter the ultimate through provisional means.

Because within the bodies of sentient beings there exists the Tathāgatagarbha in its state of being entangled [with afflictions], which is none other than the ālayavijñāna, and because the seeds of innate bodhi-wisdom are entirely contained within the ālayagarbha.

Contained within consciousness. (One should know that "Ālaya-vijñāna" combines both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms. The Sanskrit term is *ālaya*; the Chinese term is "storehouse" (*zàng*). "Storehouse" means to store. It is so called because it contains and stores all seeds.)

The seed of bodhi-wisdom is likewise contained within the *ālayavijñāna*. If one’s faculties and nature are matured and one encounters a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they will lead one from the provisional to the ultimate, causing the Great Mind to arise—this is precisely the *bodhicitta*.

As for the "three kinds," these are ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). "Refining" refers to smelting metal; "polishing" refers to grinding and polishing.
These two characters are used metaphorically to manifest cultivation: it means that the practitioner, following the instructions of a virtuous friend, [proceeds].

By means of precepts and meditative concentration, one subdues the mind and is able to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*). It is like grinding an object with a stone until it is transformed from existence into non-existence;

by polishing and refining all phenomena (*dharmas*), they are brought back to the single mind (*ekacitta*). It is like smelting gold in a furnace until the chains are dispersed and formed into a single ingot.

Having realized that all phenomena are but mind, one also realizes that extension and brevity are without obstruction, and thus no longer fears that the Buddha-way is long and distant. Furthermore, [one attains...]
Because one does not fear enduring diligent suffering for a long time, it is called "cultivating sublime conduct. "Permanently severing the lower" refers to:

through a single moment of mental application (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta*), severing the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and abandoning attachment to a self (*ātma-grāha*) to realize the nirvāṇa of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); and severing the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and abandoning attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
One realizes the emptiness of phenomena and nirvana. Having severed the two attachments and departed from the two obstacles, one then attains the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding Dharmakāya;
this may be called "entering the ultimate from the provisional.

The final two lines conclude [the argument], stating that the wondrous fruit of Bodhi does not exist separately outside the mind, but is always present within the sphere of the heart and mind, never having been separated for even a moment; thus, it is certainly not difficult [to attain].
It is established. That which you find difficult is the true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); indeed, such a one is difficult to encounter.

For those who have the karmic affinity to extinguish existence, encountering a true spiritual friend means being exhorted toward the higher, sublime state; it is like transforming iron into gold—how could this be difficult?
Just as the dragon girl attained Buddhahood on the spot upon meeting Mañjuśrī, and as Jiashan saw the Way at the boatman’s oar-head;
having thus extensively cited examples to exhort the upholding [of the teachings], this section is concluded. △ Eighth: Verses Teaching the Essential Points of the Dharma.
All Bodhisattvas who cultivate the supreme path should know these four essential dharmas: first, to draw near to virtuous friends; second, to listen to the true Dharma;
third, to contemplate according to principle; and fourth, to practice and realize in accordance with the Dharma.
All the great holy lords of the ten directions have cultivated these four dharmas and realized bodhi. You, O elders...
To the great assembly and the faithful lay practitioners (*śrāddha-upāsaka*) of future ages: these four dharmas of the bodhisattva stages must be cultivated to achieve the path to Buddhahood.
For all bodhisattvas who have universally signaled their resolve for enlightenment and who cultivate the supreme path, they do so for the sake of generating the resolve and initiating practice.
Regarding the phrase "the practice": the four types of "inferiority" refer to the essential points of the method of cultivation, intended to cause the practitioner to resolutely observe them;
therefore, it says, "one should know. Regarding the phrase "approaching": this explicitly sets forth the four meanings. First, one must approach a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
"Approaching" means bowing to them as one's teacher; "associating closely" means not departing from their side. Morning and night, one must never be negligent.
As for performing menial tasks such as tending the hearth or carrying out the pounding of grain—submerged in lowly service—I have never shunned such toil.
Yet, in my desire for them to take me as their model, I find that "if one does not meet a master at the outset, one will end up confused and muddled in old age.
This should be understood as the first difficulty. Next is the hearing of wisdom: whatever true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) speak is entirely the True Dharma.
I shall listen. Next is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*):

I shall contemplate according to what I have heard, so that every word dissolves back into myself and every phrase accords with my own fundamental mind. Next is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*):

I shall cultivate according to what I have reflected upon, such that practice and understanding become one, transcending mind, intellect, and consciousness, and illuminating the principle through right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). At that moment, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all...
Emptiness. When all sufferings are simultaneously transcended and wisdom accords with principle, this is called "personal realization.
The four methods mentioned above are the practices universally cultivated by the Great Sages of the ten directions; hence the phrase "the ten directions, etc.

The final four lines, beginning with "You all," serve as a concluding exhortation to the elders. Because of the single person Zhiguang, it benefits five hundred others and extends to all beings. Therefore—
"Great assembly" refers here to the instruction for the present congregation; the following phrase extends it to the future congregation.
"Pure-faith lay devotee" (qingxinshi) refers to one who possesses refined and pure faith.

"Thus" and so forth—the character *di* (ground)—refers to the four essential dharmas, which constitute the causal ground (*nidāna*) for a bodhisattva’s attainment of Buddhahood. "Essentials" and so forth means that one desires to achieve [Buddhahood].
The path of the Buddha requires that one practice four dharmas; by treading them and cultivating them, by perfuming oneself with them and training in them, the path of the Buddha may be accomplished.
For the aforementioned reasons—that the King’s kindness is profound and his status noble—I have inferred his past causes, which arose from pure observance of the precepts.
Therefore, I have extensively praised the dharma of the precepts. If one seeks pure precepts, one must first perform repentance.

In the section on Repentance within the Dharma-gate of Confession (*chàn-fǎmén*), he further distinguishes between the contemplation of phenomena (*shìguān*) and the contemplation of principle (*lǐguān*).

He states that one seeking to receive the precepts must seek out a holy master (*shèngshī*), and to ward off demons, one must further seek external protection. He extensively cites the Three Jewels (*sānbǎo*) and exhorts with all his might to uphold them, repeating these points in several successive layers.
This concludes the four dharmas. Because I perceive that the Tathāgata’s sincere heart is for the sake of the multitudes, I have not grown weary of prolixity;

nor is it that I delight in prolixity, but rather that my compassion is exceedingly earnest. The section on the kindness of the sovereign has now concluded. △ Fourth, the kindness of the Three Jewels, in two parts:
First, a general restatement of the four debts of gratitude.
"Sons of good family, you should listen attentively. Regarding the four debts of gratitude spoken of by the Tathāgata.
△ Second, the separate verses on the Three Jewels, in three parts. First, the verse on the Jewel of the Buddha, in two parts. First, a general verse on the virtues of the Buddha.
The grace of the Buddha Jewel is supreme; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he gave rise to the Great Mind.

Throughout three *asaṃkhyeya* great eons, he fully practiced hundreds of thousands of ascetic deeds. His merit was perfected, pervading the entire Dharma realm, and having reached the culmination of the ten stages, he realized the three bodies (*trikāya*).
The three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas are as explained in the two-volume commentary. Regarding the *mahākalpa*: the *Dharmasaṃkhyā* states that there are three kinds of kalpas: first, the *antarakalpa*.
When the human lifespan is ten years, it increases by one year every hundred years until it reaches eighty-four thousand years; this constitutes one period of increase.

Then, from eighty-four thousand years, it decreases by one year every hundred years until it reaches ten years. This constitutes one period of decrease. [This cycle of increase and decrease is one *antarakalpa*.]
One decrease—such a single cycle of increase and decrease constitutes one *kṣudra-kalpa* (minor eon). Regarding the two *madhyama-kalpāḥ* (intermediate eons):

twenty such cycles of increase and decrease as previously described constitute one intermediate eon. Regarding the three *mahā-kalpāḥ* (great eons): these refer to the periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness;
each consists of twenty cycles of increase and decrease, and together they constitute one great eon. One who fully cultivates ascetic practices will thereby sever delusions and realize the Truth.

In the interim, he traversed all paths and practiced the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) in equal measure. He extensively benefited both himself and others, taking the cultivation of myriad practices as his function and the attainment of meaning through those functions as his virtue.
Because his merit and virtue were fully perfected, they are called "complete" (*paripūrṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "pervading the *dharmadhātu*," this reveals the virtues in terms of spatial scope and possesses three meanings. First, while practicing the causes of Buddhahood, the Buddha’s performance of deeds extends throughout the entirety of the empty *dharmadhātu*. Why?

First, there is no place where he does not reach. As the Sūtra says: "One contemplates the trichiliocosm and finds that there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed where it is not a place where the Bodhisattva has sacrificed his body and life.
Second, the fruit manifests the virtue of the cause; his fame is universally heard throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Third, every single practice he performs is able to accord with the nature (dharmatā). Since the essence of the nature is all-pervasive, his practice is likewise pervasive.
"Universal" (*pian*): this refers to the perfection of the cause. "Below the ten stages" (*shidi xia*) refers to the fulfillment of the fruit.

From the initial generation of the mind, one passes through the successive stages—from the stage of faith (*xin*) to the stage of abiding (*zhu*), and so on up to the tenth stage—until finally attaining Buddhahood.

Vertically, this spans three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas before one first realizes the Buddha of the three bodies (*trikāya*). These three bodies are the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). First, the realization [of the Dharma-body].

All have realized it. △ Second, the specific verses on the three bodies, in four parts. First, the verse on the Dharma-body, in two parts. First, the explicit clarification of the virtue of cessation:
The essence of the Dharma-body pervades all sentient beings; myriad virtues are凝然 (quiescently constant), its nature eternally abiding, neither arising nor ceasing, without coming or going.
Departing from oneness and difference, permanence and annihilation; the Dharma-realm is all-pervasive like space. All Tathāgatas together cultivate and realize it.
All conditioned and unconditioned merits rely upon the Dharmakāya, which is eternally pure. The intrinsic nature of the Dharmakāya is like space;
it is far removed from the six sense-objects and remains unstained. The Dharmakāya is formless and free from all characteristics; it is beyond the perceived and the perceiver.
All marks are entirely empty. Thus, the wondrous Dharma-body of all Buddhas is the cessation of the marks of conceptual proliferation and verbal expression;
it is far removed from all discrimination, the sphere of mental activity has ceased, and its essence is identical to suchness.
As for the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), it takes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as its body. Its substance is all-pervasive: vertically, it pervades all time, darkly penetrating the three periods;
horizontally, it pervades all places, filling the ten directions and encompassing the ten voids. It contains within itself the profound and the deep.

The statement that [the Buddha-nature] pervades all sentient beings means that the Dharma-body is not possessed by the Buddha alone; rather, it is possessed by all four classes of noble ones and the six realms of ordinary beings.
Because all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, Buddha-nature is precisely the Dharma-body of sentient beings.

Generally, as long as ordinary beings remain entangled in afflictions and have not yet attained liberation, they are unable to awaken to or realize [the Buddha-nature]. Although they possess its essence, they have not yet attained its enjoyment.

Now, through the exhortations of Master Zhiguang and his disciples, they are urged to engage in self-reflection, so that they may know the existence of the Dharmakāya and understand that sentient beings can attain Buddhahood.
"The ten thousand virtues" refers to all the dharmas of merit, wealth, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom.

Wisdom and so forth are the inherent qualities and functions naturally possessed by one's nature; because they are not newly acquired through cultivation, they are said to be "stably and eternally abiding.
One should know that the Dharmakāya has two meanings: first, it is richly endowed with myriad virtues, as explained above;

second, it is utterly free from even the slightest speck of dust, as explained below. This does not mean falling into the views of arising and ceasing, coming and going, identity and difference, or annihilation and permanence.

All these belong to the realm of existence (*bhava-dvāra*) and involve relative opposition. The Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*), being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), transcends all such opposition; therefore, it is described as "unborn" and so forth.
The phrase "the dharma-realm" (*dharma-dhātu*) here appears to be inverted; it would be more consistent to say "pervading the dharma-realm. If it were not so, [the meaning would be lost].
One should say "the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is all-pervasive," or simply state "the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is all-pervasive"; both the phrasing and the meaning would then be consistent.
That the two characters for "Dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu) appear at the beginning here is either a reversal in the translator’s wording or a scribal error.

Generally, for those who lecture, it is best to follow the logical sequence. As for the phrase "like space," this is a metaphor used to manifest the Dharma; it is because space itself is also all-pervasive.

Because it is complete; yet it remains a partial metaphor and has not attained total identity. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Empty space exists within the true mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky.
From "All things below" onward, [the text] reveals the essence and function (tǐyòng) realized in common by all Buddhas.
There are two phrases concerning the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). These reveal that the Dharma-body is the basis for all virtues.
The conditioned refers to the myriad practices of Bodhisattvas and the activities of the transformation Buddhas; because there is purposeful action, these are called conditioned merits.

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) refers to the path realized, namely the wisdom of suchness and reality (*tathatā-jñāna*), which is devoid of purposeful activity; these are called unconditioned merits.
The phrase "relying upon [the dharmakāya]" and so forth clearly demonstrates that the dharmakāya is the basis for all qualities.
Since all virtuous qualities rely upon the dharmakāya, there is nothing that is not integrated with it; because the dharmakāya is pure, everything is pure.
The Dharma-body is truly eternal; therefore, all things are truly eternal.

Just as the myriad streams flow into the sea and share the same salty taste, the following eight phrases all clarify the state of being free from faults and transcending all that is non-virtuous. As for the characteristics of subject and object: where there is form, there are characteristics.
Since there is no physical form, there are no manifest characteristics. Since there are no manifest characteristics, how could there be subject and object?
One should know that the two terms "subject" and "object" are relative phenomena; for example, as space is revealed by form, form is the revealer and space is the revealed.
Because both subject and object are transcended, it is said that all is empty. The following words dispel conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); that is to say, there is only...
Words and signs merely call out to others without reaching them; because words lack the efficacy of attaining the principle, they are called "vain proliferation" (*prapañca*).
One should know that the two characters for "quiescent extinction" (*śānti*) cannot be explained through the principle, for words are incapable of expressing quiescent extinction.

The latter two phrases [of the verse] are set aside, as all things—such as the sacred and the mundane, the environment and its inhabitants, defilement and purity, cause and effect—are merely conceptual constructions.
Therefore, it is said that "all" [dharmas] are so. The Dharma-body is fundamentally non-existent in its own essence; hence, it is said to be "far removed.

Regarding the phrase "the sphere of mental activity ceases": "mind" refers to the deluded mind; "sphere of activity" refers to the objects perceived by the deluded mind; and "ceases" means that one does not cling to those external objects.

Because the spheres of activity of the deluded mind are all unattainable, one is free from the marks of mental objects. Above, by extinguishing conceptual proliferation, one is free from the mark of verbal expression;

by distancing oneself from discrimination, one is free from the mark of names and words. Generally speaking, the fundamental nature is empty and quiescent; not a single dharma can be grasped by the mind.
This is what is called the unconditioned Dharmakāya, which does not fall into any numerical categories. II. Conclusion and Exhortation to Practice and Realization.
Desiring to realize the body of a Tathāgata, the Bodhisattva skillfully cultivates the ten thousand practices. The essence of wisdom is the unconditioned true *dharmatā*;
in both form and mind, all Buddhas are identical. It is like a flying bird reaching a mountain of gold; it causes the bird’s body to become the same color as that mountain.
All Bodhisattvas are like the flying birds, while the *dharmakāya* of the Buddha is like the golden mountain.
This means that just as the Buddha was able to realize it, you all should likewise realize it. "Tathāgata" refers to the Dharma-body;
"bodhisattva" refers to the person who is capable of cultivation; and "ten thousand practices" refers to the efforts from cause to fruition.
This means that those who wish to attain the fruit of Buddhahood from its cause must skillfully cultivate the ten thousand practices; only then can they realize and attain it.
However, for one who truly desires to practice the ten thousand deeds, such practice constitutes the efficacy of a bodhisattva’s cultivation and the wholesome dharmas of benefiting others.
Within the gateway of diligent effort, one must give rise to all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), sever all delusions, and depart from the two kinds of death;
only then can one personally realize ultimate *nirvāṇa*. How could this be easily accomplished? Furthermore, it cannot be achieved without personal cultivation.
The realization of the essence [of Buddhahood] cannot be accomplished without benefiting others; thus, it does not constitute an adornment.

The Dharma-body takes myriad virtues as its adornment, for these cannot be perfected without myriad practices. Regarding the two phrases following "the essence of wisdom": cause and effect must necessarily correspond.
That the essence of wisdom is unconditioned means that wisdom is the enlightened illumination of the Bodhisattva, which is *sākṣāt-bodhi* (initial awakening). True *dharmatā* is...
This is original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*). Because both the initial and the ultimate are entirely free from conceptual discrimination, it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).
This statement means that both wisdom and principle are identical to those of the Buddha. The subsequent phrase further states that both form and mind are also identical to those of the Buddha.

"Form" refers to the five sense organs (the eye organ, ear organ, nose organ, tongue organ, and body organ) and the six objects (the two kinds of visible form—shape and color—as well as sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects). "Mind" refers to the mind organ (*manas*).
The ālayavijñāna, the six preceding consciousnesses as the mind-kings, and the fifty-one mental factors.
Since these two categories of phenomena—form and mind—are expanded into the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements, they are called "all. That which all Buddhas share is this.
It is said that when the Buddhas, through their unconditioned wisdom, accord with unconditioned principle, all form and mind are entirely fused into the *dharmatā* of true suchness (*tathatā*).
This is why they attain Buddhahood; the intent is that you Bodhisattvas, by practicing and attaining realization, shall likewise be identical to the Buddhas.
The next two lines provide an analogy: "For example, it is like a flying bird alighting upon gold."
The mountain: because the color of the golden mountain is supreme, it can cause the bodies of birds to become the same golden color as it. All [verses] below are combined here;
this means that the Bodhisattva is like a bird and the Dharma-body is like a mountain.

When the Bodhisattva once realizes the Dharma-body, all form and mind likewise melt into the true nature of Suchness (Tathatā), becoming identical with the Buddha. △ Second, the verse on the Reward-body (Sambhogakāya) has two parts.
First is the Body of Self-Enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).
Each of the various marks and signs of the Body of Self-Enjoyment pervades the lands of the ten directions. With the four wisdoms perfectly luminous, it experiences the bliss of the Dharma.
The essence of the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future is identical. Although it pervades the entire Dharma-realm without obstruction, such a wondrous realm is...
It is inconceivable. This body abides eternally in the reward-land of the Buddha, experiencing the bliss of the Dharma for itself without interruption.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The self-enjoyment body refers to the infinite, true merits produced by the Tathāgatas through their cultivation of immeasurable provisions of merit over three incalculable eons; it is moreover supremely perfect, pure, eternal, and all-pervading."
The physical body continues in a state of profound stillness, reaching to the end of the future, constantly enjoying the vast dharma-joy of self-enjoyment.
