It is further said that each of its sense organs and marks of excellence is boundless; this sutra states that these are the various marks and excellences of the self-enjoyment body.
Each one pervades the lands of the ten directions, as stated in that treatise. The *Awakening of Faith* says: "The body possesses infinite colors;

each color possesses infinite marks; each mark possesses infinite secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*); and the supporting fruits upon which they reside likewise possess infinite varieties of adornments, manifesting accordingly," and so forth.
"Pervading the lands of the ten directions" refers to what is described in that treatise as being eternally pervasive.
Regarding the "form body" (*rūpakāya*): that [text] says each is boundless, while this [text] says each is all-pervasive.

This refers to attaining the perfect reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) through the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), which fills the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpasaṃbhava-lokadhātu*). This is because the untainted five aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) are omnipresent in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Regarding the phrase "the four wisdoms" and below: it means that the Reward Body Tathāgata transforms the categories of consciousness and mind to achieve this.

The four wisdoms (namely, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, the Wisdom of Equality, the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done). "Perfectly luminous" means being fully complete.
"Dharma-joy" refers to the sovereignty of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), which is joy in its very essence; it is precisely that which is enjoyed by oneself and is not known by others.
"The Buddhas before and after" and so forth refers to meeting and uniting with all Buddhas; it means that one is able to realize that their essence is non-dual.
Because they are distinct, it is said that they are all identical. Although the following section universally addresses doubts, one might fear that a skeptic would say:
"If the marks and signs (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana) pervade the lands of the ten directions, how can this be reconciled with the principle of spatial obstruction? Therefore, the text explains:
"Although the marks and signs pervade the Dharma-realm, they nevertheless possess no obstruction. This merely establishes the premise; the subsequent explanation states: "Such are these marks..."

Excellent. Together with all objective realms, the body and its objects are mutually fused and do not obstruct one another; they are all empty, luminous, profound, and wondrous, beyond the scope of thought.
How could the path of the intellect dare to harbor doubts regarding them? As that treatise states: "As is the measure of the Pure Land, so too is the measure of the body.
Below this section on the body, the text clarifies the land upon which the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya) relies. The Reward Buddha is itself...
The totality of his enjoyment for others consists of the land, which is the Land of True Reward Adornments; the body, which is the Body of Self-Enjoyment;
and the permanence, which refers to his constant dwelling within that Land of True Reward. That treatise states:

"The Body of Self-Enjoyment relies upon its own land, namely the pure consciousness associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, resulting from the self-benefiting practices cultivated in the past."

It is untainted (*anāsrava*). Through the maturation of the causes and conditions for a purely pure buddha-field, from the moment of initial attainment of buddhahood until the end of the future, it continues to transform into a purely pure buddha-field, circular and boundless, adorned with various jewels; this is the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).

It dwells constantly in reliance [upon this]. As the Sūtra says: "Receiving bliss without interval" means that from the moment of first attaining Buddhahood until the end of the future, one enjoys the bliss of the Dharma without interruption;
this is identical to that treatise. △ Second, the Body of Enjoyment for Others has three parts.
First, the body, land, marks and signs, and preaching of the Dharma.

The various marks and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-anuvyañjana*) of the Enjoyment Body (*sāmbhogika-kāya*) manifest in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings without increase or decrease.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "The Enjoyment Body refers to the subtle and pure body of merit manifested by all Tathāgatas through their Wisdom of Equality;
this is precisely the collection of marks and secondary characteristics. The long prose section of the second fascicle of the present sutra states: "Endowed with..."

Because there are eighty-four thousand marks and embellishments (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), it is called "various. This verse states: "Manifesting in response to capacities" means appearing in accordance with those capacities.
"Without increase or decrease" means that while the true essence remains unmoving, its function can manifest in accordance [with conditions].

It manifests without manifesting; thus the fundamental essence does not decrease. It manifests while being non-manifest; thus the fundamental essence does not increase. This section is explained in detail in the prose commentary (*gadya*).
This has merely been explained in brief. △ Regarding the twenty bodies that expound the Dharma of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*):

in order to transform the various bodhisattvas on the stages, a single Buddha manifests ten kinds of bodies. These manifestations differ according to what is appropriate for each, increasing progressively by multiples until they reach the infinite.
Teaching the essentials of all dharmas in accordance with their faculties, he causes them to receive the joy of the Dharma and enter [the path].
The One Vehicle: As they attain supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), these gradually increase; the Dharma-gates they realize are likewise so.
Bodhisattvas of lower stages give rise to wisdom, yet they cannot fully comprehend the higher stages. The capacity to transform and those who are transformed increase according to the stage.

Each belongs to its own sphere according to their original conditions (*pratyaya*). Sometimes a single bodhisattva is transformed by many Buddhas; sometimes many bodhisattvas are transformed by a single Buddha.
The Long Discourse states: "All Tathāgatas, in order to transform the assembly of Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, manifest ten kinds of bodies of enjoyment for others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*).
Now, the first two phrases serve as a brief heading, while the subsequent two phrases explain them.
That they are each different refers to the differences among the ten bodies. The section beginning with "successively" provides a general verse summarizing the distinctions between the ten bodies.

"Distinct" means that they proceed sequentially. "Multiplying" means that each subsequent stage is twice as superior as the preceding one. Regarding "reaching the infinite," the *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"The first body sits upon a hundred-petaled lotus flower and preaches the 'Illumination-Gate of a Hundred Dharmas' and so forth for Bodhisattvas of the First Ground...
up until sitting upon an ineffable, wondrous jewel lotus flower to preach for Bodhisattvas of the Tenth Ground."
“Sa. This refers to the "Gate of Illumination of All Ineffable Dharmas" and so forth. That [text] is detailed while this is concise; hence it says "reaching the ultimate.
This "ultimate" is precisely the aforementioned "ineffable. The two phrases following "according to the faculties" (*gen*) explain the meanings of "differences" and "multiplicative increase.
"According to" (*cheng*) means "in accordance with. "Faculties" (*gen*) refers to one's innate endowment. "The essentials of all dharmas" refers to the hundred... [etc.]

Regarding the passage "The Dharma, the thousandfold dharmas, etc., causing them to receive the joy of the Dharma, etc.": this means that the Buddha causes those in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth to realize according to their faculties and enjoy the joy of the Dharma;
though their levels differ in depth, they are identical in entering the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which is to say, entering the ultimate from the provisional.
All of the above is based on the Buddha’s teaching. From the phrase "They obtain... onwards, it is based on [the disciples].
The "expedient teaching" refers to those who are bodhisattvas of the ten stages (daśabhūmi) who have attained supernormal powers (abhijñā). This is as stated in the *Longer [Prajñāpāramitā]*:

"Once the bodhisattva has awakened, he manifests great supernormal powers and transformations that fill hundreds of buddha-worlds, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
The phrase "gradually increasing" likewise carries the sense of what follows being superior to what precedes it. Since this is the case for supernormal powers, so it is for the others.

The Dharma-gates are likewise thus; hence it says, "that which is realized," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "lower stages" and so on: this correctly clarifies that the realizations of each stage differ in their depth.
For example, although a Bodhisattva of the first stage gives rise to wisdom, they do not know the matters of the second stage.
This is because the former is considered "lower" and the latter is considered "higher. However, the reason they do not know them is that they are obscured by ignorance (*avidyā*). Because...

On each stage (*bhūmi*), one abandons a portion of ignorance and realizes a portion of ultimate truth. Because the first stage has not yet abandoned the ignorance of the second stage, it is obstructed by that [ignorance] and thus cannot fully comprehend it.
Regarding "the capacity to transform others" and so forth, this clarifies the correspondence between the capacity of the recipient and the teaching.
The "capacity to transform" refers to the Buddha and the Dharma-gates he expounds; the "those to be transformed" refers to the capacities of the practitioners on each respective stage.
"Increasing according to the stages" means that it gradually increases in accordance with the successive stages of transformation. "Original conditions" (*mūlapratyaya*):
"original" refers to the inherent endowment of each respective stage, while "conditions" refers to the cause for its cultivation and transformation;

this means that the inherent endowment of each stage serves as the very cause for its cultivation and transformation. "Belonging to what is subsumed": "subsumed" (*śeṣa*) means "appropriate" or "corresponding. It relies upon...

"Relying upon. This means relying upon fundamental conditions (*pratyaya*). It is for this reason that it is said their realization is not the same. Alternatively, the first [section] directly reveals the differences:
those of sharp and dull faculties are each distinct. Or there is a certain type who, although possessing the capacity (*indriya*) for the Mahāyāna, is dull;
even a single Buddha cannot transform and deliver them, such as Cūḍapanthaka, whom five hundred bhikṣus together could not instruct.
A single verse may cause one to gain the former while losing the latter, or gain the latter while losing the former; this case is also like that. As for the necessity of relying upon many Buddhas:
it is because when there are many Buddhas, the conditions are superior. Since the duration of the process is long, do not allow for interruptions; plan for it over a long period.

Thereafter, they attain the Way. There may be those of equal and most sharp faculties; though such people are very numerous—whether by the hundreds, the thousands, or even in immeasurable numbers—because their faculties are sharp, a single Buddha can transform them.
Just as a single word of ultimate truth transforms an ordinary person into a sage, the *Lotus Sutra* states:
"Immeasurable bodhisattvas surge forth from the ocean; all of them are Mañjuśrī."
These are those whom he has transformed and delivered. △ Third, the conclusion revealing the path realized by the ten bodies:
Thus, these ten Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment, each sitting beneath a bodhi tree of the seven treasures. As one Buddha enters nirvana, the next attains enlightenment;
they do not appear like transformation-buddhas who manifest over the course of kalpas. Upon the lotus pedestals where these ten Buddhas sit, there are each a hundred [petals] extending everywhere.
Chrysanthemum petals: within each individual petal is a Buddha-land, which is itself a trichiliocosm. Within each such world-system are ten billion suns, moons, stars, and planets;
four great continents; the six heavens of the desire realm; the four dhyānas; and the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The first two lines conclude by manifesting the attainment of enlightenment. As for the "ten Buddhas," these refer to the ten Buddhas who respectively appear at each of the ten stages (*bhūmi*);
all of them manifest the attainment of enlightenment. Each sits upon a seat, following the prose section of the second fascicle. The subsequent two lines are questionable;

they should not be present as they do not correspond with what precedes or follows. They emerge abruptly, and it is unclear why they are there. I shall now provide an explanation to resolve this doubt.
This is explained as follows: Fearing that those who doubt might say, "The Dharma-body is eternally abiding, without birth or extinction;

it is not known whether the Reward-body and the Supreme Response-body undergo birth and extinction," he therefore clarifies: "The former Buddha enters extinction while the latter Buddha achieves enlightenment.

This is unlike the transformation-buddhas who appear throughout the kalpas. This is because, according to the previous classification, the self-enjoyment reward-body has a beginning but no end, exhausting all that is yet to come.
The future limit is ultimately non-extinguished; it is eternally abiding from this point onward. This refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) for others' enjoyment.
Since it responds to Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, it is the "supreme response body" (*viśiṣṭa-nirmāṇakāya*), which also manifests according to the karmic conditions of sentient beings.

As for the "former Buddha," this is the body manifested in initial response to those on the ten stages. Regarding "entering extinction," this refers to extinction through the concealment of the body, not through annihilation.
Regarding its "extinction": although those in the tenth stage possess great capacity (*mahā-vimukti*), there are times when they fail to evoke a response;

the Buddha likewise conceals his body and does not appear. Thus, this concealment is termed "extinction. As for the "subsequent Buddha who attains [enlightenment]": that which previously concealed itself is considered the "prior Buddha.

If those of great capacity again evoke a response, the Buddha again manifests in accordance with their needs; this is the "subsequent Buddha. "Attaining" refers to birth. It is not said that he is "born," but rather...
Regarding "attainment" (*siddhi*), there is a distinction between sudden and gradual. Regarding "birth," it is like a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*):

manifesting birth from a womb constitutes "birth," yet one does not escape the gradual process of growing up before subsequently attaining enlightenment. Here, we speak first of "attainment," which refers to sudden manifestation;
it does not necessarily involve undergoing birth, for its marks, signs, and radiance are spontaneously perfected. Nevertheless, as for whether the Buddha manifests or does not manifest—
This concerns whether the capacity of the sentient beings' faculties perceives [the Buddha] or not; this is the distinction made by the subsequent phrase.

That is to say, although the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) Tathāgata has periods of concealment and manifestation, his True Body (dharmakāya) is eternally abiding. This is unlike the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) Tathāgata, who only appears once after passing through many kalpas.
The section beginning with "The ten Buddhas" extensively clarifies the characteristics of the excellence of the seat. The preceding passage spoke of attaining enlightenment.
Although it is said to be "under a tree," this teaching of the Dharma actually refers to a flower pedestal (*padma-pīṭha*).

Regarding the term "pervasive" (*pariṣphuṭa*), this refers to the first stage (*bhūmi*) being pervasive throughout a hundred Buddha-worlds and so forth. As for the phrase "each having a hundred or a thousand petals," the expression is general while the meaning is specific.

The general expression is "each," whereas the specific meaning refers to the number being either a hundred or a thousand. For example, the flower pedestal of the first stage has a hundred petals; [the second stage...]
"Chrysanthemums and the like" below expand upon the characteristics of their environment.

Since there is a Buddha-field within each individual petal, one should know that these petals are not lotus leaves, but rather flower petals. The subsequent phrase states that these Buddha-fields are furthermore not small;
they are indeed trichiliocosms. Within each such realm, there are ten billion suns, moons, and so forth, as well as the four [continents].
The dhyāna heavens: the "sphere of space" refers to the Heaven of Infinite Space; the "sphere of consciousness" is likewise [the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness].
"Non-perception" refers to the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception. As for the term "etcetera," it refers to the Heaven of Nothingness. (To explain more precisely:

as with one Mount Sumeru, one sun and moon, one set of four great continents, and one set of the six heavens of desire, which are covered above by the First Dhyāna Heaven—this is called a "small world" and cannot be called a "thousand. One thousand such small worlds, covered above by the Second Dhyāna Heaven, constitute a "small thousand-world system. One thousand [of these]...)

A small chiliocosm is covered above by the third dhyāna heaven; this constitutes one medium chiliocosm. A thousand such medium chiliocosms, covered above by the fourth dhyāna heaven, constitute a great trichiliocosm. Because the word "thousand" is repeated three times, it is called a "trichiliocosm of three thousandfold worlds.

Within it are ten billion suns and moons, with the four heavens of the formless realm situated above. This is because within a single leaf there is a great trichiliocosm. Just as the first stage (bhūmi) contains a hundred leaves—meaning one hundred great trichiliocosms—the second stage contains a thousand, and so on until the tenth stage, which contains unspeakably many great trichiliocosms.

When illuminated from beginning to end, they are layered and inexhaustible; this is the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*). Alas! This is the realm of the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*).
...this excellence. Truly, it is inconceivable! △ Third, the verse on the transformation bodies:
In each of the four continents, and specifically in Jambudvīpa in the south, there is a Vajrāsana and a great Bodhi tree king.
Within those [realms], the various transformed bodies of the Buddhas simultaneously realize the path of enlightenment and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma.
The trichiliocosm. Bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas attain the fruits of sainthood according to their respective faculties and dispositions.

Regarding the "four lower [realms]" below: this refers to the origin of the transformation buddhas. As for the "four continents," these are the ten billion sets of four continents within the trichiliocosm;
within each set of four continents, there is a Jambudvīpa, and thus there are ten billion Jambudvīpas. One...
Within each of the four continents, there is a Vajrāsana and a King of Bodhi Trees;
these are the places upon which the Nirmāṇakāya Buddhas rely for their attainment of enlightenment.

Correspondingly, as there are ten billion Nirmāṇakāya Buddhas who rely [upon them], there are likewise ten billion King of Trees and jewel thrones. These Nirmāṇakāyas simultaneously [reside] beneath these ten billion trees.
He attained enlightenment. Having manifested his attainment of enlightenment, he must have turned the wondrous Dharma within ten billion great trichiliocosms.

Because the teaching is able to accord with the capacities of beings, it is called the "wondrous Dharma" (*saddharma*). Since those who are its recipients are the assembly of the three vehicles, they are referred to as "bodhisattvas and others.
Regarding each phrase, there are two meanings. First, according to their respective faculties and dispositions, each attains [realization].
The "sacred fruits" refer to those of the Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas; these teachings constitute the Three Vehicles. Both cause and effect are provisional.

Second, according to the suitability of their faculties, the provisional is opened up. Those who achieve the sacred fruits enter the real. Initially, they follow the provisional and each realizes the sacred fruits of the Three Vehicles;
ultimately, they enter the real and all attain the Buddha-fruit of the One Vehicle. Since it is so in one instance, it is so everywhere.

It is thus everywhere; hence it is said, "each and every one," and so forth. However, the former interpretation follows the literal text but its meaning is shallow, while the latter interpretation is concise in text but profound in meaning.
It is better to follow the profound, as it does not lose the subtle significance. △ Fourth, the summary of the three bodies.
The Buddha of the three bodies thus described is supreme and peerless, and is therefore called "Jewel" (*ratna*).
This means that among the four objects of gratitude, the Jewel of the Buddha is the highest. △ Second, the verse on the Dharma-Jewel has three parts:
first, a general summary with a heading and enumeration.

The teachings spoken by the two bodies—the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the Transformation Body (*saṃbhogakāya*)—consist of the Dharma-Jewel, comprising doctrine, principle, practice, and fruit. Regarding these two bodies:

the "Response Body" refers to the inferior response body, which manifests according to the conditions of those who perceive it. Whether among devas it appears as a deva, or among humans it appears as a human, and so forth;
the size of its body and the quality of its appearance are entirely indeterminate, responding to conditions and meeting the needs of sentient beings.
It is like an echo in an empty valley or the bright moon reflected in a pond; in reality, there is no coming or going, yet it causes those who hear and see it to perceive it as such.
As for the "Transformation Body" (nirmāṇakāya), this refers to the manifested body.

It is like riding the sun-wheel or the fragrant elephant, being entrusted with lineage in the royal palace, experiencing fear upon visiting the four gates, leaping over the palace walls to leave the home life, entering the Snowy Mountains to practice the Way, and beholding the light.

...attaining Buddhahood under the Star [Constellation], and so forth. They have attained Buddhahood from time immemorial; furthermore, after the realization of the fruit, they manifest through transformation, appearing as Buddhas, and are thus called "Transformation Buddhas" (*nirmāṇa-buddha*).
Both of these two types of Buddhas are capable of preaching the Dharma. The sounds, names, phrases, and syllables that express this are called "Teaching" (*śāsana*).
The distinctions in the meanings and principles of what is expressed are called "Principle" (*tattva*). To advance in practice according to this principle is called...

Practice. When practice is fulfilled, that which is realized is called the fruit (*phala*). These four dharmas are all capable of serving as a standard and support; they are collectively termed "Dharma" (*dharma*).
Because they are esteemed by the world, they are honored as "Jewels" (*ratna*). 2. That which is the Teacher of all Buddhas.
All Buddhas take the Dharma as their Great Teacher; it is the path to Bodhi realized through the cultivation of the mind.

The Jewel of the Dharma is unchanging throughout the three periods of time; all Buddhas alike turn to it for study. I now prostrate to Sarvajñā (Omniscience), and therefore declare that the Jewel of the Dharma is the Teacher of the Buddhas.
Even if one enters a raging fire, it cannot burn them; they shall immediately attain true liberation at the appropriate time.
The first two lines state that the Buddha attains the path to Bodhi by practicing in reliance upon the Dharma; therefore, the Dharma is the Teacher of the Buddha.

The four lines following "Dharma Jewel" correctly explain the meaning of "Teacher": it means that from ancient times to the present, it remains consistent, and from ordinary beings to sages, it is equally honored;
thus it is said to be "unchanging. Because all Buddhas universally rely upon it, it is said that they "all study" it. *Sarvajñā* (薩婆若) means "all-encompassing wisdom," which is to say—
This refers to the fruit of Buddhahood. Regarding "prostrating," although this is a venerable fruit, it is in fact an expression of reverence for the cause;

since the fruit is accomplished by means of the cause, one specifically attributes the debt of gratitude to the Dharma. Therefore, it is said that the Dharma is the Teacher of the Buddha. The final two lines derive from the *Ratnārthasamuccaya*.
This refers to the Dharma that is able to serve as a standard and sustain reality. It is empty and signless, never having been abandoned since antiquity, and ultimately indestructible.

Therefore, it is said that "even entering fire, one is not burned. If a person follows the teaching and practices accordingly, cultivating and realizing the essence itself, they will attain true liberation in a single kṣaṇa.

Thus it is said, "In accordance with the time [the fire cannot burn]. As for the statement that the fire cannot burn: if this refers to the *dharma* (the signified), it certainly cannot be burned; if it refers to the *dharmas* (the signifiers), it pertains only to sounds and names.

As for the phrases and sentences, they are especially incapable of being burned. If one considers white paper and black ink, it is not necessarily the case that they cannot be burned. Why? Because paper and ink are impermanent things; yet, if there is a sincere heart that moves the divine response, even these cannot be burned.

This was because when the Buddha-dharma first arrived, the Daoist masters of the Five Peaks wished to test the authenticity of the teachings against those of the two masters, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna. Emperor Ming ordered each side to take their own scriptures and set them on fire, decreeing that those which did not burn were the true ones.

At that time, the Daoist scriptures were completely consumed by the flames, while the Buddhist scriptures remained unharmed. Consequently, the Daoists converted to Buddhism. Nevertheless, the emphasis lies in the sincerity of the response, and this is not a general rule. △ Third, explaining extensively through analogies.
The Dharma Jewel can destroy the prison of birth and death, just as a vajra shatters all things.

The Dharma Jewel can serve as a sturdy ship, capable of crossing the river of craving to reach the further shore. The Dharma Jewel can bestow happiness upon sentient beings, just as the celestial drum responds to the hearts of the gods.
The Dharma Jewel can relieve the poverty of sentient beings, like a maṇi jewel raining down all manner of treasures. The Dharma Jewel can act as...
The Stairway of the Triple Gem. Hearing the Dharma and cultivating its causes leads to rebirth in the higher realms. The Jewel of the Dharma is the Golden Wheel, the Great Holy Sovereign;
by means of the great power of the Dharma, it destroys the four māras. The Jewel of the Dharma can serve as a great precious chariot, capable of transporting sentient beings out of the burning house.
The Jewel of the Dharma can serve as a great guide, capable of leading sentient beings to the place of treasure. The Jewel of the Dharma can blow the great Dharma conch, awakening...
It awakens sentient beings to the path of Buddhahood. The Dharma Jewel can serve as a great lamp of Dharma;
it can illuminate all the darkness of birth and death. The Dharma Jewel can serve as a vajra arrow; it can stabilize the national borders and subdue all enemies.

The Dharma taught by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time can benefit sentient beings and liberate them from the bonds of suffering, leading them into the city of nirvāṇic peace and bliss. This is called the grace of the Dharma Jewel.
It is difficult to repay.
This differs from the two-fascicle prose version in that some elements are concealed or revealed, and others are increased or decreased.

According to the prose, there are three metaphors for clothing, armor, and a sharp sword, yet the metaphor of blowing a conch shell is absent; it is now supplied within these verses. [The word "conch" (螺) follows.]

It possesses the merit of providing an exhortation. By using the Dharma to elucidate the Buddha-nature within sentient beings, it causes people to awaken and attain Buddhahood, much like blowing a conch shell to alert a multitude.
The remainder is as explained in the long prose commentary; since that has already provided a detailed exposition, it will not be annotated again here.

From "The three periods of time" onwards, this section summarizes how all Buddhas collectively preach [the Dharma], with the intent of encouraging faith. From "Able to benefit" onwards, it specifically reveals liberation.
"Delivering from the bondage of suffering": This introduces the specific manifestation of the grace of leading [beings] to the realization of the Way.

The phrase "is named below" concludes by manifesting that the grace of the Dharma is difficult to repay (one should know that "suffering-bondage" applies to both cause and effect and pervades the Three Vehicles. Regarding the cause, there are three types: first, the afflictions and karma of the delusions of view and thought in ordinary beings constitute the cause of the suffering of out-flowing birth-and-death;

the birth-and-death of segmented transformation constitutes the fruit of suffering. Both cause and fruit are capable of entangling and binding, and are therefore termed "suffering-bondage. Second, for Śrāvakas, the failure to resolve upon Bodhicitta is the cause of suffering; being bound by the birth-and-death of transformation is the suffering).

The fruit also carries the sense of bondage. Third, because Bodhisattvas have not yet exhausted ignorance, it serves as the cause of suffering; and because they have not yet attained direct realization of Bodhi and still abide in the state of transformation (nirmāṇa), it serves as the fruit of suffering.

Thus, there is briefly the sense of bondage. The section on the grace of the Dharma Jewel is hereby concluded. △ Third, the verses on the Sangha Jewel in three parts: first, the verses summarizing the three types.
"Elder Jñānaprabha, listen attentively. The monastic community, both mundane and supramundane, has three designations: Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and the assembly of noble and ordinary beings.
They are able to benefit sentient beings and serve as a field of merit."
"Designation" (chēng) means to call or address. Those of the Mahāyāna are addressed as Bodhisattvas; those of the Hīnayāna are addressed as Śrāvakas.
Those for whom birth and death have been exhausted are designated as sages (ārya); those who have not yet exhausted them are designated as ordinary persons (pṛthagjana).
"Field" refers to land where the five grains are sown. If a person plants seeds in the earth, they will obtain grain in the autumn; the Jewel of the Saṃgha is like this.
If one draws near to and makes offerings to such a person, one will obtain merit; therefore, they are called a "field of merit" (bhadra-kṣetra).

[One should know that there may be errors in the transcription of the characters, such as writing "zhēng" (稱) instead of "zhǒng" (種), meaning that each of the Three Vehicles has its own type]. II. Verse on the Separate Explanation of the Two: the Holy and the Ordinary. A. Verse on the Holy Sangha.
1. The Bodhisattva Sangha.
Mañjuśrī, the Great Holy Honored One, serves as the mother of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The initial resolve of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions is entirely due to the power of Mañjuśrī’s teaching and transformation.

All sentient beings throughout every world who hear his name, behold his body or his radiant marks, and witness his various manifestations according to their kind, shall all achieve the inconceivable path of Buddhahood. Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Dharma Prince, from the first moment he resolved his mind [on enlightenment], he has abstained from eating meat. For this reason, he is named Maitreya.
Desiring to bring all sentient beings to maturity, he dwells in the fourth heaven, Tuṣita, within forty-nine kinds of palaces that fulfill all wishes.

Day and night he constantly teaches the practice of non-retrogression, delivering humans and devas through countless skillful means. There are ponds of water with eight virtues and exquisite flowers. All...
All those with the necessary conditions shall be born together. I now entrust my disciples to Maitreya; within the assembly of the Dragon-Flower, they shall attain liberation.

O sons of good family in the final dharma age, by giving even a single morsel of food to sentient beings, through these roots of goodness you shall behold Maitreya and attain the ultimate path of Bodhi.
The section on the Bodhisattva Saṃgha in two fascicles is extremely concise in its prose, providing only the names; it is, however, detailed in the verses.

Mañjuśrī’s Chinese and Sanskrit names are found in detail in the first fascicle of the list of names. "Great Holy Honored One" (Dàshèng Zūnzhě) is a title of supreme excellence, referring to one who has long since attained the Buddha-way yet continues to practice the causes while manifesting the fruits, assisting the Buddha to propagate the transformation [of sentient beings].
The passage beginning with "The three periods of time" explains the meaning and manifests his grace, stating that:

It is not that only a single Buddha defers to her; rather, the Buddhas of the three periods of time revere her as their mother. Speaking in terms of the vertical dimension, she precedes the past and follows the future;
hence, she is called "the Three Periods. Speaking in terms of the horizontal dimension, she encompasses the east, the west, and so forth, down to the nadir;
hence, she is called "the Ten Directions. Taken together, she is the mother of all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods for the sake of ordinary beings.

At that time, he first causes [beings] to resolve their minds [for enlightenment]; this meaning encompasses the ultimate attainment of Buddhahood as well, all of which is due to the power of Mañjuśrī’s transformation and teaching.
This constitutes his supreme benefit to the Buddhas. Furthermore, he also benefits sentient beings in an inferior manner:
some, upon hearing his name, admire his virtue; some, upon seeing his body, recognize him as a sage; and some, upon beholding the light he emits, as well as the light...
The manifestations appearing therein, as well as the bodies manifested through transformation according to the capacities of beings, enable all sentient beings to attain the path of Buddhahood;
by virtue of their wondrous spiritual power and the grace of their teaching, they are truly inconceivable.
"Generating the mind" refers to the bodhicitta (which is comprised of the three minds and four vows). "Maitreya’s descent" specifically reveals the grace of Maitreya. From the beginning... [etc.]

He utters the name of Maitreya. The reason he is called Maitreya is that from his first generation of the mind of enlightenment, he has not eaten the flesh of sentient beings, because all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, throughout successive lifetimes, they have been one another’s parents.
Therefore, with a heart of compassion and pity, how could he bear to eat them? It is by virtue of these causes and conditions of abstaining from meat that he is known as Maitreya.
Therefore, he is named Maitreya. It is truly because sentient beings of the animal realm all possess Buddha-nature, yet worldly people slaughter them for food to satisfy their own mouths and bodies;
they merely crave a momentary delicacy, unaware that they are binding themselves with the enmity of lifetimes.
Please observe those who slaughter: some stab the heart with sharp knives, some sever the throat or split the shell, some flay the skin or scrape off the scales;
even to the point of extracting entrails and lungs, or breaking bones and beating the marrow, causing them agonizing pain and the loss of life, yet they do not consider it wrong.
Moreover, when people of the world are reviled by a single word, they harbor resentment for a lifetime—how much more so for killing?
When one’s own body eats meat, how can this not involve harboring resentment and grievance? If one returns again to birth, how could it not result in retribution as an enemy?
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "A person dies and becomes a sheep; a sheep dies and becomes a person. Throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they prey upon and kill one another."
Furthermore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "To kill sentient beings for profit, or to use wealth to ensnare various meats—both are evil karmas;
after death, one falls into the Raurava Hell. Alas! Who would dare not believe these sacred words?

May those fortunate people with good roots quickly turn their minds, cease killing, and abstain from meat. Furthermore, they should encourage others toward goodness and release living beings, widely practicing compassionate relief. If this is done...
It is not only Maitreya who is Maitreya; rather, all people are Maitreya. This is intended to manifest the grace [of the Buddha] below.
Tuṣita—translated here as "Contentment"—is the fourth heaven of the Desire Realm. It consists of an inner court and an outer court;
Maitreya dwells in the inner court, acting as the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi (Hùmíng). As for the Hall of Sovereignty (*Yìrúì-diàn*), this is where he preaches the Dharma within the inner court.
This refers to the halls and palaces. Among the forty-nine categories of dharmas, none fall outside this scope; it is what is meant by "the meaning revealing the profound and secret.

As for the "non-retrogressive practitioner," this refers to Maitreya’s teaching on the exhortation to practice the three types of non-retrogression (the explanation of the three non-retrogressions is found in the preceding text).

In general, these are the ultimate, perfected, and real dharmas. As for "expedient means" (*upāya*), these are either the provisional dharmas of the Small or Initial [Vehicle]; they are supplemented by these.
Thus, because there are [explanations by way of] causes, conditions, parables, and so forth, it is said to be "innumerable. Regarding the water of eightfold merit (*aṣṭāṅga-vāri*):
because this water possesses eight kinds of merit—first, the merit of clarity; second, the merit of coolness; third, sweetness; fourth, lightness and softness; fifth, lubricity; sixth, tranquility;
seventh, the removal of afflictions such as hunger and thirst at the time of drinking; and eighth, the ability to nourish the sense faculties after drinking—it is called the water of eightfold merit.

Regarding the "Exquisite Flower Pond": Just as there are pools of the seven treasures in the World of Ultimate Bliss containing lotus flowers within them, wherein sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha entrust their physical forms, here it is likewise.

These must be exquisite jewel-lotuses that receive and sustain those with a karmic affinity who maintain mindfulness and vow to be reborn there; all such individuals are born together within these very lotuses.

They are born by transformation (*upapāduka*). "I now [entrust them]" and below: the Buddha once charged Maitreya with the disciples who have not yet been delivered in the present age, commanding him to teach and transform them at the first assembly under the Dragon Flower Tree so that they may attain true liberation.

(The details of the Dragon Flower assembly and so forth are explained in two fascicles. In the final two lines, he specifically charges the disciples of the future Dharma-ending age, thereby manifesting the dragon...
Regarding the three assemblies at which the Buddha preached the Dharma and bestowed predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), all were disciples of Śākyamuni.

The meaning is that in the first assembly he delivered [the teachings for] the disciples of the *saddharma* (True Dharma) period; in the second assembly, those of the *pratirūpakadharma* (Semblance Dharma) period;

and in the third assembly, those of the *paścimadharma* (Final Dharma) period. These are all matters concerning the entrustment to Maitreya and the bestowal of predictions as recorded in the *Āgama* sūtras.
Now I shall merely recount this. From the phrase "Virtuous son" (*kulaputra*) downwards, it also includes women.

Should anyone offer even a single morsel of food to hungry sentient beings, though their roots of goodness may be slight, they shall all be able to behold Maitreya and attain Bodhi, ultimately achieving the Way.
This reveals the grace of Maitreya, which is difficult indeed to repay. The above is merely...
This reveals the two individuals, Mañjuśrī and Maitreya; in meaning, it includes all the great bodhisattvas.
Generally speaking, whoever benefits others is considered a noble monk (*āryasaṃgha*). △ Second, the śrāvaka-saṃgha.
The great śrāvakas such as Śāriputra transform sentient beings through wisdom and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Their wisdom was like that of Śāriputra, and their supernormal powers were like those of Maudgalyāyana.

As for the term "such as" (*ādi*), it refers to those who, like Pūrṇa, were skilled in preaching the Dharma, or like Kātyāyana, were skilled in debate—all of whom were able to deliver and transform sentient beings. Someone may ask: regarding the holy teachings...
Question: It is said that the Śrāvakas are incapable of saving sentient beings, yet this sutra speaks of "transforming the multitudes of living beings. Are these not contradictory? Answer:
That which the Buddha disparaged refers to those Śrāvakas of fixed nature who extinguish their bodies and obliterate their wisdom.

At the time they realize the nirvāṇa of extinction, they do not dare to return to the triple world to save sentient beings, seeking only their own liberation; therefore, he disparaged them as being inferior to Bodhisattvas. However, as for...

Those who are "rejected" are of fixed nature; they cannot be compared to those of indeterminate nature, let alone to Śāriputra and others, who were originally great manifestations of expedient means (*upāya*).

How could there be any principle by which they do not deliver [beings]? Consider this: if it were ultimately impossible for them to deliver beings, then their wisdom, supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), eloquence, and skill in debate would all be useless. Furthermore, he asked: "In the assembly of the Vaipulya sutras..."
"Are those whom Vimalakīrti rebuked not the likes of Śāriputra? Answer: "One should know that Vimalakīrti, Śāriputra, and the others were all of one class of great *mahopāya* (great skillful means).

Their intent was to censure the provisional (*prajñapti*) in order to awaken the real (*bhūta*). Since this present sutra is what the Buddha spoke with his own mouth, how can one use that [incident] to challenge this?
Part Two: Verses on Ordinary Monks. Section One: Preaching the Dharma while Fully Possessing the Precepts.
Monks,
if one can accomplish the precepts of liberation, such a person is truly one who practices right view; teaching the Dharma to others and transmitting the Mahāyāna,
such a field of merit is foremost.
Liberation is precisely the Prātimokṣa precepts. "Liberation" is explained in detail in Volume Two. △ Second, the Sangha of those with Right Faith who have violated the precepts:

There may be a class of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) within the Sangha whose collection of precepts is incomplete yet who give rise to right view. They praise and recite the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle;

as soon as they commit an offense, they repent, whereby their hindrances are eliminated. Thus, such ordinary beings also become the cause for all sentient beings to attain Buddhahood. Such are the ordinary beings.
The Sangha Jewel: Just as the saffron flower, though withered, still surpasses all other exquisite flowers, so too is the bhikṣu of right view;
he is beyond the reach of the four kinds of wheel-turning kings.
Regarding those whose precepts are incomplete: having already received the precepts, how could they not wish to uphold them?

That there are nonetheless those who transgress is due to what is called "preferring the correct yet being firmly attached to the perverse," or "desiring purity yet being biased toward defilement. This is surely brought about by the seeds of karmic habits from past lives.

Although they may have transgressions, their right view remains undeluded; they still possess the altruistic intention to benefit others, praising and extolling the One Vehicle and expounding the subtle Dharma (*praśaṃsā* means to praise with beautiful words and extol virtues;
*gīta* means to chant and laud; *vyākhyāna* means to lecture and analyze; all these are the virtues of right view and altruism). Following the section on transgressions below.
It may happen that, encountering certain conditions and circumstances, one is momentarily deluded; unaware, one follows along with them and commits an offense.
This is precisely being led by past habitual tendencies and does not arise from one's own volition. To repent immediately is what constitutes right view;
it means attaining awakening at once, for once one regrets, it is too late. As for the elimination of hindrances, it is said that "offenses arise from the mind."
It returns and is extinguished from within the mind. The commission of an offense is like firewood; the mind of repentance is like fire.
Just as fire burns wood until the ashes fly away and the smoke vanishes, it is said that "obstructions are removed. The phrase "for all" seems to be inverted relative to the preceding phrase;
it should be placed beneath "the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle. Whichever single phrase is transgressed, it should be positioned above "such ordinary beings. Thus...

Upon examining the text and its meaning, all is consistent. Thus, since one is already able to praise and chant the wondrous Dharma, they transmit the Buddha’s seal of the One Vehicle mind, which permeates the hearts of sentient beings;
how could this not serve as the causal seed for attaining Buddhahood?

Furthermore, since one immediately repents upon committing an offense, karmic obstructions are already eliminated. Such an ordinary person, possessing great shame and remorse, may likewise be considered a member of the Saṃgha.
It is like the *kuruvinda* flower; even when it has withered, it still surpasses all other flowers, for its character and quality are different.

The following two lines provide the analogy: the *kuruvinda* flower represents right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), withering represents the violation of precepts, and the various flowers represent the four types of wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*) and so forth.
This means that although a bhikṣu who possesses right view may violate the prohibitions, he does not destroy his right view.
Upon seeing this, one feels shame and remorse; thus, the mind becomes empty and transgressions are extinguished. This is even superior to that of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin). Why is this?

Although the rank of a Wheel-Turning King is most exalted and supreme, if he indulges his own mind and remains deeply attached to the five desires, he cannot attain the "first place" of an empty mind.
Therefore, the analogy is used to manifest such superiority. △ Third, the verse concludes by summarizing the kindness of the Saṃgha.
These four classes of noble and ordinary Sangha work tirelessly for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings; they are called the world’s excellent field of merit.
This is known as the great benevolent virtue of the Sangha Jewel.
Ordinary monks pervade the world, while holy monks respond throughout the ten directions. Ordinary monks cause the flames of wisdom to form a continuous fragrance;
holy monks manifest the eternal presence of the Dharma-body. Thus, where could one not see the Sangha? When could the Dharma not be preached?
Therefore it is said that the benefit and happiness of sentient beings never cease for even a moment. Since they possess this virtue of benefiting and gladdening others, they are therefore...
It is indeed true that [the Buddha] is a virtuous friend and a field of merit for sentient beings. The final phrase concludes the theme of gratitude.
Because he is a field of merit, he is a treasure; because he is able to bring benefit and joy, he possesses gratitude. △ Fifth, the summary of the four debts of gratitude, in two parts.
First, the formal conclusion.
The meaning of the four debts of gratitude as I have explained them is called that which can create the field of the world;
all things arise from this, for without these four debts they could not be obtained.
The "creator" refers to birth. The "field" is the earth; because all things and crops grow from the earth, it is called a field.
The field is a metaphor for the four debts of gratitude. "Worldly" refers here to the world of sentient beings, specifically the four types: parents, kings, and so forth.
Just as a father can give birth to one and a mother can nourish one, parents are thus the field that gives birth to one.
When a king possesses the Way, devas and nāgas provide protection; wind and rain follow their proper seasons, and the people attain peace and happiness.
Thus all things flourish and grow, attributing this grace to the king, regarding him as the field for the production of living beings.

As the Three Jewels transform the world, extinguishing evil and giving rise to good, and turning the ordinary into the holy, the Three Jewels are therefore the field for the path of living beings—the source of grace for all sentient beings.
The meaning lies in their mutual production. Because they have previously been one's parents, all myriad things arise and flourish through the four kinds of grace.
The final phrase serves as a reductio ad absurdum: if one were separated from these four graces, nothing at all could be obtained. △ Second, citing an analogy.
Just as all material forms in the world arise from the four great elements that create them,
so too is the world of sentient beings established by means of those four debts of gratitude.
For example, "the world" refers here to the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), such as the great earth, mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees.

Regarding the term "various" (*nānā*) applied to the objects of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*), there are distinctions; for instance, among those objects perceived by the eye, there are various forms (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) in terms of size, and manifest colors (*varṇa-rūpa*) such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
Furthermore, there are the three kinds—odor, taste, and touch—which the eye cannot see. This is because...
Invisible and resistant form refers to fragrance corresponding to the nose, flavor corresponding to the tongue, touch corresponding to the body, and sound corresponding to the ear;
these are all the objects of form (*rūpa-āyatana*). As for the "four great elements" (*mahābhūta*) that act as the creators, they are earth, water, fire, and wind;

they are called "great" because they can produce all things. The objects of form are the derived forms—fragrance, flavor, touch, and sound—which constitute the four [remaining] sense objects. This encompasses...
Exhausting all things in the universe, take any single object at random: when observed it possesses form; when smelled it possesses fragrance;
when tasted it possesses flavor; when touched it possesses tangibility. Because form, fragrance, flavor, and tangibility can delude the true nature, they are called "dust" (*rajas*).
Yet, these must necessarily have earth and so forth as their producers. Earth is simply soil; all things depend upon soil [to exist].
Birth occurs; without water, there can be no nourishment, and what is parched does not grow. Therefore, water is that which enables birth. Fire is warmth;
all things must be warm before they are born. Thus, fire is that which enables birth. Wind is able to move and activate;
all things depend upon it for their development. Therefore, wind is that which enables birth. Were it not for these four great elements, all things could not exist of themselves.
It is born. The following two lines combine the metaphors. The "sentient world" (*sattva-loka*) refers to living beings; this corresponds to the "world of form-objects" (*rūpa-dhātu*).

The "four debts of gratitude" (*catvāri ṛṇāni*) correspond to the "four great elements" (*mahābhūtāni*). This means that it is because of these four debts of gratitude that sentient beings are established.

How magnificent is the World-Honored One! Acting as father and son of a single light of wisdom, he has penetrated to the very root; thus, he is worthy of praise. This is what is meant by "instructing others."
[He is] untiring. None surpasses the Buddha. Truly, the grace of the Buddha-Jewel is inconceivable.
Thus, the Tathāgata’s verse of repeated praise is concluded. △ Fourth, the Resolve of the Father and Son, Jñānaprabha: Part Three.
First, Jñānaprabha receives the teaching and inquires about repaying the debt of gratitude. Part Two: First, praising the knowledge of gratitude.
At that time, the elder Jñānaprabha, together with his sons and others, having heard the Buddha’s teaching on the four kinds of great kindness, attained what they had never experienced before.
With palms joined in joy, they addressed the Buddha, saying: "Excellent, excellent, O World-Honored One of Great Compassion!

For the sake of sentient beings in this defiled and evil age—who do not believe in cause and effect, who are unfilial toward their parents, and who hold false views—you have preached the true and wondrous Dharma for their benefit and happiness."
In this world, Jñānaprabha and his sons were those whose faculties were ready to receive the Dharma; upon hearing what the Buddha taught, their minds attained clear awakening.
They conceived a sense of great fortune, and before they realized it, joy filled their hearts. Thus it is said: "They obtained an unprecedented state of joy."
He joined his palms, and with a heart filled with the joy of the Dharma, his words were expressed outwardly;

unconsciously, he praised with his voice until he uttered the double phrase "Excellent! Excellent! to marvel at this extraordinary report. Only with the single phrase "Great Compassion" did he finally praise the Buddha.
Compassion (*maitrī*) must necessarily be accompanied by pity (*karuṇā*). Among the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), each one of them is fully present within compassion.

Because he is uniquely honored as transcending the world, he is called the World-Honored One of Great Compassion (*mahāmaitrī-lokanātha*). "For the sake of the turbid and inferior" correctly praises the intent of his compassion. "Turbid" refers to the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*);

because these five turbidities obstruct one's nature, all affairs turn out poorly, and thus it is called an "evil age. The character "for" (*wei*) correctly reveals true compassion; this is that which the Buddha is able to provide.
The mind [of giving] (the character *wei* is glossed as "to give" and "thereby"; it refers to the compassionate mind with which the Tathāgata gives). To disbelieve in cause and effect is wrong view.
This is because the two terms "cause" and "effect" constitute the certain and responsive functioning of both the mundane and supramundane realms.

Whether one receives a favorable or unfavorable retribution for good or evil karmic conditions is invariably like a shadow following a form or an echo following a sound, without fail. Yet, worldly people are obstructed by delusion and, in their every movement—

Holding onto birth gives rise to doubt; because the nature of cause and effect is profound and obscure, it is called "lack of faith. Because one acts in opposition to one's parents, it is called "filial impiety.
These are all instances of worldly people being deluded and inverted; thus, they are able to invoke the cycle of birth and death and sink into the three miserable realms.
Now, from a heart of compassion, the Buddha has expounded the Dharma of the Four Graces and the Rite of Repentance; this is truly a sublime Dharma that brings benefit and joy to the world.

(It is called the "True Dharma" because it is spoken in accordance with reality; it is the "Sublime Dharma" because it is taught to suit the capacities of beings. This is especially so when the Buddha speaks of the grace of one's parents.)

To awaken unfilial sentient beings and cause them to practice filial piety; because they practice filial piety, they are moved to be reborn in the wholesome realms—this is their benefit and happiness. Furthermore, those who are unfilial will inevitably be disloyal.

By means of the Buddha’s teaching on the kindness of kings, he causes those disloyal individuals to give rise to a loyal heart and repay the virtue of their sovereign; thus, they may achieve renown in this life or be reborn in a good place in a future life, which constitutes their benefit and happiness.

For sentient beings who do not believe in cause and effect, by means of the Buddha’s teaching on the kindness of sentient beings toward one another, he causes them to know that throughout kalpas they have been each other's parents, yet due to changing heads and faces, they are deluded and unaware of it. He causes them to understand causes and recognize effects, turning their minds toward goodness so that they shall obtain wholesome fruits—this is their benefit and happiness. For sentient beings with false views who hold irrational and erroneous [notions]...

[They] calculate [things wrongly], denying cause and effect, and clinging to the views of annihilationism or eternalism. The Buddha spoke of the grace of the Triple Gem to use the correct to refute the heterodox, thereby inspiring right faith; this may be called the truly wondrous Dharma, the ultimate means of benefit and joy).
△ Second, receiving grace and seeking recompense.

We pray that the World-Honored One will explain the meaning of repaying kindness. Having now awakened to the profound nature of the four debts of gratitude, we do not yet know what wholesome deeds we should cultivate to repay this kindness.

Upon hearing the Dharma, the elder and his son wished to repay it so as not to辜负 (disappoint) what they had heard. The son possessed a heart of filial piety toward his father, and the father possessed the aspiration to enter the Way.
This may be called knowing gratitude and repaying kindness; from the outset, they did not fail the intent of their coming.
II. The Tathāgata’s Teaching and the Ten Pāramitās. (Two parts. A. First, recounting the previous extensive explanation.
The Buddha addressed the elder: "O sons of good family, I have already extensively explained this for the five hundred elders, as was detailed and elucidated in the second fascicle.
II. A brief analysis has four parts. First, the primary teaching on the profound point of repaying kindness."

Now, for your sake, I have briefly explained but a small portion. If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, seeking to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, diligently practices the ten *pāramitās* yet perceives something as being attained, they have not yet repaid my kindness.
If a person, even for a brief moment, can practice a single act of goodness with a mind free from attainment, only then is it called repaying my kindness.

"A small portion" refers to a brief explanation. If those who are virtuous and so forth are the persons seeking awakening, then *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is the Buddha-way sought. "Diligent" means one must not be indolent.
Regarding the ten *pāramitās*, there are three types mentioned within the two fascicles of the text: namely, giving (*dāna*), intimacy (*upāya*), and reality (*bhūta*). Although these exist...

The ten perfections (daśapāramitā) have their designations, yet they lack specific names for each; the present case is likewise: there are the designations but no detailed explanations, and only the benefits are stated.
If one were to follow the second fascicle which speaks of giving (dāna) alone, and since the name "giving" does not appear here, why must one be so rigidly attached?
What harm is there in interpreting this according to the usual explanation of the ten perfections? Regarding the Sanskrit term *pāramitā*, this—
Regarding "reaching the other shore": this is a metaphor used to reveal the Dharma. Although this has already been explained previously, it will be stated again for the sake of beginners.
For example, in the world, the near side of a great river is called this shore (*tīra*), and the far side is called the other shore. The middle of the river is the midstream.
This shore is characterized by suffering, while the other shore is characterized by bliss. Just as people in the world, when oppressed by suffering, desire to escape—
This is suffering. Seeking to reach the other shore, one is obstructed by the waters of the Nai River and cannot cross by oneself; one must wait for a boat or raft to ferry across.
This is because the "this shore" is a metaphor for birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the "other shore" is a metaphor for nirvāṇa, and the "midstream" is a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*).
The analogy of the boat and raft refers to the ten dharmas, such as giving (*dāna*).

If a person, mindful of the suffering of birth and death, gives rise to the bodhicitta and seeks the great nirvāṇa of the fruit of Buddhahood, yet finds that afflictions (*kleśa*) cannot be severed by themselves, they must practice giving and the other [perfections] to cross over all delusions, just as one boards a boat to cross a river. For instance, giving can cross over the affliction of stinginess.
Through this, one attains liberation and reaches the further shore. It is the same for all nine dharmas: through ethical discipline one transcends transgressions;
through patience one transcends anger; through diligence one transcends laziness; through meditative concentration one transcends dullness and agitation; and through wisdom one transcends ignorance.
Skillful means deliver one from guarding emptiness; the aspiration-deliverance delivers one from retreating; power delivers one from timidity; and wisdom delivers one from ignorance.
By means of these ten, one can deliver one from the ten obscurations and cause people to achieve the Way, just as boarding a boat enables one to reach the other shore.
If there is "inferiority" below, it is because of having something to attain—this is a dharma of attachment to marks; subject and object have not yet been extinguished. All [is thus].
To fall into conditioned effort—how could this constitute repaying the Buddha’s kindness? This statement means that such an approach does not accord with the Buddha’s intention.
From the words "If a person" onwards, [the text] correctly teaches the method for truly repaying the Buddha’s kindness:

if a person, even for a brief moment, can practice a single act of goodness with a mind that attains nothing—that both subject and object are empty, and the three spheres are all quiescent—this is what accords with the Buddha.
This is what is called repaying kindness. If this is so for a single good deed, it is likewise for the ten perfections;
one may thus be said to know kindness and repay kindness, sharing the same resolve as the Buddha. △ Second, the inquiry and explanation of the profound meaning and its cause.
Why is this so? Because all Tathāgatas attained the Buddha-way by touching upon non-attainment, thereby transforming all sentient beings.
Following the preceding passage, it may be sufficient that the mind has no attainment for one’s own benefit; what further benefit is there in calling this "repaying the Buddha's grace"?
It is said that when all Tathāgatas had not yet become Buddhas, they attained it by touching upon non-attainment.

One attains Buddhahood. The character "touch" (觸) should be understood as "directed toward" (向). This means that regarding all phenomena and principles toward which one is directed, both the subject (the grasper) and the object (the grasped) are empty;

even the characteristic of emptiness itself is transcended. As the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) says: "One distances oneself from illusion, and distances oneself from that distancing as well.
One distances oneself from the distancing from illusion, and distances oneself from that too. Only then is this truly 'having nothing to obtain' in principle. Regarding this principle:

Only when these factors coincide can one benefit both oneself and others; thus, one is able to attain Buddhahood and transform sentient beings. △ Third, exhorting the practice of the profound Dharma as a repayment of gratitude:
If there are sons of good family with pure faith who hear this sutra, and who believe, understand, accept, uphold, explain, and transcribe it.

By means of non-apprehension, the three spheres are realized as empty. To privately preach the Dharma of four lines for a single person, thereby eliminating their mind of false views and causing them to incline toward Bodhi—this is precisely what is called repaying the four debts of gratitude.

To have no doubt is called faith (*śraddhā*). To awaken to the principle is called understanding (*avabodha*). To receive and accept is called receiving (*vedanā*). To practice with devotion is called upholding (*dhāraṇā*). To explain the meaning is called interpretation (*vyākhyāna*).

To lecture is called preaching (*deśanā*). To dip the brush is called writing (*lekhanā*). To model and draw is called copying (*likhanā*). All of the above are practices for the dual benefit [of self and others].
Taking "non-attainment" as the standard and "the three wheels being empty in essence" as the explanation follows from what was previously stated regarding "non-existence."

Regarding that which has been attained: fearing that others may not understand it, the Tathāgata himself provides this explanation. That is to say, when practicing any single practice, if one does not perceive a self, then the grasping at a self is empty;
if one does not perceive phenomena (*dharma*), then the grasping at phenomena is empty; and if one does not even cling to emptiness, this is the departure from attachment to phenomena.
To practice in this manner is for the three spheres to be empty of essence. This is for one's own benefit, and is considered "private" [practice].
Next is benefiting others. Now, as for the fact that one must necessarily act secretly while seeking to benefit others, this is done to manifest the superior through the inferior.
The "inferior" refers to those who are isolated, narrow-minded, and of little learning, whose speech is clumsy and vulgar, and who are unable to preach amidst the high halls and vast assemblies.

It may only be privately shared with a single person; furthermore, one cannot explain it extensively. According to their individual understanding, one explains the Dharma of the four lines (*catuṣpāda*).
Although these four lines are subtle, they are the Buddha’s True Dharma (*saddharma*). They are truly capable of destroying the heterodox and can also bring about the realization of the Way.

Regarding all matters of principle and practice, when one penetrates the three emptinesses (*trividha-śūnyatā*), only then does it become the profound Dharma for the twofold benefit (*dvaya-hita*). This excludes the heterodox.

There are two points. Both [self-benefit and benefiting others] are appropriate. If explained in terms of self-benefit, regarding attachment to signs as wrong view, one is able to eliminate it by realizing the three emptinesses (*trīṇi śūnyatāni*).
Having realized the three emptinesses, this is precisely the sublime practice for proceeding toward *bodhi*.
If explained in terms of benefiting others, one causes others likewise to realize the three emptinesses, eliminate wrong views, and proceed toward *bodhi*; thus, [it benefits both].
The mind of all things must certainly not be non-existent. If one can truly put this into practice, the four debts of gratitude will all be repaid.
△ Fourth, a repeated inquiry and further explanation regarding transformation and teaching.

Why is this? Because such a person shall attain unsurpassed bodhi and, in turn, teach and transform immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to enter the Buddha-way so that the seeds of the Triple Gem shall never be severed.
This inquiry is most critical: if one must preach the Dharma through the threefold emptiness as an act of repaying kindness, for what reason is this so?

It is because for such a person, the three spheres (trimaṇḍala) are empty in essence; thus, benefiting both self and others constitutes the correct practice for attaining Buddhahood, and they shall surely attain unsurpassed bodhi.
Because it must be transmitted from teacher to disciple, it is called "successive teaching. "Successive" refers precisely to this transmission.
Furthermore, that which is immeasurable must necessarily proceed from the few to the many; from this point forward, it will become increasingly vast as time goes on.

Therefore, those who are transformed are immeasurable sentient beings, all of whom shall attain the Buddha-way. As for "the Three Jewels not being severed," this means to perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas.
Since one has thus ensured that the seed of the Buddhas is never interrupted, this constitutes the actual practice of repaying their kindness. (This person...)

[He is] the one who is able to expound the four propositions. △ Third, the benefits obtained by the father and son, Jñānaprabha and others, upon hearing the Dharma. First, Jñānaprabha attains non-retrogression.
At that time, after the elder Jñānaprabha had heard these verses, he attained the samādhi of patience (*kṣānti-samādhi*) and developed weary detachment from the world. He attained...
"Non-retrogression.
This is the phrasing employed by the compiler of the sutra. The samādhi of patience need not be explained separately;

it is simply that upon hearing the preceding verses and the phrase regarding the non-apprehension of the mind, one attains a profound and silent realization, which is intuitively grasped within the heart, like a person enduring a hardship.

Whenever he encountered humiliation, he did not debate with others, but silently endured it within his heart; this was likewise so. He attained realization through silent awakening and never presented his understanding to others;
thus the compilers of the sutras recorded it. *Samādhi* is called "right reception" (*zhèngshòu*);

it means not receiving any [defiled] sensations while being in accord with the Way, for one spontaneously attains its enjoyment. Therefore, it is called *samādhi*. As for "those who weary of and leave the world":

Through hearing that the mind has no attachments, one enters the sublime practice of the Path. Only then does one realize that the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) of the world cause attachment wherever they are encountered;
thus, one gives rise to wearying detachment from desire and renounces it. This is the most excellent mental state for a beginner and serves as a model for future monastics.
As for Bodhisattvas of the profound stages, they do not even cling to emptiness, let alone be defiled by sensory objects. Therefore, [they remain] ever...
Wandering through the three realms and delivering sentient beings according to their needs—why must one necessarily feel revulsion? This beginner cannot be compared to others;

therefore, it is precisely because of this sense of revulsion that one seeks liberation. As for attaining non-retrogression, it need not be discussed solely in terms of the stages of the three types of non-retrogression.
Rather, it refers to having attained a profound, intuitive realization such that the single thought of revulsion toward and detachment from the mundane world no longer arises.

He did not dare to retreat. Therefore, in the fourth fascicle, he finally seeks ordination; in the fifth fascicle, he requests the Buddha to preach the Dharma of pure joy and the practice of seclusion.
The Buddha first instructs him in the twelve *dhūta* practices. This is largely based on the correspondence between the preceding and following textual meanings.
Such is my brief and superficial explanation. If one follows the meaning rather than the literal text, since Zhiguang has already...
Such a person of great capacity, having not regressed for even a single thought-moment, has already entered the stages (bhūmi) and shattered the delusions of ignorance.
Never again losing the right mindfulness of the Middle Way, they may truly be called a Bodhisattva of the stages. Both meanings apply here. 2.
The Sons and Others Resolve upon Bodhicitta.
At that time, the sons of the Buddha, eight thousand in number, attained this samādhi and all gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment, which is equal to the unequaled.
This samādhi is also patience (*kṣānti*). Terms such as "anuttara" (unsurpassed) may be understood accordingly. Regarding "the peerless among peers" (*asamasama*):
among all types of generated minds, the bodhicitta is supreme. While other minds might be equal to the bodhicitta, there is no other mind that can be equal to the bodhicitta itself.
This statement refers to raising one's head while including the multitude. Furthermore, there is another explanation: "equal" (*sama*) means equality. It says:
There is no mind equal to it, nor even equal to the bodhicitta; therefore, it is called "unequaled" (*asama-sama*).
This is because even the hundred parables of the *Avataṃsaka* cannot equal it. △ Third, the assembly attains the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Forty-eight thousand people also realized this samādhi; they were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.
These were the members of the assembly who were present at the outset. The samādhi is the same as before.

"Distanced from dust" and so forth refers to the benefits obtained from the non-apprehension of the mind. Dust has both coarse and subtle aspects; defilement has both shallow and deep aspects. The coarse refers to the six [senses].

"Dust" (*rajas*) refers, in its subtle sense, to the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Regarding the "defilements" (*mala*), there are degrees of shallowness and depth: the shallow refers to deluded consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*), while the deep refers to the craving for gnosis (*jñāna-tṛṣṇā*).

As for the "Dharma-eye" (*dharmanetra*): "Dharma" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and "eye" refers to true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). This means that those with such sharp faculties, upon hearing [the teaching] once, find nothing to be attained in the mind;
suddenly, both mind and objects are empty. When the attachment to phenomena is empty, this is "distant from dust. When the craving for gnosis is absent, this is... [freedom from defilement].
It is "free from defilement. Having already become free from intellectual attachment and craving, true wisdom is revealed, and one personally beholds the Dharmakāya;

hence it is said that one "attains the purity of the Dharma-eye. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Conceptual appearances are the dust, and cognitive emotions are the defilement. When both are left far behind, your Dharma-eye shall immediately become clear and bright.
This refers precisely to this point. The above has discussed the cultivation of the Buddha-mind-ground. [End of citation]
The exposition on the four debts of gratitude that ought to be repaid is hereby concluded.
